events.title: What smart people are saying about Jensen Huang's new statement
events.summary: Jensen Huang broke his silence on Tuesday. Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg via Getty Images Jensen Huang said he'd be "honored" to return to Nvidia. The ex-CEO broke his silence on Tuesday after resigning in the wake of affair allegations. Here's what business leaders think of his new statement. Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang finally addressed his resignation publicly — and he'd be happy to undo it if invited back. In his statement, Huang said he owned his "mistakes completely" and that he was cooperating with an internal investigation. The statement adds new pressure to Nvidia's board and interim leadership hours before the company reports quarterly earnings after the closing bell. Here's what business and tech leaders and personalities are saying about Huang's statement: Travis Kalanick, Uber founder Travis Kalanick Zak Bennett/Bloomberg via Getty Images Kalanick, who's pushed publicly for Huang to be reinstated, celebrated the statement on X. The Uber cofounder was famously pushed out of his own company in 2017. "Let's bring Jensen back!!! LFG," he wrote . Dan Ives, tech analyst and partner at Yorkville Ives Dan Ives. Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images Nvidia's board could now face increased pressure, Ives and his colleagues wrote in a research note for Yorkville Ives. "Clearly Jensen wants to come back as CEO, and the statement moves the fight from a petition to the board," the note reads. The research note said Nvidia's bylaws allow a critical mass of shareholders to call a special meeting — and with President Donald Trump , Elon Musk, and many employees on board, "that coalition is no longer unthinkable." But the fight over Nvidia's next CEO will play out in Washington, where federal authorities will want an outsider and compliance with export controls, according to Yorkville Ives' note. "The board's decision now sits between a founder who has publicly asked for his job back, a shareholder base with the means to force the question, and an administration split between a President open to his return and a Treasury Secretary demanding an outsider," the note says. On X, Ives posted, "This could be next step in Nvidia saga." Jason Calacanis, angel investor and "All-In Podcast" co-host Jason Calacanis said that the ban was "smart" because of the risk of terrorism. Bloomberg/Getty Images Huang's got a fan with at least one of the All-In Podcast hosts. "Bring @JensenHuang back 🫡," Calacanis posted . Gavin Baker, chief investment officer at Atreides Gavin Baker predicted $100 billion in annual recurring revenue. Bloomberg/Getty Images Baker, an Nvidia shareholder who co-wrote a letter to its board urging it not to rush to judgment with its CEO search, praised Huang as an "exceptional" CEO during an interview with CNBC's Sara Eisen on "Squawk on the Street." Huang put out his statement moments before Baker appeared on TV — and Baker was glad to see Huang say he would cooperate with investigations. "I think this is all good," he said on CNBC. "I think this is good for America. I think this is good for Nvidia." Baker said he wanted to see Huang back at Nvidia. "America loves comebacks and second chances and I would like to see Jensen, if he is cleared of these charges, given a second chance as to be the CEO of Nvidia," Baker said. Ruben Gallego, US Senator U.S. Sen. Ruben Gallego Finn Gomez/Getty Images The Democratic senator from Arizona warned Huang not to get too ahead of himself. "Slow your roll there," he replied to Jensen's post . "You have to answer some questions first. We need to know if you allowed Blackwell chips to be siphoned to China? Where you ever told the Megaspeed was a problem. Did you know that Megaspeed was under investigation in 2024 and if so why did you allow the sales to go forward?" Huang has agreed to testify behind closed doors before three House committees on December 1. Gallego's questions hint at the investigations Huang and Nvidia might face as Democrats — who were swept into power during the midterms in part due to backlash against tech companies — regain majorities in Congress starting in January. Casey Newton, "Machine Gods" podcast host and founder of The Platformer Casey Newton Jerod Harris/Getty Images for Vox Media Newton cracked some jokes at Huang's expense. "This man's commitment to delivering chips to Alice Huang is simply inspiring," he said on X , referencing the Megaspeed CEO whom Huang allegedly had an affair with. Newton later had an idea : "Instead of coming back to Nvidia directly, Jensen should try to route himself through a holding company in Malaysia or Singapore." events.title: FAA pauses tech upgrade linked to nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration is halting the installation of new routers following Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop , the agency confirmed Tuesday. Why it matters: The technology rollout is suspected to be connected to massive travel disruptions that continued through the weekend, inconveniencing travelers across the country. Catch up quick: Over 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, and thousands more were delayed. The issue stemmed from routine work to upgrade the FAA's aging telecommunications network, replacing copper wires with fiber-optic connections. The agency is adding Juniper routers to the network as part of the transition. The FAA said its system became overwhelmed by roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds after a router was installed, disabling communication and radar in 17 of the nation's 22 regional air traffic control centers. Investigators identified two potential sources of the problem — one in Arkansas and another in Texas. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the device functioned as programmed by the installer and wasn't faulty. The FAA is still investigating the root cause. What they're saying: "We believe we have addressed the initial cause of the disruption by immediately disabling the functionality of the originating Juniper routers," the FAA announced in a statement . "As a precaution, we disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers in the system, and we have paused installing them." The pause comes after a group of Democratic senators demanded the agency halt the router installation on Tuesday. It was unclear whether the senators prompted the move or whether the FAA had already paused installation before sending the letter to the Transportation Department and the FAA. Zoom in: "DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote in a letter to Transportation Secretary Scott Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. "Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed." "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety," they wrote, adding that identifying the problematic router is not the same as determining why it malfunctioned. The senators — all part of the Senate Committee for Commerce, Science and Transportation — requested a response to its questions by no later than Nov. 23. By the numbers: The FAA is slated to convert more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices, and 400 are already installed, per the senator's letter. Just 69 are operational. The FAA did not respond to Axios' request for comment. Go deeper: What we know about what caused the FAA's nationwide ground stop Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: Speed camera fault may have allowed drivers to escape fines
events.summary: Published 17 November 2026, 12:35 GMT Further problems with the accuracy of speed cameras on English roads have been uncovered which may have allowed drivers to slip through the cracks and escape fines. National Highways discovered issues with speed cameras last year , affecting 154 out of 400 cameras but, following an investigation, said it had found another fault on units monitoring roads including those running between Huntingdon and Cambridge. The Home Office has revoked approval that allows footage from the cameras to be used as evidence in legal proceedings. US firm Verra Mobility operates the cameras but National Highways said it will now end the contract. Roads minister Justin Madders said: "We can't take chances with this. "If we're going to prosecute people, we need to be confident the system is working as it should. That's why we've taken the action we have." In a statement, Verra Mobility said it "remains fully committed to delivering reliable, innovative technology that helps make roads safer". The fault affected all of the variable speed cameras on smart motorways, and a section of the A14 between Huntingdon and Cambridge as well as the A1 approach junction to the A14. A spokesperson for National Highways said that Verra's camera system had been selected on the basis that it maintained Home Office approval. The agency said that since that was no longer the case "we are ending our contractual relationship to use the cameras for enforcement". It added: "We are considering all further commercial and legal options that may be appropriate." The BBC has contacted Verra Mobility for comment. Madders said that the enforcement of speed limits continues to be conducted through a range of different tactics, including mobile cameras as well as marked and unmarked police patrols. But he admitted that the camera system will not be fully fixed until sometime next year. Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC motoring organisation, said: "Malfunctioning speed cameras on smart motorways do more than just let speeding drivers get away with breaking the law and endangering lives – they further undermine confidence in the very types of road we know drivers already have serious misgivings about." There are 4,000 cameras across the entire road network. In December 2025, National Highways, which runs England's motorways, blamed an "anomaly" in how variable speed cameras were interacting with speed limit signs on some A roads and motorways. For example, on a road where the speed limit increases, a driver may see a sign showing 60mph but the camera recording it may still be working on the basis of a previous 40mph speed limit. The fault led to 2,650 wrongful speed camera activations between 2021 and the end of last year. Those who had been wrongfully fined have been reimbursed. As National Highways continued to test the system, it discovered a further problem "relating to how some of these cameras may activate in specific and rare circumstances". It said that according to its calculations, "the circumstances in which the latest issue could occur are extremely rare, and there is no evidence to suggest it has impacted enforcement". Nevertheless, it said it was "taking immediate steps to ensure compliance is maintained at relevant locations". It said it would out further traffic officer patrols in place to monitor the sites. events.title: AI companies lost voters on narrative and execution, Alphabet’s Porat says
events.summary: Alphabet’s longtime investment chief acknowledged that Google — and AI companies generally — came up short convincing US voters that the trillions of dollars being plowed into data centers across the country were worth the cost. A bipartisan backlash against data center building galvanized voters, who almost uniformly moved to block expansion across the country in local measures earlier this month, and elected lawmakers in the midterms who largely backed a slowdown in the AI buildout. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta have been at the center of that expansion — either directly financing massive projects or signing up as the anchor tenants there. “I’ve been traveling the country quite a bit and the pain you saw reflected in polls, I’m hearing firsthand around affordability,” Porat told Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Like many executives at the heart of the buildout, Porat argued that most Americans are willing and excited by the job opportunities that the AI frenzy presents. “I think what’s most potent is when I have these conversations across the country,” she told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman. “What I hear time and time again is ‘this is creating opportunity that I hadn’t seen in my town.’” Porat also defended the dilutive — and expensive — capital that Alphabet and other big companies were using to finance their ambitions. “It’s expensive, but the reason we’re investing is we see the extraordinary opportunity,” Porat said. “None of us have lived at a time like this.” Google is expected to spend up to $205 billion in capex this year, and has forecast even higher numbers for 2027. The company’s free cash flow has turned negative in recent quarters, worrying investors who believe that the company — and Big Tech generally — may be getting ahead of its skis. “We want to make sure we’re showing up with a full-stack approach that delivers value and a balance sheet that’s a fortress balance sheet so that we can continue to deliver in a high-quality way,” Porat said. — Rohan Goswami

events.title: Home Depot names Richard McPhail as new CEO, beats earnings expectations
events.summary: Home Depot named Richard McPhail as its new CEO effective next week. McPhail currently serves as CFO. CEO Ted Decker had been on a temporary medical leave of absence but has since returned, according to Home Depot. The company made the announcement as it posted earnings and revenue that beat expectations. Home Depot on Tuesday announced its chief financial officer, Richard McPhail, will become CEO of the company, succeeding Ted Decker, effective next week. Alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot said Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to succeed McPhail. Decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The company said on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said. "I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession plan." McPhail has been with the company since 2005, holding multiple executive roles. "We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick. He said the company will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using artificial intelligence tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market. Home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the company has previously said it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects. The CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The company said comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount. Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.86 adjusted vs. $3.84 expected Revenue: $43.4 billion vs. $42.80 billion expected The company reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86. Revenue rose 4.9% compared with the year-ago period. "We also are confident that we are taking material share from the market and from competition," McPhail said on the call with analysts. In the third quarter, the company said online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric. The company said it saw positive comparable sales numbers in 13 out of 16 of its merchandising departments, including notable strength in the power department, which posted double-digit percentage growth. For the full year, Home Depot said it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase. Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase.

events.title: One app, many ways to pay: How DBS is shaping the next wave of digital payments with PayLah!
events.summary: Building on over a decade of innovation, DBS is charting PayLah’s next chapter with more ways to pay and more personalised experiences for customers across generations DBS is extending PayLah! to more cross-border QR payments, including China, offering customers a convenient way to pay overseas. For millions of Singaporeans, paying with DBS PayLah! has become part of their daily routines – from buying meals at hawker centres to paying at heartland shops and malls. What began as a peer-to-peer mobile wallet more than a decade ago has grown into one of Singapore’s most widely used payment platforms, with over three million users. DBS is now building on this foundation, extending the convenience of PayLah! beyond Singapore’s shores and into more payment situations. From shops across the Causeway to storefronts in China, PayLah! users can scan to pay just as they do at Singapore’s hawker centres – where PayLah! accounts for more than 60 per cent of QR transactions. “The way people pay has evolved significantly over the past decade, and so have their expectations. Today, customers value not just the ability to pay digitally, but how simple and seamless the experience is,” said Chan Sow Han, head of Payments and Unsecured Lending at DBS Singapore. “Our focus is to build on what customers already know and use, extending that ease of payment across more situations and locations so they can use PayLah! to pay wherever they are, while continuing to enhance the experience to better serve their needs.” QR payments are widely used across Asia, but payment systems and practices differ across markets. In China, for instance, customers may scan a merchant’s QR code or present their own for the cashier to scan. DBS is addressing this through its latest expansion of PayLah!, which enables users to make QR payments at over 100 million participating Alipay+ and Weixin Pay merchants across China. On top of existing UnionPay QR connectivity, DBS is the first and only bank in Singapore to support both payment methods across China’s three major QR payment ecosystems. The development marks another milestone in DBS’ efforts to extend the payment habits Singaporeans are accustomed to at home across international borders. According to DBS, in 2022, it became the first bank in Singapore to enable consumers to make QR payments globally using a local app, through its partnership with UnionPay International. Since then, PayLah!’s overseas reach has grown through partnerships with payment networks. These include DuitNow in Malaysia, PromptPay in Thailand and QRIS in Indonesia, allowing customers to scan to pay when travelling to these destinations. This year, DBS said it also became the first Singapore bank to connect to Taiwan’s TWQR network, allowing PayLah! users to scan to pay at over 250,000 participating merchants in Taiwan. “While QR payments are increasingly common across Asia, different markets have their own payment systems and ways of transacting. Our approach has been to work with established payment networks and partners to bridge these differences, so customers can enjoy a more consistent payment experience when travelling,” said Chan. The TravelLah! Debit Card offers zero foreign exchange fees and zero DBS fees on overseas ATM withdrawals, with no cap on the amount or frequency. These efforts have translated into growing customer usage. Last year, PayLah!’s cross-border QR transaction volumes have grown 2.5 times year-on-year, while the number of unique users has doubled. Average spending per customer on PayLah!’s overseas QR transactions has also increased by approximately 30 per cent in the same period. Recognising that customers have different payment preferences when travelling, DBS also introduced the TravelLah! Debit Card in September 2026, complementing PayLah!’s overseas QR payment capabilities with a debit card option. Available to customers aged 16 and above, TravelLah! offers zero foreign exchange fees, using Visa exchange rates without additional mark-ups from DBS. Customers can pay in more than 150 currencies worldwide and view indicative exchange rates directly on the PayLah! app, giving them greater visibility over prevailing rates before they spend. TravelLah! also offers zero DBS fees on overseas ATM withdrawals, with no cap on the amount or frequency of overseas withdrawals. The accompanying TravelLah! Debit Card Wallet within DBS PayLah! held in Singapore dollars can be topped up as needed, allowing customers to set aside funds for their travels without having to pre-convert or manage multiple currencies. Cardholders can also redeem complimentary basic travel insurance, subject to terms and conditions. The card has attracted interest among younger customers, with around half of those who signed up in its first month aged between 16 and 29. Beyond expanding where and how customers can pay, DBS is also enhancing PayLah! to better serve the needs of different customer groups.

events.title: Some EU countries ‘could accept unlimited young Britons’ under youth mobility scheme
events.summary: Scheme expected to be sealed in principle at EU-UK summit in Brussels on Friday but trickier elements could be postponed for six months EU countries including Germany could accept an unlimited number of young Britons under a youth mobility scheme, according to sources. Fresh details on how a scheme might work have emerged with EU leaders and the UK expected to settle on a quota of about 100,000 a year being allowed to work, travel or study in each others territories from 2028. The UK has insisted on a quota of EU citizens entering the UK under the scheme to guard against mass migration, but some countries have said they will not follow suit on the other side of the Channel and would be open to taking unlimited numbers. The quota is expected to be worked out on a country-by-country basis with smaller countries such as Malta and Luxembourg seeking a system that will not be based on a per-capita quota per EU member state. The youth mobility scheme is expected to be sealed in principle as the EU-UK summit in Brussels on Friday. In what looks like a win for Andy Burnham , however, several diplomats have said the tricky question of EU students paying the same fees as their UK counterparts if studying at a UK university under the scheme would be postponed for six months. This is to allow linkage with the Made in Europe legislation that will not reach its final stages until possibly April next year in a vote in the European parliament. The legislation is designed to give priority to EU supply chains in the car and other industries. By linking the two issues the UK can get assurances that the final detail of the deal on mobility cannot be signed off unless it has been included in the Made in Europe legislation. It is also understand that the majority of the 12-page draft joint statement has been agreed, with negotiations expected to continue to the wire and perhaps even during the summit between Burnham, the European Council leader, António Costa, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, which starts at 10am on Friday. The details came as Burnham has said there is “no rush” to decide on the UK’s longer term relationship with the EU, as he came under pressure from his own party to press the brakes on the pace of the rethink. The prime minister said he would “take stock” of the wider relationship after Friday’s summit in Brussels at which he also hopes to secure agreements on food and farming and emissions trading. In an interview with Sky News, Burnham admitted that he would now not set out the full options for a closer EU relationship until December – but denied he was “stepping back” from his previous commitments to pursue ties. The prime minister had been expected to give a speech or deliver a statement setting out options for a closer relationship early next week, probably Monday, and to argue that it would be in the UK’s long-term interest. While he may still address MPs, he is now likely to focus on the details of the deal secured at the summit, delaying his bigger plans to around the same time as his 10-year plan for the country, No 10 sources said, adding that the two were linked. No 10 insiders told the Guardian that Burnham wants to “frame the conversation, not go straight to the endgame” before testing public opinion, with even some Remain-minded MPs acknowledging there is more work to be done. These will include discussions with European counterparts to establish what the EU is willing to negotiate and whether it might be possible to get a better bespoke deal, or what the terms of rejoining the single market or customs union might be. Since Burnham announced in September that he would look again at the UK’s membership of EU, he has reiterated that the existing deal is not good enough, and that he would set out plans for a longer-term relationship this autumn. In addition to the customs union or single market, these could include trading relationships along the lines that Norway, Switzerland or Canada have with the EU, reversing Brexit in its entirety, or no change at all. But after revealing his personal preference would be to fully rejoin the bloc, Burnham has encountered some resistance, including from within the cabinet, with some MPs with Leave-voting seats anxious about reopening the debate. Senior government figures say that Burnham wants a mandate to start negotiations with the EU in Labour’s next election manifesto, but that any subsequent referendum would be confirmatory after MPs had endorsed a deal. In his interview, Burnham said: “All I’m going to do is look at what options might be available. And so that people can see the pros and cons, we’ll set those out in due course. There’s no rush to do that. The British public will be in charge of whatever comes next. “We’ll see how [Friday’s summit] goes. And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU. I’ll set that out later this year alongside the 10-year plan.

events.title: Waymo suspends freeway rides nationwide after California DMV order
events.summary: Waymo robotaxis are no longer allowed to operate on California freeways after the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles restricted the Alphabet-owned company’s operations following several incidents that raised safety concerns. California’s DMV, which regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, issued the operational restrictions on Waymo on November 11. However, the restrictions weren’t made public until Tuesday. San Francisco Business Times was the first to report the order. The DMV confirmed the new restrictions to TechCrunch, stating that the department took action after three Waymo autonomous vehicles entered an active construction closure on U.S. Route 101 near Burlingame, and another separate incident involving California Highway Patrol vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco. Waymo has complied and is preventing its robotaxis from accessing freeways in any of the markets it operates in, including those outside of California. Waymo currently has commercial operations in 15 U.S. cities. The DMV said Waymo’s freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety. “The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present, despite a prior restriction and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents that occurred on May 18, 2026,” according to an emailed statement sent to TechCrunch. The DMV said the restrictions will remain in place until Waymo can demonstrate that it has taken “effective corrective actions” to address the deficiencies. Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher told TechCrunch the company has temporarily restricted freeway operations across its other operating markets to evaluate its performance. “Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” Gallagher said in a statement. “Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.” Waymo began offering freeway rides in late 2025 , a commercial milestone that has been central to its expansion in major metro areas. Freeway access allows Waymo to connect riders to airports and other destinations more efficiently, slashing travel times by avoiding slower surface streets. That has been particularly important in the San Francisco Bay Area because Waymo’s service area stretches from the city south to Silicon Valley. Freeway access has dramatically shortened trips across the Peninsula that previously took 45 minutes or more than an hour. In May, Waymo abruptly stopped operating on highways. The company didn’t cite a specific reason at the time, but several social media posts showed Waymo robotaxis driving through traffic cones and struggling to navigate construction zones. Waymo robotaxis returned to freeways in July after the company said it updated the self-driving software system to improve performance around freeway construction zones. events.title: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
events.summary: The FAA said it would pause work to install new routers after problems with the technology in recent days. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has said an overloaded router led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop for more than four hours on Friday, but the cause of the tech problem is still unclear. Democratic senators have asked the FAA, the Department of Transportation and the companies involved in the work for clarity on what went wrong. The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday. Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause. The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic. Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong. "Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety." The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat. The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage. CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment. Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years. Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades. "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization." Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions. — CNBC's Phil LeBeau , Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

events.title: Jeffries shifts strategy amid growing Democratic divisions in US House
events.summary: The lawmaker is opting to put progressive opponents on record as he vies to become the chamber’s first Black speaker. On the eve of Democratic leadership elections in the United States House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries has confirmed plans to force fellow Democrats to take a recorded vote on his nomination for speaker. Jeffries, the chamber’s current minority leader, told reporters at the US Capitol on Tuesday he was taking the new approach instead of — as some of his top allies had hoped — a vote by acclamation, which requires no ballot. list 1 of 3 Jeffries backs Hegseth impeachment as Democrats vow probes of Trump allies list 2 of 3 Will Democrats try to strip US-Israel initiative from Pentagon funding? list 3 of 3 Why US Democrats are expected to keep Schumer and Jeffries in power The move effectively forces House Democrats to publicly weigh in on whether they support Jeffries’s leadership. Jeffries, a New York Democrat poised to become the House’s first Black speaker, argued that a recorded vote was the same method his party used when it retook control of the chamber in 2018 during President Donald Trump’s first term. “It certainly seems to me to be appropriate that we take exactly the same approach to give every single person the opportunity to weigh in, one way or the other, on who the caucus feels is best positioned … to help move us forward into the new Congress,” Jeffries said during his news conference. The strategy shift, which was first reported by Punchbowl News, comes amid growing Democratic dissent over having Jeffries in control of the party’s messaging and policy priorities in the US House. Some progressive members, particularly newly elected ones, had reportedly threatened to call for a recorded vote to extract policy concessions from Jeffries. Without unanimous backing, the vote to nominate Jeffries could highlight dissent within the Democratic Party. One of the most vocal holdouts, Congressman-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, has publicly refused to commit to Jeffries unless he received guarantees on some progressive priorities, including halting US military aid to Israel and reforming campaign finance standards set by the Supreme Court case Citizens United. “Unless Speaker Jeffries is willing to commit to enforcing our nation’s laws like the Leahy Law against Israeli genocide in Gaza, unless the speaker is willing to get to the heart of this crisis which is Citizens United, he will not have my vote,” the Ohio Democrat said in a video posted to social media. Jeffries’s preemptive countermove effectively strips progressive members of leverage heading into Wednesday’s closed-door vote by forcing them to go on record against his leadership. It also highlights a weakness in their efforts: the lack of another candidate for speaker. On Monday, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts dismissed the idea she would mount a challenge to Jeffries. Last week, she rallied her social media followers to sign a petition to shape the Democratic majority’s agenda, spurring questions about whether she would run for the speaker role. But she has since brushed those aside. “I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people,” Pressley said at a town hall in her district. When asked about the resistance he faces from his fellow Democrats, Jeffries told reporters they would “have to talk to” dissenting party members about why they oppose his leadership. “We’re going to have a vote tomorrow. The caucus is going to be able to work its will. And we’ll see what the outcome is tomorrow,” Jeffries said. “In less than 24 hours, you’ll be able to know.” Jeffries is expected to handily win Wednesday’s vote, which would give the leader an idea of the support he has when the 120th Congress is sworn in on January 3. The speakership will be confirmed in a separate roll call vote on the floor of the US House early in the new year.

Universities are also responsible for holding society accountable by researching and benchmarking AI, Li said. “It would become one of the biggest failures of our time if we don’t, as a society,” Li said, “if we don’t resource [the] public sector in a serious way.” — Jake Angelo

events.title: Infrastructure organisers of the 2032 Paralympics have no employees with disability
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Brisbane 2032's Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority has no employees with disability Brisbane will host the Olympic and Paralympic Games in 2032, with planning underway for 17 new and upgraded venues. ( ABC News: Peter Mullins ) The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority's (GIICA) latest annual report shows it has no employees with disability. Paralympians say it is a missed opportunity as the state prepares for the 2032 Games. GIICA says it has established a reference group to ensure accessibility requirements are met for the venues. The independent authority responsible for key 2032 Olympics and Paralympics venues has no employees with disability. Para-athletes say it is a missed opportunity. The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) was established in late 2024 to lead the planning, construction, and delivery of 17 new and upgraded venues for the Games. GIICA's employment headcount grew by 50 per cent in the 2025-26 financial year compared to the previous year. Its latest annual report showed its workforce, of 81 employees, included no people with disability. Brisbane Stadium at Victoria Park is one of the venues GIICA is overseeing for the 2032 Games. ( Supplied: COX Architecture and Hassell ) Dual Paralympic medallist Karni Liddell said that was "surprising". "Zero per cent is not reflective of how many people with disabilities are in Australia," she said. Ms Liddell, who lives in Queensland, said planning for the Games was not just about making stadiums accessible. She said getting to the venues was always the hardest part for people with disability. Paralympian Karni Lidell says people with disability should have a positive experience at the Games. ( ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato ) "We don't want them showing up to Brisbane and having a really negative experience," she said. In 2018, the Gold Coast hosted the Commonwealth Games' largest para-sport program, but the international event's transport to and from the venues was not accessible. How Brisbane's 2032 Games can learn from the past A report highlighting the "missed opportunities" for people with disability at past global sporting events hopes to create a "road map" for Brisbane's 2032 Games. Gravel car parks were used for disability parking, and people in wheelchairs could not use the toilets in the trains or move between carriages, a Queenslanders with Disability Network and Urbis 2024 report found. Fellow Queensland Paralympian Marayke Jonkers said the Games won't be the most inclusive and accessible if people with lived experience aren't in the rooms when decisions are made about venues. "It's a missed opportunity," she said. "Very few people with a disability are ever going to be a Paralympian, but we all do need a job." Ms Jonkers said she has been unsuccessful in applying for jobs connected to the 2032 Games. Paralympian Marayke Jonkers says an amazing legacy for the Games would be improved employment outcomes for people with disability. ( Supplied: Marayke Jonkers ) "I did not want to get a job because I was disabled," she said. "What I have experienced trying to find work after having two university degrees, started a charity, being the president of the board of very big ASIC-registered companies … it's still really hard to actually get employment." Ms Jonkers said people with disability are more than twice as likely to be unemployed compared to those without disability. She said changing that statistic would be a "pretty amazing" legacy for the games. "If we really want to do well in 2032 as a country, it's not just about the athletes for 10 days," Ms Jonkers said. GIICA was established to lead the planning, construction, and delivery of new and upgraded venues for the Brisbane Games. ( Supplied: COX Architecture and Hassell ) A GIICA spokesperson said the venues will be accessible, inclusive and welcoming for everyone. They said the authority has partnered with Queenslanders With Disability Network (QDN) and Paralympics Australia to establish an accessibility reference group to ensure requirements are met across venue design and construction. The group met for the first time in September and included people with lived experience of disability, para-athletes and accessibility advocates. "Their insights will help GIICA test ideas, identify opportunities and make informed decisions as we deliver venues that are accessible," the spokesperson said.

The new round, which comes a year after its $75 million Series A round was announced, was co-led by General Atlantic and earlier backer QED Investors. Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander co-founded the three-year-old startup after previously co-founding two other companies, including Fat Llama, a peer-to-peer rental marketplace acquired by Swedish rival Hygglo for $41.5 million in 2022. Model ML develops AI agents that integrate with clients’ systems, data, and tools, including Excel and PowerPoint. The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis. Other startups automating the routine, repetitive tasks for investment bankers and management consultants include Hebbia and Rogo, which raised $160 million at a $2 billion valuation in April. Anthropic and OpenAI have also built tools for financial professionals, but Model ML says it runs on open source models and that doing so allows it to operate at about 2% of the cost of frontier models while delivering faster results. events.title: What is a dirty bomb and how dangerous is the weapon
events.summary: President Trump warned Iran against orchestrating a "dirty bomb" attack in Washington, D.C., though the White House says there are no credible threats. The big picture: Unlike a nuclear weapon, a "dirty bomb" uses common explosives to scatter radioactive material, potentially contaminating surrounding areas, forcing evacuations and causing widespread disruption. Driving the news: Asked Tuesday about reports of a possible Iranian dirty bomb plot in Washington, Trump said, "We're looking into it." "We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added . Trump did not say an attack was imminent: "I hope it's not." Trump warned Iran would face unprecedented consequences if it carried out an attack. Catch up quick: Trump's comments came hours after CNN reported about the threat to D.C. CNN reported that unnamed officials described Iran's attack planning as "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack." "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," says Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. Iran has denied the allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei calling them "baseless." Read more about dirty bombs below. What is a dirty bomb? How it works: A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives, like dynamite, with radioactive materials, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . This is much different than a nuclear bomb. A nuclear bomb splits atoms and releases a huge blast of energy. Dirty bombs spread radioactive dust, smoke or other material that contaminate, the CDC says. How dangerous is a dirty bomb? The main danger stems from the explosion itself, which, like other explosive materials, can cause serious injuries and damage, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission . The scope of impact would depend on the size of the bomb, NRC says, as well as the type of radioactive material and weather conditions — especially if the material is inhaled. "Because people cannot see, smell, feel, or taste radiation, you should take immediate steps to protect yourself and your loved ones," the CDC says. The biggest concerns from high levels of radiation exposure would be nausea, vomiting, skin burns and radiation sickness, per CDC. Yes, but: The exposure would probably not cause immediate serious illness, the CDC says, except for those very close to the blast. What would happen if one exploded in Washington? Though the White House confirms there are no credible threats, there are plans in place to keep D.C. safe from threats. The Department of Homeland Security 's immediate response includes police and responders restricting access to affected areas, while experts investigate radiation levels. Residents may be told to shelter indoors. DHS' Securing the Cities program helps high-risk metro areas, including D.C. and its region, detect and prevent potential attacks. The DHS has provided $300 million to the STC areas through 2023 to help them buy radiation detectors, train officers and build systems for spotting potential radioactive materials. Worthy of your time: The NRC recommends staying as far away as possible from the bomb site. The CDC has tips on what to do if you're in a home, building or car when a dirty bomb goes off. Removing outer clothing may eliminate up to 90% of radioactive dust, the CDC says. Pets should also be brought inside, the CDC says. Has a dirty bomb ever been used? No dirty bomb has ever been successfully used in an attack, according to the Washington Post and other reports , though authorities have uncovered several plots and attempts. The U.S. Government Accountability Office has tracked past attempts, including multiple attempts in Russia. In 2002, U.S. authorities arrested Jose Padilla, an American accused of discussing a dirty-bomb attack with al-Qaeda operatives, potentially targeting Washington, D.C., per the Department of Justice . The alleged plot was in its early stages and never materialized. The bottom line: A dirty bomb attack doesn't appear to be imminent in the U.S., but any such strike would make a relatively small explosion into a much larger public safety crisis.

events.title: Milburn calls for tax cuts for businesses hiring young people despite union concerns
events.summary: Youth unemployment review risks clash with unions and Labour left over workers’ rights and minimum wage Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s youth unemployment report? Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people Alan Milburn has called on ministers to cut business taxes and ease regulations to encourage employers to hire more young people, setting up a potential clash with trade unions and the Labour left over employment rights. The former health secretary published the results of his year-long review into youth unemployment on Wednesday, in what the prime minister, Andy Burnham , called a “watershed moment” for young people. But while ministers embraced his central recommendation of cutting benefit and sickness payments to pay for more concerted employment support, his recommendations on workers’ rights, national insurance and the minimum wage pose potentially awkward dilemmas for the government. In the 278-page report, Milburn called for ministers to cut national insurance for companies that hire young workers, to apply a “cautionary principle” when abolishing exploitative zero-hours contracts and to slow the rise in the youth rates of the minimum wage. “ A new bargain needs to be struck between employers and government : employers should create more first chances; government should make it easier and less risky for employers to do so,” he wrote. “That is the give and the get.” Trade unions warned against some of his proposals, despite broadly welcoming Milburn’s push for a drastic expansion in state support to help the almost 1 million young people not in education or work. Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, urged the government to “crack on and deliver its guaranteed hours rights in full” in the face of lobbying from business groups. “The past decade and a half has tested to destruction the idea that low-paid insecure work is good for our economy and young people’s employment prospects. It’s for the birds,” he said. Burnham welcomed Milburn’s report on Tuesday, telling cabinet colleagues it represented a “comprehensive vision” for how to change the welfare, health and education systems for young people to help them into work. He then joined Pat McFadden in the Commons, where the work and pensions secretary told MPs the government would deliver “a new settlement for young people”. Under Milburn’s plan, the government would spend nearly £2bn a year on a youth opportunity service, which would provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work. It would involve spending just over £2bn to create more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies that hire young people. The new system would be paid for largely by replacing young people’s disability and sickness benefits with a single youth allowance, which would be considerably less than some people can currently claim. People aged 18-24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, which would be replaced by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are “well established, significant and ongoing”. The benefit cuts would be expected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn in higher tax receipts. That money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system, Milburn said. Ministers and Milburn have worked hard to avoid the response that greeted Keir Starmer’s attempts last year to cut the benefits bill by £5bn by restricting access to disability payments. The former prime minister backed down in the face of opposition from his own MPs, in a humiliating retreat that arguably set in motion his eventual departure from office. Early signs suggest the outreach efforts have been successful, with several of the architects of last year’s rebellion speaking in favour of the proposals. Debbie Abrahams, the chair of the work and pensions select committee, called the review “an opportunity of a generation”, adding: “We must change the status quo. ” Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters But while Burnham and McFadden expressed support for the idea of shifting money from benefits to employment support schemes, they did not explicitly back Milburn’s recommendations on either national insurance contributions or zero-hours contracts. McFadden told the Commons on Tuesday: “We know that employment costs matter and we will consider all these things as we move forward.” On the minimum wage, Milburn urged ministers to continue applying “caution” when judging how quickly to increase the youth rate, after Labour promised in 2024 to raise it to the same level as the adult rate. And on banning zero-hours contracts, he warned: “There is a risk that in trying to address a legitimate challenge, the solution has unintended consequences.

events.title: Food relief takes election backseat but cost of living front of mind for voters
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Cost of living bites hard across regional Victoria as voters head to the polls Susan Naveed visits Whittington Neighbourhood House weekly to help feed her and her nine-year-old son. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) Regional Victorian food relief centres fear funding that expires next year will threaten their ability to supply 100,000 meals a week. The relief centres are also struggling with food shortages due to supermarkets reducing waste. The food centres are calling on Victorian election candidates to commit to further funding. Susan Naveed never thought she would need food relief. But after leaving her job due to personal reasons a year ago, Ms Naveed is now a frequent customer of Whittington Neighbourhood House's Foodbank relief centre in Geelong. "Sometimes if it wasn't for Foodshare I don't know if my son and I would have food," Ms Naveed said. But a looming food shortage may become a reality for Ms Naveed and thousands of others, with six regional food relief centres due to run out of state government funding in July. A Foodbank hunger report in October found 69 per cent of households experienced food insecurity for the first time in the past year. A volunteer packs food at the Bendigo Foodshare centre. ( Supplied ) In the 2025 state government budget, Regional Food Security Alliance received $6 million over two years for its relief centres in Wodonga, Bendigo, Geelong, Shepparton, Mildura and Warrnambool. Neither Labor nor the coalition have committed to extending the grant. Alliance chair Cathie Steele said $12 million was needed for the next four years to meet demand. "Everyone could do with more but it's a tough time so we can't ask for more. We just need to keep our services going," Ms Steele said. "We've got to ensure that there's ongoing support for people." The Victorian government did not respond when asked by the ABC about whether funding would be continued from July 2027. A Victorian Liberals spokesperson said it was up to Labor to explain why future funding had not been secured. One Nation at the weekend committed $14 million over four years for the alliance's six relief centres if it formed government. Alliance chief executive Jacqui Watt said she had met with election candidates and current sitting members, including Carers and Volunteers Minister Luba Grigorovitch. Ms Watt said the response from all had been non-committal. Michelle Murphy says produce supplies have dropped in the past year. ( Supplied ) Bendigo Foodshare chief executive Michelle Murphy said her centre had experienced a 21 per cent drop in fresh food supplies this year and was struggling to keep shelves stocked. "We've seen less fresh produce coming through our warehouse as supermarkets continue to reduce their food waste and less produce becomes available through our statewide food relief partners," she said. Ritchies IGA supermarkets chief executive Fred Harrison said supermarkets were cutting food waste, which meant less was available to donate. "Business being tough, one of the areas you try to minimise is the amount of waste and throw-outs you might have," he said. Mr Harrison said short shelf-life products such as milk presented challenges for distribution. Fred Harrison says supermarkets have cut food waste in the past year. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) "Dairy products or small goods products are used by three or four days and logistically it's hard to do much with it once you get down to those short use-by dates." Coles told the ABC it had contributed $151 million in total community support "to promote health outcomes and build resilience". Woolworths said it had provided more than 44 million meals nationally in the past year through Foodshare and community organisations. "Our five local supermarkets in the Bendigo region donate excess food every week, rescuing an average of more than 800kg of food per week," the supermarket said. Ms Steele said the alliance was now focusing on getting supplies direct from food producers rather than supermarkets. Whittington Neighbourhood House in Geelong provides a vital service for people dealing with food insecurity. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) Shoppers switch to cheaper alternatives According to Foodbank, more than half of food-insecure households have swapped to cheaper food alternatives, such as tinned food instead of fresh products, in the past year. Supermarkets have also seen a trend towards customers buying cheaper cuts of meat and moving to products such as minced meat to make meals go further, according to Mr Harrison. Whittington Neighbourhood House offers a range of goods.

events.title: Kalshi takes down controversial Trump 'mention' markets at CFTC's request
events.summary: Kalshi has paused trading on several of its "mention" markets related to statements by President Donald Trump. A spokesperson for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission told CNBC it has placed holds on some of Kalshi's proposed mention markets' certifications. A Trump-related mention market drew scrutiny in July after it was revealed a White House teleprompter operator placed trades on Kalshi. Prediction market platform Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of "mention" contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC, the company confirmed on Tuesday. Mention markets are made up of contracts that ask traders what specific words will be used in a speech, a corporate earnings call or during a television broadcast. Earlier this year, a White House teleprompter operator used inside information to place trades in mention markets related to the president's comments. Markets paused include those asking traders what nicknames Trump will say before 2027, what the president will say in November and what countries and companies Trump will say before the end of the month. The move comes after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , the federal agency overseeing prediction markets, said in a letter to exchanges in September that mentions contracts have a greater manipulation risk. A spokesperson for the agency told CNBC that the commission has placed holds on the certification of some of Kalshi's proposed mention markets. The spokesperson cited a Kalshi contract on hold that asked what key words would Trump say before a certain date. The contract was originally self-certified by Kalshi in February 2025. "The CFTC stayed the certification of these contracts because they may be susceptible to manipulation, which is consistent with the staff advisory the CFTC put out two months ago," said Brooke Nethercott, the agency's spokesperson. In a statement, Kalshi spokesperson Dani Lever said Kalshi is complying with the order. In August, reports emerged that the CFTC was conducting an internal review into mention markets. The agency also requested that Kalshi, which is the only U.S.-regulated exchange that features the contract type, take down its sports-related mention markets in response to the inquiry. Kalshi complied. A Trump-related mention market drew scrutiny in July after it was revealed a White House teleprompter operator placed trades on markets related to the president's comments. In a settlement with the operator, the CFTC ordered a three-year trading ban on the individual and a penalty amounting to over $172,000 . Kalshi has defended mentions markets even as the CFTC has become increasingly skeptical of them, saying that the individual words of prominent people often cause billions of dollars of movement across financial markets. In addition to scrutiny regarding mention markets, the company is also facing a probe from the CFTC about its communications about new products with the agency, though a spokesperson for the company told CNBC that it was working to resolve the issues. As of Tuesday morning, a mention market asking what Vice President JD Vance would say during the New York Times DealBook Summit event on Wednesday is still active. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: 7 smart reasons to sell a stock—and my ‘golden rule’ for offloading shares, says hedge fund CEO
events.summary: Leadership Jared Diamond: What makes leaders successful Money Use 5 phrases to gracefully decline an invitation you can't afford, says financial therapist Raising Successful Kids Parents who are really good at handling tantrums do 5 things—their kids become more emotionally intelligent, says psychologist Leadership Whole Foods co-founder shares tips for launching a successful second act Leadership The RealReal CEO’s No. 1 leadership lesson Nobody is born knowing anything innately about the stock market. And if you feel like you've missed the investing class, you didn't. Usually there isn't one. So responsible people who are trying to do the responsible thing by building a portfolio for themselves and their families often find huge gaps in their knowledge and don't know where to turn. As the co-founder and CEO of the hedge fund Metropolitan Capital Advisors and a longtime panelist on CNBC's Fast Money, I know that there's no shortage of advice when you're getting started about great investments to buy. It can feel easy and gratifying, especially when your portfolio is doing well. But then things get tougher. One of the hardest things to do as an investor is to figure out when to sell. You buy a stock because you believe it will go up in value. But the decision to sell is rarely so straightforward. Personally, I've made just about every selling mistake. But over time, I've developed a framework for knowing when to sell — and when not to. Selling decisions are often rooted in emotion and cognitive bias rather than logic. One major culprit: anchoring to past performance , a flawed reference point that clouds clear thinking. Behavioral economics, particularly prospect theory , shows that we experience the pain of a loss more intensely than the joy of a gain. This leads investors to cling to losers ("just need to get back to even") and sell winners too early ("lock in the gain"). We also place too much emphasis on recent events, a phenomenon known as recency bias . If your last tech stock soared, you're more likely to chase another. If your last trade flopped, you may avoid the market altogether. And when recent trades go well, people tend to trade more — often to their detriment. Finally, selling triggers a storm of second-guessing and rationalization. Here are my responses to common excuses: "What if I'm wrong and it goes up?" What if you're right and it keeps going down? "What will I do with the cash?" You don't always need to put it to work right away, or you can buy a little more of what you already own. "If I double down and it rebounds, I'll make it all back." But if it continues to go down from here, your losses will double. "I don't like having a loss, so I'll sell once it gets back to even." What you originally paid is irrelevant. Yet for many investors, it becomes the most important factor in their decision-making. To assuage their fragile egos, they risk even bigger losses. These biases and emotional landmines are why you need a clear, disciplined plan for when to sell, including when: The original thesis no longer holds. If the fundamental reasons you bought the stock are no longer true — if earnings slow, revenue shrinks, margins deteriorate or the company loses market share — it may be time to move on. There's a regulatory risk. Legislative changes can dramatically shift a company's prospects. For example, the outlook for solar-related companies can decline dramatically when tax credits are cut for installations. Management loses credibility. Frequent earnings misses or misleading guidance suggest deeper problems. One-off surprises happen; recurring surprises reflect poor leadership. It becomes too big a slice of your portfolio. A stock that grows from 10% to 25% of your portfolio due to the superb performance of its underlying business, which fuels a soaring stock price, increases your risk from a diversification standpoint. Rebalancing is smart and necessary. The maximum I would have in any one position in my own portfolio is 20% — and that's probably too much! The stock becomes overvalued. Sometimes the hype drives prices beyond what fundamentals justify. If valuation detaches from reality, it's okay to take some profits. If it really goes nuts, I will sell enough to take my original investment off the table. You need the money elsewhere. Selling to fund a home, college tuition or retirement is perfectly valid. Opportunity cost matters. You have tax reasons. For example, tax-loss harvesting may allow you to offset capital gains or deduct up to $3,000 of losses against ordinary income. When you've decided to sell for a solid reason — especially the first, second, or third outlined above — don't hesitate. Don't wait for the perfect price. Just sell. Just as important as knowing when to sell is knowing when not to sell. Avoid emotionally driven decisions that sabotage long-term gains. Don't sell just because it went up.

events.title: Gina Raimondo criticizes Trump admin chip policy
events.summary: Gina Raimondo, former commerce secretary and CEO of RAISE US, said that when it comes to selling chips to China, the US government has to put national security above corporate revenues. Raimondo said that when she was running the Commerce Department under the Biden administration, she spent a lot of time with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, going over the rules and what they could and could not sell. “They weren’t always happy,” she said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. But she added that she always put national security first and that you couldn’t “put a price” on America’s national security. “This administration hasn’t been like that,” Raimondo said. She described the ever-changing message on chips as: “‘No, you can’t sell chips.’ ‘Yes you can, if we can get a 25% cut.’ You’re either for America’s national security or you’re not — it’s not at a price.” Referencing new export rules to crack down on China’s ability to rent compute, she said she started work on that two years ago, but then the “buzzer rang and the game was over,” she said. “Why did it take two years for that to happen? I don’t know, but I’m glad they’re moving in that direction.” She added that China “wakes up every day” thinking “how do we beat America?” When asked whether she would run for president on the Democratic ticket in 2028, Raimondo deflected. “My next job is my current job.” — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: They Suffered Brain Injuries After Riding a Six Flags Roller Coaster. Regulators Pinned the Blame on Them.
events.summary: An aerial view of the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, in September Jae C. Hong/AP Photo A 17-year-old boy died after riding the extreme X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California this summer, just weeks before two more people suffered severe brain injuries after riding the same attraction, ProPublica and L.A. Material have found. A homicide detective investigating Christopher Gibson’s death in June sent an email to the California official responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But records show that the official did not reply until nearly two months later. The lack of action raises the question of whether the brain damage suffered by the two riders the following month could have been avoided. Christopher’s death, which has not been previously reported, also raises questions about Six Flags, its flagship X2 ride and the way in which California regulates roller coasters. Billed as a “fourth-dimension” roller coaster, the X2 drew more than 16 million riders attracted to extreme thrills. It featured seats that swiveled in all directions as the ride hurtled and twisted along the track, sometimes at a rate of up to 76 mph. Guests ride the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain theme park in Valencia, California, in 2023. Eric Thayer/Bloomberg via Getty Images The X2 was shut down temporarily after two separate brain hemorrhages in July. In August, CNN reported that the X2 had been “linked to more than a dozen reports of serious injuries” and two deaths over nearly two decades. Christopher’s is a third. A ProPublica and L.A. Material investigation has found that state regulators have repeatedly failed to take swift action in the face of reported deaths and head injuries on the X2. On at least 70 occasions since 2010, Magic Mountain reported head injuries to the little-known unit within the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But rather than responding to those reports with vigorous inspections or safety checks, the regulators often did minimal or no investigation, according to a ProPublica and L.A. Material analysis of court filings, public records and internal regulatory documents. “How many more people have to die before you think, ‘Well, maybe we should look at that?’” said Mariusz Ziejewski, a biomechanical engineer who has worked with the military to reduce brain injuries and was an expert witness in a lawsuit against Magic Mountain. “I think one is already way too much.” CalOSHA and Magic Mountain instead frequently blamed riders for their injuries and in more than 35 cases alleged that people had somehow ridden the attraction incorrectly by failing to hold their heads in the right position. In one case, when a 14-year-old was hospitalized last year after losing consciousness on the ride, officials attributed it to the teenager’s menstrual cycle. Six Flags and CalOSHA did not respond to detailed questions from ProPublica and L.A. Material. However, Denisse Gómez, a spokesperson for the state department that oversees CalOSHA, said in a statement that when theme park injuries are reported, regulators evaluate whether the ride was operating correctly and according to state safety rules. The agency is “committed to public safety,” she said, adding that “because that investigation is ongoing, we are not commenting on matters involving X2 at this time.”  Six Flags provided a statement that noted that the X2 had consistently passed safety tests, and its parks undergo preventative maintenance and a comprehensive, third-party inspection program. They also said their investigation of the ride remains ongoing, and that they are fully cooperating with CalOSHA. “Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do,” a spokesperson said. When Six Flags has been sued for wrongful death or injuries related to the X2, it has maintained that injuries are rare and the ride is highly regulated by CalOSHA. In a recently settled lawsuit related to 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 in 2022, Magic Mountain’s director of public safety said in a declaration that the state has never notified the park of any “patron safety-related concerns related to the acceleration forces on the X2.” Christopher Gibson was an autistic but healthy teen when he and his mother, Leanndra Fascaldo, drove from their Colorado home to California to celebrate his high school graduation at Magic Mountain. The pair rode roller coasters for several days starting on May 31, including the X2 and the Viper, which Christopher called a “neck breaker,” according to a sheriff’s report. On their fourth day at the theme park, the teen once again rode the X2 and then the Great American Revolution before complaining of a headache. By early afternoon, they returned to the hotel. That night, the pain grew worse. His mother gave him Advil. Eventually, he moved to the hotel room’s closet, where it was darker, and went back to sleep. His mother assumed he was just exhausted, but around 2 p.m. the next day she noticed that he had stopped snoring. She looked into the closet and saw that his lips were blue and his face was covered with “white and pink foam.” She called 911. Paramedics pronounced him dead at 3:16 p.m. on June 4. Within a month, a sheriff’s homicide detective reached out to the California state office that regulates roller coasters, writing that “it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.” The detective did not receive a reply until she contacted the office again two months later. It’s been a deadly year for Six Flags. In addition to the California incident, an Atlanta school worker died in October after riding one of the theme park’s “hypercoasters” at Six Flags Over Georgia, prompting the company to temporarily close nine attractions at six theme parks across North America. Theme park rides are regulated by states, not the federal government. In 2000, the legislature gave CalOSHA, the agency responsible for worker safety in California, oversight of roller coasters. Millions of people flock to the state’s theme parks each year, and the move came after a series of high-profile accidents in the 1990s. Under the law, state officials were given new power to conduct annual inspections , and theme parks must report accidents that result in serious injury to the agency. But ProPublica and L.A. Material found that officials in CalOSHA’s Amusement Ride and Tramway Unit have frequently determined that investigations are unnecessary when accidents happen on the X2. events.title: JBL’s headphones that are great for in-flight entertainment are 67 percent off
events.summary: If you’re looking to upgrade your headphones before the big wave of Black Friday deals arrives, you can buy JBL’s Tour One M3 for a new low price of $149 ($300 off) at Amazon , Best Buy , and directly from JBL . The deal is so good that my colleague John Higgins , The Verge’s audio and TV reviewer, popped in on his day off to tell us just how much of a steal they are at this price. JBL Tour One M3 Where to Buy: $449.95 $149.95 at Amazon $449.95 $149.95 at Best Buy $449.95 $149.95 at JBL JBL’s Tour One M3 stand out largely because they come with the Smart Tx wireless audio transmitter. Frequent fliers will likely appreciate the accessory, which plugs into a plane’s in-flight entertainment system via a 3.5mm cable, allowing you to listen to audio wirelessly. It also works with other devices that lack Bluetooth support but have a headphone jack. The small touchscreen-equipped transmitter also lets you easily adjust the headphones’ noise cancellation, EQ settings, and volume. It can be used to answer calls, too. Fancy tricks aside, the headphones get the essentials right. According to John, they offer excellent passive noise isolation, and their active noise cancellation is good enough to block out low-frequency sounds, like airplane engines. He also praises their overall sound quality, though he notes that JBL’s default tuning slightly affects midrange clarity, something you can easily fix by adjusting the EQ. They also support high-resolution lossless audio over the included USB-C or 3.5mm cable, plus spatial audio with head tracking. JBL says they can last up to 70 hours on a single charge with noise cancellation off — enough to get you through multiple long-haul flights — while the USB-C-chargeable transmitter offers up to 18 hours of battery life.
