events.title: Anthropic IPO: For hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into AI startups, a big debut is a must
events.summary: Anthropic's IPO will be a key moment in the valuation of an AI startup ecosystem that captured 86% of U.S. venture capital dollars in the first half of 2026, and for infrastructure funds that boomed on the data center buildout. The VC industry has rebounded from a five-year period of underperformance, buoyed by big gains in the largest AI companies. Other alternative assets, including private credit and private equity buyout funds, have lagged. Artificial intelligence has propelled big gains in venture capital funds this year, and a flood of money — over $350 billion — into AI startups. Venture funds were up close to 18% through the first half of 2026, with 86% of U.S.-based VC investor money going into AI companies. With Anthropic set to make its public market debut this week at a reported valuation of $1.4 trillion — though sources told CNBC on Tuesday the pricing may be upped — the market's reception to the deal and early trading in its shares may set the tone for the next leg in the private market AI boom. It has been a period of increased volatility for tech stocks and the public market AI trade. In addition to concerns about balance sheet strength and valuation, midterm elections showed widespread public opposition to data centers , and the CEO scandal rocking Nvidia, the "central bank" of AI financing , has compounded risks in the sector. But on the private side of tech investing, firms are closely watching how investors react to Anthropic's IPO. "I think that will end up guiding further intentions for the VC space," said Mike McLelland, managing director of investments within private markets at Cleveland, Ohio-based Clearstead. "Once you have a couple of good exits, it gives people a little more confidence in the realization story." Anthropic is getting some deep-pocketed support for the deal. Altimeter Capital is aiming to invest $5 billion , according to its founder and CEO Brad Gerstner, who noted that was five times as much as he has ever invested in an IPO. "I think this is a cornerstone compounder for a long time," Gerstner told CNBC's "Halftime Report" on Monday. "It's where the trade is going." Chip giants Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Nvidia, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Micron are all investing, as are Google and Microsoft. The direction of the IPO market is important given that companies have been staying private longer than they did in the past and strategic exits have been relatively muted, McLelland said. A notable exception is Google's $32 billion acquisition of cloud security firm Wiz. That 2025 deal was Google's largest ever, overtaking its $12.5 billion purchase of Motorola in 2012. A very concentrated private bet on AI VC gains have been concentrated in a small number of large funds that hold the biggest AI-linked companies. MSCI reports that the 10 largest holdings make up 22% of the value of its venture index. That concentration comes amid improved performance. Venture capital funds returned 17.8% in the first six months of 2026, according to Opto Investments, using proprietary and MSCI Private Capital Solutions data. Venture fund portfolio data is reported by fund general partners on a delayed basis. The six-month gains would equate to a full year return as high as 38% if the pace is maintained. It comes on the heels of a recent period of underperformance for the asset class, with a 6.19% return over five years, according to Juan Mier, lead analyst of fund strategies at PitchBook. Venture's 10-year average return is 13% annually, according to PitchBook. For the year ended March 2026, venture capital delivered a nearly 22% return, driven in large part by AI valuations, Mier said. It is not just the largest AI companies that are venture-backed and tied to the IPO performance of the giants. Thousands of smaller companies that supply AI giants with infrastructure, component manufacturing, and data services, for example, have also seen their valuations rise quickly, said Jake Miller, co-founder of New York-based Opto Investments, which helps investment advisors design private investment programs. Notably, AI captured $355.9 billion, or 86% of U.S. venture dollars in the first half of 2026, according to Clearstead analysis of PitchBook data. Globally, AI deal value reached $521.4 billion over the trailing twelve months. That's more than double the prior year, even as AI deal count fell 21.6% from the previous quarter. Mier said venture capital returns are expected to moderate in the third quarter as valuations in the AI space in public markets have adjusted, and that flows to private markets eventually. "That may moderate returns for the second half of the year," he said. Anthropic's deal, reported to be on target for a $1.4 trillion valuation, is well below the $2 trillion deal value originally floated by bankers. But amid the AI proliferation, industry participants expect VC to continue piquing investors' interest in the coming years.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tech billionaire Sanjay Govil expresses interest in buying into Hobart Hurricanes, new stadium Sanjay Govil has expressed interest in buying into the Hobart Hurricanes Big Bash League team. ( Getty Images: Steve Bell ) Tech billionaire Sanjay Govil has expressed interest in buying into the Hobart Hurricanes and the Hobart stadium precinct. The government's appetite for such a deal is unclear, and any public-private partnership agreement for the stadium would signal a change in policy. An updated cost for the Hobart stadium project is expected in the next few weeks. Cricket looms as a wildcard in the Tasmanian government's hunt for more funds to build the new Macquarie Point stadium. And at least one American billionaire has expressed an interest in investing in the stadium precinct , as part of a potential power play involving the Hobart Hurricanes cricket team. Tech billionaire Sanjay Govil wants to buy at least a 50 per cent share in the Hobart Hurricanes, following Cricket Australia's decision to green-light the privatisation of the Big Bash League. As part of a broader cricket and infrastructure play, Mr Govil is interested in a slice of the Macquarie Point stadium and precinct, envisioning a place where American college football-style parties may be held before future Hurricanes games. "I think it's going to be very, very exciting. And to be part of that? Imagine," he told the ABC. Sanjay Govil has expressed interest in the Hobart Hurricanes and Macquarie Point stadium project. ( Supplied: Eagle Team ) Mr Govil, who founded Infinite Computer Solutions and digital healthcare company Zyter, is worth upwards of US$2 billion. Aboriginal protester guilty of trespass despite 'cultural responsibility' to forests MP declares shares in data centre developer before calling for moratorium Man charged with murder of two-week-old Hobart baby He owns the Welsh Fire, which plays in the UK Hundred competition, the Ricky Ponting-coached Washington Freedom in America's Major League Cricket competition, and is funding the construction of a 10,000-capacity cricket stadium for the Freedom in Frederick, Maryland. He wants a stake in the Big Bash League and has targeted the Hurricanes — and its prospective new stadium. "There are two elements to it, part A and part B," he said. "We would come in, and part A is the operations team, taking ownership of the Hobart Hurricanes team. The Hurricanes would then, in turn, lease the ground and facility from entity B, which would have different shareholders including us," he said. Sanjay Govil says it would be "exciting" to have a stake in the Macquarie Point stadium. ( Supplied: Cox Architecture ) The Auburn college football fan, who also owns a stake in entertainment and events company Mari, envisages a college football-style atmosphere and fan experiences before and after Hurricanes games at Macquarie Point. "That infrastructure would not just include the stadium, but a tailgating area, shops, restaurants, a whole experience centre," he said. "It's all about experience. That's the expertise I want to bring to the Hobart Hurricanes. More stadium money sought amid cost blowout concerns The Tasmanian government has begun the process of courting financial partners to help fund its Hobart stadium, as the $1.13 billion project faces a budget crunch. The prospect of cricket-induced private investment was floated with Premier Jeremy Rockliff at a September 8 meeting between him and Cricket Tasmania bosses. The government's appetite for such a deal is unclear, and any public-private partnership agreement would signal a backflip. It had previously explored a public-private partnership for the stadium, commissioning reports by Perth consultants Paxon Group and Melbourne-based Infrastructure Advisory Group last year — but ultimately decided against the model, deeming it too high a risk to the state . But with a stadium budget crunch on the horizon, a cricket-flavoured public-private partnership might become enticing to a government desperately needing outside funds to help fund the build. The stadium looks set to exceed its project budget of $1.13 billion, with state funding constrained to $875 million, as part of a government agreement with upper house MLC Bec Thomas in exchange for her support for the project in Tasmania's parliament last year. BESIX Watpac won the tender to construct the Macquarie Point stadium.

Research led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative looked specifically at hyperscale facilities, the largest class of server farms that typically support cloud computing and AI processing. The published study, " Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres ," estimates their combined electricity use approached that of a single state such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee under the highest-load scenario. The researchers identified 403 hyperscale facilities by using a larger datacenter dataset, satellite imagery, and building footprints on OpenStreetMap. Rather than reading electricity meters, the researchers worked out consumption from each site's electrical capacity, the hours in a year, and assumptions about how heavily the facility was running. Across four operating scenarios, ranging from low-intensity use to AI-heavy workloads, electricity draw was believed to total 68-99 terawatt-hours (TWh). Each of those states consumed approximately 100 TWh during the study period. The researchers also calculated carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions using eGRID2023 plant-level generation and emissions data from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons of CO 2 across the scenarios, with a central estimate of 25.7 million. That compares with 10.5 million for 2018. The study covered May 2024 to April 2025, so electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely to be even higher now, the researchers say. "What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," said Gianluca Guidi, lead author on the paper and postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard. "The datacenter boom hasn't slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we're reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026." Harvard's report also considers the mix of fuels being used to generate the electricity that powers all those hyperscale data houses. The mix varies considerably between regional grids, so where a hyperscale facility is built makes a substantial difference to its attributed emissions. Across the sites studied, roughly 54 percent of the electricity attributed to their consumption came from fossil fuels, mainly natural gas and coal. The electricity attributed to these facilities nevertheless had a lower average carbon intensity than the US grid overall. The researchers acknowledge limitations, including that there wasn't enough available data to study all hyperscale sites in the US, and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose compute versus AI-specialized operations at individual campuses.

events.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
events.summary: The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous I t’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over. Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans. The Neets review has taken on a life of its own. ITV has commissioned a four-part docudrama on the writing of the report. Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Neets: The Musical will be opening just before Christmas. And Mud’s classic, That’s Neet, That’s Neet, I Really Love Your Tiger Feet is the hot favourite to be the UK’s entry for next year’s Eurovision. At long last, a song we can all get behind and that has a realistic chance of winning. But Tuesday was the day. The day Big Al took centre stage at Google HQ to tell us he was about to tell us everything he had already told us. We just had to listen quietly and bathe in his reflected glory. And tick off all the review’s highlights as they were mentioned. Neets bingo. We were in danger of creating a lost generation. In fact we already might have done, as more than 10% of young people under 25 had been out of work, education or training for more than 20 years. It wasn’t that young people were lazy snowflakes. They had been let down. Time now to invest in this generation , not write them off. To invest in their futures like other northern European countries do. You couldn’t get hundreds of thousands of people back to work just by cutting benefits. That was delusional. Rather, a culture shift was needed. A recalibration of the way the state engaged with an abandoned generation. Almost seamlessly, the venue shifted to the Commons where Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, surrounded by Andy Burnham and most of the cabinet, was due to give his own 10-minute potted version of the Milburn review. First though, an intervention from the speaker, who wanted to put on record his concern that copies of the report hadn’t been laid before the house. Not that anyone needed a copy; we all knew it off by heart. Pat then repeated pretty much everything Milburn had said an hour earlier. The only difference being that McFadden managed to sound a bit gloomier about the whole thing. Not because he wasn’t enthusiastic, but because he was. The more engaged and upbeat Pat is, the more depressed he sounds. It’s just the way he’s wired. Gloom is his natural state of being. Even with McFadden’s rather downbeat delivery, this still felt like quite a moment. For the last two and a half years, many have criticised the government for its lack of vision. For lurching from one crisis to the next. Here, at last, was that vision. A major shift in the way the state would engage with a generation of young people who hitherto had been ignored or left on benefits. You couldn’t help feeling a bit sorry for Keir Starmer. He was the one who – albeit late in the day – had commissioned the review, but Burnham would get the credit. That’s showbiz for you. While Labour benches were packed, barely a dozen Tory backbench MPs had bothered to come for what might be a seismic shift in policy. Maybe they are the snowflakes. Or maybe they really aren’t that bothered that so many young people feel they have no future. Or maybe they couldn’t face sitting through the truly hopeless response of the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately. You really can’t blame so many Neets for feeling the odds are stacked against them when they see the rise and rise of Whately. Helen is everything the Tories believe Neets to be. Lazy, stupid. A woman without principle who has morphed into whatever shape is required to fit in with a Tory party sliding ever further to the right. If there were any justice, Whately would be one of the many people struggling to find a decent job. Or any job. Had she been born 25 years later, it would have been Helen claiming benefits. Her reply was one of the most half-witted imaginable. You can just about forgive the nastiness. That comes with the Tory territory. So of course she was demanding that billions more be cut from benefits. Because that’s the only language they think Neets understand. What was too much was the stupidity.

events.title: ‘Both utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed’: Fed advisor Marc Andreessen on AI going from boom to bust
events.summary: Marc Andreessen got the last word at the Federal Reserve’s big AI conference in San Francisco on Monday, and he used it to tell the central bank that nearly everyone in the room was going to be let down. “My line has been both utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed,” the venture capitalist said at the San Francisco Fed , “specifically disappointed by the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact, and specifically the economic impact.” Andreessen co-leads the Productivity and Jobs Task Force, which Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh set up to tell the central bank what super intelligence—“SI,” in the White House’s preferred term—will do to growth, prices and jobs. On Monday, Andreessen previewed what he’ll contribute to the group’s report. Without using the name, he described one of the oldest problems in economics: William Baumol’s “cost disease,” the reason flat-screen TVs get cheaper every year while hospital bills, tuition and rent go the other way. His case is that AI won’t cure it, and could even make it worse. The Fed hasn’t quite laid out that outcome. The task force is advisory, and Andreessen has no vote on interest rates. He co-leads it with Stanford economist Charles Jones and Microsoft executive Asha Sharma, one of five outside panels the Fed named in June to rethink how the central bank works. Its charge, per the Fed , is to assess the economic impact of “new general-purpose technologies, including super intelligence, to inform the Federal Reserve’s policy judgments.” The panels report to the rate-setting committee with recommendations due by year-end, though Warsh said in October that “some, but not all” would turn their homework in on time. The Fed’s task force page lists no ethics or recusal terms for the panels. Andreessen’s firm, Andreessen Horowitz, raised more than $15 billion in new funds in January, as venture firms raced to keep up with the AI boom. Andreessen is also Silicon Valley’s best-known accelerationist. His 2023 “Techno-Optimist Manifesto” declared, “We believe in accelerationism,” which he defined as “the conscious and deliberate propulsion of technological development.” It listed @BasedBeffJezos, the pseudonymous account behind the “effective accelerationism,” or e/acc, movement, first among its “patron saints,” and it named the enemy: “Our enemy is stagnation.” When OpenAI’s board fired Sam Altman a month later, Andreessen posted simply “E/acc!” This is the man who told the Fed that stagnation might win out over an AI-powered industrial revolution on Monday. The Fed’s three scenarios Warsh opened the day by laying out three “illustrative scenarios” Fed board staff have begun to evaluate. In one, AI lifts productivity, the gains are broadly shared and the economy stays close to full employment. In another, growth still runs above its long-term average, but automation pushes unemployment higher. In the third, AI “could disappoint after significant capital investment and stock market gains,” stocks fall, the economy slows and it eventually recovers “without the productivity gains.” All three turn on whether AI arrives in force. Andreessen’s version is duller: most of the economy just doesn’t let it in. He splits the economy in two. The “fast sectors,” like consumer electronics, media and commodity goods, take up new technology quickly, and “what those sectors all have in common is they have rapidly falling prices.” The “slow sectors”—health care, education, housing, and law and government—“are not legally allowed to have rapid change, like literally not.” The machine “cannot get an MD, cannot prescribe medication,” he said. “The machine cannot get admitted to the bar.” The slow sectors, in his telling, pair restricted supply with subsidized demand: you can’t easily build new housing or open new hospitals, and when voters revolt over the cost, Washington steps in with student loans and housing subsidies. “So, of course, prices can only go up.” Then he followed it to its end. As prices crash in the fast sectors, they shrink as a share of GDP, and the slow sectors take over. Health care, he said, “is already a fifth of US GDP and I don’t see why it doesn’t go to a fourth, a third and then half and then ultimately 80%.” (The government’s count is 18% in 2024, or $5.3 trillion, per CMS actuaries .) “You might interpret this as good news because it means the AI revolution is not going to, you know, destroy all the jobs or kill everybody,” he said. “You could also view this as very negative, which is productivity growth just simply may not grow very much. Economic growth just simply may not grow very much. We may just continue to stagnate.” Andreessen called himself “extremely optimistic,” saying that AI gives the country “a magic formula” and comparing it to being “handed this elixir to boost productivity growth.” But policy is a problem, he suggested. The decisions about what to do with AI, he said, “are going to matter actually way more than what the technology is capable of,” because without them “the technology will simply not get rolled out.” That landed in a room where, three hours earlier, Warsh had brought up “secular stagnation,” the 1930s worry that economists returned to after the financial crisis, and asked whether superintelligence “dramatically” changes that picture. A 60-year-old diagnosis Baumol, the late New York University and Princeton economist, worked this out in the 1960s, starting with the economics of the performing arts. A string quartet needs the same four musicians and the same playing time it did in Mozart’s day, but those musicians have to be paid wages set by an economy where factory workers keep getting more productive. So live music, and later education and medicine, keep getting more expensive relative to everything else, and keep taking a bigger share of spending. In his 2012 book, The Cost Disease , Baumol projected that if health costs kept growing at their recent pace, they would rise from 15% of the average person’s income in 2005 to 62% by 2105 . He was an optimist about it. “No matter how painful rising medical and educational bills may be, society can afford them ,” he wrote, because productivity elsewhere makes everyone richer. The real threat, he added, was “foolish public policy.” For Baumol, the disease was built into the work: you can’t speed up a string quartet. For Andreessen, it’s built into the law. That matters for the Fed, because an agency that sets interest rates can’t fix zoning boards or medical licensing. The economist who has done the most to bring Baumol into the AI debate was in the audience. Jones, who is on leave at Anthropic, stayed quiet because the company is preparing to go public, as Andreessen remarked to the crowd. events.title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him
events.summary: Published 17 November 2026, 16:27 GMT Jensen Huang said he would be "honoured" to return as the boss of tech giant Nvidia if the board asked him to, in his first public comments since his shock resignation. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely," Huang said on X, days after reports he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy. He said he had an "outpouring" of calls from company employees, investors and others calling for him to return as CEO of Nvidia. But, as the BBC reported on Monday, Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back to lead the company. The prospect of Huang returning at this point looks unlikely. The company's board is investigating his conduct , which includes an alleged affair with an Nvidia executive. The AI chip giant is set to report its financial results later on Tuesday, during which the company's interim chief executive, Collette Kress, may address the situation with Huang. Beyond the internal Nvidia investigation, Huang's affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing is set to see the billionaire questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead. The Nvidia founder said he had "made serious mistakes in my personal life". Nonetheless, Huang's statement appeared to show some hope he would be able to move past the major corporate scandal. Huang said people have continued to "reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics". "If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang added. Many technology executives in recent days have praised Huang's role in the artificial intelligence boom. A petition began circulating online over the weekend calling for his reinstatement at the company. Yet, by Monday, many executives were not openly calling for Huang's return. Brad Gerstner, a major tech investor who knows Huang personally and also holds a significant stake in Nvidia, last week wrote an open letter saying that Nvidia could consider Huang's reinstatement. On Monday, Gerstner said during an event hosted by Semafor that his letter had been misunderstood and the investigation into Huang's conduct needed to run its course. While Gerstner questioned the facts around Huang's departure, he added: "I don't know to what degree he misled the board. If I was on a board I would take that very seriously. Let's be clear no one is above the law." "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in the written statement, seen by CNBC. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said in the statement. In his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO last week, Jensen Huang struck a contrite tone, saying that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence contact. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in the written statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation." Huang said he had seen support from investors and employees and was willing to come back as CEO to help the company navigate "complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics." Here is the entire statement from Huang: Over the past week, I've been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life's work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation. Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours. events.title: Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents
events.summary: November 17, 2026 Category: Company News Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents Through the new AI Transparency Initiative, Microsoft is working with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to advance a common approach to AI transparency, security and governance across models and providers. Microsoft will also bring greater visibility into how AI models and agents interact with enterprise data across its products and services Microsoft Source | 5 minutes REDMOND, Wash. — Nov. 17, 2026 — Organizations can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they often cannot reconstruct what happened between a request and an outcome, making it difficult to independently verify model behavior. At Microsoft Ignite on Tuesday, Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella announced the next phase of Microsoft’s commitment to making AI safer: the AI Transparency Initiative, a collaborative effort with customers and partners to establish a common, open approach to security and governance across models and providers. The initiative reflects a simple principle: Greater AI autonomy requires greater transparency. “For security controls to be effective, every organization needs greater transparency into the model itself,” said Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security. “With this work, we will bring more transparency to all models. This is a critical step in making containment smarter and stronger, allowing us to better inform accountability and traceability.” Enterprises are connecting AI models to data, tools, credentials and infrastructure, enabling agents to take actions without human approval at every step. Existing controls can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they cannot see what happens within them or independently verify their accounts of their own behavior. This limits organizations’ ability to understand the context behind an agent’s actions. That evidence gap creates security, compliance, audit and accountability risk. Security teams need a new trust architecture to address the growing insider risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents. “As AI agents become more deeply integrated into enterprise operations, security teams need clear visibility into what those agents are accessing, what actions they’re taking and how those actions can be verified,” said Aanchal Gupta, Chief Security Officer, Adobe. “Building a common approach to AI transparency across the industry is essential to strengthening trust and helping organizations innovate with confidence while maintaining security and accountability.” From principles to practice The initiative has three parts. First, Microsoft will expand its participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s SI Agent Standards Initiative and draw on its research to develop open, industrywide standards for AI transparency, security and governance. Second, Microsoft is collaborating with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to help develop open standards for AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Third, Microsoft will incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot, enabling customers to use the resulting evidence with their security and compliance tools, whether from Microsoft or other providers. “Our clients want to move faster with AI, and they shouldn’t have to choose between innovation and safety,” said John Israel, Global Chief Information Security Officer, KPMG International. “Trust in AI requires transparency, explainability and responsible oversight. We’re proud to work with Microsoft on the AI Transparency Initiative to help establish open, industrywide standards that give organizations the visibility and control they need to deploy AI responsibly at scale.” Clear accountability Agents with access to data, tools and credentials carry the risk profile of a privileged insider but operate at machine speed and scale, making independent oversight essential. Accountability stays with the organization. When something consequential happens, leaders answer to customers, employees, boards, auditors and regulators. Blaming the AI isn’t an answer, and “trust the model” isn’t a control. The initiative is designed to work across models and providers, including closed and open-weight models, so developer teams can change or update the models powering their agents without compromising IT and security teams’ ability to govern them securely or compliance teams’ ability to audit their actions. “As organizations take the next step in their AI reinventions, they need a solid foundation of trust and confidence to build from,” said Harpreet Sidhu, global cybersecurity lead, Accenture. “Initiatives like this from Microsoft to take an open, industry-driven approach to AI transparency can help as we secure AI models and fit them with controls and governance. Accenture is proud to partner with Microsoft and other leaders in this space.”  See, verify, control Microsoft believes every organization should be able to see what AI systems access and do, verify their actions independently and control what they are permitted to do. See: Know what the AI was asked and authorized to do, which model and runtime were used, what data and tools it accessed, and what actions it took. Monitor agent activity and risk signals continuously against policies and thresholds. Verify: Agents cannot be the sole source of truth about their own behavior, and frontier models cannot be trusted to govern themselves. Evidence covering agent identity, delegated intent and actions should identify its source (the model, the runtime around it, or independent systems such as identity and policy) so model-reported signals can be checked against independently observed records. Organizations should be able to independently verify AI activity using their own security and compliance systems, without relying solely on the model provider’s account of its behavior. Control: Stay in charge of what AI is permitted to do. Clear evidence of each workflow’s purpose, owner, data and delegated authority helps organizations enforce their policies before consequential actions occur and reconstruct what happened during investigations, containment, recovery and audits. That evidence should stay with them when models and providers change. Organizations should retain control over what data their agents can access and how that access is governed, regardless of the model or provider. events.title: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before US House, says can resume CEO role
events.summary: Huang said he is ready to return as Nvidia CEO if the company’s board would like him back at the helm. Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, has agreed to appear in transcribed interviews with several United States House committees on December 1, even as he has said he would be “honored” to resume his job if the company’s board would like him to. On Tuesday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee announced the upcoming interviews, which will also include the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee. list 1 of 4 When tech founders leave, what happens to their companies? list 2 of 4 Megaspeed, firm at centre of Nvidia scandal, says Alice Huang left in 2025 list 3 of 4 Musk, Silicon Valley insiders urge Nvidia to restore Jensen Huang as CEO list 4 of 4 US moves to block China’s remote access to AI chips amid Nvidia scandal The US tech giant’s General Counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on December 2 . It was not immediately clear whether the men would attend in person or speak remotely. “We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Republican chairmen of the committees, Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, said in a statement. “The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.” Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday after reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, raised questions over exports of the company’s advanced AI chips to China. The lawmakers first called on Huang on November 5 to appear before the committees. That came amid initial reports from The New York Times that US authorities had started investigating Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which buys artificial intelligence (AI) chips from Nvidia, and with whom Huang has admitted to having an affair. US authorities have scrutinised Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Beijing gain access to advanced AI chips that are barred from shipment to China. The announcement comes as Huang has expressed a willingness to return to the company since resigning last Thursday. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a post on the social media platform X. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang’s comments come amid reports that tech industry insiders were pushing for his return to the company, alongside a petition with more than 177,000 people calling for his return. “The board’s decision now sits between a founder who has publicly asked for his job back, a shareholder base with the means to force the question, and an administration split between a president open to his return and a Treasury secretary demanding an outsider,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said in a note provided to Al Jazeera. At the same time, Nvidia has announced a board-level committee to oversee national security and export controls, marking the first major governance move since Huang resigned. The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former Goldman Sachs vice chair, Nvidia said. Directors Stephen Neal, former CEO of law firm Cooley, and John Dabiri, a Caltech professor, will also serve on the committee. US President Donald Trump welcomed the move, calling the launch of a national security initiative a good idea. Nvidia stock tumbled in midday trading on Tuesday. It was down more than 1.6 percent for the day, 11 percent over the previous five days and 29.2 percent over the previous month.

events.title: Voters broke with Democrats on ballot initiatives
events.summary: The News PALO ALTO, Calif. — Democrats swept Republicans on Nov. 3, but some of their party’s progressive ideas didn’t make it with them, as a host of liberal ballot initiatives failed and conservative proposals passed across the country. In California, where Republicans lost every major race by landslides, voters rejected a billionaire wealth tax, made it harder to create one, and likely killed a measure that would have piloted public financing of elections. In Colorado, a deep blue electorate voted to ban gender surgeries on minors by 4 points and to bar trans athletes’ participation in female sports by 5 points. A similar sports proposal prevailed by 12 points in Washington, even as Democrats padded their state legislative majorities. And in Iowa, where Gov.-elect Rob Sand led a Democratic comeback, voters endorsed a two-thirds legislative supermajority for any income tax increase. The success of some conservative ideas down the ballot — largely focused on taxes and social issues — gave some hope to Republicans after a hopeless election night. Voters rejected their party, but took multiple opportunities to oppose tax increases and roll back progressive social policies.Democrats were not taking that as advice to their party. Instead, they believe that opposition money and muddled messaging overwhelmed them, and they could win if they made another run at the ballot. “The margin was narrow enough that if we do more education with voters, we could significantly narrow it and win this,” said Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff at the union SEIU-UHW and a proponent of the California wealth tax. Saikat Chakrabarti, an unsuccessful House candidate who was a top contributor to the wealth tax campaign, agreed. “When you have nearly half a billion dollars against you, and they spend it to spread straight-up lies about an issue, it’s hard to win unless you can get your own message out,” Chakrabarti said. “The campaign had a winning issue,” he said, “but failed to get its own message out.” Different ways to lose The Proposition 40 campaign was heavily outspent, with some of California’s wealthiest residents funding its opposition. According to state campaign finance records , $152 million went into the “no” effort, compared to a bit more than $33 million for “yes.” Spending for and against Proposition 42, which bars new wealth taxes, was similarly lopsided —nearly $128 million for, and nearly $35 million against. Some of the funding to kill the wealth tax also came from members of the Democratic Party’s coalition, like Planned Parenthood, which advocated for a long-term funding source over the proposed one-time levy. Outgoing Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed it, as did Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, giving voters permission to support their ticket while voting against an idea backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. “Since it failed, I look forward to Gov. Newsom leading the fight by championing a national wealth tax, which he claimed he heavily supports,” said Chakrabati. The spending in other conservative down-ballot victories was more mixed. Supporters of Washington’s ban on transgender girls playing in girls sports out-spent opponents by a 3-1 margin. One of the coalition’s other priorities, which would have required schools to notify parents if their children identified as a different gender at school than at home, failed by 5 points. In Colorado, where transgender sports and medicine bans for minors passed narrowly, the “yes” side was heavily outspent by its opponents, the Families Not Politics coalition. “It’s unfortunate that this is an issue that’s been politicized,” said Erin Lee, the Democrat-turned-Independent whose Protect Kids Colorado coalition got the measures on the ballot. “Democrats have chosen this as a hill to die on, and Republicans have grabbed this as a political tool to wield. But when we started putting the team together, it became clear that this issue transcends the parties.” The Democratic Party in both blue states opposed the measures. Shasti Conrad, the chair of the Washington state Democratic Party, said that the sports measure “was very confusingly written,” while Republicans brought out their base to support it. Sources who worked to beat the measure told Semafor that their campaign was beset by bad planning and bad luck. The Gender Justice League, an LGBTQ+ rights group that was working against the measure, claimed to have “lost 80% of our foundation support and 35% of our government funding” as the Trump administration enforced its executive order on gender. The “no” campaign also resisted help from Third Way, the centrist Democratic think tank not beloved by progressives. Lanae Erickson, a Third Way vice president, shared research with campaigners in every state where a sports ban could appear on the ballot. “We found that most persuasive messages were around the gender checks component of the measure,” said Erickson, referring to language in the Washington initiative that required female athletes to prove their biological sex . Colorado campaigners used Third Way’s research; Washington campaigners opted not to until the campaign’s final weeks, when they ran some digital ads based on the information. Democrats in both states believed that their eventual messaging was not effective enough. “We had an extremely long ballot, and I think it was confusing to folks,” said Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo. “I think a lot of people didn’t know exactly what those provisions stood for. We have to make sure we’re protecting folks, and that we’re doing so clearly and specifically.” In no state where conservatives passed their preferred tax or social issue measures did Democrats say that their party’s position might change. Erickson, pointing to the margins in both Washington and Colorado, said that Third Way had been trying to find a winning path for trans rights for years, and that the results showed progress. “Funders kept telling us it’s an 80-20 issue, so they didn’t help us,” she said, referring to polling on trans participation in girls sports. “It’s not an 80-20 issue. But if the question is put to voters as the status quo or a blanket ban, people will say yes to the blanket ban.” David’s view Roughly speaking, there are two kinds of ballot measures – those designed to bring out voters for one of the major parties, and those designed to pass no matter what the parties do. For years, Democrats hoped that ballot measures raising the minimum wage would help them change the electorate. Two decades ago, Republicans thought the same about ballot measures that banned same-sex marriage. But in many cases, voters simply took the chance to separate their partisan preference from their issue preference. This is what happened on Nov. 3, when Republicans got no lift at all from measures that were most attractive to their hardcore voters. events.title: Microsoft and Salesforce Announce Copilotforce, Bringing Trusted Customer Context and Action into Microsoft AI Experiences
events.summary: November 17, 2026 Category: AI Microsoft and Salesforce Announce Copilotforce, Bringing Trusted Customer Context and Action into Microsoft AI Experiences Microsoft Source | 8 minutes New integrations connect Salesforce with Microsoft Copilot, Teams and Fabric, helping enterprises turn Salesforce customer insights into action while maintaining existing security and permissions. New two-way Zero Copy integrations between Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric enable organizations to securely query and analyze data across both platforms without maintaining duplicate datasets. Accenture is serving as design and implementation partner and pilot customer, deploying the integrations in its own global sales organization. REDMOND, Wash., and SAN FRANCISCO — Nov. 17, 2026 — Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ: MSFT) and Salesforce Inc. (NYSE: CRM) today announced Copilotforce, a new partnership that helps employees get more done in the tools they already use by bringing Salesforce customer context, business processes and actions into Microsoft Copilot and other AI-powered productivity experiences.   Unveiled at Microsoft Ignite, the partnership introduces new integrations across Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Fabric, including Salesforce in Copilot, a plugin available in public preview with 38+ prebuilt sales skills. Together, these capabilities help businesses move faster, reduce manual work and get more value from their existing technology investments — while maintaining the security, governance and permissions they already rely on.   Bringing Salesforce workflows together with conversations, meetings and documents in Microsoft 365 means less time spent moving between systems and more time on the work that matters. Salesforce in Copilot connects customer context with the work happening across the business so employees can make more informed decisions and take action without constantly switching applications. Microsoft Work IQ, the intelligence layer powering Copilot, provides relevant context from Teams meetings, Outlook emails and documents across SharePoint and OneDrive. Work IQ and Salesforce help sellers understand not only what’s recorded in CRM, but what’s happening across customer conversations and collaboration — and what needs to happen next.  Through authenticated Salesforce MCP access, sellers can securely retrieve customer information and take supported business actions within their existing Salesforce permissions. Salesforce continues to govern access and business actions, while Microsoft applies its existing enterprise compliance controls to communications and documents. Data, context and the apps where sellers work come to life in practical workflows across the sales cycle, including:  Grow Revenue . Use the Pipeline Review and Close Planning skills to decide which opportunities deserve attention and build a concrete path to signature. Customer priorities and deal context inform the proposals and business cases sellers develop in Word and PowerPoint, with clear owners, milestones and next steps.  Manage Risk. Connect Salesforce opportunity data with customer concerns raised in Outlook, escalations discussed in Teams and unresolved commitments. The Deal Review, Customer Health and Renewal Radar skills see beyond the recorded stage or renewal date to the customer concern in an Outlook thread, the escalation discussed in Teams or the unresolved commitment behind a stalled deal, helping sellers identify where to intervene.  Move faster. Turn customer conversations into follow-up drafts, internal recaps and proposed CRM activities using the Call Follow-Up skill. Sellers can review and confirm next steps instead of manually reconstructing conversations and updating multiple systems.    With Copilot as the front door to business process, Salesforce in Copilot allows organizations to bring together Salesforce data, workflows, agents and prebuilt skills from the systems they already rely on through Copilot’s open and interoperable platform.  “AI is only as powerful as the data and context that grounds it,” said Judson Althoff, CEO, Microsoft Commercial Business . “Bringing Salesforce customer data and sales skills together with the work context delivered by Work IQ in Microsoft Copilot allows our joint customers to unlock actionable insights across their core business applications. Copilotforce will give sales teams the intelligence they need to make faster, higher-confidence decisions while maintaining the governance and trust enterprises demand.”  “Through Copilotforce, we’re bringing Salesforce to the largest surface in enterprise software today, embedding trusted Salesforce context and intelligent sales workflows directly where sellers work,” said Miguel Milano, President & Chief Operating Officer, Salesforce . “By bringing together the #1 CRM with the #1 productivity surface, we’re transforming AI from a standalone tool into a powerful driver of productivity, smarter decisions and customer success.”  Expanding connection in the places people work   For many organizations, the work first starts in Microsoft Teams, where people share files, make decisions and hand work to each other. Sales Cloud in Teams, now available in pilot, brings Salesforce customer context directly into those conversations, so sellers can see pipeline and quota progress, get deal notifications and find briefing materials without leaving the place where decisions are already being made.   Across these Microsoft and Salesforce integrations, customer data remains protected at every boundary: Salesforce controls data access and governs supported business actions, while Microsoft ensures communications and documents adhere to existing enterprise compliance policies. Supported writeback actions to the CRM require explicit user confirmation and respect existing validation rules, so teams can act with confidence while customer records stay governed and auditable.  AI is only as useful as the context it can reach, and for many enterprises customer data lives in Salesforce while operational and financial data lives in Microsoft Fabric. Microsoft and Salesforce are bringing a two-way Zero Copy connection between Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric, so teams can work with fuller context across both platforms without building pipelines or maintaining duplicate datasets.  With Data Federation, now generally available, joint customers can now directly query and analyze supported Microsoft Fabric OneLake data within Salesforce Data 360. A service agent can see a customer’s recent purchases on their account, a marketer can build a segment from spending behavior and an AI agent can answer from current data, all without moving the source data out of Fabric. events.title: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks
events.summary: The U.S. has lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus. The director of the Pan American Health Organization made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission. It's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates help to fuel outbreaks that have sickened thousands and led to a string of preventable deaths. The U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus. The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission. In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones. "The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday. It's a devastating step backward for American public health , as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated. More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania , one in New York and two in Wisconsin . The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response efforts. The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action plan in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation. In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status. CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring. Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be " doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status. The decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence. CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities. Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated. The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission. The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.

events.title: As decision model use skyrockets, is customization the next frontier?
events.summary: In October, more than one in four requests on Vercel’s AI model router went to decision models, not LLMs — an enormous share of work for a kind of computerized intelligence that was invented only a month earlier. Decision models are LLMs that don’t produce output tokens; instead, they’re tuned to use their general intelligence to quickly and cheaply decide between preset options, while registering its level of confidence in the choice. They’re useful in production environments, where fast decisions can be more important than the reasoning provided by a slower and more expensive frontier model. TypeSafe became a $7.5 billion company after releasing its Jev family of models, which continues to dominate usage (at least where we can see metrics from services like OpenRouter, which handled more than 1.5 billion queries to TypeSafe’s models last week). However, it’s easy to make a decision model, and dozens were released in the wake of Jev. One Amazon engineer made one in a weekend, and soon every hyperscaler had its own option. On Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said that his company is rolling out its decision model, Microsoft-Decision-1.1, for wide use on Azure immediately. The action is happening on both ends of the ecosystem: Sqwish , a U.K.-based AI startup behind a decision model called kettei fat, announced a $3 million pre-seed round today. Co-founders Ushnish Sengupta and Federica Freddi, who met as Cambridge grad students, had been developing small LLMs when Jev arrived on the scene, and they realized their architectures could be repurposed as a powerful decision model. Data appears to be the key to a successful model in this category — TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida told TechCrunch that the hardest part of building Jev was finely calibrating its judgement using statistically-adjusted synthetic data. Sqwish, too, has been working with synthetic data, but its unique offering is built-in post-training tools that use a customer’s own data to improve the model’s judgement. “What makes us not a commodity, I think, is the fact that we are offering our customers the same power…they can keep uploading their production data, and just the same way that we trained our models, their models can also keep getting better at the tasks that they care about,” CEO Ushnish Sengupta told TechCrunch. Attempting to rank decision models is difficult; Sqwish’s “kettei fat” model has performed well on some benchmarks, but most builders of the technology say that the real proof is in the pudding: It’s generally simple for developers to sub in one model for another and see how it does in a specific context. “The benchmark is more of an invitation to try the model out, and then the continual tuning is the reason why they should stick to us,” Sengupta said. The Microsoft-Decision-1.1 model is also the result of the company carefully balancing across cost, latency, intelligence and calibration. Achint Srivastava, the engineering VP who led the project, agreed that too much focus on benchmarks is a mistake. “What we see is that ‘benchmaxed’ models fall flat under real enterprise usage very quickly,” Srivastava wrote in an email. “Our testing underscores just how challenging it is to deliver accuracy, reliability, speed and cost efficiency in a single model. Microsoft-Decision-1.1 and Jev are among the few that perform strongly across all four dimensions, even when evaluated on ‘held out’ or unseen benchmarks reflective of real use cases.” For startups like Sqwish, competition with hyperscalers and frontier labs is an opportunity. Freddi predicts that future systems will see so-called System One intelligence, like decision models, working in concert with System Two intelligence, like frontier LLMs. “Even in that future, System One is maybe a $10 billion, $50 billion [opportunity], and OpenAI is doing this IPO with you know $1 trillion, $2 trillion market value in mind,” she told TechCrunch. “This is all we care about; whereas for them, this is just a side project.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: My daughter made $100 selling homemade slime door-to-door. Two years later, she's running her own business.
events.summary: Karly Wrede's daughter started her own slime business. Courtesy of Karly Wrede Karly Wrede's daughter, Nora, made $100 selling homemade slime door-to-door in just 30 minutes. She turned her hobby into Bee Kind Slimes and has hosted 50 birthday parties this year. The business has taught her about money and confidence while bringing her closer to her mom. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Karly Wrede, whose daughter created Bee Kind Slimes. It has been edited for length and clarity. Two years ago, my daughter Nora wanted to buy something. She asked my husband and me for money. We gave her a list of chores she could do, and she asked us if she could sell her slime instead. She's always been a fan of making homemade slime. So she packed it all into a tote bag and started walking door to door in our neighborhood. We walked behind her. I was worried she wouldn't sell anything and thought we'd have to console her, but she came back 30 minutes later and had made $100. My husband and I were both like, "Wow, maybe this is a thing." And that's really when Bee Kind Slimes was born. At first, people bought from her because she was a sweet little girl at their doorstep, but then she asked if she could sell on social media . It kind of went from there - someone reached out and asked if we wanted to do a farmer's market; we got asked to do a holiday show; Nora started to sell her slime online, and she started doing birthday parties. Now we even teach other families how to start a slime business . We've just sort of kept saying yes, and it's been amazing to see what she can do in two years. My daughter designed her own slime cart At first, we were selling individual containers of slime , but it goes bad if you let it sit for too long. After a farmers market or show, we spent a lot of time emptying containers, reactivating the slime, and putting it all back in. I saw a collapsible charcuterie cart on Facebook Marketplace one day, and it gave us the idea to design a slime cart. Karly Wrede's daughter has her own business now called Bee Kind Slimes. Courtesy of Karly Wrede Now we can wheel it in and out of events and parties , and it's more of an experience. Kids love picking their own slime color and can choose charms and fake sprinkles to mix in. Every slime is unique, which makes it really fun and less work for us. She works 10-15 hours a week on her slime business Bee Kind Slimes is a part-time job for Nora at this point, involving making, packaging, and selling slime. Some days she takes the slime cart to back-to-back birthday parties. She's done 50 birthday parties this year. Right now, she works on the business about 15 hours a week, but during the holidays that will increase. Karly Wrede's daughter goes to birthday parties with her slime. Courtesy of Karly Wrede To make the slime, we tried making batches in a KitchenAid mixer at first, but they didn't work well. We went through five mixers in the first year. Nora applied for a grant through the Mason Makes Money Fund and received it, so we used the funds to buy an industrial mixer. Now she can make 10 times as much slime as she could in a small batch. She's still a kid, though. A big part of this is figuring out how to balance helping her learn and grow without burning her out, because this is something we get to do together for fun. My daughter has learned about money and so much more Before she started the business, Nora got $10 in allowance a week. She'd instantly go to the store to buy a toy. Now she gets paid $100 each month, but has to wait until the end of the month to get the money . It's really made her think about what she wants to spend her money on, and be proactive about thinking about saving. Now there are times when she doesn't spend much, or any, of her allowance. Karly Wrede says her daughter has learned so much about money. Courtesy of Karly Wrede I work for a nonprofit, and I also wanted to help her learn how to be generous, which she's been able to do in a variety of different ways. events.title: Chase Home Lending CEO says he plans to 'go on offense' against non-bank lenders
events.summary: Total mortgage demand, including both refinancing and new purchase loans, is now down just over 39% from a year ago, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Despite all that, Sean Grzebin, the CEO of Chase Home Lending, the nation's largest bank mortgage lender, said he's hiring and bent on increasing market share. Grzebin said he is looking to take back market share from non-bank lenders, who flourished after the financial crisis, when banks were cleaning up from thousands of failed home loans. A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. Mortgage rates shot higher again last week, after four straight weeks of declines. A hotter-than-expected monthly inflation report, coupled with new headlines from the Iran war, had the average rate on the 30-year fixed mortgage up 33 basis points to 7.5%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Total mortgage demand, including both refinancing and new purchase loans, is now down just over 39% from a year ago, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Despite all that, Sean Grzebin, the CEO of Chase Home Lending, the nation's largest bank mortgage lender, said he's hiring and bent on increasing market share. "For the last several years, we haven't really added a lot of salespeople," said Grzebin, who admits plainly that this is the worst market in decades. "We're going to hire a bunch of home lending advisors across the United States. We're going to focus on areas where we haven't had a lot of coverage, but there's a lot of mortgage activity and transactions taking place, and it really matches the expansion that we're having within the branch network on the consumer bank side." Grzebin said he is looking to take back market share from non-bank lenders, who flourished after the financial crisis, when banks were cleaning up from thousands of failed home loans. In August, JPMorganChase announced a 40% increase in home lending capital through 2035 to $750 billion. It will also hire 850 new lending agents. "I think the non-banks are all very formidable competitors. I think they've had an advantage while the banks were distracted through several decades," he said. "I think now you're starting to see the resurgence of the banks, and I think a lot of banks are actually going to grow their mortgage business through this." He said he expects to see continued consolidation in the mortgage market, especially as artificial intelligence penetrates the origination part of the business. Chase is investing heavily in AI for underwriting, he said. "We're hiring mainly in our sales functions because we think we can grow by adding people that have relationships with existing customers today, as well as them taking advantage of our branch network to help grow their business on one side," explained Grzebin. "And we think we can achieve all this growth without adding any incremental headcount in our operation because of the streamlining of the process that's happening with AI." Chase just ranked highest in mortgage origination satisfaction in J.D. Power's annual U.S. Mortgage Origination Satisfaction Study. While overall satisfaction was unchanged from 2025, just 58% of borrowers said they receive same-day responses from their lender when they ask questions, down from 62% a year ago. Fewer borrowers also say they have a main point of contact, down to 88% from 91% a year ago. "Borrowers appreciate being able to handle more of the mortgage process online, but they still want someone they can turn to when they have questions," said Bruce Gehrke, senior director of wealth and lending intelligence at J.D. Power in a release. "J.D. Power is seeing less recognition of updates and guidance that are important to keeping borrowers informed. Lenders have an opportunity to make the process more convenient while ensuring borrowers feel supported, especially as they approach closing." That appears to be what Chase is leaning into as so much of the process now moves to agentic AI. Grzebin said they focused first on the closing process, which customers said was most frustrating. Then they moved to digital tools. "There's a lot of opportunity there that we're going to be able to take advantage of in the next 12 to 24 months, just making it easier for customers to do more self-service through AI capabilities that we're going to also roll out over the next couple quarters, and so we are invested heavily in AI," he said. "We're going to see some real efficiency from it, and then on the sales side, adding salespeople, but then also figuring out a way to make them more productive.

events.title: Pedestal AI raises $4.7 million to agentify the supply chain
events.summary: Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly. On Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The company’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a plan that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world. The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal says the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments. In practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further. CEO Raj Aggarwal says contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.” Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic , launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics. As Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t. Perhaps most importantly, it’s the kind of problem that can have an immediate effect on a client’s bottom line, making it easy to justify the expense. “If you can get it right,” he told TechCrunch, “you can have really big impact.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .
