events.title: The Fed’s first close look at the AI buildout finds $3 trillion of AI commitments that aren’t on big tech’s balance sheet as debt
events.summary: The first time the Federal Reserve took a close look at how the AI buildout is being financed, it found more than $3 trillion of promises that don’t show up as debt. The Fed’s November Financial Stability Report includes a new section, “Leverage in the Data Center Buildout.” None of the report’s five previous editions, going back to 2024, had one. The closest, in November 2025, was about AI and algorithmic trading. The new section counts more than $1 trillion in leases that are signed but haven’t started yet, plus more than $2 trillion in take-or-pay contracts and residual value guarantees, at Amazon , Alphabet , Broadcom , Meta , Microsoft , Nvidia , and Oracle . Citing the report in a speech Monday in Milan, Fed Governor Michael Barr put the “potential maximum nominal value” of those obligations above $3 trillion. He said the seven largest AI firms’ on-balance-sheet debt “is expected to exceed $800 billion before year’s end.” The Fed notes the off-balance-sheet figures are undiscounted and “not directly comparable” with debt. Amazon, Alphabet, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle didn’t immediately respond to Fortune ’s requests for comment. Debt, not-yet-started leases, and guarantees and contract commitments at Amazon, Alphabet, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Oracle, through the second quarter of 2026. The Fed notes the off-balance-sheet figures are undiscounted and not directly comparable with debt. Federal Reserve Board, Financial Stability Report, November 2026 It raises the question of who takes the hit if AI demand comes in short. The report says the arrangements let companies with strong credit support weaker-credit projects “without having an immediate, direct effect on the balance sheets” of the big firms. Data-center developers use those leases to finance construction, and the riskier slices of the resulting debt are held by high-yield bond funds, life insurers, business development companies, and other private debt vehicles. The largest U.S. bank holding companies have “close to $1 trillion of exposure” to large technology firms, data-center developers, AI-related special purpose entities, private credit vehicles, and utilities, according to the Fed. Barr warned the opacity “can exacerbate selloffs when investor sentiment shifts, as it is hard to know where risk resides.” Separately, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said Monday Board staff have started modeling AI scenarios , from a growth boom to an AI disappointment. The borrowing caught up fast Debt issuance tied to advanced computing rose to more than $680 billion by October, the Fed found, about five times the $130 billion issued in all of 2023. Advanced computing’s share of nonfinancial investment-grade corporate debt issuance went from less than 6% in 2023 to about 31% this year. The Fed estimates outstanding public debt tied to advanced computing at more than $1.1 trillion and says private credit deals make the full total harder to measure. Market players are worried, too. The Fed surveyed 23 contacts at broker-dealers, banks, investment funds, and advisory firms in September and October, and 87% named AI as a salient risk to the financial system, up from 50% in the May survey. A broad correction in risk assets came next, at 52%. The report reflects data through Oct. 28, two weeks before Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned . Nvidia’s guarantees, without Huang Huang resigned Nov. 12 as president, CEO, and board member of Nvidia, and CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. Nvidia reports third-quarter results after the close today. Analysts expect revenue of about $108 billion, CoinDesk reported , and said Kress “faces questions about demand, financing commitments, and China exposure.” Nvidia’s filings show the kind of commitments the Fed is counting. In August, the chipmaker agreed to residual value guarantees with SB Energy, the landlord for an AI campus in Pike County, Ohio, where an OpenAI affiliate will be the tenant on about 4.25 gigawatts of IT load. If OpenAI goes insolvent and defaults on a lease, or fails to make payments, Nvidia generally covers the gap between the lease’s guaranteed minimum value and what’s recovered. Its total obligation is “cumulatively capped at $105 billion” for the initial commitment, subject to conditions that include the sites being ready for service, expected beginning in 2028. OpenAI has agreed to reimburse Nvidia for anything it pays. Separately, Nvidia’s latest quarterly filing lists $3.5 billion in guarantees on AI cloud partners’ data center leases as of July 26, against which those partners have put $712 million in escrow. Nvidia, SB Energy and OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Barr said such guarantees “represent the degree to which hyperscalers and GPU producers might absorb losses” if borrowers default. Telecom equipment makers tried a smaller version of this during the dot-com boom. Lucent committed $5.7 billion in credit to customers in 2000, eWeek reported at the time. One of those customers, Winstar, had a $2 billion vendor financing deal with Lucent. It filed for bankruptcy in April 2001 and sued Lucent for $10 billion. Four years later, a bankruptcy judge ordered Lucent to pay $244 million . The banks have a cushion, mostly Barr isn’t predicting a bank blowup. “Given the still-limited amount of debt backing the current boom, I’m less concerned about direct losses,” he said. The Fed calls the banking system “sound and resilient, with high regulatory capital ratios.” The New York Fed’s annual check on bank vulnerability , published Nov. 12, shows some strain. Researchers there found a measure of banks’ liquidity stress is at “a level not seen since 2014.” In a scenario replaying 2022’s rate shock, banks would face a $151.1 billion capital gap, little changed from a year earlier. Three of its four measures show rising vulnerability. That analysis uses data through June and doesn’t look at AI exposure specifically. Fortune reported in June the Bank for International Settlements found direct lending funds had quadrupled their lending to AI and IT over five years. The Fed’s first look ends on a limit to what it can see. The biggest tech firms “may absorb losses in the event of a future downturn,” the report says, but their economic exposure to one “may be substantially larger than suggested by their on-balance-sheet liabilities.” Its next report is due in the spring. events.title: Bupa GP clinic urged doctors to bill costly Medicare items to lift revenue
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Doctors and Medical Professionals A Bupa clinic encouraged doctors to increase revenue by billing extra Medicare items. ( ABC News: Nic MacBean ) Bupa emailed GPs working at one of its clinics, encouraging increased billing of chronic condition management plans, which cost more than standard appointments. Senior doctors say they are concerned corporatised GP practices are prioritising profit over patient care, but Bupa defended the email. The Department of Health says it is spending $147 million over four years to review the industry and improve compliance. A GP clinic operated by health insurance giant Bupa encouraged doctors to lift their billing of more costly Medicare items. The ABC has obtained an email from a Bupa clinic to its GPs in June, which told doctors to ensure "revenue is increasing". The email asked doctors to do this by increasing the bookings of patients for costly Medicare checks known as "chronic condition management plans" (CCMPs). It further encouraged doctors to re-book patients, if they were eligible for further checks but Medicare rules prevented them from being claimed on the same day. CCMPs are personalised plans written by GPs, designed to create a structure to improve outcomes for people struggling with complex health conditions. The plans can be used for conditions ranging from eczema to heart disease, and while often beneficial to patients, they may not be essential for everyone with a chronic condition. The Medicare schedule fee for a GP to prepare a CCMP is $160.60, compared to $87.10 for a standard GP appointment lasting at least 20 minutes. The federal government's spending on the plans is rising rapidly and it is now spending nearly $1.3 billion a year on these chronic care plans out of the $35 billion Medicare budget. 'Need to explain' why items not billed In the email, Bupa told doctors their appointment books were closely scrutinised each day through the popular software portal Cubiko, for "possible service opportunities", and notes were left about what could be billed. Bupa operates 33 medical centres. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The booking software includes a specific function to check for chances to bill patients for 'possible service opportunities', including the costly chronic care plans. The email also detailed how the "ops team" had tasked the practice managers with "ensuring revenue is increasing by ensuring there is an uptick in billings of HA [health assessments]". Cubiko spruiks that its "QuickCheck" function can help identify opportunities for billing patients more Medicare items. ( ABC News: Screenshot ) Bupa's email then went on to list the Medicare item numbers for these health assessments, including chronic condition management plans and a nurse item. GPs were reminded that practice managers need to "ensure" an increase in patients being charged for these more expensive Medicare items, otherwise practice managers "need to explain why these are not being billed". In a statement, Bupa said the email was sent at one clinic and was an attempt to remind doctors to consider preventative care. "Patient needs, clinical judgement and compliance with Medicare requirements always come first," it said. Bupa said practice managers provide "administrative support to our doctors. Patient needs, clinical judgement, and compliance with Medicare requirements always come first and we reinforce this through ongoing guidance and training". Do you know more? Share it with us here . If GPs coerced, 'it has to be stopped' Health economist Terry Barnes was a senior adviser to two health ministers in the Howard government. He told the ABC he was not surprised by Bupa's email, and it was a window into how much corporate owners of GP clinics "called the shots". Terry Barnes says optional extras like chronic condition management plans should not become mandatory Medicare billings. ( ABC News: Billy Draper ) "If corporates are putting pressure on their doctors to order health assessments or any other type of extra service, and the optional extras become mandatory, then there is a real problem there," he said. "If they are actually putting pressure on the doctors, coercing them internally, to behave in a certain way in relation to billing services and generating services then that has to be stopped." Are private health insurers moving to US-style model? Increasing partnerships among health insurers, GP centres, and telehealth services raise concerns about a potential two-tier system in which privately insured patients have more affordable access to GP consultations.

Meanwhile, only 130 wallets appeared on the event’s leaderboard, suggesting that not every dinner seat may be filled.  Like previous TRUMP dinners, the event scheduled for Nov. 22 at the president’s golf club outside Washington, D.C., offers crypto investors a chance to compete for invitations to an event featuring Trump himself. The more TRUMP tokens they buy and hold, the better their chances of securing a seat, while the highest-ranked holders can earn VIP access. But while announcements of the previous two events sent the price of TRUMP soaring roughly 60%, the latest gala has failed to spark a similar rally. The token briefly jumped 9% when the dinner was announced on Sept. 30, only to return to its previous trading range of roughly $2 within 24 hours. Since then, it has continued to decline. events.title: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
events.summary: Flight delays are becoming more common, causing financial and emotional stress for travelers CHICAGO -- New airline tickets: $300. Hours waiting for luggage: four. And the topper: a four-hour Uber ride from Detroit to Chicago that cost $400. Call it outage math, a hellish calculation spawned by ever-more-common flight delays. This one was part of Angelina and Kyle Phoenix's anniversary trip to Chicago. On Friday, they flew from Jacksonville, Florida, into the maw of the Great Ground Stoppage of 2026 with as many as a million other travelers. Instantly, the financial and emotional toll of the four-hour flight outage radiated outward from the airports as everyone involved scrambled for costly workarounds to a crisis no one expected, can fully explain or wants to pay for. Emergency child care. Outrageous taxi ride fees. Rebooked tickets, lost vacation rentals and little idea what expenses might be reimbursed. But beyond finances, travelers told The Associated Press on Monday, perhaps the most consequential cost is also the most intimate: Stress and grief over time lost — a cumulative toll that is generally not, as customer service might say, eligible for reimbursement. Kyle Phoenix got a whiff of it more than 12 hours and hundreds of dollars of unexpected expenses into the couple’s journey, as he watched chaos unfold in the baggage claim area of Detroit airport. Officials, he noticed, had stopped announcing which canceled flights would disgorge checked baggage onto which turnstiles. Answers were hard to come by. That made decisions about what to do next increasingly difficult. “A lot of confusion, a lot of scrambling from a lot of people,” Kyle recalls of the scene. “I think that was probably the roughest part, not knowing anything.” When the couple finally retrieved their luggage at midnight, the $400 Uber ride began to look like the best option. They forfeited their rebooked flight — as well as a hotel room they would have stayed in for a few hours — and embarked on the four-hour ride to Chicago. “We just took the loss,” Angelina Phoenix said. Dread lingers around such events because they're getting more commonplace, with no end in sight. Even as travelers spoke to the AP about Friday's ground stop, United Airlines suffered a malfunction and halted its flights for 90 minutes. Several top U.S. banks reported significant slowdowns. And that was after AI chaos and Microsoft’s global meltdown just a few days earlier. Ahead loomed the busy Thanksgiving travel week, when TSA agents typically screen more than 2 million passengers nationwide. It was enough to make any thinking person ask: Could everything be broken? And it forced humanity to reckon once again with the fragility of the systems that anchor modern life. Delays are accelerating faster than the increase of scheduled passenger flights since the COVID-19 pandemic, the International Air Transport Association reported in July. Between 2015 and 2025, delays affecting scheduled passenger flights generated about $10.9 billion in costs for airlines and travelers, with sharp increases in holdups starting in 2021. The issues are costing travelers time, which even the Federal Aviation Administration agrees is worth money. Federal guidance issued a decade ago valued airline passengers’ time at $47.10 an hour, expressed in 2015 dollars. That's about $66 an hour today. The figure accounted for travel time that would otherwise be available for work or leisure. More recently, an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond estimated that last year’s 43-day federal government shutdown caused roughly 1 million additional hours of passenger delays at six airports. Economist Russell Wong calculated the lost time’s value at $66 million, based on metro area wage data and the higher-than-average incomes of people who take flights. Wong excluded canceled flights. events.title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
events.summary: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source. Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River . And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.  Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September. Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.  Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.  The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.  But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study . Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.  Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA. El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions. Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

events.title: Inspiring FOSS project Crosspoint Reader has lessons about tech, communities, and LLMs
events.summary: The Ubuntu Summit isn't all about Ubuntu, or even Linux. The second day opened with a talk from CrossPoint Reader project lead Justin Mitchell, with both good and bad news for all kinds of FOSS. The talk, EPUBs, ESP32s, and Everyone's A Developer Now , was all about a FOSS project that isn't Linux-based – because the devices it targets are much too small to run even the smallest, most cut-down distro. Recently, a new generation of roughly credit-card sized ebook readers has been thriving. Some have integral magnets, which let them cling to the back of iPhones – or to models with magnetically attached wireless chargers, anyway. The idea is that instead of waking your phone and doom-scrolling, you flip it over and read a book. They are bringing about what Mitchell calls "the Tiktok-ification of reading." Many of them, though, come from their various manufacturers significantly limited by their original OSes. The strong sales are linked to the availability of free, open-source, cross-platform alternative firmware, which removes many of the restrictions that the devices ship with. For most of them, that means Crosspoint Reader . Some devices are now shipping, new, with versions of Crosspoint Reader. This runs on multiple different models of compact e-readers, and this small community project has seen impressively widespread adoption: over 300,000 installations. Early in his talk, project lead Mitchell mentioned more than 1,600 forks on GitHub, but at the time of writing, that's up to 2,300 and counting. He estimates nearly half a million users. This kind of success forced Crosspoint Reader to change from being FOSS code to a product. A peripheral example is the Brick Club List , a list of what versions work with what devices – an Excel spreadsheet that grew into a website. If you haven't been paying attention, you may not have noticed just how much e-readers have shrunk – in size and in cost – in the last few years. The Reg FOSS desk first noticed this trend in 2024, when we read about the smartphone-sized Onyx Palma , which sold for around $300 (about £225). As it happens, this was a decade after The Register first looked at one of Boox's devices . Mini e-readers – and their prices – have continued shrinking since. The $99 (£75) Xteink X4 Classic has a 4.- inch (10.9 cm) screen, and the $79 (£59) Xteink X3 is even smaller: it's the size of a credit card, with a 3.7-inch (9.4 cm) screen. As a result of their strong sales, there are now multiple similar devices on sale, such as the Boox Picco . The project's GitHub page lists 11 devices it currently supports, all of which are based around the ESP32-C3 system on a chip. The ESP32-C series chips are more powerful than the earlier models of ESP32 microcontrollers: they have a single RISC-V core, but running in the low hundreds of MHz and with some 400 kB of RAM, of which about 380 kB is available. It's very little space, but enough to have fun. Mitchell talked about some of the problems of being a FOSS project that is used by nearly half a million non-techie people. For many of Crosspoint Reader's users, it's the first time they have ever used open source. Some want tech support. Many demand features that can't fit into these tiny devices. Even when the requests are modest and feasible, such a large user base means that people want a wide range of functionality – and thanks to inexpensive cloud LLMs, even totally non-technical users can try to add new functions for themselves. The result is multiple code submissions every day. Many might fit on their own, but it's impossible to fit them all in. So many queries and submissions puts considerable stress on the volunteer maintainers. Mitchell mentioned a possibility that they – and we – had never dreamed of: that of pull requests (GitHub parlance for code submissions) from people using such extensive automation that the submitters don’t realize that they’re sending them. One submitter sent 10,000 pull requests in a single month. The problems aren't just technical, or workload-related: there's also a delicate balance of how to refuse well-intentioned and technologically viable submissions that just won't fit for non-technical reasons, such as being too niche for the typical use-case of a sub-£60 gadget. The problem is that this FOSS firmware is making these cheap gadgets so much more useful that re-flashing them is an implicit part of the purchase. That introduces all kinds of unexpected side-effects, for the users and for the developers. Crosspoint Reader is a microcosm of the rapid growth of Linux and FOSS in general – and a taste of what will happen if it ever goes truly mainstream with mass-market consumers. One of his "what I got wrong about this job" points we particularly liked was: “The scarce resource isn’t code. We have more code than we know what to do with." Instead, it's… "Judgement. Trust. Responsibility." There are lessons for the whole IT industry in there, we reckon. Even for the biggest players . In the meantime, though, these tiny cheap e-readers are an interesting new thing. As Mitchell put it, paraphrasing The Atlantic , they're: "Fun in a way gadgets haven’t been for a long time." Just being fun is a goal that is far too often forgotten… Especially in FOSS. ®

events.title: ‘What if the input isn’t the news? What if the input is you?’ Bill Gross gave away 1.2 million AI business ideas for free—the Fortune 500 is next
events.summary: A month ago, Idealab founder Bill Gross gave away 1.2 million AI-generated business ideas for free. Now he wants Fortune 500 companies to pay $250,000 a year to run the same system on their own patents. “What if the input isn’t the news? What if the input is you?” Gross told executives at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, in a session sponsored by Idealab.ai. He meant their patents, trade secrets and “all the things that you’ve shelved inside of your company.” Idealab plans to license the full system to companies at $250,000 a year, he said, and is offering five companies a one-year pilot for $25,000. The pitch is aimed at a real problem: big companies hold a lot of patents that never become products. Large firms’ patents are tied to new product launches “far less so” than smaller firms’, according to research from Kellogg’s Sara Moreira and economists at Yale and the Atlanta Fed, which matched about 1.4 million products to patents. Moreira’s explanation complicates Gross’s pitch, though: big companies often use patents as a “defensive tool” to block competitors rather than to launch anything. Some of that shelved R&D is on the shelf on purpose. The Caltech test Gross launched Idealab.ai in October after feeding an AI system news stories going back to 2000, every patent since 1980, product recalls, and complaints on Reddit and X, along with his own 31 methods for coming up with business ideas. He said it came back with 1.2 million ideas after about a month and roughly $1 million in AI costs, and that 131,000 people in 202 countries have searched them since launch. To test the corporate version, Gross went to Caltech. He is a Caltech alumnus and trustee, and he said on stage that he sits on its board. He asked the tech-transfer office for four patents. “They said, ‘Why just four? We’ll give you all 9,000,’” he said. He said the system ran all 9,978 and generated 3,867 businesses that Caltech “should either build or license.” For scale, Caltech’s tech-transfer office signed 59 licenses and options and helped form eight startups in fiscal 2024, according to its annual report . For the forum, Idealab ran the public patents of 113 attending companies through the system and printed each a sheet of business ideas “that you’re not already doing,” Gross said. “Now that’s a teaser,” he said. “What we really want to do is work with you and have you give us the things that aren’t public.” The $250,000 corporate license is meant to pay for the free public version. “Big companies with 100 billion dollar year R and D budgets will pay for it, and that way we can give it away free to entrepreneurs,” he said. Gross said he modeled Idealab, founded in 1996, on Thomas Edison’s lab, and quoted Edison: “I find out what the world needs, then I go ahead and try to invent it.” The test now is whether a corporate R&D department, which has had decades to find out what the world needs from its own patents, will pay Gross $250,000 to tell it. events.title: US Federal Reserve’s Lisa Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing
events.summary: US President Donald Trump has sought to fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook since August 2025. Lisa Cook has refused to attend a White House hearing on claims she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, saying the process is unfair and aimed at a fixed outcome. Her lawyer said she has “no legal obligation” to join what he called a “facade” to fire her, and warned it could damage the Federal Reserve’s independence. The dispute adds to Trump’s push to remove Cook since August 2025, while the Supreme Court has already blocked her firing during the legal fight. WASHINGTON – Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear in December before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome. The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook’s lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration initially demanded for Nov 6. Trump administration officials have demanded that Cook appear before the committee to address allegations she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed’s board of governors, a charge she denies. President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president’s efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed’s independence and reflect Trump’s desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs. “Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing – and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook’s lawyer, wrote in a letter released on Nov 17 to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a facade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.” In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump administration from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that “the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design.” AP

events.title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return to Nvidia as CEO
events.summary: Huang resigned last week over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple employees who reported to him Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO in his first remarks since resigning from the company Thursday. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC . Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang, according to reports from the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal. However, the company expects to report its quarterly earnings after market close Tuesday , after which it may face questions from analysts and investors about Huang’s future there. The CEO founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran the company until last week, when he resigned over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple employees who reported to him. Huang and Nvidia initially said the executive’s dealings with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean datacenter firm Megaspeed and a suspected spy, were a routine customer relationship. However, Huang disclosed the affair in an email to employees, and the board announced an investigation into its national security implications . Nvidia’s board has also created a committee to oversee exports and national security issues. The US government confirmed on Tuesday morning that the commerce and justice departments have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024. Though the government has never officially restricted sales and exports to Megaspeed, Nvidia put Megaspeed on an internal “no sell” list in June 2025 after the commerce department requested its records of any sales to Megaspeed, according to a statement from the department. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting US advanced AI chips to Chinese firms in potential violation of export restrictions. Huang’s full statement is published below. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO as supporters campaign for comeback Jensen Huang said he had not lived up to Nvidia's standards and he owned his mistakes. ( AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson ) Jensen Huang says he "would be honoured" to return as Nvidia CEO if the AI chipmaker's board decides to have him back. It his first comments since resigning under pressure over his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Mr Huang said he had been humbled by an "outpouring" of calls for his comeback. "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," he said in a statement. The statement follows a campaign, backed by tech titans including Elon Musk, calling for Mr Huang's reinstatement . According to a counter on the official "Stand with Jensen" website, more than 190,000 people have signed an open letter demanding the board re-employ him. Mr Huang said he had seen an "outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO". On Monday, local time, US President Donald Trump said he "would certainly not mind seeing" Mr Huang come back to the role. "I think he learned a big lesson," Mr Trump told reporters as he prepared to depart for a trip to Asia . The US has moved to tighten controls designed to prevent chip-smuggling in the wake of the scandal. Ms Huang worked for a company that US authorities believe may have circumvented those controls to send Nvidia's most powerful AI chips into China, according to multiple reports. Chinese economic espionage is in the spotlight after the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, and former intelligence officials say the US is not doing enough to combat it. Several congressional committees are investigating. Mr Huang has agreed to answer questions before Congress on December 1, according to a statement from the House Committee on Foreign Affairs. "The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous PRC [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," said the chairs of the committees, which also include the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee. The Nvidia board has not officially commented on the calls for Mr Huang to return, but Reuters and other news agencies yesterday reported the board was not considering asking Mr Huang to come back . events.title: Iraqi PM heads to Lebanon amid push to explore oil routes beyond Hormuz
events.summary: Ali al-Zaidi’s talks expected to include proposed project linking Tripoli in Lebanon to Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline. Beirut, Lebanon – Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is set to visit Lebanon on his latest regional visit aimed at boosting economic cooperation amid the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran. Al-Zaidi will hold a series of high-level meetings in Beirut, including with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri. High on the agenda of Wednesday’s talks will be strengthening bilateral trade, customs exemption deals and coordination on security and countering drug trafficking. Diversifying oil export routes via a pipeline linking the Iraqi city of Kirkuk, through Syria’s Mediterranean port of Baniyas, to Tripoli in northern Lebanon, is also expected to be discussed. The proposed project is aimed at potentially bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, a key energy waterway that has been severely disrupted since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February. “After the war in Iran and the story of Hormuz and exports in the Gulf, [Iraq] is looking for alternative routes to diversify their export routes,” Walid Marrouch, professor of economics at the Lebanese American University in Beirut, told Al Jazeera. Iraq’s crude oil exports were badly hit following the start of the Iran war and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world’s energy passes in peacetime. Last month, Iraq’s Ministry of Oil said crude oil exports reached about 2.7 million barrels per day (bpd), up from some 200,000 bpd in May. Before the war, Iraq was exporting about 3.5 million bpd. The increase has been boosted by the resumption of oil pumping this week through the Iraqi-Turkish pipeline at an initial capacity of 120,000 bpd. Still, Iraq has been looking for alternatives to export its crude oil, primarily through Syria, which was previously difficult due to international sanctions under the leadership of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled in late 2024. Tamer Badawi, an associate fellow with the Royal United Services Institute, said al-Zaidi’s visit to Lebanon was likely to be informed by US envoy Tom Barrack’s “efforts to diversify Iraq’s oil export routes across the region, particularly through Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Lebanon”. He added: “The broader ambition is to develop alternative export corridors connecting Iraq’s oil infrastructure to regional networks.” One of the potential proposed alternatives is Tripoli, in northern Lebanon. The impoverished city has emerged as an option because of the long-defunct pipeline from Kirkuk and a local refinery that in 1940 filtered 21,000 bpd of crude oil from Iraq, according to the Lebanese Directorate General of Oil. The refinery shut down in 1992, shortly after the end of the 15-year Lebanese Civil War in 1990. Industry insiders say Tripoli’s oil infrastructure has three legacy lines with a historical peak capacity of 900,000 bpd. While it would need to be repaired and renovated, a report this year by the Basil Fuleihan Institute of Finance (BFIF), an autonomous agency under the tutelage of Lebanon’s Finance Ministry, said “the terminal infrastructure remains a goldmine of latent capacity” with a moderate flow scenario of 300,000 to 500,000 bpd that could gain Lebanon annual revenues in the region of $80m to $275m. The revenues could be a boon to the Lebanese economy, which has been beset by a complex economic and banking crisis since 2019 that has seen its currency lose more than 90 percent of its value and the majority of its population living in poverty. Al-Zaidi’s trip to Beirut comes weeks after he met with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus. During the visit, the two countries signed a cooperation agreement to rehabilitate the pipeline running from Kirkuk to Baniyas, in a project to be carried out by US energy giant Chevron. “Upon rehabilitation, this groundbreaking project will have an initial transport capacity of 2 million barrels per day of crude oil,” the US Department of State said in a statement at the time. Experts said al-Zaidi’s visit on Wednesday was a big opportunity for Lebanon to ensure its place in a prospective tripartite agreement with Syria and Iraq – but warned that if Lebanese officials failed to act, the country could be left behind. “Lebanon can benefit, but if Lebanon does not get a seat at the table, it [could be circumvented] because Iraq can already reach the sea from Syria,” said Marrouch. Before reaching Tripoli, Iraqi crude oil would have to pass through some 250km (155 miles) of Syrian territory. Syria also has its own ports in Tartous and Latakia, with a smaller port in Banias. According to BFIF, Syria is set up to handle about 350,000 to 500,000 bpd, between refineries at Banias and Homs, “a direct Mediterranean outlet that circumvents both the Suez Canal and the Strait of Hormuz”.

events.title: Religious ruling revives memories in Israel of Rabin assassination
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? Hostility towards Palestinian participation in Israel’s government fuels fears of far-right political violence. As negotiations to form Israel’s next government continue, tensions across Israel have risen to an unprecedented high, evoking memories of the period leading up to the 1995 assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin . In a letter published last week, Rabbi Gedalia Axelrod, a former head of Haifa’s rabbinical court, invoked a principle in Jewish religious law known as din rodef, issuing a religious ruling that could be used to justify the killing of politicians accused of facilitating a government backed by Arab-led parties. The same principle was invoked by Yigal Amir to justify his killing of Rabin because he had signed the Oslo Accords with the Palestinians. list 1 of 4 Is Israel’s Eisenkot bloc less right wing than Netanyahu? list 2 of 4 Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of attempted ‘coup’ list 3 of 4 Will Netanyahu lose this time? list 4 of 4 As Knesset readies for new speaker, Israeli opposition holds powerful role “The Torah obliges me,” Axelrod later told the Israeli news website Walla. “I knew it was not easy, but if the Torah obliges, then we go. We are Jews, we make sacrifices.” Axelrod’s ruling has prompted widespread condemnation and demands for a criminal investigation. The Chabad Hasidic movement that Axelrod belongs to has also distanced itself from his remarks. Twenty former senior Israeli security, military and public figures, including former heads of the country’s intelligence agencies, have called on the authorities to investigate Axelrod. Separately, left-wing member of parliament Ofer Cassif and his fellow lawmaker Michal Rozin have also demanded an investigation, warning of the growing risk of political violence taking hold across Israel. The controversy comes after Israel’s parliamentary election in late October, in which parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel won 19 of the parliament’s 120 seats. Parties opposed to caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hold a majority in parliament, but several members of the opposition have refused to cooperate with the Arab parties. For many in Israel, mention of din rodef , or the “law of the pursuer”, immediately evokes memories of the tensions and incitement that led up to Rabin’s killing on November 4, 1995. Rabin’s widow, Leah, directly accused Netanyahu – who was then the leader of the opposition – of helping to foster that climate of hostility. She pointed to his presence at a rally a month before the assassination, at which protesters displayed an effigy of her husband dressed in a Nazi uniform. Amir justified his assassination of Rabin by arguing that the prime minister’s pursuit of the Oslo Accords endangered Jewish lives, echoing the reasoning now employed by Rabbi Axelrod, who claims that an alliance with an Arab-led party would place Jewish lives at risk. This conflation of politics and religion, while hardly unique to Israel, amounted to “political theology”, Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani explained. “By political theology, I mean the way ideas about God, sacred authority and the chosen people shape political life,” he said of the rules governing who is entitled to rule, who is allowed to belong and whose life must be protected. “Sometimes these ideas are explicit, as in a rabbi invoking divine law against an elected politician. But they can also survive in apparently secular ideas about the nation, sovereignty and historical destiny.” “Someone who accepts Arab participation in government can then be portrayed as betraying a sacred community, and violence against them can become, in the eyes of a believer, a religious duty,” he said of the rationale behind Axelrod’s ruling. “The threat of political violence is really high,” Cassif told Al Jazeera. “We all remember what happened in 1995 and the atmosphere that preceded Rabin’s assassination. This time it’s worse. Then it was just a few extremists on the fringe; now it’s the mainstream. They’re being openly encouraged by a prime minister who, I think, is ready to consider or do anything to hold on to power.” Cassif also pointed to far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s own role in the atmosphere of incitement before Rabin’s killing. In October 1995, the month before the assassination, Ben-Gvir was filmed brandishing the hood ornament torn from the prime minister’s car, telling journalists, “We got to his car, and we’ll get to him, too.” Fears of far-right violence have grown as coalition negotiations have dragged on. Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party have repeatedly sought to vilify Arab-led parties, both in their campaign ahead of the October 27 election and in their statements since. Netanyahu has accused the parties of allying with foreign and hostile powers.

events.title: Proton’s Lumo, a privacy-focused alternative to ChatGPT and Claude, arrives on desktop
events.summary: Proton , the privacy-focused tech company offering alternatives to Google’s and Microsoft’s tools for email, productivity apps, password management, cloud storage, and more, is now bringing its AI app Lumo to personal computers. On Tuesday, the company launched Lumo Desktop for Windows, macOS, and Linux, allowing users to leverage its AI to carry out local tasks on their computer involving connected apps, personal files, and other automations. The app is designed to offer users more control over their personal data, as consumer AI technology becomes focused more on AI agents that can perform tasks on users’ behalf, rather than just answering questions. Already, the major model makers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others, offer desktop tools for working with their AI technologies, but doing so invites increased risk to users’ personal data . Only this week, for instance, Apple announced it was addressing those privacy concerns with tightened security settings for apps that request Full Disk Access, as the AI desktop apps do. Proton’s idea is to offer a set of tools that let its AI access connected apps, files, and folders and automate tasks, but with more personalization over how much access the AI has. The company says users can choose which actions the AI agent takes that will need to request their approval, and it vows that the conversations and information from connected apps and files are never used to serve personalized ads or train AI models. The new app includes a variety of connectors that support local tools, like file-system access, shell execution, and browser content fetching, as well as Proton’s email app and other third-party services, including Confluence, Dropbox, and Jira. The connectors also support local and remote MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, which AI agents use to access external data sources. Proton says that users can decide for each connector which actions Lumo can perform automatically, which require approval, and which are blocked entirely. Users can also turn individual tools off from the Tools menu in their conversation. In addition, users can set up their own scheduled tasks, where each has its own set of permissions, in terms of what can be handled automatically and what requires approval. Proton notes that it uses encryption to ensure that only users can read their chat history, not the company. The company also says it keeps no server-side logs, and the limited data it does store is protected under Swiss privacy law. The data is hosted on European infrastructure, outside the scope of the U.S. CLOUD Act , which specifies how law enforcement agencies access data held by cloud service providers. The company says it’s investing in its infrastructure, with its first Nvidia B300 cluster built on Open Compute Project (OCP) standards now going live in Switzerland. Similar to other AI apps, Lumo’s desktop app supports Skills, which lets users save instructions, templates, and reference files that Lumo can reuse across their conversations. events.title: Jensen Huang Says He’s Open to Coming Back to Nvidia
events.summary: Jensen Huang said that he is open to returning as chief executive of Nvidia , five days after he resigned from the company . In a statement published Tuesday morning on X, Huang said that since stepping down he has received an “ outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote. Huang also thanked people who showed “kindness” to him and his family and acknowledged “the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met.” He reiterated his love for America and Nvidia and his remorse for his unfaithfulness to his wife, which he also expressed in a company-wide email sent last week. Huang resigned four days after Nvidia launched an internal investigation into an affair he had admitted to having with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen. Huang reportedly misled the company’s general counsel and chief marketing officer about the affair with Alice. The day before Huang stepped down, The New York Times reported that he'd had a second affair with one of his direct reports at Nvidia. After his resignation, Reuters reported on an alleged third affair with another Nvidia employee. The company’s code of conduct discourages "personal relationships" that "may create a conflict of interest." Colette Kress, Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, was installed as interim CEO upon Huang’s resignation. The New York Times first reported Jensen’s association with Alice, also known as Huang Le, in October 2025. On November 6 of this year, citing an intelligence memo that reportedly circulated among Trump administration officials last spring, The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that intelligence officials believed Alice may be an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump administration officials, including tech executive and White House Science and Technology advisory council cochair David Sacks, have questioned whether Alice was associated with the MSS. The Chinese government has rejected claims that Alice spied for the nation. WIRED reported last week that on the same day Huang resigned, Nvidia employees began using an existing petition to the board to call for his reinstatement . It gained more than 1,600 comments in just a few hours. A separate, public petition titled “ Stand With Jensen ” similarly calls for the executive’s return. At the time of writing, it has more than 193,000 online signatures, including more than 11,000 self-identified current and former Nvidia employees and more than 100,000 self-identified shareholders. On Friday, Elon Musk said that he was going to sign the petition, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan claimed that he had signed. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as CEO, adding that he believed Huang had “learned a big lesson.” Nvidia’s board of directors, however, reportedly said on Monday that it was not considering reinstating Huang as CEO. On Tuesday, the board announced that it had established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee “for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” In your inbox: For life-tested picks, sign up for our Gear newsletters Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do their chores big story: cool kids write in all lowercase —does that make you mad? events.title: AI models can be tricked into identifying civilians as military targets by telling them it’s a game
events.summary: Some AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and other leading AI labs could be easily tricked into identifying targets for military strikes — even if they include civilians or locations like schools — simply by being told they’re playing a game, according to a new research report by Vals. Vals, a San Francisco-based AI evaluation startup, tested whether leading AI models could be manipulated into participating in autonomous warfare. Researchers used simulated scenarios and a combination of generated and real imagery from Ukraine and Iran to see if the AI models would mark targets in drone and satellite imagery. The models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, and other companies frequently identified potential targets in drone and satellite imagery, including civilians and surrendering soldiers. When the models refused to cooperate, researchers were able to jailbreak them by claiming the battlefield scenarios were part of a game. The findings come amid growing fears about the immediate risks posed by AI, beyond the existential threats associated with artificial general intelligence. Earlier this year, Anthropic became embroiled in a dispute with the Department of Defense after it told the agency it could not use Anthropic’s technology for mass surveillance of Americans or autonomous warfare. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has insisted that today’s AI systems aren’t reliable enough to make life-or-death decisions without a human in the loop. Meanwhile, the Pentagon argued it should be able to deploy the technology for any lawful military purpose. The new research raises further questions about whether AI companies are capable of preventing their models from being used in warfare. Ironically, AI models from Anthropic performed the worst in these simulated scenarios. But none of the models performed particularly well. None of the researchers’ requests were blocked by a safety classifier, and refusals were uncommon. Even when models did refuse, they often complied after being told they were playing a game. Anthropic spokesperson Eduardo Maia Silva told TechCrunch the company appreciates Vals’ report, recommendations, and collaboration, and acknowledged that the outcomes were not acceptable. “The examples in the report are very clearly against our rules and we have banned and will ban users when we see this behavior,” according to an emailed company statement sent by Silva. “Even for authorized settings, Anthropic has long been firm that today’s frontier AI systems are not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons.” Anthropic told TechCrunch that its teams were already developing additional safeguards before the report was published and that those measures would be in place soon. Anthropic is also expanding its own testing and enhancing safeguards and enforcement to address any gaps it finds. OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans told TechCrunch the company prohibits using its public models to facilitate violence or for unapproved national security purposes, including in the scenarios Vals simulated. “We actively detect and disrupt misuse, including by suspending accounts that violate our policies,” OpenAI said in an emailed statement. “We’re also developing additional safeguards for our public models against misuse involving drones and drone software.” Vals notes in the report that the models were never asked to directly make strike decisions, a task the researchers said the models would typically refuse. That doesn’t mean their outputs couldn’t have dire or fatal consequences in the real world. For instance, targeting information could be used by autonomous weapons systems. In some scenarios, the models were asked to report whether people were visible. Positive reports were followed by simulated strikes and the models would see the consequences. The report relies on commercial models from frontier AI labs, not the models those companies might provide to the military. It’s not clear whether the additional safeguards would apply to military use, though. Vals also noted that technical challenges, including latency and limited onboard computing capacity, make it difficult to use general-purpose AI models for live drone targeting. Those constraints make their deployment in combat less of an immediate threat. A more immediate threat, the researchers say, is that AI models could be used to annotate battlefield footage at scale, producing training data for autonomous targeting systems. For instance, researchers relied on real satellite imagery of an Iranian school that was bombed by the U.S. in February 2026, killing more than 150 civilians. Bloomberg later reported that an “overreliance on AI” contributed to the strike. In Vals’ testing, models frequently marked the school, which sat next to a military complex, as a strike target, with Claude Opus 5.5 selecting the school in 69% of ordinary trials and 72% of game-framed trials.

events.title: Disney+ and Hulu are fully unifying by the end of the year
events.summary: Hulu is merging with Disney+ under CEO Josh D'Amaro. Jeremy Moeller/GC Images; Aurore Marechal/Getty Images Hulu's features will be fully integrated into Disney+ by the end of the year. This project, known internally as Project Gemini, has been in the works for years. The unified streaming experience is part of CEO Josh D'Amaro's plan to build a super app. The Hulu-Disney+ marriage is happening right on schedule. Disney's plan to fully unify its streamers "is nearly complete" and will be finalized in December, the company told investors on Tuesday. It could be the beginning of the end for a stand-alone Hulu app, though Disney hasn't said when the current Hulu app would be discontinued or what will happen to the beloved Hulu brand. This initiative, known internally as "Project Gemini," was scheduled to be finished by the end of 2026, Business Insider reported in May. In the coming weeks, the Disney+ app is getting its last Hulu-specific features, including the ability to watch live TV and add-on streamers for users with qualifying subscriptions. Disney has spent years integrating Hulu's content and features into its namesake streamer in an effort to lift engagement and reduce cancellations. Merging the streamers can create "a more seamless way to discover and engage with the breadth of content across our brands and franchises," Disney said in its shareholder letter as it shared earnings . The decision to move Hulu fully onto Disney+ may make the stand-alone Hulu app obsolete. An internal document obtained by Business Insider in May said that "the Hulu tech stack and app will be decommissioned after all users have transitioned" to Disney+, though it didn't specify exactly when that would happen. A Disney streaming town hall presentation in early November said that "One App Milestones" are expected to last through the company's fiscal fourth quarter, which spans early July to early October. The slide deck referenced Project Gemini, but didn't list the "One App Milestones" or explain the implications of completing them. How Hulu fits into the super app strategy Putting Hulu and Disney+ under one roof is part of CEO Josh D'Amaro's plan of building a super app where streaming subscribers can play games and buy merchandise without leaving the app. Disney's ambition is "to connect Disney+ more closely with the whole company," D'Amaro said on Tuesday's earnings call. "That means our parks, our cruise ships, merchandise, and games." This all-in-one experience will begin to shape this spring, D'Amaro said last quarter. Some media analysts think a streaming super app could boost viewership and customer loyalty while driving more revenue; others think adding games and shopping to Disney+ could make it bloated. Disney said Tuesday that it's adding creator content to Disney+ in December after announcing a deal with TikTok last quarter. The town hall presentation in early November said that Disney was planning to integrate creator content in early 2027. Employees were also told at the meeting that Disney is putting more vertical clips on Disney+, including clips from sports, news, and short-form "micro series" expected to arrive this quarter. Disney is also exploring creating a free streaming product to bring in new users, as Business Insider first reported in July. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Jensen Huang agrees to face Congress over Nvidia scandal
events.summary: Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will officially testify before Congress in early December, lawmakers announced Tuesday. Why it matters: Lawmakers want answers on whether Nvidia's powerful AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether the company did enough to protect sensitive American technology. Huang and Teter will participate in transcribed, closed-door interviews with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China select committees. Context: House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House China committee Chairman John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent letters to Huang, Teter and Commerce undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler on Nov. 12 , requesting they appear. The chairmen told Teter they were seeking information on alleged chip smuggling and the use of Nvidia products by U.S. adversaries, as well as the company's alleged export-control investigations. Kessler was expected to join a classified briefing with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, but the meeting was postponed. What they're saying: "We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the three committee chairmen said in a release . A representative for Huang did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment Tuesday. What's next: Huang will appear before the committees on Dec. 1, and Teter will appear on Dec. 2. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced last week that Huang had stepped down as CEO over an alleged affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and former executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed International. Huang's resignation ignited requests from Congress to investigate his relationship with Megaspeed , a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to Nvidia's AI chips. Megaspeed faces its own investigations for allegedly smuggling chips into China, which the company denies. The big picture: Huang ties to President Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have raised concerns from lawmakers about whether the government did enough to crack down on Nvidia's chips finding their way to China. Editor's note: This is breaking news and will be updated.

events.title: CAIR defends civil rights work against Trump’s ‘smear’
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? The largest Muslim advocacy group in the US urges President Trump to address rising hate crimes against Muslims instead of attacking its efforts. The largest Muslim civil liberties organisation in the United States has condemned suggestions by President Donald Trump that it could face a blanket designation as a “terrorist” group. The Council on American–Islamic Relations (CAIR) said the White House should be addressing violence against American Muslims, rather than attacking the rights group. list 1 of 4 Trump plays Muslim Brotherhood card against Senate candidate El-Sayed list 2 of 4 Trump dials up Islamophobia against Abdul El-Sayed at Michigan Senate rally list 3 of 4 US Muslims concerned but resilient as ‘hate’ attacks target Abdul El-Sayed list 4 of 4 Trump leans into Islamophobia and conspiracy in last-ditch campaign rallies “The Trump administration should focus on addressing this surge in violent hate, not entertaining smears against the civil rights organisation that counters such hate,” CAIR said in a statement to Al Jazeera on Tuesday. On Monday, Trump said he was considering giving a blanket “terrorist” designation to the Muslim Brotherhood and that his administration was also looking at CAIR, which is already classified as a “terrorist” group in Texas and Florida. “CAIR is another one we are watching,” he said of the organisation. When asked if he was considering naming CAIR as a foreign “terrorist” group, he responded: “I’m not going to say that yet, but it could happen.” In its statement, CAIR said that it was “fully prepared to defend our civil rights work and the broader American Muslim community from any new attempts to censor free speech, punish dissent or otherwise undermine the rule of law”. “Our advocacy for justice here and abroad is the real reason that anti-Muslim and anti-Palestinian extremists spend so much time obsessing over our work,” it said. CAIR highlighted several recent violent attacks against the Muslim community across the US, saying, “anti-Muslim extremists have murdered three American Muslims at a mosque in San Diego, firebombed multiple mosques in Minnesota, [and] attempted to burn down one of the largest mosques in Alabama”. Trump’s comments on Monday came during an exchange with reporters outside the White House, following a question about Egypt’s crackdown on the Muslim Brotherhood and whether Washington would consider a broader designation of the group. Earlier this year, the Trump administration designated the Muslim Brotherhood chapters in Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt as foreign “terrorist” organisations. Trump praised Egypt, where the Muslim Brotherhood originated, for cracking down on the group, indicating it did so at his urging. “Egypt has clamped down very hard on the Muslim Brotherhood, at my request,” he told reporters as he left the White House on Monday. “Egypt did a great job,” Trump said.

events.title: Nike lays out financial goals ahead of first investor day in 9 years
events.summary: Nike is hosting its first investor day in nine years at its Oregon headquarters as the company tries to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is working. The footwear company has been enduring a yearslong slump, including significant sustained declines in the China market. Nike said Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance. The retailer also laid out a financial framework and said that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The company said higher-quality revenue, gross margin expansion and productivity improvements would help it reach its goals. Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35. The company also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company said aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth." Nike CEO Elliott Hill told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the new initiative is about "being closer to the athletes we serve." "What's different today is the depth and breadth we're taking from an innovation perspective," Hill said. He added that Nike is emphasizing sportswear at a time when sports have never been more relevant around the world. Hill also said Nike is working to regain its cultural relevance, after a perceived dropoff contributed to its slowdown both in its home market and in China. Nike said it would focus on performance sports and sportswear opportunities "with the greatest potential for long-term growth," and said its five priority sports would be running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor. Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the company aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump. Last month, the company reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it announced a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year. Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027. The new strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031. Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have said the company is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers. At the same time, Nike announced last quarter that it's creating a new global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company said it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence. CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally. The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises.

events.title: Target aims for a Black Friday do-over after last year’s bummer
events.summary: Target is leaning on gift cards to entice shoppers to get to stores early on Black Friday. Dominick Reuter/Business Insider Target is going big this Black Friday after a lackluster promotion last year. The company said the first hundred guests at each of its stores will get gift cards of $25 or more. One winner at each location will receive a $1,000 card. Target is going big this Black Friday . The bullseye retailer said Tuesday that it will give gift cards worth $25 or more to the first hundred shoppers at each of its stores when they open on November 27. In addition to $50 and $100 cards in the mix, one winner at each location will get a $1,000 grand prize. The move could help Target regain some of the enthusiasm it lost last year after shoppers took to social media to  critique the selection  in its Black Friday gift bag, which included fun-size candy, drink mix samples, shampoo, and a deck of Uno cards. Last year, some locations had more than 500 people waiting in line, the company said, and ten shoppers at each participating store received bags with extra prizes valued from $99 to $350. Last year's gift bags were limited to the first hundred shoppers, too. In the fine print for next week's promotion, Target said store workers will hand out redemption tickets beginning one hour before opening until either the supply runs out or one hour after opening. Tickets are limited to one per eligible customer, and attempts to get additional tickets will result in disqualification. Anyone who cuts in line or uses "dangerous methods" to get a better spot will also be turned away, the company said. Beyond the monetary incentives, Target teased a Black Friday drop from a "guest-favorite" musical artist, plus exclusive new food and beverage selections from viral brands like Goodles, Katjes, and Backflip. events.title: Tech leaders tell Fed chairman Warsh how AI could transform the economy
events.summary: Just maybe, both the extreme techno-optimists and AI doom-and-gloomers are wrong about the economic impact of the technology. That's the argument that venture capitalist Marc Andreessen — who is co-leading a Federal Reserve task force on the topic — made in a high-profile panel Monday. Why it matters: The argument could help shape how the Fed assesses AI's economic consequences, with major implications for its outlook on growth, inflation and interest rates. Andreessen's argument offered an early glimpse of the thinking that will underpin his recommendations to the central bank's leaders. What they're saying: "My line has been both utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed, specifically disappointed by the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact, and specifically the economic impact," Andreessen said at the San Francisco Fed. Andreessen, a co-leader of Fed chairman Kevin Warsh's Jobs and Productivity Task Force, spoke alongside former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo at a hearing in the Bay Area, where Warsh studied at Stanford and later spent 15 years teaching and conducting research. (Fellow task force member Chad Jones, a Stanford economist on leave for Anthropic, was in the audience but did not speak because the company is preparing to go public, Andreessen said.) Zoom in: Andreessen previewed his contribution to the task force's report, arguing that the economy is divided into two groups: Fast-changing industries, such as technology and media, where innovation drives productivity gains and lower prices. Slower-changing industries, including health care, education and housing, where regulations, limited competition and other barriers make technological progress harder. The intrigue: These slower-changing sectors account for some of Americans' biggest expenses. Those sectors of the economy "are not legally allowed to have rapid change," Andreessen said. Andreessen argued that regulations and other barriers could prevent AI from transforming large parts of the economy, which he says would limit job losses and productivity gains. " You might interpret this as good news because it means the AI revolution is not going to destroy all the jobs or kill everybody," he said. "You can also view this as very negative. Productivity growth just simply may not grow very much. Economic growth just simply may not grow very much. We may just continue to stagnate," he added. The big picture: Warsh is turning to influential outsiders to challenge how the central bank thinks about the economy. Affirm CEO Max Levchin told Warsh that AI has made the company's engineers five times more productive, cutting the cost of developing new features by 80%. Stripe CEO Patrick Collison said new businesses launching on its platform each week have doubled from a year ago, an unprecedented surge in its 15-year history. Unlike established companies, startups are more willing to let AI independently develop products and fix bugs, potentially allowing them to grow faster with fewer employees. What to watch: Executives said AI is already delivering productivity gains in traditional industries — including sectors Andreessen said are more resistant to technological change. Erik Wexler, CEO of Providence, a large nonprofit health system, said AI tools that transcribe patient appointments are saving some physicians two to four hours a day on paperwork. Wexler said that one doctor called it "life-changing." What's next: Warsh has asked all five task forces to recommend ways to improve Fed policymaking by year-end, though he cautioned last month that some may miss the deadline.
