events.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit exposes succession and governance risks for companies and boards
events.summary: To join the CNBC Workforce Executive Council, apply at cnbccouncils.com/wec . Apply to the Workforce Executive Council Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has put Nvidia's CEO succession planning and board preparedness under scrutiny. Leadership experts say Nvidia's unusually flat structure with concentrated decision-making, relationships and reporting lines around Huang created outsized risk. "Succession planning is an ongoing, fundamental responsibility of the board, not something to do when a crisis hits," says Lisa Calicchio, chief human resources officer at WCG Clinical. The fallout from Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy as well as an Nvidia executive that led to his resignation as CEO of Nivida , the company he founded and grew into a $4 trillion chip giant, will likely go on for some time. But the missteps of Nvidia's board of directors offer immediate lessons, say talent and leadership experts. It shows what happens when there's no clear succession plan, the dangers of an overly decentralized leadership structure, and how companies built around one powerful, controlling leader create the kind of risk boards are responsible for preventing. In the span of less than a week — from the time Huang admitted that he was unfaithful to his wife until the board announced that he was resigning — the question became: could Nvidia, a company at the epicenter of the AI build-out, operate without him? With Huang's ouster and the appointment of CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO , Nvidia's employees, customers, and investors will begin to find out. The process will also put a glaring spotlight on why the Nvidia board wasn't better prepared for Huang leaving the company for whatever reason. "Succession planning is an ongoing, fundamental responsibility of the board, not something to do when a crisis hits," says Lisa Calicchio, chief human resources officer at WCG Clinical and a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council . She described what happened at Nvidia as "a failure of epic proportion, both on the part of the board for not fulfilling its fiduciary responsibility to ensure continued viability of the organization by having a robust succession plan, and for the behavior and risks created by the CEO." "What they're doing now is flying by the seat of their pants," she added. Nvidia's 10-member board of directors is a collection of early investors, long-time partners and business executives across a range of industries. Before Nov. 12, the company did not have a chair of the board or any clear succession plan . The board also includes directors who expressed "confidence in Jensen" before they had even begun their own independent internal review of his actions. In addition to naming Kress to the top job, the company appointed Harvey C. Jones, a tech investor and Nvidia director for the past 33 years, as its first-ever chair. After his appointment, the company announced that the board would be conducting a search of both internal and external candidates to find a permanent chief executive. 'All the risk centered on the shoulders of one man' Alan Fleischmann, founder and CEO of business advisory firm Laurel Strategies and a member of the CNBC CEO Council , says that while "the DNA of any organization is defined by the CEO, there must be a stronger board dynamic and strong leadership surrounding the CEO." "Succession planning is not simply about identifying who takes over when a CEO leaves," Fleischmann said. "It's about building an institution that can thrive beyond any one individual." The outsized role Huang played at Nvidia — in September 2025 he told CNBC's Becky Quick that he had as many as 60 direct reports — makes it even more difficult for the board to find someone who can understand the inner workings of the company while being such a visible and active hype man for its all-important AI chips. In corporate governance circles this is known as "key man" risk and it points to a company being overly reliant on one person whose death, departure, or financial or moral compromise could materially damage the organization. "This is the world's most valuable company and all the risk centered on the shoulders of one man," Calicchio says. "Flat organizations can be remarkably effective…but there are tradeoffs," Fleischmann added. "When too many decisions, relationships and reporting lines converge around one individual, the organization can become more vulnerable than it appears." Calicchio acknowledged that a CEO having numerous direct reports isn't problematic in the early days of a company, when the founder knows everyone, but becomes concerning "when a company is the size of Nvidia. I really question the rigor and discipline of their organizational policies." This same absence of rigor is evident in the lack of any obvious successors to Huang.

Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters From 72 hours to 2 months in a single quiet announcement. Careful what you ask Google's AI, because it's storing it even if you ask it not to HTML-in-Canvas ships and could make the web a lot more creative...and a lot stupider 23 hours ago Google: AI agent turned a security patch into a working exploit with no human help 1 day ago Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum 3 days ago Crackdown on UK medical record snooping after staff reported sneaking 300+ times this year 4 days ago Google promises its new smart specs won't give creeps their ideal view 4 days ago Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update. Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot. At the core of the announcement is Google's splitting of Gemini chat history settings from AI model training permissions. What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case. So far so good: Being able to have Gemini remember more of your past interactions to contextualize newer discussions is nice, to be sure. The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles. "Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes. "They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public." Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update. That's right: Prior to Monday's change, Gemini users who turned off the "Keep Activity" option only had their chats retained for three days, according to an archived copy of the same page that now states that choosing the same please-don't-store-my-AI-chats option means Google keeps them "for around two months." It's also worth noting that, even if users have the option to not store Gemini chat records enabled, submitting a feedback request on any Gemini post means that temporary retention period gets extended to three years. That was the case both before and after Monday's change, mind you, but for the privacy-conscious it's definitely important to note. Sending feedback to Google about a Gemini response also means that humans will be reviewing that particular conversation, as well as any associated files and conversations that can be associated with the one in question. Submitting feedback also means that Google assumes the right to use the conversation and its associated content to improve its services and improve its AI models. In other words, even if you opt out of having your conversations stored, your Gemini history could still end up being used to feed the Google machine. events.title: I moved from California to Japan and make $90,000 a year. Salaries are lower here, but life is more affordable.
events.summary: Kaito Itokazu moved from California to Japan three years ago. Business Insider Software engineer Kaito Itokazu moved from California to Japan three years ago. He earns around $90,000 annually while living in Tokyo. His budget covers his $840 rent. He saves up to $3,500 monthly, spends more dining out than on groceries, and travels across Asia. This is an as-told-to essay based on a conversation for Business Insider's video series, The Pay Check, with Kaito Itokazu, 25, who lives in Tokyo. It has been edited for length and clarity. I'm a software engineer living in Tokyo , earning around $60,000 a year as a salaryman, plus around $30,000 from side gigs. I'm originally from Los Angeles, and I moved to Japan three years ago. Salaries in Japan are much lower than in the US. When I tell my friends in America and Japan my salary, I get the exact opposite responses. My friends in the US are shocked and worry about how I make it work. When I tell my friends in Japan, they're like, "Oh wow, that's really good for your age." This is because it's much cheaper to live in Japan . Even with a lower salary, it's possible to live comfortably. Each year I tend to evaluate whether this coming year is worth the opportunities, experiences, and connections I can create — as opposed to when I was growing up in the US — and every year has been yes. In the past three years, I've switched jobs, moved apartments, and now I'm starting a side business. Compared to the national average, my salary is on the higher end, which gives me more opportunities and experiences and allows me to live in Tokyo. I am extremely grateful and fortunate for that. Side income and housing in Japan For my side business, I create websites and web applications and help businesses integrate AI into their workflows. I also teach kids basic computer programming. With my side gigs, I'm projected to make an additional $30,000 a year. That's around $90,000 a year in total. A lot of the money I get from my side business is expensed or reinvested into it. My base rent is around $840 — that's almost double my previous rent when I was living in Yokohama . The size is around the same, so what I'm really paying for is the prime location. Kaito Itokazu's base rent in Tokyo is around $840 a month. Business Insider Moving into a new apartment is pretty expensive in Japan. You have to put down a deposit that you don't get back — mine was $2,000. Because of the nature of my apartment, they wouldn't let me move things on my own, so I had to hire a professional company to move the furniture, which cost around $500. For utilities, I pay around $57 a month for gas, water, and electricity. I also spend around $250 on AI tools. In total, from housing to utilities to streaming, it comes to around $970 a month. Day-to-day spending in Tokyo Being in the city, I don't really need a car. Most of my transportation is by subway and bus. When I go to work, I get my transportation fee reimbursed. So I usually spend $120 a month on public transportation for fun outings. If you're not careful, the trains can add up. I spend $130 on groceries, $250 on eating out, $70 on cafés and coffee shops, and $70 on convenience stores. Those numbers are pretty embarrassing to admit; I could definitely spend more on groceries and less on eating out. Kaito Itokazu shops for groceries in a supermarket in Tokyo, Japan. Business Insider Yet, one of the things I really like about being in Japan is the amazing food . To me, it's worth a little extra money to try new places and eat out. The $70 for the convenience stores comes from items like snacks, rice balls, yogurt, and ice cream. I also tend to eat out with friends or coworkers most of the time. Compared to the average Japanese person, I spend a little more on food and groceries. I like to play soccer or futsal — that adds up to around $38 a month. Recently, pickleball and paddle have been trending, so I spend around $26 on them and $51 on my gym membership. After that, around $65 goes toward nightlife and bars, and I spend about $32 on a haircut every month. I also love to travel within Japan , Asia, and to America. If I happen to go home to the US, it can be around $1,000, but on average I spend around $470 a month. I recently went to Busan, South Korea, for a $200 round-trip flight; I visited my grandparents in Kagawa for a $120 round-trip flight; and I also went to Mount Fuji for around $31. Managing finances in Japan For health insurance, $212 is deducted from my paycheck each month for standard healthcare from my employer. I broke my wrist three years ago, and when I wanted to get it checked out in the US, it would take me around two weeks to get an appointment. While I was in Japan, my wrist started bothering me, and I was able to get it checked out immediately. I went in that same day for X-rays and scans. I initially paid for the surgery, but my insurance reimbursed 70% of the cost. The total came to around $300. On average, I save around $1,500 to $3,500 a month. Of that, 30% goes to investments, 30% to an emergency fund, and the rest goes back into my side business. In Japan, we also have a residence tax that applies to you a year after you move. You get taxed on your previous year's salary at around 10% of your salary, fixed. I went to Chapman University in the US and recently paid off my student loan debt . I was fortunate to be in a position to receive a scholarship and use money from my internships to pay off my student loans. Kaito Itokazu said that discussing one's salary is taboo in Japan. By sharing his story, he hopes to help others considering a move there. Business Insider Now, I'm trying to find a balance between being financially smart and being able to experience and spend money how I want to. I have a budget range, and I don't want to go over it. I also have money saved up in case something goes wrong with a fund or if I want to invest it — but I also have some money I use to travel or experience new things. If I decide to settle down in Japan, I think I'm on track financially. As I build a community and make more connections, Japan starts to feel less like a temporary place and more like a second home. That makes it much harder to leave. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Yemeni parliament approves law designating Houthis as ‘terrorists’
events.summary: The law targets the group’s financing and activities as renewed fighting threatens to derail efforts to end Yemen’s war. Yemen’s parliament has unanimously approved a law designating the Houthis as a “terrorist organisation” and criminalising the group’s activities and financing, as fighting intensifies between the group and forces loyal to the internationally recognised government. The vote, held over two sessions by videolink on Monday, comes seven years after the measure was first proposed. Parliament said it had deferred the bill, first tabled at a session in the city of Seiyun in April 2019, to give peace efforts a chance. list 1 of 3 Houthi advance on Aden may spur resurgence of Yemen’s southern separatists list 2 of 3 Is the US-Israel war on Iran turning into a ‘frozen conflict’? list 3 of 3 Yemeni army reports 661 attacks on Houthis as group advances towards Aden It noted that the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, had attacked government-held areas of Yemen and Saudi Arabia, and accused the Iranian-backed group of brushing aside “all options for peace”. Yemen’s cabinet approved the draft law on October 11. The country’s National Defence Council had designated the Houthis a “terrorist” organisation by executive decision in October 2022. The United States also lists the group as a “terrorist” organisation, and Saudi Arabia treats it as one. According to the state-run Saba news agency, the legislation was formally submitted to Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, on Tuesday to be signed into law. It runs to 55 articles and designates the group – including all of its political, military and civilian formations – “a terrorist organisation” and a “rebellious faction”. It also toughens penalties for offences including seizing state authority, besieging cities, attacking civilians, laying landmines and attacking international shipping. Certain offences would carry the death penalty. The law also sets out procedures to identify, trace, freeze and confiscate assets linked to the group and its affiliated entities. The vote comes amid months of renewed hostilities after several years of relative calm on Yemen’s front lines. In late June, the Houthis announced an escalation against government forces and Saudi Arabia, saying the move was aimed at lifting what the group describes as a “blockade”. In early September, a Houthi ground offensive on the western coast gave the group control of parts of Taiz and Hodeidah governorates after government forces withdrew from the port city of Mocha and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb area. Government forces launched an operation called “Dawn of Yemen” in early October to retake Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa. It initially made limited gains in recapturing territory lost on the Red Sea coast, but on Sunday, pro-government forces withdrew from those areas, allowing the Houthis to advance further. Heavy fighting continues in Marib, al-Jawf and Lahij governorates, and the Houthis are pressing to take the city of Taiz, which the government and rights groups say is under a tight siege. The Houthis have also stepped up attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia, while the Saudi-led coalition says it is striking facilities that fund the group’s war effort. The Houthis seized Sanaa in September 2014. United Nations-sponsored talks and regional mediation have failed to end the war since then. Ismail al-Suhaili, a political science professor and senior researcher at the Mokha Center for Strategic Studies, said the law marks a shift towards a tougher government position after the failure of peace efforts. Moving the designation from an executive decision to parliamentary legislation gives it wider legal force, he said. He said it could complicate future negotiations by shifting their focus from power-sharing towards restoring state institutions, disarmament and UN Security Council Resolution 2216. Al-Suhaili warned that the law could put additional pressure on banks, traders and companies operating between government- and Houthi-controlled areas and deepen Yemen’s financial split. Donors and aid organisations could also become reluctant to work in Houthi-held areas, which could disrupt the delivery of essential supplies to civilians. The Houthis, he said, could respond with further military escalation or with countermeasures targeting government leaders. Tawfiq al-Hamidi, head of the SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, told Al Jazeera the law was “a late step” but provides a legal basis for holding those responsible for abuses to account and compensating victims. While the law narrows the space for political negotiations in favour of military action, al-Hamidi said, it does not entirely rule out a future settlement.

events.title: Nvidia stock falls ahead of earnings as company reels from Huang resignation
events.summary: Nvidia reports earnings after the bell Tuesday. Investors have been weighing the fallout from former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management. Nvidia shares slipped on Tuesday as former CEO Jensen Huang released his first public statement since his resignation and the company prepares to report earnings after the bell. Huang said he is open to returning as Nvidia's CEO and that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his behavior. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in a statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber . "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation." "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang continued. Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, following reports that he had a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. Outlets also reported that Huang also had an affair with a vice president at the company and an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second employee. Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025. Lawmakers also announced Tuesday that Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on Dec. 2. An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO drew more than 190,000 signatures , including Elon Musk . But Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday. The chip giant is also facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips. Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members, the company said in a statement. events.title: The man who sold Aetna to CVS for almost $70 billion says the deal was cover for problems ‘they never really fixed’—just as CVS breaks itself in two
events.summary: Mark Bertolini sold Aetna to CVS Health for almost $70 billion in 2018. On Monday, he told a room of Fortune 500 executives what he thinks CVS was really buying. “The real intention” of the purchase, Bertolini said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, “was just to take the earning stream and revenue stream from [Aetna] to hide a bunch of other things that they never really fixed.” He tied that directly to the breakup CVS is going through now: “You’d never do that deal now.” The comments land two weeks after CVS said it will split in two . CVS Health will keep Aetna and its Caremark pharmacy benefit manager and spin off its roughly 9,000 stores and MinuteClinic as a separate company, CVS Pharmacy, by the first half of 2028. CVS shares closed down 12.5% on Nov. 4, the day of the announcement, wiping out nearly $15 billion in market value. For employers, insurers, and anyone with a pharmacy benefit, it’s the partial unwinding of the biggest bet on vertical integration in American health care. CVS declined to comment on Bertolini’s remarks. “This is the right decision, at the right time,” CVS Health spokesperson David Whitrap said of the split in an email to Fortune, adding that the company is “getting ahead of the external market dynamics from a position of strength. Each of our businesses are thriving.” He confirmed that Aetna and Caremark will stay together and that the separation should be finished by mid-2028. Where’s the queen? Bertolini ran Aetna from 2011 through the sale and has been CEO of Oscar Health since April 2023. He had been asked by Fortune ’s Kristin Stoller whether—after decades running one of the system’s biggest players—he worried he’d made it worse. He started with what he called “an admission against self-interest.” Bertolini said he was part of the team that took Express Scripts public, back when “we thought the PBM [pharmacy benefit manager] was a great idea.” “I thought it would never last, but it did,” he said, comparing it to a card hustle on a New York street corner: “Where’s the queen?” The Aetna deal was supposed to be something else. Bertolini said the idea was “a new front door for health care,” with customers shopping for care at the front of CVS stores. In 2017 he pitched it as “10,000 new front doors to the health care system.” He said that vision “never got pulled through because it took a lot of intensity to do it,” and he was moved to the board. On CEO succession, he was blunt: “There can only be one CEO.” CVS cut him from its board in February 2020 as it shrank from 16 directors to 13. Bertolini told the Wall Street Journal at the time he was being pushed out before the Aetna integration was finished. A CVS spokesperson said at the time “the board felt it was the right time for Mark to focus on his other endeavors.” The stores, the front door in Bertolini’s pitch, are now the part CVS is cutting loose. Bertolini said the strategy stopped making sense after the pandemic and the shift to virtual care. CVS CEO David Joyner’s explanation is that the split is possible because things are going well. “The businesses are running really well,” he told Reuters . “We’ve been afforded the opportunity to make different decisions than we, than I could have two years ago.” Morningstar’s Julie Utterback noted “CVS has the most exposure to vertical integration in the industry.” ‘Eliminate employer-sponsored health insurance’ Asked by Stoller to name one complexity that “maybe your own companies even benefit from” and should be eliminated, Bertolini didn’t hesitate: “Eliminate employer-sponsored health insurance.” His argument is about bargaining power. Doctors, hospitals, and insurers each competed for a bigger share and consolidated along the way, he said, so an employer with 20,000 or 30,000 workers that could get a good network deal 15 years ago can’t anymore. Bertolini said 74% of large employers are now considering defined contribution, where the employer gives workers a set amount of money instead of a plan. He wants that money in portable accounts, like HSAs or HRAs, that follow workers through job changes, gig work, and Medicaid or Medicare. “Americans always pick the best solution last,” he said. Employers are paying a lot for the current version. Family premiums for employer coverage passed $28,000 in 2026, with workers paying $7,471 of it, according to KFF’s annual survey . Zach Reitano, CEO of the cash-pay telehealth company Ro, who shared the stage, gave the same answer: “Most frequently in the healthcare system, the patient is not the customer,” he said, adding that creates “suboptimal outcomes just based on incentives.” Reitano borrowed the old line about democracy being the worst form of government except for all the rest: “In our mind, a patient is sort of the worst person to determine their healthcare except for everyone else,” he said. Oscar’s own math Bertolini is talking from a stronger position than he had a few years ago. Oscar, which sells plans on the Affordable Care Act exchanges, reported third-quarter net income of $167.3 million, against a loss of $137.5 million a year earlier, on revenue of $5.14 billion, up 72%. Membership was about 2.69 million, according to its results . Onstage, he said 67% of Oscar’s coding is now done by AI agents, that the company runs 40 large language models, and that it has taken $1.2 billion out of its operating costs over three years. Closing out his answer on CVS, he came back to his earlier point: “We try everything else until we get the right one, which is the last one, and that’s the consumer.” CVS expects to finish the split in the first half of 2028. Aetna will stay with Caremark, and the front door will be on its own. This story has been updated with comment from CVS Health. It has also been updated to clarify the context of Bertolini’s final quote, which closed his answer on the Aetna-CVS deal, and to quote the moderator’s question that prompted his answer on employer-sponsored insurance. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ if allowed to return as Nvidia CEO
events.summary: In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signaled his willingness to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the company’s best interest. Huang’s statement, posted in full on X , reads as follows: Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours. Jensen Huang resigned after reports of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Nvidia’s chip exports have faced intense scrutiny since the revelations, and Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1. In Huang’s absence, Nvidia has formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance. Still, many investors and employees associated with Nvidia have called for Huang to return as CEO, at least until an investigation can provide clearer evidence of guilt. An open letter circulated earlier this week attracted the signatures of more than 10,000 current and former Nvidia employees, as well as prominent tech figures like Elon Musk, Amjad Masad, and Travis Kalanick. “We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter reads. “If the Board believes his continued absence is necessary, provide a specific, evidence-based explanation of why it serves NVIDIA’s best interests.” Still, many see such a return as unlikely. On Monday, an unnamed source on Nvidia’s board told The Washington Post there were no plans to reinstate Huang. There’s also significant resistance to the idea in Congress, where Huang still faces significant questions about his role in chip exports to China-linked firms. events.title: My family history of cancer was giving me so much anxiety. I finally learned to stop turning to Dr. Google.
events.summary: The author said she used to let her health anxiety send her down an internet rabbit hole before her doctor's appointments. Courtesy of Linda Wolff. I have a family history of cancer, and every lump and symptom pushed me to turn to Dr. Google. Compulsive Googling of my symptoms only stressed me out, leading me to feel even worse. I now avoid self-diagnosis by focusing my time and effort on things I enjoy. My first real scare came at 36. A swollen lymph node on the left side of my neck during a routine checkup raised my doctor's concern. "How long have you had this?" he inquired. I held my breath as his fingers traversed the lump hovering above my collarbone. He jotted down the name of a surgical oncologist. The room began to spin. After several anxiety-ridden months of visiting the local cancer center to have my lump observed, the surgical oncologist insisted we remove it. During the weeks that led up to my surgery, I made the fatal mistake — no pun intended — of Googling "lumps on my neck." The information took me down a rabbit hole, from ordinary viruses to malignant cancer. Of course, I ignored the benign and focused on the worst. Lymphoma and Leukemia kept popping up in my nightmarish searches at 2 a.m. Naturally, I assumed I was dying. My parents and siblings have all had cancer. I fear I'm trying to outrun my fate. Each time I go for a checkup, scan, mammogram, colonoscopy, or blood work, I brace myself for devastating news. My worry was sucking the life out of me, overriding the voice in my head telling me that instead of taking each moment for granted, I should be enjoying my existence. My worry has lingered for a long time I was 16 when my beloved father first complained of stomach pain. My mother assumed it was from blue cheese dressing that turned. But when the pain became severe, his doctor suggested exploratory surgery. He found pancreatic cancer. I don't think I ever fully recovered from my father's devastating six-week-long decline from diagnosis to death. It's no surprise that I struggle with a PTSD-like fear whenever medical issues arise. When I was faced with having surgery to remove my lymph node, my children were small, and the thought of them growing up without me tore me to pieces. I told them I was having a "pimple-ectomy," which sounded silly so they wouldn't be scared. I held it together in front of them, but fear and anticipatory grief consumed me as I cried myself to sleep. Thankfully, it was benign. The worry sometimes felt like wasted time Over my decades, I've had a multitude of suspicious bumps, polyps, and cysts tested and removed. Each clean bill of health comes with tremendous relief, and a side of guilt for being one of the lucky ones and the awful awareness of the all-consuming time and energy I wasted that I'll never get back. Instead of going down a symptom rabbit hole, I could have been learning a new language, making a photo collage of my grandbabies, or at the very least, watching adorable puppy videos. Eventually, one of my doctors saw how my anxiety was affecting my health . I recall the tears streaming like the fountain of Bellagio as I hiccuped my worst fears during an abdominal ultrasound. The 24-hour information drip I did prior to my appointment, Googling my symptoms, didn't calm my fears; it amplified them. I can't help but think this must be contributing to my high blood pressure, IBS, insomnia, and vertigo. I knew my doctor was right when they told me I had to stop. And I finally did. I'm keeping myself distracted with more fun things I'm not saying I don't worry anymore. I do. But now I avoid the armchair analysis on my computer or phone and let the medical professionals do their jobs. Instead, I try to remind myself of all the instances my worrying was for nothing and did nothing but rob me of precious time and peace of mind. Now when I'm tempted to do a deep dive on an ailment, I take a breath and remind myself that the search will only make me suffer. Choosing instead to engage in something joyful or productive, like planting in my garden, playing with my grandchildren, or penning my novel. The distraction is wonderful. I feel better, too. events.title: Disney beats fourth-quarter estimates, targets $3 billion in savings through cost-cutting efforts
events.summary: Disney topped Wall Street estimates for revenue and earnings per share for its fiscal fourth quarter. It's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029 via measures that include layoffs, CFO Hugh Johnston told CNBC. The company's results were once again boosted by strength in its streaming and parks divisions. Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and announced it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029. Those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month . Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs." Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the company's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy." "They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company," he said. "At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth." The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026. The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%. Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks. "The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston said. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded." The company will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July. Here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3 , compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG: Earnings per share: $1.77 adjusted vs. $1.67 expected Revenue : $25.95 billion vs. $25.18 billion expected Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77. The company's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions. Disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion. The division is already a top performer for the company, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year. While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston said. Growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney. Still, D'Amaro said he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with new additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027. "Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he said. "And new capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits." The company expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March. Sports, streaming and entertainment Over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion. Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney said. The segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the company saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5.

events.title: Photos: Tens of thousands rally in France over living standards and wages
events.summary: France witnesses its third major public sector strike since September, as protests highlight wage and service concerns. Demonstrators have gathered across France after unions called a nationwide strike by public sector workers in a bid to secure pay rises, as protests over living standards and squeezed public services continue to roil the country. France’s 5.8 million public sector employees were urged to mobilise on Tuesday after talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Friday failed to satisfy union demands for across-the-board pay rises, following last week’s minimum wage boost for private-sector workers. It is the third united day of strikes and protests in the public sector since September, after a previous mobilisation earlier this month drew hundreds of thousands of workers and saw police fire tear gas as clashes broke out in several cities. More unions joined the call to strike after Lecornu’s meeting, saying the government’s proposed measures did not address what they describe as an urgent pay and cost-of-living crisis. In Paris, a major rally was taking place in the east of the city, with dozens of other demonstrations planned nationwide. Police sources told AFP that between 40,000 and 80,000 people were expected to demonstrate in the capital, and up to 300,000 across France. In Paris, university professor Nicolas Prevot said he was marching to defend human rights, protect public services and keep the far right from power in next year’s presidential election.

events.title: Iraq resumes pumping crude oil for export through pipeline to Turkey
events.summary: Iraq has resumed pumping crude oil for export through Turkey in a move expected to boost the economy and revitalise an industry paralysed by the war in Iran . Crude will be pumped through the 960km Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline at an initial rate of 120,000 barrels per day, Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Khudair said, the state-owned Iraqi News Agency reported on Tuesday. That will be gradually increased to hit a capacity of 500,000 bpd, after the “successful completion of maintenance, rehabilitation, technical and operational tests”, he added. “This achievement represents an important strategic step in enhancing Iraq's export capacity and diversifying crude oil export outlets.” It will also help in “generating additional financial revenues for the national economy, especially since exporting through the northern outlet allows for the marketing of crude oil without price discounts”, he added. Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations. More than 90 per cent of Iraq's budget is funded in dollars from oil exports, almost all of which must pass through the Strait of Hormuz. The regional conflict has led to a sharp supply collapse for Iraq. Exports fell from 3.36 million bpd in February to 131,000 bpd in April. The result was a drop in monthly oil revenue that previously hovered around $7 billion. Baghdad has also announced the start of work on a new pipeline linking Basra to Haditha with a capacity of 2.5 million bpd, as it seeks new routes to export crude. But the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline remains crucial. In August, Iraq and Turkey signed a ​one-year agreement ⁠to continue crude oil ⁠flows at an export capacity of 750,000 bpd. Iraq is also driving efforts to boost its standing. At September's UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi appealed to the world to invest in Iraq as he pitched his economic and anti-corruption plans. Last month, the International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said it was advancing discussions with Iraq , as well as Lebanon , as part of broader efforts to support vulnerable countries in the Middle East and North Africa. Iraq is also debating a draft federal budget for 2027 that would be the biggest in its history but the plan is also the most detached from the country's financial reality.

events.title: Thousands demand cancellation of Nathan Cofnas talk at Oxford University
events.summary: Online petition with more than 32,000 signatures demands the university ‘cancel Nathan Cofnas’s invitation to speak’. Thousands of people have signed a petition and protests are planned at the University of Oxford against the appearance of Nathan Cofnas, an American academic and self-described “race realist” accused of racism. Cofnas, who had accused the late Professor Jason Arday of plagiarism last July, is due to give a talk at Oxford’s Oriel College on Tuesday evening at an event organised by the Oxford Reform student society, which is linked to the far-right Reform UK party. list 1 of 4 Who is DEI critic and Jason Arday accuser, Nathan Cofnas? list 2 of 4 Jason Arday’s death is institutional murder list 3 of 4 University suspends US academic leading Jason Arday plagiarism accusations list 4 of 4 Nathan Cofnas on whether he feels responsible for Jason Arday’s death Cofnas has drawn controversy for years with his eugenics-linked views tying race to intelligence, writing that Black people were less intelligent than others in an article which led to his dismissal from his position at a college at Emmanuel College, Cambridge. He was suspended as a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University in Belgium in August after making plagiarism allegations against Arday, a Black Cambridge professor. Arday consistently denied allegations of plagiarism but acknowledged errors in his work. Arday was later found dead in his home after resigning his post amid the ballooning scandal. Cofnas was later allowed to resume some academic work at Ghent remotely, without teaching, while an investigation continued. The Oxford Reform student society defended its event – titled “Is DEI Undermining Higher Education?”, referring to diversity, equity and inclusion – and said it is “committed to broadening participation in university life”. In a statement, Oxford University said the event being hosted on its grounds “does not imply endorsement by the College of the views of its speakers”. An online petition demanding the university “cancel Nathan Cofnas’s invitation to speak” has more than 32,000 signatures. “Ideas platformed at Oxford do not stay in the lecture theatre”, the petition said.

events.title: Daydream’s new AI agent acts as your personal stylist — and can shop for you, too
events.summary: Can an AI agent serve as your personal stylist? That’s what e-commerce veteran Julie Bornstein’s fashion startup, Daydream, aims to find out. On Tuesday, the company launched “Daydream Agent,” an AI agent that is described as a personal stylist that can help you plan a look, virtually try on clothes, surface relevant pieces based on your taste, and more. The idea, the company explains, is to put a personal stylist in everyone’s pocket. This application of AI could be promising, given that early adopters of consumer AI agents like Meta’s Muse have found that online shopping is a key use case. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently noted that shopping was a top activity for Muse’s over 10 million users and that 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily. In Daydream’s case, the fashion startup has been focused on using AI to deliver personalized shopping results to its users. Its new AI agent builds on its earlier work with an AI chatbot that could help users find outfits and make suggestions, but not complete purchases. Now the company says its Daydream Agent expands on that experience by remembering each shopper’s own personal style, fit preferences, and budget to refine its recommendations. Shoppers can also upload a photo to have the agent reuse that image to virtually try on any item they’ve saved. When they find something they like, the agent can complete a purchase through a one-click checkout process. The agent can also handle other fashion-related tasks, like keeping an eye on when items go on sale or when brands have a new drop, or providing weekly updates or spotting new fashion trends. Also, instead of leaving items in their cart, shoppers can save pieces they’re interested in to a persistent “clothing rack” so they can compare options and think about their purchases before deciding what to buy. Shoppers can also connect their own closet and their calendar to the agent, helping them to build outfits around what they already own and plan what to wear for upcoming events. The tech works by pulling real-time pricing and availability information from its catalog of over 10,000 brands, then combines that with its fashion-focused artificial intelligence. It’s powered by a combination of OpenAI, Gemini, and Claude models, which it fine-tuned, along with its own trained models designed for particular use cases. However, considering that fashion is more of an art than a science, the company says it’s keeping humans in the loop. To do so, this month it brought on its first stylist in residence, Francesca Salih , an international fashion stylist and the founder of StyleGrid. Salih provides the startup with styling content that helps shape how the agent pulls together outfits and offers advice. This advice is part of the company’s fashion knowledge database, which the agent experience relies on. Bornstein, formerly Stitch Fix’s COO and the founder of The Yes ( exited to Pinterest in 2022 ), started Daydream in 2023 as an AI search engine . The company, backed by $50 million in funding from Forerunner Ventures, Index Ventures, GV, and True Ventures, says more than 2 million shoppers have used Daydream to discover apparel and accessories since its June 2025 launch. events.title: I visited London’s viral GTA 6 merch pop-up, where shoppers waited for hours and scrambled to buy whatever was left
events.summary: I went to Selfridges' GTA 6 pop-up to see what was worth queuing for. Georgia Hennessy GTA 6 is arguably the most-hyped game in history, and that hype is on display at a London pop-up. I joined a long line for the pop-up at luxury department store Selfridges on a gray, rainy morning. Once inside, customers scrambled to buy whatever was left on the mostly empty shelves. London's main shopping thoroughfare, Oxford Street, was quiet on a grey, drizzly morning. Outside the luxury department store, Selfridges, a queue had formed for its much-hyped GTA 6 pop-up. The shoppers, mostly men, stood bundled in raincoats, hoods and scarves, waiting to see what merchandise was left after the collection sold out online. A delivery truck nearby filled the air with the smell of fish. Well-dressed Selfridges customers glanced at the line as they passed with the particular dry curiosity Londoners reserve for an inexplicable crowd. The answer was Rockstar Games’ next Grand Theft Auto release — which drops on Thursday — and the chance to buy a piece of the anticipation surrounding it. Shoppers waited outside Selfridges to see what GTA 6 merchandise was left. Georgia Hennessy Outside, I spoke with shoppers who had joined the queue for very different reasons. "What I want to know is, who's this for?" said JD, a retail worker who spoke to me quietly; he didn't want anyone to know that he had come to conduct what he called "competitor analysis." "If you're willing to spend £2,000 (about $2,650) on a jacket, surely you're not going to be queuing up with the rest of us," he said. JD said he was primarily there to study the visual merchandising, the promotional car, and the type of customer the pop-up was attracting. The car, a Ferrari Testarossa with a custom blue-and-pink paint job, is the pop-up's centerpiece and is on sale for $1.3 million. The car is also the model for one of GTA 6's in-game supercars, the Grotti Cheetah. A Ferrari Testarossa, or in GTA 6 parlance, a Grotti Cheetah on display. It is for sale for $1.3 million. Robert Scammell/Business Insider "It's a cultural moment," JD said of the game's release. But he was skeptical of the prices. "From what I've seen, the prices are unreal for some of this merch," he said. The rain began again as we waited. I pulled my scarf over my head as a makeshift hood. Someone barged past and stepped on my foot. Behind us, a 10-year-old named Jonny began to play with the barriers, humming songs I recognized from TikTok. He was visiting London with his father, Jon, 45, from the Netherlands. The pair had spotted the pop-up the previous day and returned early the next morning, hoping to get inside. Jon and his son Jonny hoped to buy a hat during their visit to the pop-up. Georgia Hennessy Jonny had preordered GTA 6 months earlier and hoped to buy a hat. "He's nervous!" Jon told me. Further along the queue was David, 33, a Paris-based visitor to London. He said he had seen reports online of much longer waits and had decided to stop by only if the line was manageable. "I thought I might as well just come and check," he said. "I wasn't going to wait ages." When I asked if he was a fan, David shrugged. He had played “most of” the earlier games, he said, much like other people his age. David said he might buy a relatively inexpensive item, such as a T-shirt or cap, but had not come to resell merchandise. After I mentioned the booming resale market, though, he looked it up on his phone and showed JD and me an eBay listing: a keyring sold at the popup for $10.50 was being offered for $80. The three of us looked at the screen. "Wow," JD said. Shoppers were only allowed to purchase 3 items each, with no duplicates. Georgia Hennessy Inside, the stock shortage was plain to see. A tall man paced the shop floor clutching a roll of cash. He asked several assistants about the items he wanted, but each told him there had been no more deliveries. Eventually, he found an employee folding a football jersey — apparently the only one available on the floor. It was a return. The man unfurled it in the middle of the shop, only to discover that it was an extra-small women’s crop top. He scowled and put it back down. Some of the only GTA 6 T-shirts that were for sale at the Selfridges pop-up, Georgia Hennessy Among the items on display were a mirrored dish featuring an alligator wearing sunglasses and the words “Vice City Leonida,” a small silver spoon, and a razor-blade keyring. It was a more adult side of the pop-up than excited children outside might have expected. Some of the items leaned into the video game series' adult themes. Georgia Hennessy Elsewhere, JD got hold of what appeared to be the last baseball cap. Jon and Jonny, who had also hoped to buy one, approached the till empty-handed and began chatting to the smiling worker. Then, with something close to sleight of hand, a "burger-shot" visor appeared out of nowhere for them. They bought it immediately. Jon placed it on Jonny’s head, and the boy grinned. Many display cases were empty or had only one of each item displayed. Georgia Hennessy Earlier, as we waited outside, a group of children on a school trip, who looked about 7 or 8 years old, passed by the queue in high-visibility jackets. Several boys whooped and pointed at the pop-up. One literally jumped with excitement, his eyes wide. They seemed almost too young to know what GTA was . But that may be the point of the pop-up: GTA 6 is no longer just a game release for longtime players. It has become a retail event, a social-media moment, and, for a growing number of shoppers, an item to collect before someone else flips it online. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honored' to return as Nvidia CEO in first public remarks since exit
events.summary: Ousted Nvidia chief Jensen Huang said Tuesday that he would be ‘honored’ to return as CEO, in his first public remarks since resigning from the US chip giant after revelations of extramarital affairs. In a statement, Huang said he had witnessed “an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” and would return “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.” Huang acknowledged making “serious mistakes in my personal life,” adding that he was cooperating with the Nvidia board’s independent investigation. “I love our country, and I love NVIDIA,” he said. The machinations surrounding Huang have overshadowed expectations for more sky-high profits in the chipmaker’s latest earnings Tuesday. Interim CEO Colette Kress, appointed in the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation following revelations of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, faces a raft of questions over the chip giant’s outlook . The company has already formed a new board committee for oversight of national security issues. Kress’ reported reluctance to support Huang’s strategy to backstop and invest in many of the companies driving the technology will also be of particular focus: Any sign Nvidia is pulling back will have huge ramifications for the sector, and the global economy. — Prashant Rao

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Ride-hailing biz says stolen credentials allowed crooks to help themselves to driver's license data China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion 1 day ago US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough) 1 day ago Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric 1 day ago Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia 1 day ago Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 3 days ago Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's attorney general puts the number of victims at 149,346. Among the data the crooks got their hands on were images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers. Uber doesn't name the supplier in its filings with US state attorneys general, but told TechCrunch it was Fireworks AI, the inference outfit whose security woes we covered last week . According to a breach notification filed with Iowa's attorney general, Fireworks alerted Uber to the intrusion on October 9. Uber cut off the supplier's access to its data and, four days later, established that the attackers had accessed drivers' personal information on October 7. Uber had set up a dedicated cloud storage environment for the AI biz, complete with security monitoring overseen by its own cloud security team. Unfortunately for Uber and its drivers, the crooks were using legitimate credentials, so none of the alarms went off. The ride-hailing firm says those credentials couldn't be used to access its other systems, and says it has since revoked or changed the credentials associated with the supplier. Uber hasn't said why it handed images of thousands of driver's licenses to an AI inference outfit. The Register has put that question to both companies, and asked Uber if any drivers outside the US had their data exposed. Fireworks, which provides infrastructure for developers to run and fine-tune AI models, had a particularly miserable October. The company first disclosed a security incident on October 9 after discovering that someone had been using its internal credentials without permission. Fireworks initially said it had no evidence that the intruders had gotten their hands on personal information or customer datasets. The company was hacked again later that month and, on November 9, disclosed that some customer data had indeed been compromised. The AI biz acknowledged that attackers had accessed billing records, some customer datasets, and incomplete model weights. Productivity software maker Notion was among those affected, with some of its customers' conversations with its AI assistant exposed. Fireworks suspects the involvement of financially motivated criminals in the business of flogging unauthorized access to large language models. Whether the crooks have any plans for the haul of Uber drivers' personal information is unclear. Uber began notifying affected individuals on November 10, more than a month after learning of the breach. It's offering victims free credit monitoring and fraud assistance, though drivers have just 90 days from the date of their letter to sign up. This isn't Uber's first brush with cybercriminals in recent months. In August, the ride-hailing giant's logistics arm, Uber Freight, confirmed a break-in after the Helix extortion crew claimed to have made off with almost a million files, including data pilfered from mailboxes and OneDrive accounts.

events.title: Election-winning student movement enters Serbia’s new parliament
events.summary: Hundreds hail Student List lawmakers as the new parliament meets for the first time. Following the October 25 vote that upended Serbia’s political landscape, the new parliament is meeting for the first time in Belgrade. The vote redrew Serbia’s parliamentary map as a grassroots, student-led movement won the largest single share, removing President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). The Student List group was backed by 2.3 million citizens, altering the previous parliamentary arithmetic and balance of power. It holds a majority with 140 parliamentary seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with the Serbian Progressive Party’s 104. Tuesday’s session is chaired by the oldest member of parliament until a new speaker is elected, assisted by the four youngest MPs from the largest electoral lists. Hundreds of supporters cheered the new lawmakers as they entered the National Assembly. The new speaker could be announced later on Tuesday. The formal agenda follows a clear legal framework: verifying parliamentary mandates based on a report by the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), taking the solemn oath of office, electing the speaker and deputy speakers, appointing the secretary-general, and forming parliamentary committees and permanent delegations to international bodies. But beyond legal formalities, the political atmosphere is complex and large sections of the public have high expectations. Political analyst Djordje Vukadinovic told Al Jazeera, “Everyone is eagerly awaiting it. I would avoid making any predictions, because with the current opposition structure, you never know what might happen or what stance they will take.” He added, “What I do know is that this is only the beginning of establishing a new government, and I believe not everything will be wrapped up today.” Ahead of the session, a group of students wrote to the new lawmakers, reminding them of their “serious” responsibilities. “All of you are becoming members of parliament in the highest legislative body of the Republic of Serbia for the first time. And only that. Nothing more. The fact that the highest state offices have for decades been presented as ‘comfortable armchairs’ is a systemic flaw. The people elected you. We are the people. You are the people. Act accordingly,” warned the Student Plenum of the Higher School of Civil Engineering and Geodesy in Belgrade in an open letter. Aleksandar Cupic, an incoming Student List MP and an assistant professor in engineering, said new lawmakers must demonstrate institutional maturity. “We do not plan to speak about our candidate for five or 10 hours, because that is neither in the spirit of the values we will represent nor is it rational. We owe it to the citizens to proceed with electing the speaker of parliament,” Cupic told reporters ahead of the session. He said political groups had been consulting one another in a more moderate atmosphere than reports have suggested. But on Tuesday, tensions were seen outside parliament. A woman threw yoghurt over Lidija Vukicevic, a well known actress who supports the SNS, outside parliament and the crowd booed Vucic as he walked in. The Serbian actress and former MP Lidija Vukicevic, who is backing the ruling SNS party, had yoghurt poured over her as she arrived at Serbia’s National Assembly for its first session following elections won by a student-led opposition movement. The swearing-in session marks the start of a critical political countdown – a 90-day constitutional deadline to elect a new government. Should that expire without parliament voting in a new cabinet, Serbia’s constitution mandates the dissolution of the National Assembly and the calling of snap parliamentary elections. The developments are being watched across the region, as well as in European and global political circles. Observers say the new political leaders will have to govern the state and rebuild sustainable cooperation with neighbouring countries and the European Union – ties that have been strained in recent years. Echoing that point, Student List representative Aleksandar Baucal told the international EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels that a peaceful transfer of power is only the start of a complex array of work. “Changing power through non-violent and democratic means is only the first step,” Baucal said in Brussels. “Serbia now faces the task of rebuilding institutions that will prevent the personalisation of power and serve all citizens, regardless of who they voted for. I am convinced that from now on, the news coming out of Serbia will be largely positive.” In a similar vein, the European Democratic Party (EDP) weighed in on the eve of the parliamentary session. “Serbia must now heal the wounds of recent years through truth, justice and accountability … we sincerely hope a new chapter of freedom, democracy and reconciliation will begin,” the EDP said, adding that the session will test whether Serbia is ready for institutional reform.

events.title: UAE’s Al Tajir family sells Scottish ‘ghost’ golf course to Gleneagles
events.summary: A Scottish championship standard golf resort which has never opened to the public has been sold by its UAE owners to its neighbour, the Ryder Cup venue Gleneagles Hotel. Gleneagles West, known as gWest, in Perthshire, was put up for sale in September by the UAE’s Al Tajir family and has now been sold for an undisclosed sum. Mahdi Al Tajir, who in 1971 became the first UAE ambassador to the UK, was named the richest man in Scotland by The Sunday Times in 2013 and owns the Highland Spring water company which is based nearby. The family bought the land in 2007, completing its tournament-standard golf course two years later but barely a shot has been played at the private-gated resort in the years since. A combination of the financial crisis, the Scottish independence debate and referendum, Brexit and Covid-19 meant the family felt the time had never been quite right to take it to the next stage of investment. The 18th-century-inspired clubhouse remains a shell and development of the rest of the resort – it has permission for up to 170 residential plots, a hotel and spa, leisure and entertainment facilities and staff accommodation – was shelved. Gleneagles Hotel is owned by Mumbai-born London businessman Sharan Pasricha. He founded hotel company Ennismore in 2011, buying The Hoxton in London's Shoreditch in 2012 and Gleneagles in 2015. A Gleneagles representative told The Courier newspaper, which first reported the sale: “The Gleneagles Hotel has acquired a neighbouring expanse of Perthshire countryside, bordering the hotel and its iconic King’s and Queen’s Courses. “Surrounded by the rolling Ochil Hills and breath-taking scenery, this land shares the same natural beauty and character that has defined The Gleneagles Hotel for over a century. “Nestled within this landscape is a golf course quietly whispered about, one of the lesser-known treasures of Perthshire. The acquisition offers an opportunity to extend our stewardship of this remarkable landscape that has always been integral to the spirit of the hotel. “We look forward to sharing more as our plans take shape, guided by the same care and consideration that have shaped this special place for over a century.” At the time the resort went on sale, Euan Kelly, partner at Knight Frank Edinburgh, described it as a “once-in-a-lifetime asset: a substantial consented resort development site, with a golf course designed by a celebrated architect, in one of Scotland’s most prestigious leisure locations”. Course architect David McLay Kidd designed the championship-standard course and described the resort as “the best inland site I’ve ever seen for a golf course”. It sits in one of Scotland’s best-known golf and leisure corridors, to the west of Gleneagles between Perth and Stirling. The UK’s golf industry generated revenue of around £2.7 billion ($3.64 billion) in 2024/25, which is expected to rise to £3 billion for 2025/26. There are about 560 courses in Scotland – one fifth of the total in the UK. Speaking in 2020, Mr Al Tajir’s son, Mohsin, said: “You want to invest. The next phase of gWest is another £50, £60, maybe £100 million. And as a family we're not willing to put that sort of money in if we don't know what the future is.” He said with concerns that taxes would go up, rather than Scotland becoming a tax haven if independence were to happen, “maybe it's not the place I need to put my money”.

events.title: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing
events.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook's attorney gave the strongest signal yet that Cook will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry." President Donald Trump's "decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf. The "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation" in a hearing, Lowell wrote. Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook 's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook. The committee established last month by President Donald Trump , who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf. "Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday. The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties. While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name." Jensen Huang slated to appear before House panels Dec. 1; Nvidia lawyer due to testify Dec. 2 Republicans outspent Democrats in record 2026 midterm ad blitz But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett . Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3. He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome." Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue." Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing. "Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote. "Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote. Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote. The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter. Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden . Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September. Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal. The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."
