events.title: Jensen Huang open to Nvidia return in first statement since resignation
events.summary: Jensen Huang on Tuesday indicated he is willing to return as chief executive at Nvidia if the company's board of directors ask him to do so. In his first public remarks since resigning last week, Mr Huang said he was aware of the push from inside and outside the company for his return, and said he would "be honoured to to answer to answer these calls and return as CEO". "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO," Mr Huang said. "Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. Nvidia is a once-in-a-generation company." Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an… — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026 US media have reported that Nvidia's board of directors has no interest in Mr Huang returning after his affair with a technology executive purported to be have ties to China's intelligence services, which has caused considerable fallout for the world's most second-most valuable company by market capitalisation. The woman, Alice Huang , was previously chief executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which is under investigation by the US for allegedly smuggling chips to China. Megaspeed denies the allegations. Adding to the harm were accusations that Mr Huang knowingly tried to circumvent laws designed to prevent certain US technology from being used in China. US President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday he would like to see Mr Huang return. Mr Huang has also agreed to appear for transcribed interviews with three US House of Representatives committees on December 1, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said in a statement. Nvidia's general counsel will appear before the committees on December 2. "The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," said US Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford. Mr Huang said he is committed to co-operating with the Nvidia board's independent investigation. "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," he said. Nvidia 's board of directors earlier on Tuesday said it had formed a committee to oversee its security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. Mr Huang's affair has rocked Washington politics, particularly among hawkish members of Congress who say such a relationship could have given China access to Nvidia's most advanced AI chips . The US has banned the sale of those chips to China, citing national security concerns. Nvidia's existing national security and global trade compliance teams will report directly to the newly established national security and export control oversight committee, and to the interim chief executive, Colette Kress. "Nvidia recognises that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and super intelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said in a statement. “As the world’s leading advanced computing company, Nvidia has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges." The announcement came a day after the US Commerce and Justice departments revealed they had initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for possible export control breaches. “While we don't typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting,” the statement said. Joint Statement from Department of Commerce and Department of Justice on Megaspeed Investigation. pic.twitter.com/aAdtN9aDfF — U.S. Department of Commerce (@CommerceGov) November 17, 2026 The agencies said investigators at the Commerce Department in May 2025 requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to the Singapore-based company. Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025. That same month, agents from the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, along with law-enforcement officials in Singapore, conducted an in-person check at Megaspeed and interviewed Ms Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead in Megaspeed's criminal investigation, they said. Earlier on Monday, the Bureau of Industry and Security released an interim final rule tightening access to advanced AI chips and servers. The department said the rule was designed to ensure existing restrictions on access to sensitive US technology would not be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries. “The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes, while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” the agency said. The announcement came as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced growing criticism his agency did not do enough to curb exports of advanced AI chips to China.

events.title: ‘They learn the job doing the job’: the project helping UK’s Neets into work
events.summary: Labour’s plan to get young unemployed people into work involves overhaul of welfare support, but for those with disabilities, specialist help is crucial When Rory Bowman finished school he joined the cohort of almost a million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – around the country. The 21-year-old has autism and said he was exhausted after struggling for support in mainstream education for years. He didn’t think he could manage university, but couldn’t find a job or training that would accommodate his neurodivergence. Then he came across Project Search, a nationwide year-long transition-to-work programme that helps young people with learning disabilities or autism move into permanent paid employment. It changed his life and now Bowman is thriving in his work as a personal trainer at Pure Gym. “Getting actual experience in workplaces, understanding how they function, what would be expected of me and how to interact with people, it was exactly what I needed,” he said. “And having a job coach who does half the jump with you.” Alan Milburn’s report on how to get the UK’s Neets into work has recommended an overhaul of welfare support for young people , including moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits and on to a new “youth allowance”. In return, eligible 18-to-24-year-olds will be guaranteed a fully funded, six-month job if they have been claiming universal credit for 12 months. Milburn said this was about prioritising “their longer-term life chances” over “immediate shorter-term finances”. Interns and staff at the Project Search course run by Phoenix College in Tower Hamlets welcomed the bold commitment to get more young people into work, but there were concerns about cutting support and the quality of job opportunities being offered. Bowman said he disagreed with the proposal to cut benefits like the personal independence payment (Pip) for young people to help push them into work. “I think alongside any workplace initiatives, Pip is still absolutely a must-have. I would argue it’s more important to have if you’re going to be engaging in a structured programme – for me, things like noise-cancelling headphones are essential,” he said. “I need that funding more to enter the world of work than I did when I was sat at home playing video games.” Staff said getting young people, especially those with extra needs, into a long-term sustainable job wasn’t as simple as filling a vacancy – many students need holistic support and extra help even once they’re in work. “We’ve been noticing a lot more interns coming in with serious mental health conditions and that requires extra help,” said Renato Marques, principal of Phoenix College. “But here, even for our very high-needs students, everything is geared towards getting them into a workplace. “They learn the job doing the job. A lot of courses say they are preparing students for work, but they are not taking them into work.” Rather than studying at a traditional campus, their interns learn in classrooms hosted in partner businesses – including a global law firm, a large distribution company and Queen Mary University of London – and they rotate through daily 9am to 3pm work placements. Over the past six years, 68% of students ended up in employment at the end of the course – four times higher than the national average rate of disabled young people who are Neet. All graduates also have access to a follow-on service they can use for advice in the first few years of their career. For students with higher levels of need, the college developed a pre-supported internship combining two days of workplace experience – supported by an on-hand job coach – with extra training in social skills and independent travel. Osman Osman, assistant principal for Project Search, said Milburn’s plan would only work with better paid and resourced careers advisers in schools, and high-quality work experience and job offers. “You see careers advisers managing schools with a thousand kids, and they’re expected to meet with every single one, and it’s a very, very hard job to actually get those young people work-ready,” he said. “We spend a long time building our young people’s confidence and skillset in the field they’re interested in. “And any job offer has to be meaningful placements because inset days, taster sessions or a week’s work experience often lead to no actual outcomes for young people.” Tawhid Ahmed, 21, said finding work or apprenticeships after finishing school had been overwhelming – he now works at Phoenix College after building confidence and social skills on the course. “I have a learning disability, and it was hard because I’ve been rejected for so many jobs. The fact that I was able to find Project Search really was a blessing,” he said. “Now I do admin and I have really good colleagues who help and support me. I want to help students face challenges that I’ve faced as well.

events.title: Hoping for Britain to rejoin the EU with Andy Burnham? You may be waiting a long time | Timothy Garton Ash
events.summary: Hoping for Britain to rejoin the EU with Andy Burnham? You may be waiting a long time The PM’s first big speech on the UK and Europe was cautious and disappointing. Don’t expect any great leaps towards a new deal E ver since Andy Burnham became the British prime minister this summer, people all over Europe have been asking me one question: “Will the UK rejoin the EU?” Sometimes they add: “And if so, when?” None of the intermediate options between the current hard Brexit and Brejoin are of any interest at all to most other Europeans. Measured against these great expectations, Burnham’s first big speech on Britain and Europe, delivered on Monday evening amid all the pomp and circumstance the City of London could furnish, must be considered a disappointment. It was both a cautious and a curiously old-fashioned speech. Cautious in diagnosis: his bold statement that “we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years” was immediately followed by “the hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain”. (So a soft Brexit would be fine?) Cautious in prescription: beyond the welcome modest steps to be agreed at this Friday’s UK-EU summit (easier access for food and agricultural products, linking our carbon emissions markets, creating a youth mobility scheme), anything this government does during the term of the current parliament will stay within Keir Starmer’s “red lines” (no rejoining the customs union, single market or freedom of movement). Burnham will, however, explore “options for our long-term relationship” with the EU, “to inform decisions in the next parliament”. Unless we have an early election, that means not before 2029. This caution is easily explained. Roughly half of his cabinet doesn’t want even to mention Brexit. Roughly half of his MPs are in constituencies that voted leave in 2016. The country at large thinks Brexit was a mistake but dreads the prospect of rerunning the debate and isn’t sure it would vote for rejoining if the UK didn’t have its previous opt-outs, including from the euro and the Schengen free travel area. For all the great expectations that were raised, Burnham himself had actually only said in interviews that he hoped Britain would rejoin the EU in his lifetime. He’s a robust 56-year-old, so that could take us to about 2060. More surprising was how old-fashioned his speech was, albeit delivered with demotic verve. Here, for starters, was the weary old trope of Britain always having to “lead” in whatever it does (nine references to leading, if my count is correct). Then there’s the curious way in which Britain’s commitment to European defence and support for Ukraine is totally divorced from all the other dimensions of European security and strength, which self-evidently involve the EU. Instead, there’s a relentless narrow focus on what’s good for Britain economically. At the heart of his speech was what he called the “Makerfield test” – that is, what would deliver economic benefits for the hard-pressed people of his constituency of Makerfield, which in 2016 voted to leave the EU. Oddest of all was the way he harked back to a 1948 speech in which Winston Churchill conjured Britain’s position at the intersection of three majestic circles. Gliding over the fact that the first circle Churchill mentioned was “the British Commonwealth and Empire ”, Burnham talked at some length about the Commonwealth before coming to Europe. For obvious reasons (don’t offend the egomaniac in the White House!), he also glided over the fact that Churchill’s second circle was “the English-speaking world”, with its superpower being the US. Yet if we are highlighting, as Burnham did, how the world has changed since 2016, then the drastic change under Donald Trump in the US approach to its allies, including Britain, should be top of the list. Oh, and by the way, Churchill’s third circle was “United Europe”, which he talked of in visionary terms long before it ever existed. Now, with something called the European Union , much of Europe is at least halfway there. Unlike in Churchill’s speech, in fact unlike in everything that great British and European leader said and did, here there was no sense of a wider European story in which Britain has always played an important part. Instead, Burnham spoke of Britain’s reset “with Europe”, as though Britain were not part of Europe and “Europe” only means the EU. The most European things in London’s Guildhall on Monday evening were the Polish vodka served by the Polish-South-African-British lord mayor of London, Bronek Masojada, and a few words in Dutch that he addressed to the prime minister’s wife, Marie-France van Heel. But enough about the words. What of the actions to follow? I’m not sure how long these conversations with EU partners about “options” need to last. An hour or two might suffice. For the EU has repeatedly spelled out the current ones as it sees them.

events.title: We can't afford to hire under-25s, say firms. Will Milburn plans help?
events.summary: Published 17 November 2026, 15:20 GMT Lowering employers' National Insurance (NI) payments for those between 21 and 24, and cash incentives to take on some workers are among proposals put forward in Alan Milburn's report to get more 18-24 year-olds working. Many companies have complained that recent increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to take on staff. We talked to firms and business groups about the issues they face when hiring younger works and what they make of the proposals. Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says he cannot justify the extra cost of training up new staff Cutting NI costs is "right in the sweet spot of what firms need to hit the hire button", said the Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC). The Milburn report proposes NI thresholds could be raised over the next five years, from £5,000 to £10,000 for those aged 21 to 24, and suggests prioritising the retail and hospitality sectors. Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says the high costs he faces currently make it difficult to employ young people with no work experience. "My labour costs are already over 45%. We simply cannot justify the extra cost to put on an extra staff member to train someone up for three months," he says. "In hospitality our margins have been squeezed and squeezed and squeezed" As a result, he says it currently makes more sense to employ someone who already has experience. Major report proposes welfare changes, apprenticeships and tax cuts to help 440,000 young people into work At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 8 hours ago Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, says the recommendation to raise the threshold is "the right one" and "would be an immediate shot in the arm for job creation". But the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) argues the Milburn report does not go far enough in tackling costs facing businesses. It says while the NI proposal is welcome, the change should be wider than just retail and hospitality, otherwise it "risks adding complexity and blocking off potential career paths". Ally Fir says if a state scheme was running she'd "jump on it right away" Other proposals put forward by the Milburn review include cash incentives to employ younger workers. Employers who take on any young person who has been Neet - not in education, employment or training - for six months should receive a £3,000 payment, and small businesses - with less than 50 employees - that do so should receive an extra £2,000 There would also be an extra £2,000 payment if the young person has been in care or is disabled. Ally Fir runs a bookshop in Westbourne, alongside her partner Matt, and thinks more state support is needed. She says incentivised schemes for small business "would help us to employ more, especially young people. If a scheme like that was going we'd jump on it right away." Fir says she gets job applications "every single day". She'd like to take more people on but "it is the cost of employing people that makes that impossible". Tom Parsons has already had experience of using government schemes to employ young people at his design consultancy, Aetha, in Poole, Dorset. The Kickstart Scheme in 2020 meant he could take on two young people in fully funded six-month job placements offering 25 hours a week. Tom Parsons says the old Kickstart Scheme was a game-changer for those employed under it "One of them stayed with us for five years and the other one I think about three years. And it completely changed the game for them," Tom told the BBC. "So if there was a scheme like that, again, that would really help us." He says he wants to employ young people but costs remain a huge barrier. Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds? Published 7 hours ago Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036 Published 6 hours ago One of the government's flagship employment rights reforms risks weakening the hiring of young people, according to Milburn's report. Ministers are abolishing what they call ''exploitative'' zero-hours contracts and replacing them with guaranteed hours contracts which would be based on the number of hours people normally work. Much of the detail is yet to be finalised but the Employment Rights Act is due to be enacted next year. Milburn is concerned that the changes could cause problems "at a time when the youth labour market is already weak'.' The REC said companies were "particularly worried" over the guaranteed hours measure. It added that addressing the Neets problem gave ministers "the perfect opportunity" to reconsider the issue. Young people should have a legal right to a route into education, training or work, and would be supported to do so under an "opportunity guarantee", Milburn has proposed. This could help firms which are struggling to recruit. Thirty-five-year-old Dean Greene, a sales director at waste management facility Williams Environmental, says it's tricky finding staff.

events.title: I left my hometown for a dream opportunity in Los Angeles. Within a year, I was back in the Midwest.
events.summary: The decision to leave my hometown at 22 was a no-brainer. Jennifer Yuma I left my Nebraska hometown for an opportunity in Los Angeles, but had a tough time there. When I learned my dad was struggling with his health, it felt important for us to be together. I moved back, and five years later, I'm still here — and I realized there's no rush to leave home . Leaving my home state of Nebraska wasn't hard for me. As much as I appreciated the town that raised me, by my early 20s, I'd outgrown it. My medium-sized town wasn't necessarily a place I felt particularly attached to. My parents both fled to the United States as political refugees during the Congo War in 1997. The main reason my father chose Nebraska as a home was that he knew one Congolese person in the state, and nobody else in the entire country. As I got older, the gratitude I felt for my parents' journey sparked my desire to live up to their American dream. When I received a prestigious internship opportunity at age 22, saying yes was a no-brainer — even though I'd have to move to Los Angeles with just two months' notice. My future in Los Angeles was right in front of me; all I had to do was push that door open. I figured that if it didn't work out, I'd move on to the next major city . I never expected to come back to Nebraska. Moving to LA was a dream come true, but the reality was tough I loved living and working in LA, but I felt like I was drowning. Jennifer Yuma By the time I moved to LA, I was ready for a fresh start. I'd spent my last two years of college attending classes from an apartment due to COVID-19 social-distancing guidelines , which only made me feel more claustrophobic. I was also excited to relocate to a more diverse city, one where more people would look like me and think like me, and where I'd likely have more opportunities as an aspiring writer. I connected with another intern who agreed to be my roommate and found our apartment in LA. In the spring of my senior year, I packed up my bags — with only enough savings to buy my plane ticket — and moved to Los Angeles. My family helped me pay for my security deposit, and I was able to cover the first month's rent with early graduation funds. As I expected, I loved LA, but a month in, I was embarrassingly broke and struggling to get around without a car. After unsuccessfully navigating an unpredictable bus system and spending all of my money on Ubers for red-carpet events in place of groceries, I realized I was drowning … but this was still my dream. I wanted to make it work so badly. My parents and I both kept secrets from each other I didn't mention my struggles to my parents, even though I desperately needed their help, emotionally and financially. They were telling everyone that this — me graduating from college , getting an internship, and thriving — is why they came to the US in the first place. I wanted them to feel that pride, even if the truth was a bit more complicated. There are so many things I love about being a child of immigrants, from the duality of culture and language to my values, like accepting all people and working hard. On the flip side, though, there's pressure to live up to high expectations because of the struggles my parents endured to come to America. They came to the US without the language, the money, or the resources — and I couldn't make it in another state? I didn't consider the fact that they didn't put those expectations on me; I did. While I was hiding my hardships from them, I found out they were keeping something from me, too. About halfway through my internship, during a weekly family catch-up over the phone, my mother mentioned that my father was dealing with severe health issues. After learning about my family's struggles 1,500 miles away, my mental health declined, along with my work commitments. The realization hit: My father was sick, and I wasn't there. He didn't tell me because he didn't want me to worry; meanwhile, I didn't tell him my shortcomings because I didn't want him to worry about me. In December, when I was planning to stay in Los Angeles, I booked the first flight back home to Nebraska to check on my dad. I moved back to Nebraska, and I'm content here for now Living here as an adult has brought me closer to my parents. Jennifer Yuma When I left Los Angeles, I had every intention to return. I hoped I'd find another job in the same field after my internship ended, or see where else the city would take me. The longer I stayed in Nebraska, though, the happier I felt to be spending time with my family, even if it halted my career aspirations. It's now been five years, and I'm still in my hometown . Since then, my dad's health has improved, but I want to stay close to my parents for as long as I can. Although I am itching to move again, I've found myself growing into the person I have always wanted to be and becoming closer to my family in a way I didn't prioritize when I was younger. I think I needed to stick around a bit longer to fully realize that. I still hope to eventually move somewhere else for my career and see my dreams actualized again. I'm not in a rush, though. When I leave my hometown next, I know it will probably be for good, so why not stay for a little bit longer? The goal of making my parents proud has not changed. But I believe I still am, by being here. Read the original article on Business Insider

Mckenna Grace turned herself into the arena with one of her gowns. It's time to go back to Panem. On Friday, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" finally hits theaters. Based on Suzanne Collins' prequel novel " Sunrise on the Reaping, " the film focuses on the experience of a young Haymitch Abernathy during the 50th Hunger Games. Joseph Zada is stepping into the role Woody Harrelson originated in "The Hunger Games" trilogy, though Harrelson is set to appear in the film alongside Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson . Anticipation has been building for months, and it's only heightened in recent weeks as the film's stars have walked red carpets in outfits that pay homage to "The Hunger Games." Elle Fanning has channeled Effie Trinket's signature whimsy, while Mckenna Grace brought the arena itself to life with one of her gowns. Take a look at the wildest outfits stars of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" have worn to promote the film. In Paris, Joseph Zada stepped out in a power suit. events.title: I've been to 25 national parks and forests around the US. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon is the most underrated.
events.summary: Business Insider's reporter has visited both rims of the Grand Canyon — the North was more unique and less crowded. Joey Hadden/Business Insider If you want a crowd-free experience at the Grand Canyon, go north. The South Rim is often packed, while the North Rim gets far fewer visitors. I visited the North Rim and felt like I'd discovered a hidden gem in the tourist hot spot. I've never felt smaller than I did sitting on the edge of the Grand Canyon , a natural world wonder visible from space . I've been to the national park three times. Each visit was as awe-inspiring as the last. I'll never get tired of the views and will travel back again and again. With expansive views of eroded rocks that formed over millions of years, it's easy to see why the Grand Canyon is one of the most visited national parks in the US and has been overcrowded in recent years. The park historically averages 4.5 million visitors a year, according to the National Park Service . In the summer, I've seen people pack themselves onto the edges of the canyon, obstructing views of one of the most beautiful places in the country — but only on the South Rim. While more than 90% of visitors go to the South Rim, only 280,000 trek to the northern side of the canyon each year on average, according to the NPS. In my experience, the North Rim is the park's best-kept secret. I visited the South Rim once in 2022 and the North Rim twice — most recently in 2019. While the South Rim was packed with cars and crowds when I went, I've only had peaceful, remote experiences on the North Rim that take me out of the stress of my busy lifestyle. It's a hidden gem in the otherwise crowded national park. The North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park is one of my favorite places in the US. Joey Hadden/Business Insider From Yosemite in California , to Zion in Utah , to Acadia in Maine, I've visited many US national parks. Each has surprised me with unique geographic features and diverse plant life. But the North Rim of the Grand Canyon amazed me the most. With a higher elevation than the South Rim, it has cooler temperatures, snowy winters, and more plants and trees. Unlike the more popular South Rim entrances, which are open year-round, the North Rim entrance is only accessible from May to October for overnight stays and through November for day trips (depending on the weather). The North Rim of the Arizona national park isn't as easy to access as the South Rim. Google Maps The northern side of the national park borders Kaibab National Forest . It's harder to reach the North Rim than the South Rim from other popular destinations in Arizona, like Phoenix and Sedona, because of the roadway. The last time I went to the North Rim, I was coming from Sedona, and it was a four-and-a-half-hour drive. But I experienced fewer crowds and saw a unique perspective of the canyons. Wild Horizons/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Although it has fewer visitors, I expected to see some crowds at the North Rim since it is smaller than the South Rim and has only one entrance (the South Rim has two). I was thrilled to be wrong: the North Rim entrance had no line during my July 2019 visit. Although some clusters of people were at viewpoints, I rarely encountered other hikers on trails. Outside the national park, I found the most beautiful campsite I'd ever seen — and it cost nothing to pitch my tent there. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The North Rim has fewer lodging options than the South Rim, but I found a free campsite outside the park that was unlike any other I'd been to. I discovered it on freecampsites.net while planning my first trip to the North Rim in 2015. I was so impressed that I returned for my 2019 trip. The site is in Kaibab National Forest's Locust Point area and borders the canyon's rim. There are miles of rough forest roads on the way. I distinctly remember getting out of the car to remove large branches during one of my visits. But I thought it was worth the trek when I pitched my tent about a yard away from the edge. It's important to note that this is a remote campsite without bathrooms. All that's provided is a fire pit right next to the edge — be careful not to fall. From my campsite, I saw a Grand Canyon landscape unlike any I'd seen on Instagram. Joey Hadden/Business Insider My campsite was right off of Rainbow Rim Trail, which goes from the North Rim to the South Rim. The views were mesmerizing. While the South Rim is home to the canyon's most iconic scenes that are mostly red and brown, the North Rim is lush with forests. The canyon beneath my campsite was filled with rich green trees that stood in stark contrast to the warm-toned canyon rocks. Inside the national park, I avoided looking up popular hikes and simply stopped when I saw trails. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Most of these hikes were entirely free of people during my visits. Aside from whistles of birds and breezes through the tall trees, the trails were quiet. I had truly detached experiences from the rest of the world. These hikes took me to unique rock formations that made me wonder how they came to be. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The formation that stumped me the most was this rock with a triangular hole near the top, towering over the surrounding cliffs. The North Rim's peaceful atmosphere and surprising landscape helped me reach a place of presence I'd never before experienced at a national park. Joey Hadden/Business Insider During most of my national park experiences, crowds have made it difficult to live in the moment. But sitting on the edge of the North Rim, I easily forgot about work and the daily stressors of my busy lifestyle. My mind was clear up there — and I can't wait to return. Although my last visit was in 2019, the North Rim remains significantly less popular than the South Rim. I can only hope for more isolated experiences in the future. events.title: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
events.summary: Builder confidence in the single-family housing market fell four points to 25, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index. In November, 46% of builders cut prices, the highest share in the post-Covid era, according to the report. Buyer traffic fell two points to 16, its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020. Sentiment among U.S. homebuilders dropped to the lowest level in 14 years, as higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence, led to more builders cutting prices. Builder confidence in the single-family housing market fell four points to 25, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, or HMI. That is the lowest since April 2012, when the market was just recovering from the housing crash and foreclosure crisis. Last November, the index stood at 38. Mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, but surged higher again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed hit 7.51% on Monday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Last year at this time it was 6.38%. Of the HMI's three components, the index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, and future sales expectations dropped two points to 30. Buyer traffic declined two points to 16 — its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020. "Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today's economy," Bill Owens, NAHB chairman and a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a release. "Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction." More builders are now cutting prices as they try to get buyers in the door. In November, 46% of them reduced prices, the highest share in the post-Covid period, according to the report. The share of builders using sales incentives also hit a post-Covid high of 68%. That was the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders used them. "The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability," Robert Dietz, NAHB's chief economist, said in the release. "Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back." In the three-month moving averages for regional HMI scores, the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27, and the West posted a three-point decline to 23. events.title: Federal Reserve's Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing
events.summary: Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome WASHINGTON -- Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome. The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook's lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration initially demanded for Nov. 6 . Trump administration officials have demanded that Cook appear before the committee to address allegations she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed's board of governors, a charge she denies. President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president's efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed's independence and reflect Trump's desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs. “Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook's lawyer, wrote in a letter released Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.” In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that "the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design.” Trump officials have threatened to move ahead with the hearing even without Cook, and in a Nov. 3 letter said that the three-member committee “reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you” for not participating. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The unusual “committee of inquiry” set up by the White House consists of Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, whom Trump appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s pick for Labor Secretary. The Supreme Court said in a footnote to its June ruling that Trump could try again to fire her if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry is an effort to meet those conditions. Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor “for cause,” but the Supreme Court didn’t address whether Cook’s actions met that standard. The committee will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, the White House has said. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Intune feature blocks normal sign-ins without wiping data, while another test build drops Offline Maps settings Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’ now Hackers smash 'n' grab AI vendor: Take off with license data of Uber drivers 3 hours ago 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour 6 hours ago Opinion pollster Ipsos 'fesses up to 'cybersecurity incident' 8 hours ago Up to 99% of UK civil servants rely on Microsoft for comms, minister admits 8 hours ago A new experimental Windows 11 build previews security features including an Intune-controlled Remote Lock, while a beta build clears away another relic from the halcyon days of Windows Phone. The security changes include viewing and individually removing passkeys stored on FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) security keys, plus a preview of the Microsoft Pluton Cryptographic Provider. For enterprise administrators, though, Remote Lock is the main attraction. Finding a lost Windows device has been around for years, and you can also remotely wipe a device to prevent data from falling into the wrong hands. Remote Lock lets an administrator lock a managed device through Intune without wiping it. The instruction takes effect at the device's next check-in. Windows signs out of every active session, hides every sign-in option, and shows a locked screen. The lock survives restarts and the device going offline – only an administrator can lift it remotely. Microsoft's documentation spells out the restriction: "There is no offline or local unlock. No PIN, password, local admin, or web sign-in works on a locked device; unlock arrives only through Intune." Once the lock is applied, even stolen credentials won't restore access through the normal sign-in screen. The user's account itself is not affected; this applies only to the specific device. Though still in preview, the feature will allow IT teams to respond non-destructively to a report of a missing device. It doesn't erase data or isolate the device from the network (Microsoft directs admins to other Intune controls if that is required). The lock doesn't block Safe Mode, Windows Recovery Environment, or booting from external media. Microsoft advises keeping BitLocker enabled to protect the data. Now for the beta build, where Microsoft, in time-honored fashion, gives and takes away. The latest Windows Insider build hammers another nail into the coffin of Microsoft Maps. The Maps app was removed from the Microsoft Store and made nonfunctional in July 2025. Now Offline Maps settings are following it out, as Microsoft retires the Windows UWP Map control and Windows Maps platform APIs. The original Maps app dates back to Windows Phone 7 and appeared on the desktop with Windows 8. It continued through subsequent versions before Microsoft stopped preinstalling it with Windows 11 version 24H2. For those with a nostalgic streak, it's another piece of Windows Phone disappearing off the map. ® Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’ If you design a test to find misalignment, you will find misalignment America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states Harvard study claims emissions attributable to datacenters are two to three times higher than in 2018 The future of datacenters depends on behind-the-meter energy generation PARTNER CONTENT: PARTNER CONTENT: Hyperscalers and colos have distinct power strategies, but for both, securing flexible, fast power relies on self-generated solutions Inspiring FOSS project Crosspoint Reader has lessons about tech, communities, and LLMs Cheap tiny e-readers and the perils of LLM-generated drive-by pull requests – plus much more We don't need no education platform evolution.

events.title: The 25 best places in the world to travel to in 2027, according to National Geographic
events.summary: Safari, Liwonde National Park, Malawi, Africa. Marka/Universal Images Group via Getty Images National Geographic released its annual list of the best places to travel to in 2027. It features 25 destinations across six continents, each offering different cultures and landscapes. From Ancient Mayan ruins to small maritime provinces, here are the top places to visit next year. From a total solar eclipse in Egypt to Grenada's 150th Spicemas carnival, 2027 is shaping up to be a bucket-list year for travel. In its annual "Best of the World" list for 2027, National Geographic picked 25 destinations across 22 countries and territories for travelers to consider for their next trip. This year's list includes major cities with big festivals and new museums, as well as smaller offbeat regions where travelers can get outdoors. Here are the 25 best travel destinations featured in National Geographic's 2027 list. Vestland, Norway The farming village of Dyrdal with its pretty white church on the shore of Naeroyfjord, a UNESCO world heritage fjord which is an arm of the Sognefjord. (Photo by: Martin Berry/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) : Martin Berry/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Vestland is known for its fjords, glaciers, waterfalls, and hikes, including Trolltunga, "troll's tongue," a rock ledge that sits above a lake. Bergen offers a break from the wilderness with its historic wharf, seafood, and restaurants. Direct flights to Bergen have become more commonplace, and the seven-hour overnight train from Oslo has become comfier, after Vy, the national railway company, installed convertible lie-flat seats. Penang, Malaysia GEORGETOWN, PENANG, MALAYSIA - 2025/04/21: People walk down a street in Georgetown, Malaysia. George Town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its rich cultural heritage and diverse architecture, attracting tourists with its unique blend of history and modernity. The tourism sector significantly contributes to the local economy, supporting traditional trades and boosting the overall economic growth of the region. (Photo by Stephen J. Boitano/LightRocket via Getty Images) Stephen J. Boitano/LightRocket via Getty Images Penang gives visitors a mix of George Town's heritage, street art, Chinese-Malay food, beaches, and rainforest. A new cable car is expected to open in 2027, which will take travelers from the botanic gardens to Penang Hill for views and hiking trails. Luxor, Egypt Hot air balloons are seeing during a ride over the ancient city of Luxor on September 10, 2017. / AFP PHOTO / KHALED DESOUKI (Photo credit should read KHALED DESOUKI/AFP via Getty Images) KHALED DESOUKI/AFP via Getty Images Luxor is home to some of Egypt's largest ancient sites, including Karnak Temple, the Valley of the Kings, and King Tutankhamun's tomb. It will be especially busy on August 2, 2027, when a total solar eclipse will darken the city for more than six minutes. Madison, Wisconsin State Street in Madison, Wisconsin, looking toward the state capitol building. (Photo by: Education Images/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) : Education Images/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Set between two lakes, Madison, Wisconsin, is known for its biking and walking routes, farmers markets, and more. In 2027, the LakeWay Project will begin adding trails and public space along Lake Monona's waterfront. Puerto Rico Sun setting over Castillo San Felipe del Morro in San Juan - Puerto Rico. (Photo by: Edwin Remsberg/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) : Edwin Remsberg/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Puerto Rico is known for its beaches, rainforests, Old San Juan, and mountain towns. National Geographic highlighted that visitors can take bomba and plena classes in Loíza, try fritters and seafood in Piñones, or visit ancient ceremonial sites and petroglyphs inland. Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland UNITED KINGDOM - APRIL 08: View of Caerlaverock castle, 13th century, Dumfries, Scotland, United Kingdom. (Photo by DeAgostini/Getty Images) DeAgostini/Getty Images This region of Scotland is a good choice for stargazing, biking, coastal walks, and castle visits. A new Scottish Dark Sky Observatory is set to open in 2027, while the Tour de France's Grand Départ will come to southern Scotland that July. Niigata, Japan Trees and snow are reflected on a river in a mountainous area in Yuzawa, Niigata Prefecture, Japan, on Tuesday, May. 7, 2019. For Japans growing flood of foreign tourists, one of the top internet search terms is onsen, the traditional hot springs where travelers have soaked since the days of the samurai. Now some of the worlds oldest businesses are attracting big new money. Photographer: Shiho Fukada/Bloomberg via Getty Images Shiho Fukada/Bloomberg via Getty Images Niigata is best known for deep snow, skiing, sake, and fermented foods. The 2027 Echigo-Tsumari Art Triennale will bring installations to abandoned schools, rice fields, tunnels, and villages across the prefecture. Chengdu, China Illuminated Anshun Bridge over the Jin River at night in the provincial capital of Chengdu in Sichuan, China. (Photo by: Arterra/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) : Arterra/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Visitors likely come to Chengdu for giant pandas and its spicy Sichuan food, but stay to learn about its ancient Shu kingdom. In 2027, Chengdu will mark 100 years since the discovery that led archaeologists to the civilization, and the Jinsha Site Museum will reopen after renovations. Pacific Coast Highway, California Rugged ocean view of Notley's Landing Big Sur off Route 1, PCH, Pacific Ocean and Sea rocks springtime and green grass, California. (Photo by: Joe Sohm/Visions of America/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) : Joe Sohm/Visions of America/Universal Images Group via Getty Images The Pacific Coast Highway is again open after a long closure near Big Sur, giving road-trippers access to its cliffs, beaches, redwoods, and coastal towns. In 2027, Laguna Beach will celebrate its 100th anniversary as an artists' colony, while Fort Bragg will debut a new redwood-inspired textile exhibition. events.title: Tech titans attempt their own recursive self-improvement
events.summary: Shelly’s view It rarely rains in Silicon Valley, but when it rains, it storms. Perhaps it’s the sogginess in the Bay, the post-midterms soul-searching, or the ethical questions underlying the Jensen Huang/Nvidia scandal (and the Save Jensen movement), but signs are emerging that the tech industry is — like its most famous product — developing the capacity for recursive self-improvement. “ Heroes have flaws, ” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti, when asked how he’s coming to terms with Nvidia’s chief resigning from the company he founded 33 years ago and built into the backbone of the AI ecosystem. Altman said he couldn’t answer whether he thought Huang should be allowed to come back to the helm at Nvidia, but admitted the whole episode has shaken the industry. He sounded similarly chastened about the AI referendum that swept over the US midterms: “There is this long-term question about what are people’s roles going to be in society, and what is the balance of power going to look like … between people and AI.” Altman and his peers seemed to share a new willingness to adapt to a volatile political environment — even as much of Washington turns hard on Huang and Nvidia, and US voters show little sign of laying down their pitchforks. We’ve been here before, of course: There were tech “reckonings” on everything from the #MeToo movement to social media and kids. But onstage and in unguarded moments, the most important people in the room here at Silicon Valley & The World seemed to be realizing that their problems are not just about optics or telling their story better. The question they face is whether they can build the next big thing with the people outside the Silicon Valley bubble. Notable Altman wasn’t the only CEO to defend Huang ; leaders from across the tech world defended the former Nvidia CEO at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World.

events.title: Investor Steve Eisman says the AI neocloud stocks are in 'big trouble' from Nvidia fallout
events.summary: Investor Steve Eisman said the so-called AI neocloud stocks will be the biggest losers from the unfolding Nvidia scandal. Nvidia was essentially a "virtual vertical holding company and it's unwinding," said Eisman of "Big Short" fame on CNBC's "Squawk Box ." "I think neoclouds are all in big trouble though because they are part of that vertical holding company and I think they're about to get ejected." Neoclouds, which used borrowed funds to build data centers, have been among the hardest-hit stocks during the recent pullback in the artificial intelligence trade. CoreWeave and Nebius are each down more than 50% the last three months. All eyes on Wall Street are on chipmaker Nvidia as it reports earnings on Tuesday after the bell while grappling with a potential Chinese espionage scandal. Founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday under a cloud of controversary revolving around his affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The Commerce Department has subsequently moved to close a loophole on China's remote use of data centers. Investors are worried as scrutiny increases on Nvidia's China revenue, it may pull back on its extensive financing that supported the AI industry. Frontier algorithm company Anthropic is expected to make its public debut on Thursday as concerns about the company's profitability potential linger amid the rapid and ongoing commodification of AI. Eisman said he doesn't think the much-ballyhooed offering is very important anymore to the AI trade because expectations have come down. "I don't think anybody really cares," the investor said. Instead, Eisman is focusing on how much Democrats will restrict data center building when they take control of Congress and various governorships in January. "I think the biggest issues by far are how much are, how much are local and state governments going to slow AI data center construction? Is it going to be 100% moratorium? That would obviously be — that would put the country into recession overnight. Or is it something like 10% to 30%?" he said. In the event of a 10% to 30% slowdown in data center construction, Eisman said the group of companies within the AI trade that he favors the most are the hyperscalers. "The group that makes out the best are the hyperscalers because they go cash flow positive again," he said. Correction: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday. An earlier version misstated the day.

events.title: Here's what Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told employees in a memo after earnings
events.summary: Disney's Josh D'Amaro has prioritized technology since becoming CEO. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Disney Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro thanked staffers and alluded to coming cuts after a strong earnings report. Disney has to "reimagine the way we work," D'Amaro said in a memo. See what else D'Amaro told employees. Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro expressed confidence to employees about the company's future in a Tuesday internal memo, while hinting at coming layoffs . "I'm more optimistic about Disney's future than I have ever been," D'Amaro told staffers in a memo, viewed by Business Insider, that was sent after the Mouse House exceeded revenue and earnings expectations in its October quarter. D'Amaro also said in the memo that Disney has to "reimagine the way we work" and that some changes will "impact people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company." Disney finance chief Hugh Johnston told CNBC that the company did "expect more layoffs" after three significant staff reductions so far in 2026. Disney said in its letter to shareholders on Tuesday that it expected to deliver $3 billion in annual savings by fiscal year 2029 from a cost-cutting program. The planned cuts come amid major investments in technology , including the decisions to hire a companywide tech chief from Character.AI and spend $60 million annually to hire 66 staffers from the chatbot startup, which filed for bankruptcy in October. This year, Disney has focused on unifying teams, including the marketing and brand units , and on bringing consumer products and games closer to the creative side. The Disney CEO said in his memo that these changes were done so that "the people building those experiences work directly with the teams creating our stories and characters." Read D'Amaro's entire memo to employees: Dear Fellow Employees and Cast Members, This morning, we reported strong fourth quarter and full year results, and I want to start by saying thank you . We finished the year strong because of all of you. Disney+ engagement kept growing, Experiences welcomed a record number of guests, ESPN delivered another standout quarter as football returned, and our studios and television businesses kept bringing audiences together through great storytelling. You can read more about what we delivered here. Earlier this year, I said Disney is in a category of one, and I meant it. No other company has our library of stories and characters that stay with fans for life, our ability to meet billions of fans wherever they are, or our commitment to innovation and excellence. Each is a strength on its own. Together, they compound. Our priorities are clear. Great storytelling will always be our North Star. Technology helps us serve our storytellers and fans in new ways. Operating as One Disney makes the first two stronger. To get there, we also have to reimagine the way we work. Some of this has already begun. We hired Disney's first Chief Technology Officer. We brought marketing and brand together under one leader for the first time. We moved Consumer Products and Games closer to our creative businesses, so the people building those experiences work directly with the teams creating our stories and characters. These steps are important to building a company that can move faster, and that allows us to invest more in the premium content and technology that will drive our long-term growth. Not all of these changes have been or will be easy. They will impact people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company. The industry has changed, and our company needs to change with it. That's what One Disney will do. It starts with the fan, so that someone who loves a story in one place can find more of it everywhere else. It is also how we run the company. One Disney is about synchronization, not centralization. Each business keeps its own creative identity, and we stay closely connected internally to create a better experience for fans and more opportunities for growth. Toy Story shows how this works. What began as a film more than 30 years ago moved into our parks, our homes, Disney+, and products that became part of everyday life. This summer, that fandom helped Toy Story 5 become the biggest film in the franchise's history, earning more than $1.1 billion at the global box office. We see the same opportunity with Marvel. With Avengers: Doomsday arriving next month, Marvel engagement on Disney+ has more than doubled, and August was the strongest month ever for Marvel Studios on the service. And you will see it again as we head into our first Super Bowl on ESPN this February. It's an extraordinary moment for ESPN, and an even bigger opportunity to show the world what Disney can do when we bring everything we have together. Teams across the company are already working side by side to make the most of it, and I'm very impressed by what I've seen. You'll hear more about it in the coming weeks. I'm more optimistic about Disney's future than I have ever been. At a moment of real change, you have stayed focused on delivering for our fans. We should all be proud of that. What we can build from here, as one company, is even bigger. Thank you for everything you do for Disney and for our fans every day. Josh Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ikea ditches plans for new UK stores, blaming high business taxes
events.summary: Retailer’s British boss says John Healey ‘missed opportunity to back retailers’ in October’s budget Ikea has ditched some planned store openings in the UK blaming the cost of business taxes , which it said were the highest in Europe. As its annual UK sales little more than flatlined at the Swedish flatpack furniture retailer, its UK boss, David McCabe, said: “There are locations where we were planning to open a new unit, and those plans have been abandoned due to the cost that we experience and the complexity within the market. “I would hope that we’re able to bring those projects back to life,” he added. “But it’s a very real impact here in the UK, when those investments will go to other countries in Europe.” The planned investments were smaller UK stores, but the retailer declined to comment on exact locations. Ikea has been pushing further into smaller high street shops , rather than its traditional out-of-town outlets. Ikea’s UK arm pays the most business taxes of its operations in Europe, and the third highest in the world, after the US and China, he said. The retailer’s UK sales edged 0.5% higher to £2.26bn in the year to the end of August. Sales rose 4.7% in the first four months of the year but fell in the second half as weak confidence and “sustained pressure” on household budgets led consumers to pull back on big purchases. McCabe said he had talked to customers in stores in recent weeks who were planning to replace an entire bedroom, but then decided to just buy one or two smaller pieces of furniture and a refresh with new textiles to save money. “We are seeing a change in the way that customers shop and we do anticipate a difficult period going forward,” he said. “We don’t think that there’s going to be a sudden, miraculous turnaround in confidence.” McCabe described John Healey’s recent budget as a “missed opportunity to back retailers under real pressure”, but said Ikea continued to talk to the government. The company has spent £54m on reducing prices by an average of 20% on 425 products, including its popular Billy bookcase , Hemnes daybed and the cantilever Poäng armchair. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Ikea is using seasonal offers to pull in customers, for example discounts on extendable dining tables, folding chairs and soft toys in the run-up to Christmas. McCabe said smaller stores, between 1,000 and 2,000 sq metres, had been popular with customers, in sites such as Oxford Street in London and retail parks. As well as the Oxford Street shop which opened within the former Topshop flagship site, Ikea opened stores in Brighton, Norwich and York last year, followed by a small store in Chester. It also opened a “plan and order” site – dedicated to kitchen, bedroom, and living room planning – in Dundee, and one in Aberdeen last month.

events.title: Once a month, I travel an hour to shop at Trader Joe's. Here are 10 items I always stock up on.
events.summary: In my opinion, Trader Joe's chicken-noodle soup and vanilla cold-foam creamer are worth the long drive. Tawnya Gibson Once a month, I travel an hour each way to shop at Trader Joe's for my family of three. While there, I stock up on easy meals like garden-vegetable soup, chicken-noodle soup, and burritos. I also love using Trader Joe's vanilla cold-foam creamer to make dirty sodas. I've been shopping at Trader Joe's for nearly 20 years. Unfortunately, though, after moving, the closest store to me is now about an hour away. So, once a month, I make the trip to stock up on items for my family of three. Here are 10 products that always make it into my cart. My husband loves Trader Joe's Fiberful granola bars. Tawnya Gibson Trader Joe's Fiberful granola bars go into my husband's lunch every day. They're a great way for him to easily up his fiber intake, and they taste great. We add some meat to Trader Joe's garden-vegetable soup. Tawnya Gibson In the fall and winter months, we find ourselves eating Trader Joe's garden-vegetable soup a few times a week. To make it a heartier meal, we like to cut up leftover steak or add hamburger or chicken meat. We've found the taste is less salty and more tomato-y than other store-bought versions we've tried, and the added meat pairs well with the chunks of vegetable. Trader Joe's Italian datterino cherry tomato and roasted-garlic pasta sauce is delicious. Tawnya Gibson What I love most about Trader Joe's Italian datterino cherry tomato and roasted-garlic pasta sauce is the consistency. It's thick but not chunky, definitely not watery, and clings to the pasta nicely. It also pairs well with a nice piece of crunchy bread on the side. As someone who doesn't usually love chili, I think the Trader Joe's version is a must-buy. Tawnya Gibson To be honest, I'm not a big fan of chili, and I usually don't love canned versions at all. However, Trader Joe's organic vegetarian chili is the exception to both points, as I love the consistency and subtle flavor. I keep a hearty stock of cans in my pantry for quick meals — and to add on top of baked potatoes. Trader Joe's bruschetta helps me make a quick and easy lunch. Tawnya Gibson I hate making lunch while I'm working from home , and Trader Joe's bruschetta is the perfect solution. I just grab a bagel, add some of this bruschetta, and sprinkle a little cheese and Everything but the Bagel Seasoning on top. Then, I throw it in the air fryer for a couple of minutes, and suddenly, I have a quick pizza bagel to get me through my afternoon workload. I always stock up on Trader Joe's chicken-noodle soup. Tawnya Gibson With thick noodles, chunks of chicken, and delicious carrots, this is simply the best-tasting canned chicken-noodle soup I've had. It's not super salty, so I find myself going back to it time and again, whether I'm sick or just need a quick dinner on a cold night. My whole family loves Trader Joe's fruit bars. Tawnya Gibson Trader Joe's fruit bars come in several varieties, but my favorites are the apple-and-banana and apple-and-strawberry flavors. If my son is home, I grab a few of the coconut options as well. These are always in my bag in case I need a little something to eat on the go. I'm a big fan of Trader Joe's refrigerated burritos. Tawnya Gibson Although Trader Joe's sells a few different refrigerated burrito varieties, the black-bean-and-cheese version is my favorite. That last little bite of tortilla that houses all the gooey cheese? I think that might be what heaven tastes like. I also like the beef, bean, and cheese flavor and always keep some on hand. Trader Joe's beef birria is a versatile freezer staple. Tawnya Gibson Trader Joe's beef birria is great for tacos, as an addition to the garden-vegetable soup, and over potatoes. However, my favorite way to prepare it is for tostadas, mixed with a little jalapeño cream cheese and some refried beans. I can't get enough of Trader Joe's vanilla cold-foam creamer. Tawnya Gibson I can't get enough of the dirty soda craze , so I use Trader Joe's vanilla cold-foam creamer in my Diet Coke. It also makes a nice topping for yogurt and berries. Keep reading our Trader Joe's diaries to see what other shoppers are putting in their carts. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes off in Texas, with dozens of cities to follow
events.summary: Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership announced earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup. The commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas. But the companies have far larger ambitions. Uber and Zipline plan to launch drone delivery services in dozens of additional U.S. cities in their collective bid to make one million deliveries per day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029. Zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour. Zipline drones don’t land. Instead, the drones lower the orders, which are encased in a small protective pod, to the customer’s location using a tether. Uber Eats customers in service areas will be able to tap a new “drone” icon on the app’s home page to view all participating restaurants. Uber said that at launch in the Houston area, several nationwide chains, including Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, along with dozens of local restaurants such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal, will offer drone delivery. “In partnership with Uber Eats we’re going to create a new expectation for delivery in America,” Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton said in a statement that underscores those aspirations. Those nationwide goals mirror the ambitions of other drone delivery companies, including Alphabet-owned Wing and Amazon’s Prime Air service. And those plans have started to collide with concerns from residents in some locations who complain about noise and worry that the drones will disrupt wildlife and pose a risk to safety and privacy. Companies trying to scale in this nascent industry have argued that delivery via drone is a net benefit for society, citing advantages such as traffic reduction. Customers won’t need to hop in their cars and drive to the store for that forgotten item or takeout order, instead relying on a drone, industry proponents have said. And while Zipline and other companies have been developing their drones for years, the industry is still in its early days, as is adoption in the communities where services are available. Zipline, which was founded in 2014, has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software. The California-based company’s initial focus was delivering blood in Rwanda, but it eventually expanded its scope to the United States. Its business in the U.S. scaled quickly after receiving its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration in 2022, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to conduct long-range commercial drone deliveries. Uber’s partnership extends beyond a commercial relationship with Zipline. The ride-hailing giant also invested in the startup. Neither company has disclosed the investment amount, but Zipline announced last week it had raised $1.5 billion in a round led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, and included backing by Uber, among others. events.title: US bank services returning to normal after major outage
events.summary: Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services, though Chase said its issue has now been resolved. Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems was behind the glitch and it was not a cyber security incident. A spokesperson said "this was not a systemic issue" but noted the impact may have affected other banks "only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us". The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage and a network failure that grounded all US flights . In addition, United Airlines also reported a "widespread system outage". The problems with the banks started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website. Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News, though Chase Bank told the BBC that customers still had access to their accounts and funds. A Chase Bank customer in Texas told CBS that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details. Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage Published 3 days ago Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech Published 3 days ago Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds". The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US. The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank. Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported. Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions. US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent. Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments. Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted. As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages. Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights". That issue resolved within a few hours. The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity. The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines. The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) , but comes as other industries report different outages around the US. On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues. The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel. events.title: Meta launches Direct, a stand-alone messaging app for Instagram
events.summary: Meta is testing Direct, a new stand-alone messaging app that houses Instagram’s direct messages. Direct is initially launching in Turkey and Thailand, and can be used with or without an Instagram account. With Direct, Meta is likely looking to retain users who use Instagram primarily, or even exclusively, for messaging. Over the years, people have often sought various ways to use Instagram’s direct messaging features without having to deal with the rest of the platform. Direct appears to be Meta’s answer to that demand, as the company says it is designed for chatting one-on-one or in groups with friends and family. The new app also gives the company a way to keep these users within its ecosystem rather than risk losing them altogether, and count them as active users within its ecosystem, even if they don’t use Instagram itself. Besides usual messaging features like reactions, voice notes, and emojis, Direct also features a “Draw” feature that lets you doodle and sketch directly inside chat threads. There’s also “Notes,” which are the short status updates that appear at the top of your Instagram DMs. Meta says users can create custom stickers, add audio effects to replies, and personalize chat backgrounds with custom themes. Users in Turkey and Thailand can sign up for Direct using their email address or phone number. Those with an existing Instagram account can log in using the same username and password, and their existing conversations will be synced across both apps. Meta says only people in your contacts or those you’re already connected with can start conversations or add you to group chats. Users can also report, block, restrict, or remove contacts at any time. The company also says it will use its age-estimation technology to identify and address potentially inappropriate interactions involving young users. Parents will also have access to supervision tools that let them see who their teens are messaging, manage safety settings, and set daily usage limits. Teens who use their Instagram username and password to access Direct will have to work with all the same messaging restrictions as Instagram’s Teen Accounts. Meta did not say when or if it will bring Direct to additional countries. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .
