AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Standing committee will oversee export compliance following allegations its GPUs were diverted to China China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion 1 day ago US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough) 1 day ago The Jensen Huang saga could be the beginning of the end of the AI bubble – or just a boon for competitors 1 day ago Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia 1 day ago Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 3 days ago Nvidia's board has created a national security and export control committee amid intense scrutiny over co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang's departure and allegations that Singapore-based customer Megaspeed diverted GPUs to China. The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee , announced on Tuesday, will monitor Nvidia's national security policies, export compliance, and global trade risks. It will meet at least quarterly. The committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. Nvidia's existing National Security and Global Trade Compliance teams will report on day-to-day operations directly to this new committee, as well as to interim CEO Colette Kress. The panel will oversee efforts to strengthen Nvidia's national security and trade compliance teams and retain independent legal, national security, and trade experts. The announcement follows the resignation of Huang last week after he admitted to an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, and was allegedly involved in a second relationship with an Nvidia employee. US authorities reportedly suspected Alice Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, an allegation that has not been proven. Megaspeed has separately faced scrutiny over suspected export control violations. The US Department of Commerce and Department of Justice confirmed on Tuesday in a joint statement that they were investigating Megaspeed back in 2024. The agencies said they would pursue any criminal conduct uncovered by the investigation. However, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs stated that US authorities had provided only "limited assistance" when they were investigating the activities of Alice Huang and Megaspeed, as The Register reported. The New York Times also reported that US investigations into Megaspeed were halted last year after an Nvidia executive contacted Commerce Department officials. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued new regulations tightening up restrictions on AI technology exports and cloud operators offering remote access to it. The US also expanded its Pax Silica initiative , getting allied nations to sign an agreement that "guarding AI supply chains" is a shared responsibility. Nvidia says it recognizes that advanced silicon and AI technologies present challenges for national security, and it has a responsibility to address them. "We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," said Harvey Jones, chair of Nvidia's board of directors.

events.title: Voyage Labs raises $12 million for a specialized AI travel assistant
events.summary: Planning a trip is a favorite demo for personal AI assistants — you can try it with Muse, or with Gemini, or half a dozen other choices. But while most pitches use travel-planning as part of a general-purpose agent pitch, a new startup from a Google Maps alum is betting that a specialized travel-planning agent can beat the competition. The company is called Voyage Labs , and on Tuesday it announced $12 million in seed funding led by Kleiner Perkins, with participation from SignalFire and SV Angel. The company plans to use the funding to expand supplier partnerships and grow its engineering team. Voyage Labs’ flagship product, called Atlas, is meant to work as a personal assistant for your trip-planning, available today in private beta . “People can use it to plan and book and manage their entire journey, from the time they have an inspiration to the time they come back home,” says co-founder and CEO Manik Gupta. Atlas is designed to serve as an always-on assistant throughout the planning process, fielding ideas and doing research on every idea that’s raised. The long time horizon means Atlas can tailor recommendations based on weeks of conversation, while also monitoring real-time price fluctuations and ultimately booking flights and hotels. For the Voyage founders, it’s an ideal match between technology and use case. “Trip planning is a project that has its own lifecycle,” says Yogesh Jain, co-founder and CTO of the company. “You’re planning across days and weeks — so long-running agents as a technology matches that very well.” Travel assistants are already a crowded field, but Voyage will be starting with a lot of experience in the space. Gupta was previously the director of Product Management for Google Maps, followed by four years as chief product officer at Uber. As he puts it, “I spent eight years where my only job was to wake up in the morning and go build the map. I’m just very obsessed with that problem.” The biggest question is how Atlas will compete with the multi-purpose AI assistants built by frontier labs. But as Gupta notes, the space is still changing fast, and it’s hard for anyone to be sure what form factors will thrive in the coming years. Ultimately, Voyage is betting that travel is specialized enough to need a specialized product. “We are making a bet that this vertical around travel and outdoors is a large enough vertical that it needs a focused product solution,” Gupta told TechCrunch. “Ultimately, we believe we can actually stitch together an end-to-end experience that will help users.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Instagram’s new tool for creators targets unauthorized reposts and AI-modified videos
events.summary: Instagram is introducing a new tool to help creators protect their original videos, the Meta-owned company announced Tuesday. The feature, called “content protection,” is already available on Facebook and is designed to detect when creators’ original videos are being used without their permission. The company is also expanding the tool to address AI content, not just conventional reposting. The announcement comes in response to creators’ concerns over how easily original content can be copied and redistributed across social media platforms, especially considering how generative AI has made it easier to manipulate existing videos. Instagram says the content protection tool continuously scans Instagram for unauthorized uses of creators’ protected videos. When Instagram detects a match for one of a creator’s Reels uploaded by another user, it sends the creator an alert. Creators can then choose to block the video from being viewed on both Instagram and Facebook to hide the matched content. They can also choose to add an “original by” label on the content that links viewers of the matching video back to their original video. Additionally, creators can choose to keep the match visible while monitoring its performance or release their claim on the reel, allowing it to remain visible on Meta’s platforms. The tool will also begin detecting AI-generated videos that reuse audio from creators’ original content, even when the visuals have been altered. This update will initially be tested with a small group of creators in the coming weeks. The company plans to expand access to this feature to creators who enroll in content protection on both Instagram and Facebook. Instagram says it’s exploring ways to limit the reach of accounts and content that repeatedly use AI tools to repost others’ work. Creators who are eligible for content protection will see a notification in their activity feed. Once they enroll, every original video they post to Instagram going forward is automatically protected. They can also choose to retroactively protect eligible videos they’ve already posted by manually selecting them. If creators have permitted certain profiles to use their work, such as their second profile or a brand, they can add them to their allow list so their videos won’t be flagged as matches. Tuesday’s announcement marks another step in Instagram’s ongoing efforts to give creators greater control over their content and protect the originality of their work. events.title: Dubai's Al Maktoum Airport to undergo year of tests before first passengers arrive
events.summary: Moving operations from Dubai International Airport (DXB) to Al Maktoum International (DWC) will be a complex transition, with the two airports initially running in parallel, operator Dubai Airports’ chief executive Paul Griffiths said. The new Al Maktoum International Airport will undergo at least a year of testing before its first passengers arrive, as the emirate prepares for one of the biggest operational moves in global aviation. Construction at DWC is continuing at full pace despite the Iran war, with the first phase due to open in 2032. More than 100,000 workers are on site at the $35 billion development, where piling and groundworks are under way, Mr Griffiths said in a media briefing on Tuesday. “The budget is something like $35 billion and I know major contracts are being discussed as I speak,” he said. “There are more than 100,000 workers on site. Piling is commencing. Groundworks are well under way. So, it's definitely a live project.” The testing programme will cover critical systems including baggage handling, check-in processes , Wi-Fi and other airport technology, with the aim of ensuring the airport is fully operational before passengers start using it. “The good thing is we have got the test period … of having DXB to test all this new technology before we migrate there, so there will be at least a year of testing before we even allow the first customer to cross the threshold,” Mr Griffiths said. “Then, of course, the transition is going to be enormous.” 'Particularly complex move' Mr Griffiths added that the move would be unprecedented in scale, involving several times the 20 million passengers affected when Hong Kong relocated its main airport in the 1990s. “We will be nearly five or six times that by the time we move from here. So that’s never been done on that scale,” he said. Dubai Airports has awarded Dh13 billion ($3.53 billion) worth of contracts this year for construction of the new DWC terminal, with another Dh55 billion to be awarded by the end of 2026, Mr Griffiths said in August. The move from DXB to Al Maktoum International will be particularly complex because of the scale of operations involved, he said on Monday. The transition will also require extensive recruitment and training. “The fact that we are about five years away from the opening of the new airport fills me with dread because there’s so much to do. We’ve got to recruit so many more people. We’ve got to train them. We’ve got to operate two airports, and then we’ve got to condense down to one airport. So, all of these challenges are pretty enormous,” Mr Griffiths said. “Our task here is to keep everything going to make sure that the transition between the two is covered.” The 70km shift from DXB to DWC in Dubai's south is not simply an airport infrastructure project but a wider urban development challenge, Mr Griffiths said. “We are taking the entire top left corner of Dubai, where we are sitting now, and we are transplanting it in the bottom right-hand corner, 70km away,” he said. “So that’s much, much more than just an airport project. The whole city has got to move.” Workers living in Dubai and the Northern Emirates will face significantly longer commutes to the new airport, making it necessary to develop communities closer. “All of those people living in the Northern Emirates, they won’t be able to commute every day all the way down to Al Maktoum International. So we’ve got to build cities for the airport sector workers as well,” Mr Griffiths said. Dubai Airports has already advanced its operational planning for the transition, with the concept of operations and master plans well developed. Critical contracts for DWC’s baggage-handling system and automated people movers are also under discussion, Mr Griffiths said. The broader objective is to ensure that the move does not constrain the emirate’s passenger growth or disrupt airport services. “Our real measure of success is: can we keep growth going in the city without constraining the supply of capacity, and can we seamlessly manage the transition?” he said. The first phase will give the new terminal an annual capacity of 150 million passengers. Ultimately, the airport is set to reach a capacity of 260 million passengers and 12 million tonnes of cargo a year when complete.

events.title: Interior designers share 6 things you should never have in your bedroom
events.summary: Some bedroom decorations and design choices can just add visual clutter to a space. Andreas von Einsiedel/Getty Images Interior designers shared designs and other items they think people shouldn't have in bedrooms. Exercise equipment and certain family photos should be kept in other rooms of the house. Low light fixtures and furniture that's too small can hurt a room's overall look. Although bedrooms aren't widely considered to be the heart of a home, most people spend a lot of time in them. So, the stakes for designing them are high — the furniture, decorations, and even  wall colors  you choose can make or break the vibe and look of the space. With that in mind, Business Insider asked interior designers what kinds of things people should avoid having in a bedroom . Here's what they said. Say no to cool-white bulbs. The bulbs you put in your light fixtures can make or break a space. CreativaStudio/Getty Images Bulbs are nearly as important as fixtures when choosing the best lighting for a bedroom . Ariyan Parvaresh, interior designer at AP Design , recommends skipping any cool-white bulbs. "People should avoid them because they're incredibly unflattering and tend to make you more alert, hence why they're used in markets and commercial spaces more," she said. Warm-white bulbs will give your space a much softer glow that's better for relaxing around bedtime. Lighting that hangs too low can be troublesome. A large chandelier shouldn't be too close to your bed. KUPRYNENKO ANDRII/Shutterstock There are many lighting options for bedrooms, but interior designer Perla Lichi said it's essential to avoid fixtures that hang too low. Poorly placed lights can interfere with a bed, windows, or TV. If you have low ceilings, she suggested trying flush-mount lights. Furniture that's too small for the space can cause issues. Morsa Images/Getty Images Lichi told Business Insider that you should be intentional when choosing furniture for your bedroom . Pieces that don't properly fit the space can quickly make the room look cluttered or empty. "It's best to start with your signature bed and measure accordingly. Leave enough room for end tables, corner vases, plants, and a chaise lounge/lamp for reading by the window," Lichi said. Pass on hanging photos of anyone besides you and your partner. You can also hang paintings instead of photos. NazariyKarkhut/Getty Images Although hanging photos of loved ones can make a space feel comforting, interior designer Rachel Larraine said it's important to be selective about the pictures you display in your bedroom. "I do not recommend having anyone else's photo in your bedroom except for you and your partner, if you have one," she said. "It can be really awkward having your mother-in-law staring at you while you get intimate with your partner." Rethink placing exercise equipment in your bedroom. Helin Loik-Tomson/Getty Images It's not uncommon to use the bedroom as a dual-purpose space, but you may want to set some limits. Sarit Marcus, interior designer and founder of Minted Space , suggests anyone reconsider putting bulky exercise equipment near their bed. "Ideally, a bedroom is a tranquil place to promote healthy, restful sleep — having exercise equipment like a treadmill, stationary bike, or elliptical machine creates a different energy in the room," Marcus said. Try to avoid having a bed without a headboard. Headboards can complete a space. CreativaStudio/Getty Images Larraine said people should always choose to have a headboard, even if they're opting for a low-profile platform bed. A headboard gives a bed a "finished and complete look" and creates a focal point in the bedroom. "Headboards also act as mountain energy in Feng Shui. events.title: Isomorphic Labs raises $5B as it looks to take drug candidates to clinical trials
events.summary: Isomorphic Labs , the AI drug-discovery platform that was spun out of Google’s DeepMind in 2021, has raised $5 billion in a Series C funding round as it seeks to take its drug candidates to clinical trials. The funding was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, with new investor Andreessen Horowitz and other investors also participating. All of the company’s existing backers, including Alphabet’s venture divisions GV and Capita G, Thrive Capital, MGX, Temasek, and the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund, also invested. Isomorphic Labs builds an AI drug-design engine that uses a slew of simulation AI models that explore various areas of chemistry to help the company design drugs. The company, whose work builds on DeepMind’s breakthrough AlphaFold protein-folding AI model , said its program has yielded “positive preclinical results” in oncology and immunology. The lab has struck deals with pharma giants like Eli Lilly, Novartis, and Johnson & Johnson. The new funding, which comes on the heels of a $2.1 billion Series B round in May, will be used to continue developing its drug-design engine, as well as to foray into more types of medicine. The Series C is Isomorphic’s first fundraise since its founder and CEO, Demis Hassabis, left his position as head of DeepMind to focus on drug discovery, which also saw him moving into a chairman role at DeepMind. Hassabis and then-director of DeepMind John Jumper won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for the lab’s work on AlphaFold, a system that predicts the 3D structure of proteins with nothing more than their genetic sequence. Isomorphic did not disclose its new valuation. Bloomberg reported earlier this month that the lab was looking to raise funding at a $50 billion valuation. events.title: I tried Dolly Parton's holiday mashed potatoes. They're a delicious and quick Thanksgiving side dish.
events.summary: Dolly Parton's final cookbook has a whole section dedicated to Thanksgiving recipes. Nathan Congleton/NBC/NBCU Photo Bank via Getty Images In 2024, Dolly Parton published a cookbook with her sister called "Good Lookin' Cookin.'" It features an entire section dedicated to Thanksgiving recipes, including her holiday potatoes. The mashed potatoes include sour cream, cream cheese, and plenty of butter — deliciously luscious. Dolly Parton was universally beloved for her voice, songwriting skills, and generous heart. She was also a fabulous home cook . The queen of country music was a devotee of Southern cuisine. In one of our past interviews, Parton told me she loved whipping up "mashed potatoes, coleslaw, and a big ol' hunk of cornbread " for her goddaughter Miley Cyrus . Parton later published her mashed potato recipe in the 2024 cookbook "Good Lookin' Cookin': A Year of Meals," which she wrote with her sister, Rachel Parton George. "When the holiday season arrives, why not dress up your mashed potatoes! That's what we do," the sisters wrote in the recipe's description. "All it takes is some cream cheese, sour cream, a little garlic, and your mixer!" Here's how to make it. Parton's mashed potatoes include cream cheese, butter, and sour cream. Dolly Parton and her sister Rachel Parton George in 2009. Bruce Glikas/FilmMagic To make the Parton sisters' holiday potatoes at home, you'll need: 5 pounds of russet potatoes 4 ounces of cream cheese, room temperature 1 cup of whole milk 1 stick (8 tablespoons) of butter, room temperature 1 garlic clove, minced ½ cup of sour cream 2 tablespoons of fresh parsley for garnish 1 ½ teaspoons of salt First, I prepped the potatoes. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I washed, peeled, and quartered the potatoes. Then I placed the potatoes in a colander and rinsed them under cold water. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider The recipe says to wash the potatoes "until the water runs clear." I threw my potatoes into a large pot and filled it with cold water. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider The recipe says to cover the potatoes with two inches of water, then add one teaspoon of salt. I brought the pot to a boil and then lowered the heat to medium. I allowed my potatoes to cook for 20 minutes until they were fork-tender. I drained the potatoes and placed them in a large bowl so I could add all the seasoning. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I threw in the butter, cream cheese, sour cream, ½ cup of milk, and ½ teaspoon of salt. Then I whipped the potatoes with an electric hand mixer. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I blended the potatoes on medium speed as I mixed everything together. Then I added the remaining half cup of milk and mixed the potatoes on high speed until they became fluffy, which took a few minutes. I saved two tablespoons of butter to drizzle over the mashed potatoes, along with parsley and pepper. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I served these holiday potatoes alongside Dolly's recipes for mac and cheese and cornbread stuffing, and it was my favorite dish of the three. The holiday potatoes are deliciously rich and luscious with the addition of cream cheese and sour cream, while the chopped parsley adds a nice pop of color. They also had a lovely whipped texture, which paired well with the other Thanksgiving-inspired dishes on the table. If you're looking for a last-minute addition to your Thanksgiving menu , the Parton sisters' holiday potatoes will definitely impress the whole family. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Trump administration weighs Marshall for FDA as Overton wobbles
events.summary: The Scoop Republicans are discussing Sen. Roger Marshall as a potential replacement nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration as Heidi Overton’s confirmation struggles in the Senate, according to four people familiar with the matter. The Kansas Republican, who just lost his reelection bid, is seen as a stronger potential nominee than Overton, who faces opposition from both anti-abortion activists and moderate Republicans in her bid to lead the agency. Republicans face a severe time crunch if Overton’s nomination is pulled or fails in committee; they have a month and a half left in the majority to confirm President Donald Trump’s nominees. “Marshall is viewed as an alternative if Heidi can’t make it through,” a Trump administration official told Semafor. “Senators have an easier time getting confirmed, traditionally. At this point, it’s hard to get anyone approved.” The Senate health committee is scheduled to vote on Overton’s nomination on Wednesday. Marshall, a doctor who served two terms in the House before his Senate election in 2020, currently serves on the health committee. It’s unclear how quickly the White House might move on any alternative nominee, whether it’s Marshall or another contender. No final decision has been made on abandoning Overton, though there’s quiet acknowledgment internally that her path to confirmation is exceedingly difficult. “There is a growing view in the Senate that a senator would be the only person while we’ve got a majority so Roger Marshall’s name is quickly percolating as a person who would be confirmable,” said a senior Republican aide. The White House did not immediately comment. Marshall’s office declined comment. The FDA has operated under acting leadership since former Commissioner Marty Makary was pushed out in May after clashing with the White House over whether to authorize flavored vapes. He also faced pressure from anti-abortion Republicans who are pushing for restrictions on abortion pill mifepristone. Kyle Diamantas, a lawyer who worked as the agency’s top food official, was tapped as acting FDA commissioner and earned a reputation as a competent leader who helped stabilize the agency. But the Trump administration official said Diamantas — who did not want the top job on a permanent basis — is eyeing a departure from FDA regardless of what happens with Overton’s nomination. Notable If Marshall had defeated Kansas Democratic Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton this month, he may have been in line to take the health committee’s top GOP spot, as Semafor reported .

events.title: Shoppers slowed spending in October with high prices leading to caution
events.summary: Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their moneyRetail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a revised 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce De... NEW YORK -- Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their money ahead of the unofficial start to the holiday shopping season. Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce Department's report released Tuesday. Sales at gas stations rose 1.5% last month after spiking 30.3% in September, according to the Commerce Department. Excluding gas stations, retail sales rose just 0.1%. Overall retail sales were pulled down by decline in sales at motor vehicle and parts dealers. Auto vehicles and parts dealers had a 1.6% drop in sales in October, reversing a 1.3% increase in September. “There are hints of weakening consumer spending as prices rise," wrote Carl B. Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics. “Let’s call this report a mixed report card on the health of the consumer." Spending was mixed across different sectors. Business at furniture and home furnishings stores fell 2.3%, while clothing and accessories stores declined 0.7%. Sales at consumer electronics and appliance stores were unchanged. Sales at online retailers rose 1.2%. The data offers only a snapshot of consumer spending and doesn’t include activities like travel and hotel stays. But the lone services category – restaurants registered a 0.2% increase. The weaker sales data followed new evidence that inflation continued to weigh on Americans last month. Higher energy prices are ricocheting into other parts of the economy, with airfares, public transportation and shipping all jumping in price. Grocery prices, for example, increased 0.4%, a painful uptick after years of increases, according to new Labor Department data. Massive investments in artificial intelligence have exacerbated inflation by driving up computer chip prices and, in turn, prices for laptops, phones and other consumer electronics. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Retailers are preparing for a surge in business over the Thanksgiving weekend, the unofficial start of the holiday shopping period. Stores have heavily advertised deals to lure customers who increasingly buy when they think prices have dropped. Companies like Kohl’s and Target and Walmart are trying to drive the affordability message home through marketing. Target said it’s offering more than 8,000 new gifts for the winter holidays, with more than half exclusive to the retailer. Most of the new holiday items at Target are $20 or less, including thousands of items that are priced at $5 and under. Kohl’s has increased the number of gift sets across different types of merchandise. Americans, despite the rising cost of credit, continue to rely on cards to finance spending, and credit experts say that defaults have been stable. “More Americans are carrying credit cards than ever, and they’re handling them well,” said Charles Wise, head of global research and consulting at the credit reporting agency TransUnion. Wise noted that outstanding credit card balances as of last month hit $1.17 trillion, up 5.1% from the year-ago period, based on data covering 178.5 million consumers who held an active credit card as of last month. Yet serious delinquency rates held steady, he said. That signals that “consumers remain disciplined borrowers heading into the holidays,” he added. events.title: Hakeem Jeffries shifts tactics ahead of House Democrats' internal speaker vote
events.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) plans to force his members to take a tallied vote this week on whether to nominate him as speaker of the House, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Why it matters: The plan represents a shift in tactics — his allies had previously hoped to nominate him by acclamation — that would help reveal whether he has the votes to become speaker on Jan. 3. If he loses more than 40 votes, he may be in trouble. If not, he likely sails through even if some of his members ultimately oppose him on the House floor. Jeffries and his allies are confident he has more than enough support to get the 218 votes needed to become speaker even as some of his freshman members express skepticism or even outright opposition to him. "Jeffries will win," a senior House Democrat told Axios. Jeffries' plans were first reported by Punchbowl News. Between the lines: This new strategy would exploit the fact that, as of Tuesday, no other House Democrat has announced their candidacy for speaker. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who is often floated as a possible alternative in constituent phone calls to lawmakers urging them not to back Jeffries, told Axios he is not running for speaker. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), who has become the focus of a recent draft movement, has also told allies she is not interested in the role, as Axios previously reported. Pressley, asked about running for speaker at a town hall event in her district on Monday, told attendees : "I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people." State of play: House Democrats are set to meet behind closed doors starting Wednesday morning to elect their leadership team for the 120th Congress. In addition to nominating a candidate for speaker, they are set to vote on electing a House majority leader and whip, an assistant speaker, and a Democratic caucus chair and vice chair, among other leadership positions. Most of the candidates for those senior roles are running unopposed and are still expected to be elected by voice vote because "people don't want long votes," said the senior House Democrat. Any recorded votes would still be secret ballots, unlike the Jan. 3 speaker vote in which members must stand on the floor and announce their choice.

events.title: Wind power's high cost-saving potential
events.summary: Adding wind power to solar and battery storage can cut the cost of meeting nearly all of global electricity demand by close to 20% , demonstrating how renewables can deliver reliable power when it is needed at low costs. Analysis by global energy think tank Ember found that the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand falls from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour when wind complements solar and batteries to generate power on short winter days and prolonged periods of cloud cover. The analysis assumes the remaining 10% is met by gas or diesel backup. In most countries, the trinity of wind, solar, and batteries reduces the need for energy storage systems, although it has little impact near the equator. It also significantly diminishes the risk of a solar and wind lull striking at the same time — a weather phenomenon often described by the German term , which refers to a dark and windless period. High costs of capital in some parts of the world, such as Africa, increase the cost of clean power, however. — Chloé Farand

What privacy? The 100 most-visited English-language sites are flouting European data protection laws on a massive scale, according to a privacy researcher's investigation. Forensic data analysis , published by Alexander Hanff, an attorney, computer scientist, and occasional contributor to The Register , with the support of SOMI (Stichting Onderzoek Marktinformatie), a Netherlands-based privacy group, details the dubious data flow. From October 1 to 3, 2026, Hanff took a clean Google Chrome browser profile and measured what happens when the browser loads the 100 most visited English-language websites for five minutes, without any consent banner interaction. At these 100 sites, visits were made to 265 pages – the home page, the privacy page, and the cookie notice when available – which resulted in 518,770 privacy events without any consent. All 100 sites produced what the report characterizes as Tier 1 events – interception, exfiltration, or high-entropy fingerprinting (a total of 14,675). Tier 2 consists of storage on the device, capturing device characteristics, and script loads without consent (284,463 events recorded). Tier 3 includes protocol mechanisms and passive reads used for tracking (219,632 events). The median website triggered 2,695 events, for a total of 28,695 events deemed high or critical. And 92.4 percent of the servers contacted during this process were on networks outside the European Economic Area (EEA). Most of these servers – 1,247 out of 1,400 – were in the US, and 1,034 belonged to third-parties. The EU General Data Protection Regulation governs the transfer of personal data outside the EEA. The EU allows data transfers to the US for organizations participating in the EU–US Data Privacy Framework. Beyond that, according to Hanff and SOMI, a valid legal mechanism like a contract must be in place or the transfer may fail to meet GDPR or the ePrivacy Directive. In some cases, California Penal Code section 631 (interception) and section 502 (computer access) may also be relevant. On these 100 websites, there were 89,437 fingerprinting events, 1,492 cookies set without consent, 7,456 scripts loaded from other origins, 18 websites implementing CNAME cloaking, and 37 websites delivering code to use the browser's built-in AI interfaces. The privacy and cookie notices on these websites imposed a median reading time requirement of 28 minutes and none fully matched what their pages did. Among the sites' consent banners, 115 out of 165 used dark patterns, like steering visitors with emotional language about a "safer" or "better" experience, or "we care about your privacy." The report, released in conjunction with a presentation at the Field Talk conference , also calculates the estimated environmental impact to load all this third-party content on websites without consent: 1,271,444 kWh per year, or enough to power 353 homes in Europe at 3.6 MWh per home annually. SOMI is hosting a data finder to help people request access to the personal data companies have collected about them. Hanff in an email told The Register that he would be shocked if these findings fail to get the attention of lawmakers and regulators in the EU, UK, and US, given plans to file privacy complaints with relevant authorities. "Complaints will be filed against all of them and the EU supervisory authorities have a legal obligation to investigate them all – so we will have to wait and see," he said.

events.title: US data center emissions rival entire countries
events.summary: The largest data centers in the US collectively emit an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon emissions annually — almost as much as Denmark, according to a study published in the journal Nature Sustainability. Harvard researchers found 403 data centers used almost 2% of US electricity , with most of the power being generated from fossil fuels. Sites in Iowa, Ohio, and Virginia accounted for about half the estimated emissions. The study provides the first peer-reviewed estimates of emissions generated by US data centers since the start of the AI boom, although it is not a comprehensive inventory. Without a publicly available list of facilities, researchers pieced together information using a commercial dataset, satellite imagery, and data on the power mix supplying each regional electricity grid. The findings are likely an underestimate as they exclude data centers that researchers could not sufficiently verify, as well as facilities that rely on on-site power generation. — Chloé Farand

events.title: Nvidia faces its own Lehman moment
events.summary: The position of Nvidia’s Colette Kress — a relatively unknown CFO, a rare female executive in an industry dominated by men, promoted in a storm and taking the mic for the high-stakes earnings call this afternoon — will ring familiar to old Wall Street hands. In March 2008, the day after the Bear Stearns rescue, Lehman Brothers put Erin Callan, its finance chief of barely three months, in front of analysts to clear some blood from the water and defend Lehman’s books. She was poised and persuasive, and the stock soared. Then short seller David Einhorn started picking apart her numbers. By June, Callan was out and Lehman was in a crisis of confidence from which it wouldn’t recover. Callan became a textbook case of the “glass cliff” — women promoted into the spotlight just as things go over the edge — and disappeared from Wall Street before a reputation-mending book tour. Kress, now interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigned amid a probe into his affair with a suspected Chinese spy and allegations of further affairs with subordinates, faces a different test today. Nobody doubts demand for Nvidia’s chips and its balance sheet is enviably strong. But she carries some of the same baggage, including a Wall Street Journal report that Huang called her a “deer in the headlights” in an August meeting. And she answers to a board that got its first-ever independent chair last week and will decide how long the interim title lasts. She got a vote of confidence from Citi’s Jane Fraser, who told me yesterday : “The company with Colette, at the moment, at the helm … is in very able, capable hands.” — Liz Hoffman

events.title: AI isn't out of energy yet
events.summary: Tim’s view The US data center buildout isn’t screeching to a halt quite yet, and the energy companies behind it still see plenty to look forward to. Between Democrats’ sweep of Congress and Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, the AI bubble has rarely looked so close to bursting. More restrictions are almost certainly forthcoming in newly Democrat-led states like Texas, and the wellspring of capital from Nvidia, both for hyperscalers’ construction ambitions and the comparatively modest needs of energy startups , could start to ebb. At Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World event this week, leading capital allocators, including Citigroup’s Jane Fraser and Mubadala’s Khaldoon Al Mubarak , pointed to warning lights in the digital economy. But neither seemed exceptionally worried. And as you can read below, Bloom Energy’s KR Sridhar sees “nothing but a huge opportunity” ahead. Last week at COP31, the CEO of power developer Acwa, which just made a $4 billion bet on US data centers, said the current trepidation is a “blip” that can’t reverse the undeniable and unchanging need for more electricity. Goldman Sachs said in a recent note that it hasn’t changed its expectation for $1.4 trillion in AI-related hardware spending by the end of next year; Mark Daly, head of data centers at BloombergNEF, told me he agrees that “the midterms didn’t present anything concrete that would cause us to significantly revise our views.” Even Fermi, the Texas AI energy startup that nearly imploded this year as it struggled to nail down an anchor customer, just landed a nearly $300 million deal with Amazon . Undoubtedly companies in this space will be prone to talking up their own books, and not every data center energy project will pan out. And there’s a big climate issue that hasn’t been adequately addressed: Only a handful of small countries have so far signed on to a COP31 pledge to “power and build AI infrastructure and hardware sustainably.” But no matter who’s in charge at Nvidia, US power demand is only going up. Notable The carbon emissions of US data centers are nearly as large as that of entire countries—such as Bolivia or Denmark— a new study found.

events.title: Science Corporation’s brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding
events.summary: Science Corporation , the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the company said in a blog post . Investors in the new round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech. Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain. Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for new conditions. Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt. With the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S. Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses. events.title: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
events.summary: Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in May Published 17 November 2026, 10:22 GMT As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors. On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models. South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market. But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China. This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , external , a US-based think-tank. China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests". This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips. One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO . Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands. The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said. Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University. But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient". Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand. These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent. But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips. The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment. Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms. A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure". Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls". The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week. Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models. Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI.

events.title: Deutsche Bank shares sink as whistleblowers reveal Epstein payments, Trump tax leak, Russia bets
events.summary: More than 15 million leaked Deutsche Bank files reviewed by an international media consortium detail alleged failures in risk management, compliance and governance over many years. The Financial Times reported $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein and an accidental 2017 disclosure of tax information tied to Donald Trump. Deutsche Bank says the matters are largely historical and cites 7 billion euros invested in its control environment from 2019 through 2025. Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media reports revealing alleged historic failures across its risk management and financial crime controls. These include suspicious payments linked to late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and accidental leaks of President Donald Trump 's tax statements. The leaks contain board minutes, emails, internal investigations and other material that point to systemic failures across the Frankfurt-listed lender's business functions stretching back two decades. Deutsche Bank processed $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, the FT reported . Suspicious payments are not, by themselves, proof that every transaction was criminal. The German lender also mistakenly leaked details of U.S. President Donald Trump's taxes in March 2017, during his first term in office, the FT said. The blunder — described by CEO Christian Sewing, who was then Deutsche's private banking head, as "an awful mistake" — was kept secret from the White House. The wide-ranging investigation — which was led by a consortium of more than 200 journalists worldwide including the FT, Der Spiegel and Le Monde — also said Deutsche Bank had failed to offboard around 28,000 problematic investment bank clients who had been identified for removal by early 2018. It also alleges that the bank concealed information around cost targets in 2021, when external monitors in New York reportedly warned that Deutsche's risk appetite was running ahead of controls. The files also contain details of the bank's relationships with oligarchs and transactions that the investigation links to Russian money-laundering concerns. It was these ties that motivated whistleblowers to send the information to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife. The reports once again put Deutsche Bank's risk management practices and controls under the spotlight following years of regulatory scrutiny. The bank — which has been raided multiple times by German officials this year — has, since 2012, paid out some 18.6 billion euros ($20.5 billion) in settlements over alleged market manipulation, money laundering, mis-selling and misrepresentation, among other things, the FT said. In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years. "Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said. The bank said it has undergone a "fundamental transformation" under CEO Christian Sewing, pointing to 7 billion euros of investment in its risk controls between 2019 and 2025. "Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters." CNBC has reached out to BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, for comment.

events.title: Silicon Valley leaders forge a 'save Jensen' faction
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s Silicon Valley compatriots continue to rally around him. “This narrative of the Chinese spy is falling apart,” David Sacks, President Donald Trump’s former AI and crypto czar, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday, joining a chorus of (admittedly geographically and ideologically cloistered) allies casting doubt on the crux of the scandal that bounced the Nvidia CEO from his job last week. Sacks said that the public has been too quick to judge, a sentiment echoed by Bill Ackman: “If it’s a personal foible … I think there’s a very powerful case for putting him back in place.” (The longtime activist investor, who has lately hung up his sword, laid out a tactical playbook for reinstating Huang, while saying he was unlikely to get involved.) Replit CEO Amjad Masad, who signed an online petition to bring Huang back, called Huang’s ouster “ an attack on open models, ” feeding a theory that frontier AI labs threatened by Nvidia’s Nemotron model contributed to his downfall. Huang’s absence from Nvidia “would be a huge loss and it would potentially bring about a world where there’s only the frontier model labs that exist,” Masad said. Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner urged the Nvidia board to reconsider Huang’s ouster , saying the company needs to find all the information in order to “get this right.” Trump, for his part, put it more directly, telling reporters on Monday that he “wouldn’t mind” if Huang was reinstated. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Nvidia’s first big move after Jensen Huang’s exit targets national security
events.summary: Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company’s customers. Nvidia said Tuesday that the new standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang’s alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. The Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia. The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia’s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call. Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the company to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations. This is the first major action by the company under the leadership of Colette Kress, the company’s CFO who took over as interim CEO after Huang stepped down last week. The committee, which will meet at least quarterly, will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include fellow directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. Nvidia already has a national security team and global trade compliance team. Those teams will now report to this board committee and Kress on day-to-day operations. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress later this month. events.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
events.summary: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. It’s “worse than a bug” Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.” Read full article Comments

events.title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
events.summary: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: GROMACS: An agent from KTH Royal Institute of Technology repairs broken GROMACS setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single DGX Spark, it fixed 81% of test cases. SETI Institute: At the Allen Telescope Array, an agent took a one-line prompt to plot a methanol line. Buck explained that it then retuned for Doppler shift on its own [NGC 869 vs. 896, check slide]. Nsight AI Porting Agent: NVIDIA’s new agent ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to GPUs, Buck said, speeding it up more than 5x using about 150 million tokens. Agents lean on CPUs to run tool calls between model steps, Buck explained. “That’s exactly what agents need,” he said. “They need a CPU that can run, evaluate, run the tool, perform the operations, gather the results.” DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, expected in early 2028. Buck said it joins Vera systems already announced at Texas Advanced Computing Center. Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform, built for science, engineering, analytics and AI, Buck said. It supports precisions from FP64 to FP4, adds sparse-data acceleration and connects over seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink. With more than 50,000 CUDA cores, it has about three times as many as Hopper, Buck said. It is expected in 2028. Buck said a simulation on Jülich’s JUPITER supercomputer showed that a technique called magic state cultivation can cut the operations needed for one logical step tenfold. The work is being added to CUDA-Q. NVIDIA, IBM and Fermilab announced plans today for a quantum computing co-design platform to support error-correction and applications research. NVIDIA and IBM are pairing NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk. Buck also introduced a new breakthrough for quantum decoding. The goal, Buck explained, is to cut decoding latency from about 300 microseconds to 10. A new CUDA-Q decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, cuts error-correction research computation from 12 weeks to 45 minutes, he said. Buck also showed one of the first deployments of NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics switches, at Lambda . He said they are 15x more reliable on bit errors and link flaps. events.title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
events.summary: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue? Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication. Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N . N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors. VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N 2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N 2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N 2 . In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N , not N 2 . So the energy used will scale as N , not N 2 , as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied. Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10 -19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10 -14 and 10 -12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000. But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements. McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.” It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law . “Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.” With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data. Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. events.title: Spotify’s new tool aims to stop deepfakes from being attributed to real artists
events.summary: As AI-generated slop continues to flood music-streaming platforms, Spotify is rolling out an “Artist Profile Protection” tool to all artists, giving them control over the music appearing under their name. The official launch comes eight months after the company began beta-testing the feature with select artists. Spotify says the tool is designed to address a long-standing issue across streaming services, where music can end up on the wrong artist profile due to deliberate impersonation, metadata errors, or shared artist names. The update comes as Billboard reported last month that Sony Music had requested the removal of more than 260,000 deepfake songs from digital platforms, nearly double the number the label disclosed in March. With this new feature, Spotify is aiming to give artists more control over their digital identities as the volume of music uploaded to streaming services continues to grow. Artists can enable the feature through Spotify for Artists to receive alerts when new music is submitted under their name. If a release doesn’t belong to them, they can remove their association with it to stop it from appearing on their profile. By default, releases go live as scheduled unless an artist intervenes. If artists want greater control, they can choose to switch on an advanced setting that requires them to manually approve or reject releases before they appear on their profile. “Artists should never have to find someone else’s music under their name, said Sam Duboff, Spotify’s Global Head of Marketing and Policy, in an email to TechCrunch. “Their artist profile should be in their control. Starting today, every artist on Spotify can use Artist Profile Protection to review what shows up on their profile and prevent spammy and incorrect releases from ever reaching their page or their fans. We’re the first and only streaming service with a solution to the industry-wide problem of content mismatch, and we hope it sets a new standard for streaming platforms.” The company says it worked with thousands of artists during the beta-testing phase to refine the tool and make it easier to protect their profiles without disrupting release schedules. events.title: Genesis AI raises $500M to deploy glove-wearing robots
events.summary: Genesis AI has “cracked dexterous manipulation,” CEO and co-founder Zhou Xian says. To make his case, Xian hosted TechCrunch at Genesis AI’s Silicon Valley facility, where its physical AI model operated a pair of off-the-shelf robotic arms. In one demo, the arms picked up two small cardboard boxes, scanned them, placed them in a larger cardboard box, folded it closed, taped it shut, and then plucked a label off a strip of printer tape and applied it to the box. It’s an impressive demo, exactly the kind of complex workflow that today’s robots struggle to complete. And while Genesis wouldn’t let your reporter mess with the robot’s mise en place to test its wiles, the company did agree to rerun the presentation. During the second go-round, the robot fumbled a box and had a heck of a time peeling the tiny adhesive label off the printer tape. A mistake, but also the kind of edge case that can be used to improve a model — “hiccup data,” a Genesis executive suggests. This is the exact gap — between a lab demo and reliable automation — that Genesis , and the rest of the humanoid physical AI ecosystem, need to bridge if they want to avoid another robot winter. To do so, Xian’s company is announcing a $500 million Series A round led by Khosla Ventures, Premji Invest, and Eclipse. Xian and Genesis president Théophile Gervet, who met as graduate students in a Carnegie Mellon University lab, co-founded the company in 2024. Genesis announced its $105 million seed round in July 2025. The company’s strategy is vertical integration: generating the bulk of its own training data, developing its own generative AI model, and doing both in concert with the design and construction of a humanoid robot. “We wanted to ship the best robot, end-to-end product,” Xian said. The startup’s focus on dexterity — the robot’s ability to do stuff with its hands — and gathering the right data to achieve it sets it apart from competitors like Figure or Agility. Genesis gathers force data (apparently the unlock for effective manipulation) using a sensor-enabled glove. The gloves, and accompanying headset cameras, are worn by more than 100 real workers around the world, whose activities contribute to a training dataset that feeds into the company’s model. The company’s robots wear the same sensor-equipped gloves, and their “hands” are designed to mimic the proportions of human hands. That fidelity, Xian says, enables the robots’ capabilities in sorting and wire manipulation. The other big investment the company has made is in simulation. One of its advisers, Minchen Li, is a co-author of an influential physics algorithm used by the startup to create millions of high-fidelity models of the robot’s experience. Still, about that robot: Xian said that the company’s model was more capable when operating Eno, Genesis’ flagship humanoid robot. But Eno wasn’t ready to demonstrate its abilities for TechCrunch. A handsome machine bearing more than a hint of the late Steve Jobs’ influence on tech gadgets and their marketing, Eno reflects “the feeling” the company wants to deliver to its customers. That means less of a Terminator-style metal skeleton and more of an iMac on wheels. Genesis said it has built 30 to 40 Enos but wasn’t ready to share how many it would make in the year ahead. The company would only say that a mass-manufacturing contractor had been chosen to start work next year in the U.S. and that the design of the mass-produced version had been finalized. The company is piloting the machine with a handful of undisclosed customers. To realize the company’s vision, Xian says the key bottleneck is hardware capability, both in mechanical design and in the supply chains needed to produce industrial-grade machines. Right now, the company’s dexterous hands can only operate for a few weeks of regular work before they need to be replaced. For truly generalized robotic intelligence, Genesis needs more data. Xian pooh-poohs the finer distinctions between architectures like vision-language-action models and world action models . In his view, the software is ultimately transformers and attention, so “what really matters is the whole infra — the training infrastructure, the data infrastructure, and the quality of the data.” He estimates that “the model architecture contributes to maybe 10% of the final [result].” “I don’t think we expect or we need another fundamental scientific leap,” he told TechCrunch. “No, we have all the recipes. It’s just about execution.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. All have one thing in common: they use Optimizely's Web Experimentation software. Optimizely allows businesses to tweak the content and layout of their websites without changing the underlying site code. Unfortunately, someone other than its paying customers figured out how to do just that. The attackers abused a feature that allows Optimizely customers to add their own JavaScript to web pages. The malicious code was distributed alongside the legitimate stuff from Optimizely's own content delivery network, giving customers little reason to suspect anything was amiss. Optimizely has since confirmed that the criminals exploited a vulnerability, dubbed "OPTIMJACK" by researchers, in the sign-up process for its experimentation software, adding that it had patched the hole, removed the offending code, revoked tokens, and notified affected customers. "Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects,” the company said. “We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered." Of the 1,611 Optimizely scripts examined by Helme and his team, 188 contained malicious code, including those used by Optimizely's own website and login portal. Given the researchers examined only a subset of the scripts, the number of affected businesses could be higher. The malware underwent several revisions over the course of Monday, with cryptocurrency theft among the crooks' money-making schemes. Copy a wallet address to your clipboard and the malware could quietly swap it out for one belonging to the attackers, diverting any funds sent to that address. A card skimmer added later in the day grabbed card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes from payment forms. However, according to a separate analysis by StepSecurity , card details entered into an iframe hosted by a third-party payment processor were beyond the malware's reach. There was something nasty in store for Apple users, too. The malware attempted to deploy the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits on iPhones and iPads running older versions of iOS, though how many devices the criminals managed to compromise is anyone's guess. Helme traced roughly $7,000 in cryptocurrency to the attackers' wallets on Monday, though there’s no telling how much more the crooks stand to make from stolen payment card details. By 2152 UTC on Monday, TalkTalk was the only organization remaining on Report URI's list whose Optimizely code still contained the malware. All that money spent securing corporate websites, and the attackers found their way onto them via a bit of software the marketing department uses to tinker with web pages.
