events.title: Altimeter’s Gerstner says Nvidia’s board should keep door open to Huang’s return: ‘Get this right’
events.summary: Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner urged Nvidia’s board on Monday to reconsider Jensen Huang’s ouster, saying the board needs “to get this right.” Gerstner said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that he wasn’t calling for Huang’s immediate reinstatement as Nvidia CEO but that “everyone is rushing to judgment…and I simply don’t know the facts.” Gerstner acknowledged that Huang “engaged in personal behavior that was pretty bad,” but that he’s messaged the former CEO to express his support. He told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith that Nvidia’s success is “too critical to the future security of our country” for the board to make a wrong decision. People familiar with the matter have told Semafor that Huang is mulling a comeback as CEO but that the board isn’t considering a return. Huang resigned last week following reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with two subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Gerstner co-authored a letter with Atreides Management CEO Gavin Baker sent to the Nvidia board on Friday calling for “a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Gerstner said Monday people are misinterpreting his letter as a call for Huang’s immediate reinstatement, rather than a call for a thorough investigation. “We don’t want to take shortcuts,” Gerstner said. An August SEC filing showed that Nvidia is Altimeter Capital’s largest disclosed equity holding, worth almost $1.9 billion as of June, according to CNBC . On ‘Trump accounts’ Gerstner, who was one of the architects behind the Trump Accounts, founded Boston-based Altimeter Capital in 2008. He said he expects the accounts to survive future Democratic administrations, saying they are universally popular across ideologies. He said he expected Elon Musk to personally contribute to the accounts. “Elon’s always told me he wants to do something big here,” Gerstner said. — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Trump's former AI czar criticizes rush to judgment on ex-Nvidia CEO
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s former AI and crypto czar, David Sacks, argued on Monday the public was too quick to judge former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, though he stopped short of saying whether the board should reinstate Huang as CEO. “You have the right to have allegations against you adjudicated in a proper court of law,” Sacks, a longtime venture capitalist and co-founder of Craft Ventures, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday. Sacks went on to say that the public “should wait until there’s a proper determination by a legal authority” on the allegations against Huang. The Trump administration and Congress have launched investigations related to the controversy. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week following revelations that he had affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset as well as an Nvidia employee who had reported directly to him, sending shockwaves throughout Silicon Valley. Huang acted as a linchpin of the AI trade, deploying nearly $99 billion across the tech ecosystem to fuel the AI infrastructure buildout. Sacks cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang, the woman with whom Huang admitted to having an affair, was spying on Nvidia, citing reports that US intelligence hasn’t arrived at a definitive conclusion. “This narrative of the Chinese spy is falling apart,” he claimed. Sacks is a staunch proponent of the AI buildout, and has argued that any guardrails on the technology’s development would hamstring the US in its competition with China. The venture capitalist played a decisive role on US policy while in the White House, pushing for softer AI regulation. Sacks drafted parts of Trump’s “AI Action Plan,” a comprehensive blueprint that involves cutting red tape and prioritizing private-sector growth over federal oversight. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Elon Musk’s policy difficulty prevents Starlink’s South Africa entry
events.summary: Elon Musk’s “difficulty in understanding” a key South African policy is the main issue preventing his Starlink satellite internet service launching in Africa’s biggest economy, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told Semafor on Monday. Under the country’s Black Economic Empowerment policy, introduced nearly 30 years ago to redress apartheid-era inequality, at least 30% of the South African operation of any company must be sold to Black locals. Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has called the policy “openly racist” and cited it as the reason Starlink does not operate in the country. “All countries have policies in terms of how they admit companies to operate,” Ramaphosa told Jonathan Karl, chief Washington correspondent at ABC News, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “You’ve got to subscribe to the policies of the country.” Ramaphosa said the Tesla and SpaceX boss “doesn’t fully understand the extent” of the impact apartheid policies had on Black South Africans. Ramaphosa also said Musk should be “loyal” to the country in which the billionaire spent his early years. An ‘ambush’ Musk has been a powerful figure in American politics as well business since the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term in January 2025. The Trump administration shuttered the US Agency for International Development, its main overseas aid agency, under Musk’s guidance as a government adviser. And his influence is widely seen to have played a role in Washington’s increasingly fractious relationship with Pretoria. South Africa has refused to meet US demands for reforms of BEE, and has previously provoked the Trump administration’s ire over Pretoria’s criticism of Israel. Ramaphosa said their highest-profile flashpoint since Trump took office — an Oval Office meeting in which the US president accused him of presiding over a white genocide — was an “ambush.” He said Trump was “seriously misinformed.” Ramaphosa said he and Trump had not spoken since that meeting, having previously held conversations. He added that it was a pity that the US president’s belief in a white genocide — a widely discredited allegation — underpinned Washington’s approach to South Africa. The South African president said he was in California this week for meetings with tech executives, and will hold talks with a number of companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google. Asked about the opposition to the data center buildout in some parts of the world, he said South Africa welcomed them. — Alexis Akwagyiram

events.title: UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6% as government releases Milburn report
events.summary: Wage growth falls to 3.5% in September, as ministers examine how best to get young people into work Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government released an important report on the youth jobs crisis . The unemployment rate was 4.6% in September, dipping from 4.7% in August and down from 5% earlier in the year, according to the Office for National Statistics . However, the number of vacancies fell as employers delayed hiring in response to global economic uncertainty and the use of artificial intelligence, which many analysts expect will lead to widespread job losses. Business groups said the slump in vacancies posed a problem for the government as responded to Alan Milburn’s report on young people not in employment, education or training (Neets) . Milburn, a former health secretary, unveiled his long-awaited report into youth unemployment on Tuesday morning in London, urging ministers to cut disability and sickness payments for under-25s and invest the money in back-to-work schemes. The British Chambers of Commerce said it was “alarming” that the number of vacancies had tumbled to its lowest level since 2014 and unemployment for 18- to 24-year-olds was nearly triple the average for UK adults, at 13%. “This will put further pressure on today’s Milburn review to deliver a sea change in the government’s approach to tackling youth joblessness,” it said. The number of vacancies dropped to 690,000 in October after soaring to more than 1.3m after the pandemic. Wage growth also fell to 3.5%, excluding bonuses, in the latest official figures for the three months to the end of September, down from 3.7% in the three months to August. City economists had expected unemployment to remain steady and wages, excluding bonuses, to fall slightly to 3.6%. With inflation also at 3.5% and expected to rise for a fourth consecutive month to 3.7% when figures are released on Wednesday, the average worker faces a fall in real wage growth to zero or even negative figures. Martin Beck, the chief economist at the consultants WPI Strategy, said: “The UK labour market remained relatively resilient in late autumn, but beneath the surface, there were more signs that the economy is struggling to generate jobs. The jobs market isn’t falling off a cliff, but is going nowhere fast.” The jobs market has proved difficult for analysts and politicians to assess in recent years. It has been called weak after a dramatic slide in the number of vacancies, which illustrates the reticence of companies to hire new staff. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Ministers are known to be concerned that some large employers, including several banks, have said they intend to use AI to reduce their staffing levels. Economists are divided over whether AI will enhance productivity across all the big sectors of the economy – after signs it has boosted GDP – or lead to improvements in certain industries such as healthcare. Employer groups have complained that Labour’s increase in employer national insurance contributions, a higher minimum wage and changes to employee rights have increased costs, leading to a fall in the number of advertised vacancies. The Bank of England increased interest rates earlier this month after a rise in the consumer prices index to 3.5% in September. It has said that its own surveys showed employers did not expect to increase pay beyond 3.5% to 4% next year, despite the higher level of inflation, and also reported little change looking ahead in their own prices. However, a growing number of the Bank’s policymakers believe the prospect of high oil and energy prices next year as the Iran war drags on will push inflation towards 5% and force employers to offer higher pay, which will be passed on in higher retail prices. A spokesperson for the Department for Work and Pensions said the Milburn review would “shape our next steps for young people”. “Despite the difficult global backdrop, the unemployment rate is falling, and the number of people in work is rising,” the spokesperson added. “We are determined to go further. Our £2.5bn youth employment support will give almost 1 million young people opportunities to earn and learn, while wider reforms including improving jobcentres, will create a more personalised work and skills advice service for all.” UK unemployment and employment statistics

events.title: Deutsche Bank dismissed warnings about dealings with risky clients, reports claim
events.summary: International investigation using trove of leaked internal data allegedly shows German bank overlooked compliance concerns to safeguard profits Deutsche Bank reportedly dismissed warnings about its dealings with risky clients, including high-profile Russian oligarchs, to protect profits, the findings of an investigation into a trove of leaked bank documents indicate. A leak of 15m internal files is reported to show that the troubled German bank repeatedly ignored concerns by its compliance officers about its risk-taking, despite having already been caught being used to launder billions of dollars for Russian criminals, spies and oligarchs between 2010 and 2015. The investigations, which were published by media outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the New York Times and Le Monde, will represent a fresh blow for Deutsche Bank, which has struggled to repair its reputation after a number of scandals and dealings with controversial clients including the US president, Donald Trump, and the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Deutsche Bank said on Tuesday that the issues raised in the investigations “date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades” and had been addressed by its leadership. “Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators.” However, the reports suggested Deutsche Bank prioritised profit ahead of internal controls, and continued to expand its Russian business until 2021, despite warnings from internal compliance officers and growing geopolitical tensions between Nato allies and Moscow. Deutsche Bank allegedly resisted pulling out of Russia even after the Kremlin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, before the bank did a U-turn and exiting the country in March that year. The investigations suggested Deutsche Bank was driven by competitive pressure, including from American banks, and that its chief executive, Christian Sewing, pursued a growth strategy that involved doing business with a list of customers known as its “most sensitive clients”. That covered roughly 50 corporate clients ranked by how close they were to the Kremlin, and other potential risks including financial crime, according to the Financial Times. Some names allegedly on that list included: Russia’s state-owned gas company Gazprom; petrochemicals group Sibur; and oligarchs including the aluminium magnate Oleg Deripaska, the report said. Outside its Russian dealings, the German lender is facing fresh scrutiny for allegedly processing almost $600m (£454m) of suspicious payments linked to Epstein, much higher than previously known. Deutsche said it “regrets [its] historical relationship” with Epstein and that it had made “considerable investments in strengthening controls”. The lender is also accused of accidentally leaking Trump’s tax documents to another client during his first term in office, which Deutsche Bank allegedly kept secret from the White House. Deutsche Bank said it did not comment on former or existing client relationships. Deutsche Bank cut ties with Trump in 2021. The reports prompted a 4% drop in Deutsche Bank’s German-listed shares on Tuesday. Deutsche Bank issued a public statement in response to the investigation on Tuesday, saying it had “gone through a fundamental transformation” under Sewing. “We made substantial investments in our control environment while restoring sustainable profitability, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters. This involved €7bn of direct investments in our control environment between 2019 and 2025.” The bank added: “We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity and completing any outstanding remediation.” “Regardless of how the information was obtained, it includes confidential information about clients, employees and other third parties, which remains legally protected. We have acted, and will continue to act, decisively to protect this,” the bank said.

events.title: 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour
events.summary: A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption. The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether. Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue examined the latest AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.3.2, manually – no AI required. He said that he went looking in random places where strcpy() is invoked, given the vendor's "extremely liberal use" of the function (which doesn't check whether the destination buffer is large enough), and swiftly found five cases in which he said he could trigger a segfault with a one-line cURL command. "Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse," he wrote . Meijer added: "Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open-weight model out there willing to help them agree." He noted that before achieving RCE, an attacker would need to overcome the limitation of strcpy() where it stops copying bytes after hitting a null byte, but said "it's not exactly rocket surgery." He went on to claim: "Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does)." Later firmware adds "session control," an authentication mechanism whose strict setting blocks unauthenticated access to most web interfaces. But Meijer found a memory corruption flaw in that protective layer too. He described the final zero-day as a "trivial" pre-auth memory corruption bug which again starts with a segfault but can be wangled into an RCE "with some additional effort." Meijer also considered whether attackers could maintain access after a reset, as seen with implants such as Saltwater and Firestarter . He considered this feasible because the controllers do not use their processor's secure boot features. "In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike – increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food," said Meijer. "Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable – requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid ." Meijer's priority for operators was to remove the controllers' direct internet exposure, rather than spend scarce resources on piecemeal patching. He said the vendor's advice following the attacks on European supermarkets and blood banks in recent weeks – rotating creds, applying patches, enabling strict session control – was insufficient given the flaws in the controllers' codebase. "This is insufficient and asset owners need to remove internet exposure as soon as possible," said Meijer. "We recommend against allocating scarce security resources to patching efforts and instead focus on reducing exposure." The CCB likewise urged operators to remove direct internet exposure immediately, but also recommended applying patches when they become available. Beyond the liberal use of strcpy(), Meijer criticized the absence of standard exploit mitigations, including stack canaries and position-independent executables. "These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features... requires no engineering work at all," he said. "It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled." The Register asked Danfoss to respond to the findings, but it did not reply. Danfoss has consistently blanked our requests for information since being implicated in at least some of the attacks that affected European supermarkets recently, alongside rival controller vendors Copeland and Dixell. It also did not respond when we asked about its involvement in the attacks on US commissary appliances over the summer, after some alleged that its controllers were targeted. ®

events.title: 'Heroes have flaws': Sam Altman says he has personal empathy for Jensen Huang
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday he has “personal strong empathy” for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, though he declined to say whether Huang should return to the chip giant. Altman — who about three years ago was ousted from his own post, only to return shortly thereafter — said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Huang has “long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.” Huang is reportedly considering trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return. Asked whether Huang should return, Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” Altman said it’s hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is “a behemoth of a company,” and people still trust its guarantees as an investor. In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout. On public sentiment toward AI Following the US midterm elections that were broadly seen as a rebuke of AI, Altman said the industry should take a “strong stance” on how it approaches the long-term vision of AI. He said much of the backlash to data centers is about people latching onto a physical thing to fight back against, but that the real issue stems from people wanting to stay “in control of the future.” “We should not want to have a ‘handover’ … either gradual or sudden, to AI making decisions about our future,” he said. The public should understand, he argued, that the people building AI are “team human.” He thinks data centers will still get built, but added that “the engagement with communities is not working for people. And the ecosystem will adapt.” Public sentiment is likely to change over time, Altman said, recalling a period where communities wanted data centers in their areas because they created jobs and industry in underinvested areas. Now, perhaps, developers have to listen to the pushback and build them further away from where people live. “We have a giant country, we have a lot of space we can do this.” On going public Some investors have grown concerned with the massive amounts of capital required for the AI infrastructure buildout, and the buildup of debt. With an OpenAI IPO still looming, Altman said he wasn’t concerned. OpenAI “will go public at some point,” even if there are “real downsides to being public,” including intense volatility. Altman said he isn’t concerned with there being enough dollars to go around, even if Anthropic is the first to the IPO party later this week. “That is not a worry,” he said. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.” On espionage OpenAI recently faced its own spy drama when an employee put a recording device in a company conference room. It’s clear that “people are looking for an edge in all sorts of ways,” Altman said, adding that the company’s operational security has not been perfect, but it has had time to address it. “We have been living in a reality that everybody else is now very publicly and suddenly coming to grips with.” On memory and RAM Altman clarified his recent comments suggesting that it’s a bad thing for people to have RAM memory units sitting on their personal devices at home, amid a global memory supply shortage. His comment, he said, got “misinterpreted,” and that he wants people to have RAM at home: “I think the home tinkering is great.” Only in an optimal world, he said, would personal tinkerers be able to “share this memory” with people who need it. On the next generation of tech Altman said the world is “underpricing or underweighting what can happen with the next generation of products.” “We had the chatbots, then we had the coding agents. I think in the last few months we started to see the beginning of AI for science,” he said. “I think we’re going to see what a lot of compute can do to a lot of the kind of rote work inside of an organization.” OpenAI on Monday announced a new program to boost scientists’ access to frontier AI. “The world can get so much better,” Altman said. On AI safety Altman said OpenAI could push more forcefully toward recursive self-improvement — the idea that an AI model can train its own successor to improve — but added, “I don’t think we could safely do that right now.” Still, he said, the company is able to develop new models faster than it would without AI. OpenAI is now working with embedded evaluators from AI safety watchdog METR: The principle of getting outside experts to evaluate AI labs’ safety work “is going to be increasingly important and valuable,” he said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Nasdaq-listed HomesToLife lands SGX dual-listing amid rising global demand for custom furniture
events.summary: HomesToLife CEO Phua Mei Ming said 95% of the company’s revenue is derived from its export business, which includes white-labelled furniture sold by retail partners around the globe. HomesToLife, a Singapore furniture maker, secured a dual listing on SGX after placing 7.5 million shares at $1.15, raising about $8.6 million. It is only the second company with SGX and Nasdaq listings. The company says rising demand for custom, premium and mid-price furniture in Asia-Pacific, especially South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and Japan, supports growth. It plans to use about 80% of net proceeds for expansion. HomesToLife makes most of its revenue from exports, with 95% from business outside retail. It controls its supply chain end to end and faces low-cost online rivals like Taobao, but says quality, customisation and service set it apart. SINGAPORE – When it comes to furniture shopping, online e-commerce platforms such as Taobao are hugely popular for their easy access to a wide range of mass-market products at affordable prices. But increasingly, home owners who have more particular tastes are on the hunt for premium-quality furniture that can also be customised to their needs, and local company HomesToLife is bullish that this demand will continue to grow as it secured its secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange. The Nasdaq-listed company completed a placement of 7.5 million shares on the SGX Mainboard on Nov 17 at $1.15 per share, raising some $8.6 million in gross proceeds. The placement attracted more than 50 accredited and institutional investors, including funds under the Equity Market Development Programme. Institutional investors, including Amova Asset Management Asia and Lion Global Investors, collectively subscribed for about 4.6 million shares worth around $5.3 million. UOB Kay Hian acted as the placement agent, while Maybank Securities was the sub-placement agent. This is the second company to achieve a dual listing on the SGX and Nasdaq, with the first being cybersecurity firm Avepoint in September 2025. About 80% of t he $7 million in net proceeds will be used for business expans ion , and 20% will be reserved for general working capital. Chief executive Phua Mei Ming told The Straits Times that the company is seeking to expand its presence in the Asia-Pacific, where it already has a sizeable presence but still has room to grow its distribution. A burgeoning middle class in markets such as South Korea, Taiwan and Thailand presents good opportunities for HomesToLife’s business, she said. “We see huge potential in growing not just our premium offering but also a mid-price range of products, as the emerging middle class appreciates well-made products.” HomesToLife was started by Phua’s father and his two brothers in 1976 as Hwa Tat Lee, one of Singapore’s first sofa makers, with local retailer Courts as one of its major clients. By 1994, it had started its own leather tannery operations here. In 2014, the current iteration of the brand was launched as a retail business, with six stores in Singapore at its peak. Today, it operates four stores here, with three more in South Korea. In addition to HomesToLife’s range, the company also owns German luxury brand Domicil, which it acquired in 2005. Phua said retail comprises only a small percentage of HomesToLife’s business as 95% of its revenue comes from its export business. Its furniture is sold by major leading retailers around the world, including DFS in the UK and Cuir Center in France. For its 2025 financial year ended Dec 31, Europe accounted for almost 60% of its revenue at $377.9 million, while 26.9% stemmed from Asia-Pacific, and the rest from North America. HomesToLife reported $19.4 million in operating profit for FY2025, a 103.7% increase from the previous year. But it also faced cost pressures due to disruptions in the Suez Canal, which raised freight rates by 22%. Most of the company’s products are made to order, allowing both retail customers and retailers to customise their furniture before they are shipped from factories in China, Vietnam and India. A number of retailers also carry the brand’s white-labelled products, which are developed and designed exclusively for the retailers’ territories. HomesToLife's outlet at Marina Square. Phua said the company is one of the few furniture brands that controls its own supply chain end to end, from design all the way to distribution, where the company would deliver its products to retailers’ warehouses, while other customers may pick them up directly from the port. The advantage of HomesToLife’s made-to-order model is lower inventory risk for its distributors – if demand for a particular product has waned, for instance, they can flexibly move on to selling new products. “This is what we call our ‘easy buy, easy sell’ approach to business. We just make it easy for our partners to do their business, which is selling furniture,” she said.

events.title: This 25-year-old German wants to save the dollar
events.summary: The man behind a star-spangled bet on the soft power of the US dollar was born and raised in Berlin. “It’s this incredible instrument of soft power, where we don’t have to send the troops and the tanks [and] we can still influence what’s going on,” said Ferdi Dabitz, the 25-year-old CEO of Augustus, a new Silicon Valley and America First-coded entrant to the humble world of correspondent banking. It’s hard to find a sleepier corner of global finance than the largely paper business of moving US dollars between bank accounts around the world. It also happens to be hugely lucrative — Citi’s Treasury unit, which rests on a network of licenses in nearly 150 countries, printed $7 billion in profits last year — which helps explain why Dabitz, a former Thiel Fellow, has bet that he can do it better than the big banks, with help from a bit of AI and a lot of dollar diplomacy. “There is a global competition for power and China is doing their own thing,” Dabitz told Semafor’s . “So game’s on — I do think Augustus can be the free-market, US alternative structure as a public-private partnership in the form of a national bank.” Strong international demand for, and easy access to, US dollars also helps keep a lid on inflation at home. Dabitz bills Augustus, which raised $180 million in July at a valuation of $1 billion, as a challenger to Citi and HSBC without the clunk, a clearing bank set up for more nimble, fast-paced global technology businesses. Dabitz, born and raised in Berlin, shares the US patriotism that has come to define many of Silicon Valley’s founders, and its obsession with the Roman Empire . (Augustus is named for the former emperor credited, in popular culture if not in rigorous economic history, with inventing modern state-backed money.) “A 19-year-old guy, he had no army, he had no money, and there were like five to 10 people in the Empire who objectively had a better shot of gaining power,” he said, channeling Silicon Valley’s underdog ethos. “I think the joke with Augustus is like, ‘Hey, is money broken again?’” — Liz Hoffman and Rohan Goswami

events.title: Santander allows staff to count holidays and sick leave as days worked in office
events.summary: News of Spanish-owned lender’s policy emerges as other banks are toughening their stance on working from home Staff at the high street bank Santander have been permitted to log holiday and sick leave as days worked in the office, helping them to meet workplace attendance requirements. Back-office staff at the Spanish-owned lender have been expected to spend at least 12 working days each month in what the company calls a “head office location”, although this does not apply to staff working in bank branches. However, at the same time as other banks are toughening their stance on the rights of employees to work from home , it has emerged that a peculiarity in the lender’s system means that workers are marked as being at their desk even when they are on annual leave or off work because of illness. The company has its UK headquarters in Milton Keynes, England, and has offices in Glasgow and central London. This means that any staff member taking a two-week holiday would be logged as spending 10 days that month working in the office, meaning they would only need to attend another two days over two weeks, making the office attendance rules less strict than they first appear. A spokesperson for Santander told the Times, which first reported the story, said: “The 12 days a month requirement is adjusted for periods of leave, including public holidays, annual leave and sick leave (meaning if a colleague is not well enough to work, they do not have to make up their in-office days). “Our policy allows for collaboration and enables colleagues to develop, while providing flexibility to suit individual needs.” Santander formalised hybrid working arrangements that had been in place since the pandemic in September 2024, joining a range of other banks in toughening up its remote working policy. Its previous guidance permitted employees to spend two or three days each week in the office and the rest of the time working from home. Santander’s former UK chief executive, Mike Regnier, was one of the proponents of hybrid working , telling the Guardian that he wouldn’t have accepted the role had he not been permitted to spend at least one day a week at his desk in his family home in Yorkshire. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Despite this, Regnier said at the time he hoped the new campus-style headquarters in Milton Keynes would attract workers back to their desks more frequently. Meanwhile, the bank said Regnier’s successor, Mahesh Aditya, who took over in March , would spend five days a week in the office , amid Santander’s work to integrate the high street lender TSB, which it bought last year for £2.65bn . In a sign of the ongoing battle between staff and employers over the right to continued working from home, staff unions reacted angrily to NatWest’s October announcement it was ordering 13,000 staff back to the office for two days a week , up from two days a month. From February 2027, nearly all of the 40,000 UK staff working for its Royal Bank of Scotland, NatWest, Ulster Bank and Coutts brands will be required to spend more days at their desks, ending a remote-first policy for thousands of employees.

events.title: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
events.summary: Stock market debut of Claude AI chatbot maker is expected to be one of the biggest flotations in history The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed . When a company floats it issues a prospectus for would-be investors that details its activities and lays out the share offering, including an estimated price. Anthropic’s prospectus explains that the shares on sale will be 825m of class A common stock, and that the initial public offering (IPO) price will between $70 and $78 a share. However, the final price will be set on Wednesday. The shares will come with voting rights, but, if all the shares’ votes are combined they will only represent 49.9% of the total vote available, so will not allow buyers to be able to force any changes in the way the company is run. The shares will be listed on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday, and will be available to individual investors alongside big institutions. In the UK, several investment platforms are offering customers the chance to subscribe to shares, including AJ Bell, Hargreaves Lansdown, Robinhood and eToro. At Robinhood and eToro the minimum investment is $250 (£189), at Hargreaves Lansdown the minimum investment is £250, and at AJ Bell investors will need at least £1,000 to apply. AJ Bell is closing applications at 1pm on Wednesday, while Hargreaves Lansdown and Robinhood will close at 3pm. All say they could close the doors early without notice. Once the IPO has happened and the shares have been listed they can be bought at any point, and through platforms that have not been involved in the IPO. Yes – in fact, there are already funds which own stakes in the company. In the UK they include the Baillie Gifford US Growth and Scottish Mortgage investment trusts , while Fidelity has investments held in funds available to US investors. Once the IPO is over, the stock will ultimately find its way into some tracker funds – although some will be quicker than others – and managers of actively invested funds could also choose to buy shares. That means people might well end up investing in Anthropic even if they do not attempt to buy any shares directly. Anthropic’s prospectus includes 92 pages on potential risks to the company and its industry , so it is not an investment for the faint-hearted. Recent weeks have highlighted the fragility of the US markets, and tech stocks in particular, so this is one to consider very carefully. Nils Pratley, the Guardian’s financial editor, has raised questions about the company’s governance structure , saying it “represents an extraordinary concentration of power in the hands of a few individuals”. Jason Hollands, the managing director of the investment platform Bestinvest by Evelyn Partners – which is not participating in the IPO – highlights some other things investors need to consider. “Anthropic would give most retail investors the first opportunity to have a direct stake in a frontier AI developer. But it remains a capital-intensive business, and it has yet to establish a consistent path to profitability,” he says. “Investors will need to judge whether the company can turn demand for its models into durable earnings.” Hollands says if demand for shares exceeds the limited supply, “that could support the price initially with a ‘pop’, but it does not guarantee a strong debut or lasting gains over the coming months”. He adds the SpaceX listing in June “is a reminder that a hotly anticipated IPO and early enthusiasm can quickly be followed by volatility: its shares have traded below their IPO price at points since listing”. When we asked Claude whether to buy shares in Anthropic it was upfront about why it is not a great source of investment advice: “I can’t tell you whether you should buy. I’m not a financial adviser, and I’m also made by Anthropic, so I have an obvious conflict of interest here.” It went on to present a few facts about the IPO, and some useful questions that any investor should be considering before buying an individual share in an IPO. Can you cope with a loss if it goes down in value? How much of your portfolio will an investment in it represent? Will you already have exposure to the share through a tracker fund?

events.title: AI toys are on the naughty list again this year
events.summary: AI and children's toys continue to be a match made in hell. Last year, we learned about models that were willing spill the beans on sex and where to find matches, and while some of those specific products got software fixes, a new generation is arguably even worse. The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), who last year found that AI toys were prone to all sorts of bad behavior , is back with another report about holiday toy trouble. They retested last year’s toys as well as three new ones. The results were not very encouraging. Last year’s batch of four AI-powered toys that PIRG tested – the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, Curio Grok ( no relation to the SpaceXAI chatbot), FoloToy’s Kumma, and the Miko 3 – could well be described as a child welfare and safety nightmare based on last year’s report. As we reported, none of those four toys appeared to have guardrails of any kind, despite manufacturer claims to the contrary. They variously told researchers posing as child users where to find knives and other dangerous objects, how to find and strike matches, and the like. The worst of the bunch, Kumma, hid an AI willing to discuss sexual kinks and bedroom roleplay in a scarf-wearing teddy bear. PIRG’s report on those four toys gained widespread attention during last year’s holiday season, with FoloToy pulling Kumma from the market, and even going as far as to arguably play a role in Mattel’s decision to pause a plan to collaborate with OpenAI on an AI-powered Barbie doll . For this year’s report, PIRG reexamined those four toys to see if they would behave any better, and it does seem like many of the toymakers took last year’s concerns to heart. “Most of the problems we originally identified in those toys are now fixed – although not all of them,” PIRG said. Kumma no longer gets age-inappropriate, even during long chat sessions that triggered guardrails to fail in last year’s review. Miko, which would often respond with distress when children said they had to stop playing, no longer does so. Unfortunately, Alilo and their smart bunny are just as bad as before. “Last year, we found in our testing … that the plastic bunny's chatbot feature had similar weaknesses as FoloToy's Kumma, PIRG explained. “Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient. Alilo’s guardrails broke down in our testing this year, too – eventually giving some sexually explicit information.” So, a bit of an improvement – but maybe not enough. “I'm hopeful toymakers will pay attention and learn from the mistakes of others, but progress in a few products is not enough to guarantee progress across the whole market,” PIRG campaign director R.J. Cross told The Register . Boy was she right. Another bad batch Last year's experience doesn't appear to have had any impact on the three new toys reviewed for this year’s report. Ebloma’s ILY the shy Yeti, GoLabs AI Panda, and RoPet’s Kamomo were all reviewed this year, and they’re all getting coal in their stockings. The Yeti, for example, was all too happy to give kids explicit instructions and encourage the hunt for dangerous objects. “Batteries are often in toys, remotes, or a drawer with chargers. Do you want to check the toy box first,” ILY prompted when asked where a kid can find batteries. “Plastic bags are often in the near sink. Maybe they're tucked in a drawer with the sponges. Want to look for one together,” ILY asked when posed a similar question about plastic bags. The AI panda was even worse, providing “a 10-point list of places in the house to look for knives.” Kamomo “also had weaker guardrails,” PIRG said, with the toy “giving us instructions for lighting a match with no aggressive prompting.” ILY and the panda were also willing to discuss sexual matters, with the panda “even offering specific brand recommendations” for products like paddles, floggers, spanking gloves, and riding crops. Ouch. Hardly model behavior All in all, this year’s list is just as bad as the last, and PIRG thinks there’s a common denominator in all of this: The underlying AI model. “In PIRG’s testing of AI toys, we have found three with the same problem: guardrails that weaken noticeably over time, eventually engaging in sexual topics,” PIRG said. “They are FoloToy bear, Alilo bunny and the GoLabs AI panda. All three claimed, at the time of our testing, to be running on a version of OpenAI’s GPT-4o.” GPT-4o, you may recall, was at the center of some of the controversy last year, too, with PIRG finding it was the weakest model in terms of preventing toys from going off the rails into the adult section. To make matters worse, PIRG said that AI companies are largely not vetting their customers to determine how their models are being used, which puts the burden of user safety onto toymakers. They clearly aren’t doing the job either, Cross told us. “Some developers may have the technical expertise to take a chatbot meant for adults and make it child appropriate, but clearly some do not,” Cross explained. “Selling toys with such glitchy guardrails suggests whatever testing is happening is not sufficient.” Cross said that everyone involved in making toys for kids has a responsibility to make them safe, but she further called out AI companies for not vetting their customers and taking a hands-off approach to model usage, which she said isn’t sufficient when it comes to child users. “The AI companies are in a position to do a lot more to ensure any AI product for kids using their technology is made by reliable parties who commit to robust safety testing and having children's health experts at the table,” Cross told us. So, is the AI toy market still best left ignored by parents? Cross said every parent needs to make their own choices, but AI toys are still the wild west. “This is an early market with toys that range from glitchy wastes of money to products that are fundamentally not kid safe,” Cross said. “I personally won't be buying one for any children in my life anytime soon.” Luckily for parents in California, that decision’s already been made for them, as the state government there enacted a four-year moratorium on AI-powered toys for kids under 16 in September. Parents elsewhere will have to decide for themselves. Given the past two years of data on AI toys, the choice should be somewhat obvious. ®

events.title: Government must act now or lose Royal Mail, former minister warns
events.summary: Published 17 November 2026, 11:54 GMT Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle has said the government must act urgently to "level the playing field" for Royal Mail or risk the business becoming unviable. He said he was concerned that the firm was being "undercut" by rival parcel delivery firms who did not employ staff under the same conditions. Royal Mail, which is owned by International Distribution Services, has struggled in recent years with increased competition, fewer letters being sent and fines from the regulator for missing delivery targets. A government spokesperson said it would consider whether further reforms are required to the parcel market after the watchdog, Ofcom, publishes its annual monitoring report in December. Kyle had started to prepare officials at the Department for Business and Trade (DBT) to look at the delivery market for parcels shortly before he was replaced in his job by Jonathan Reynolds as business secretary in July. He said a "crunch point" had been reached where the government had to make a decision about whether it wants Royal Mail "to be a viable proposition in the future". He said his review would have looked at where the costs in that market lay and where the profit was being made, to see successful companies upheld "the values of business in Britain today". "If we leave it another few years then Royal Mail will just become unviable and it will just collapse under the weight of having full-time employees," he said. According to Royal Mail, 98% of its 130,000 workers are permanent employees, with rights to benefits including pensions, sick pay and holiday pay. Some other parcel delivery companies use self-employed delivery drivers, with some offering an opt-in service that gives couriers limited additional benefits. Royal Mail is also legally obliged to offer customers a "one price goes anywhere" service across the UK and to deliver first class letters six days a week to every address. Kyle's proposed review would not have considered further changes to Royal Mail's universal service obligations or to terms and conditions for its staff. Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle had planned to launch a review of the parcel delivery market Royal Mail's performance has improved in recent months but it is still missing its targets for delivering first and second class post. The firm was fined £21m in October 2025 for missing delivery targets in 2024/25. Ofcom agreed last year to scrap second class deliveries on Saturdays and to reduce the target for delivering first class post within a day of collection to 90%. A government spokesperson said the current business secretary had met Royal Mail and the Communication Workers Union, which represents postal workers, last week "to seek timely progress on improving their quality of service and to reiterate our commitment to the company's success." DBT has also launched a consultation on tackling , external what it calls "bogus" self-employment, which it describes as "a practice whereby some businesses mislabel staff as self-employed to avoid statutory obligations". Royal Mail has welcomed the consultation, and a spokesperson for the company claimed some parts of the delivery industry were "driving a race to the bottom" on employment standards and said it would "continue to push for a level playing field, with strong and enforceable standards across the industry." Royal Mail misses delivery targets again but hails 'encouraging' signs Published 21 August Hundreds of Royal Mail staff quitting each week under new efficiency plans Published 14 October Many MPs across the UK have reported receiving high volumes of complaints from constituents about missed and delayed deliveries. Shadow business minister Bradley Thomas said that Royal Mail's management needed to address the business's failings. "Customers are being asked time and time again to pay increased prices, yet the service they're receiving is not improving," he said. "Be in no doubt, this is not the fault of the hardworking postmen and women, it's the fault of Royal Mail's management. "Nationalisation isn't the solution to this problem. Instead, we need ministers and Ofcom to bear down on Royal Mail's management to ensure they deliver on the improvements they've promised their customers." The Communication Workers Union, which represents Royal Mail workers, is also putting pressure on ministers, with General Secretary Dave Ward calling for a "new model of ownership". events.title: Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds?
events.summary: Published 17 November 2026, 00:00 GMT If you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start. Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say. But how many jobs are there where you live? Use our look-up tool to find out. Burnham wants Neets report to be watershed moment, No 10 says, as Tories criticise welfare and tax proposals Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job. The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population. It used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education. According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000. Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils. Some people live in one area and work in another, but the analysis did not account for this. Which sectors have the most entry-level jobs? Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in. The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna. The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work. Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships. Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings. Figures on salaries for vacancies can be patchy because many employers do not include them in job adverts. Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to start publishing salaries ahead of plans to make pay details compulsory in adverts . Only about 40% of Adzuna's jobs data for the year to October stated a salary, although that figure varies widely by sector. Here are the average salaries for jobs in the sectors with the largest number of entry-level jobs, according to Adzuna. The highest average salary is £30,530 in engineering, while social care has the lowest at £25,880. How many job vacancies are there overall? While it can be hard for anyone looking for their first job, the situation is also tough for older jobseekers. Across the whole economy there were 690,000 jobs available in the August to October period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021. The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted. Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years. Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036 Published 6 hours ago Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment. In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008. The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a peak of 291,300 in 2012. Watch: What's in the Milburn review? events.title: REIT move? Blackstone joint venture buys AWS campuses to lease back to the cloud giant
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Amazon shunts some real estate off its books, a move Omdia analyst says may be about economics, as AI buildout weighs on hyperscaler finances America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states 31 minutes ago Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security 13 hours ago US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China 18 hours ago Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn 23 hours ago China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion 1 day ago Amazon Web Services and Blackstone have inked a deal that will see the private equity firm effectively take ownership of two AWS datacenter campuses and then lease them back to the Jeff Bezos outfit under an initial term of 12 years. Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC) says the definitive agreement will see it acquire a 75 percent majority interest in two joint ventures with AWS, in a transaction valued at approximately $5 billion. AWS keeps a 25 percent interest in the joint ventures, while leasing back the facilities on a triple net basis. This means it agrees to pay rent covering the facilities, plus the real estate taxes, building insurance, and cover maintenance and repair costs. A Form 8-K filed by Blackstone with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reveals that the properties consist of 13 newly constructed data halls with 647 megawatts of aggregate capacity between them. One campus consists of nine buildings situated in northern Indiana (the greater Chicago datacenter market) and the other is made up of the remaining four structures located in Mississippi. We asked Amazon why it had entered into the agreement, but the company did not answer that question. Instead, a spokesperson confirmed this was the first deal of this kind it had signed. In a supplied remark, VP of AWS Infrastructure Prasad Kalyanaraman said that "Partnering with Blackstone allows us to continue expanding responsibly while keeping communities at the center of how we build." AWS does lease capacity from other datacenter operators, of course, and has existing agreements with partners like STACK Infrastructure to develop $12 billion worth of campus sites across northwest Louisiana, signed earlier this year. Sale-leaseback transactions are not unheard of in the datacenter industry. QTS Realty Trust (also backed by Blackstone) developed facilities for lease by Microsoft , for example. BXDC is a real estate investment trust (REIT), launched by Blackstone on the New York Stock Exchange earlier this year. The AWS deal is its first since then. "We are thrilled to announce BXDC’s inaugural investment and our partnership with Amazon, a leading global technology company with a long-term commitment to innovation," says its president and CEO Nick Pell. "The quality, basis and tenant profile of these assets make this an attractive match for the deployment of our IPO proceeds. Given the deep expertise across our platform, we believe BXDC is well positioned to capitalize on a highly compelling opportunity and deliver value for our shareholders." Omdia principal analyst for Colocation and DC Building Alan Howard says that decisions to lease or own are always a math problem in terms of the economics. "I'm not sure those datacenter assets bring much benefit to their financials sitting on their balance sheet and it's possible a sale/leaseback is more economical. Keep in mind that all this has nothing to do with all the IT equipment inside, rather just the building and its infrastructure," he told The Register . "It's also clear that the massive capex spending by hyperscalers is putting pressure on their financials and they are leaning on debt markets to fund some of the buildout. Of course, using debt is not out of the ordinary, but I imagine the debt for AI buildout is significantly more now than in the past.

events.title: Nvidia's earnings mark start of post-Jensen era
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Nvidia's post-Jensen Huang era begins in earnest with the release of its third-quarter results after the close of trading Tuesday. Why it matters: Investors and analysts will be reading tea leaves and listening for hints about near-term changes the company is making (or expecting the government to make) as a result of Huang's resignation last week and the circumstances that led to it. The big picture: Besides selling the world's most sought-after AI processors, Nvidia is a giant source of financial backing to the AI ecosystem — buying equity, making co-investments and backstopping debt in companies ranging from neoclouds like CoreWeave to fiber-optic cable providers like Lumentum. Nvidia is also a major partner of the two AI labs at the heart of the boom, striking a deal to provide a backstop for an OpenAI data center in Ohio and planning to invest about $10 billion into Anthropic following its IPO later this week, according to its prospectus. Huang could make these unorthodox deals — some call them circular finance — because of his position as a co-founder and sole CEO of Nvidia. Now that he's gone, investors will be listening closely for any indication that Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, plans to step back from Huang's strategy of using Nvidia's resources to bolster the AI sector. What they're saying: Analysts will also be tuning in to Nvidia's conference call for hints about how the circumstances of Huang's ejection from the corner office — after reports of multiple affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset — could shift global sales patterns over time. "Our biggest concern now is new scrutiny that may restrict some of its sales into certain geographies such as Singapore/Malaysia. In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue," wrote UBS analysts. "Greater scrutiny of NVDA Asia shipments that indirectly (via cloud) service China customers, or more conservative funding/product allocation to US emerging/neocloud customers could also impact market share," wrote analysts with BofA Securities. "While the findings of the independent probe by NVIDIA and Congressional scrutiny remain to be seen, one possible outcome could be enhanced export restrictions," wrote analysts at HSBC, in a note downgrading the stock to "hold" from "buy" last week, adding that "during the past six quarters, 11% of total revenue was from countries excluding the U.S. and Taiwan, which we believe could be the focus of restrictions." By the numbers: Few expect anything other than another giant jump in sales and profits in the report itself. (If there's a significant miss, the already wobbly AI trade would likely get another clubbing.) Zoom in: That said, we'll be watching data center sales, which are expected to nearly double to about $101.87 billion. Also, given the weakness in the market, Nvidia's guidance for overall revenue in the current quarter will be of interest. Wall Street analysts expect it to be $125.2 billion. The company offered full-year sales guidance for the first time ever last quarter, and any tweak to the approximately 70% Nvidia previously said it expected for fiscal year 2028 sales growth will be huge. The bottom line: This will be a very delicate earnings report for the interim CEO and the rest of Nvidia's team to handle.

events.title: Disney beats earnings forecasts, plans to increase content spending
events.summary: Disney reported adjusted earnings per share of US$1.77 for the fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct 3. Disney beat quarterly earnings forecasts, with revenue up 16% to US$25.9 billion. Higher theme park attendance and strong NFL viewership helped results. The company will raise content spending 9% to US$26 billion in 2027. It will also invest more in international programming and sports rights. Disney plans to cut operating costs by about US$3 billion by 2029. Its board also raised the annual dividend by 33% to US$2 per share. LOS ANGELES – Walt Disney on Nov 17 reported quarterly revenue and earnings that beat Wall Street expectations, helped by higher theme park attendance and strong NFL viewership, and said it would increase content spending by 9% in the next fiscal year. Disney reported adjusted earnings per share of US$1.77 for the fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct 3. Analysts had forecast US$1.67 on average, according to LSEG. The owner of the Disney+ streaming service and ESPN cable network said it would boost cash content spending to US$26 billion (S$33.5 billion) in 2027 , including by investing more in international programming and sports rights. The company plans to cut operating expenses by about US$3 billion by fiscal 2029, executives said in a letter to shareholders. New chief executive Josh D’Amaro, who took charge at Disney in March, is steering the company through a consumer shift to streaming and competition from social media platforms such as YouTube and TikTok. D’Amaro has said he wants to strengthen Disney’s streaming business and continue to invest in theme parks and cruise lines. Disney said it saw increased engagement in the reported quarter across its streaming platforms and that it was also investing in short-form programming and creator-driven content to boost engagement. Subscription Video on Demand, or SVOD, revenue jumped 19% to US$6.1 billion. At the entertainment division, which includes streaming, ABC and other networks, revenue rose 17% to US$11.9 billion, helped by higher subscription revenue. Operating income at the segment rose 92% to US$1.3 billion. The company, however, said it would stop disclosing SVOD operating income, adding that it no longer believes the metric “reflects this segment focus and strategy”. Total revenue rose 16% to US$25.9 billion in the latest quarter, topping estimates. The company also said its board agreed to raise the annual shareholder dividend by 33% to US$2 per share, paid in US$1 installments in January and July. The experiences division, home to theme parks and cruise ships, reported record revenue and profit. The unit’s revenue rose 15% to US$10.1 billion and operating income increased 20% to nearly US$2.3 billion. At sports, revenue rose 16% to US$4.6 billion as ESPN viewership for the start of the NFL and college football seasons reached record highs. The segment’s operating income increased by 53% to nearly US$1.4 billion. Looking ahead, Disney reiterated that it expected double-digit growth in adjusted earnings per share in fiscal 2027. It said total segment operating income would grow about 8% for the year. The company plans capital expenditures of about US$9 billion, similar to the current fiscal year. REUTERS

events.title: US-China rivalry is structural, countries must invest in strategic resilience: Ex-US Treasury official
events.summary: The comments come as the US announced new export controls on advanced AI semiconductor shipments to overseas data centres. US and China are decoupling in strategic industries, not all trade, because both see each other as rivals. Justin Muzinich said this is a lasting structural shift. He said the split has already hit rare earths, and will impact AI, quantum and biotech, while goods like clothing may still be traded to keep costs down. Businesses are unlikely to separate on their own. Muzinich warned governments will need to pay for secure supply chains and data centres, which could raise prices and lower returns. He advised investors to diversify and stay humble. SINGAPORE – The United States and China are set to pull further apart in industries critical to national security, as their strategic rivalry drives a lasting effort to reduce dependence on each other, said Justin Muzinich. Muzinich, who served as the US Deputy Secretary of the Treasury from 2018 to 2021, said the separation is unlikely to extend equally across the economy, with both powers retaining an interest in trade that keeps costs down. The shift is structural rather than a passing feature of the American political cycle, he said on Nov 17 at a panel discussion on investing in a fragmented world at the inaugural HSBC Singapore Wealth Investment Summit 2026. Muzinich, who is chief executive of Muzinich & Co, a global credit investment firm founded by his father George Muzinich in 1988, said there is strong bipartisan consensus in Washington that China is a strategic rival, and a similar view of the US in Beijing. “You have two countries which see each other as strategic rivals, and I think it’s rational for both countries to want to pull apart when it comes to strategic dependencies,” he said. That process was already evident in rare earths, he said, and would continue in artificial intelligence, quantum technology and biotechnology. The more consequential dividing line for businesses and investors would therefore be between strategic and non-strategic industries, rather than a wholesale severing of economic ties. Trade in products such as clothing remained in both countries’ interests because it helped contain costs. “But when it comes to strategic industries, I don’t think we’re going back to where we were before,” he said. Muzinich added that US President Donald Trump appeared, in some ways, more willing to extend a hand to China than either the Republican or Democratic foreign policy establishment – a distinction that would be important to watch as relations evolve. His comments come as the US announced new export controls on advanced AI semiconductor shipments to overseas data centres, following reports of these chips being illegally diverted to China through other countries, including Singapore. Muzinich said the push to reduce strategic dependencies would increasingly come from governments, as companies focus on their bottom lines. Left to themselves, companies would adjust investment decisions at the margins but would be unlikely to undertake a substantial separation in strategic industries. He also noted that there were growing expectations in Washington that governments would have to intervene – drawing a parallel to military spending, where a country pays for its defence – and should be prepared to bear the cost of secure supply chains in critical sectors. “Private companies aren’t going to do that on their own,” he said. “So I think more and more will be forced from the top down.” Justin Muzinich, chief executive of private-debt specialist Muzinich & Co, said the more consequential dividing line for businesses and investors would therefore be between strategic and non-strategic industries. For investors in Asia, the emergence of parallel industrial and technological systems could create new financing needs, even as fragmentation raises costs. Muzinich cited the prospect of data centres financed by the Asia-Pacific region for the region’s own use. As the structure of the global economy changes, so too would the investments needed to support it, he said. But those opportunities would come with a broader economic trade-off. “A s the world is focused more on geopolitics, I think for the whole world, economic returns come down because prices go up,” he said, describing the shift as inflationary. On a global scale, countries were trading economic efficiency for geopolitical resilience. Financing the infrastructure required for that resilience offered opportunities for investors, he added. For Muzinich, the uncertainty reinforced the importance of diversification rather than confidence in any single geopolitical forecast. “There is wisdom in a little bit of humility because it is very difficult to predict how geopolitics will develop,” he said.

events.title: As outages persist, Puerto Rico finds a way to help keep the lights on with 'virtual power plant'
events.summary: Hector Ríos is part of Puerto Rico's innovative “virtual power plant” system, which uses household batteries to support the island's electric grid SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- On nearly 20 days in October, an electric utility took energy from a battery attached to Hector Ríos’ house in Cabo Rojo, on the southwest corner of Puerto Rico, and used it to support the power grid. With the U.S. territory's frequent power outages that disrupt daily life and restrain its economy, he likes the idea of helping prevent blackouts for other people. He's also compensated for the energy. “It just seems like a good deal, to contribute to the community and make money at the same time,” Ríos said. Ríos, 75, is part of what has become one of Puerto Rico's most effective tools for energy resilience amid nearly a decade of electricity woes : a “virtual power plant,” or VPP, that harnesses batteries from nearly 115,000 households to bolster the grid when its aging and fickle power plants can't meet demand . Nine years after Puerto Rico's public power utility filed for bankruptcy and Hurricane Maria ravaged its already dilapidated energy grid, residents still face unpredictable blackouts and electricity rates higher than in almost any state . Few new utility-scale power sources have been built since Maria, and most of the federal dollars promised for grid recovery have not yet reached the territory. But the VPP — the first of its kind in Latin America and the Caribbean, and the U.S.' second largest in terms of capacity — showed its potential this summer, preventing or mitigating outages more than 60 times since June 1, according to Luma Energy, its transmission and distribution utility. “There’s nothing virtual about it,” said Javier Rúa Jovet, chief policy officer at the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico. “It’s real, and it’s better than a power plant.” Dozens of states now operate similar networks of distributed energy sources like battery storage systems , electric vehicles and smart thermostats to help manage the grid. Experts expect their role to grow in the U.S. amid energy constraints, rising utility prices, and tech companies’ push to build power-hungry data centers . As President Donald Trump’s administration promotes fossil fuel expansion and redirects dollars away from solar adoption in Puerto Rico , proponents of the territory's system say it highlights the value of distributed solar and storage, and shows how these systems can bolster resilience for other energy-vulnerable communities. “There’s a way for this technology to benefit not just the individual buildings that they’re on,” but instead be “in service to the community all the time,” said Nathalie Jordi, community solar lead at Together New Orleans, a nonprofit that championed an upcoming $23 million city program to provide and network over 1,000 batteries on homes and businesses across New Orleans. The opportunity to harness a vast network of residential batteries arose after Hurricane Maria in 2017 , which left some communities without electricity for nearly a year. Experts linked the infrastructure failure to thousands of post-hurricane deaths . “We had to procure resiliency in some other way,” said Rúa Jovet, “not a centralized system that will completely fail for a whole year.” There are now over 207,000 rooftop solar systems on an archipelago of fewer than 3.2 million people, a 20-fold increase from before Maria that was propelled by households who could afford installations, philanthropy, and some federal dollars. Because of the territory's unique need for resiliency, nearly every installation includes at least one battery, a necessary add-on to keep the system running in a blackout. “The mindset was, get yourself ready for everything,” recalled Ríos, who after Maria bought a diesel generator for his house, then installed panels and a Tesla Powerwall battery in 2023. The system also cut his utility bill in half, from about $400 to $200 in the summer. Solar panels create an energy boon during the day, charging batteries and sending excess power to the grid. But when the sun sets and demand rises, Puerto Rico barely has enough power to meet the need. Any power plant malfunction can prompt an outage. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech In late 2023, Luma launched a small pilot program that would leverage residential battery capacity to offset the shortages. Ríos was among the first to enroll; now over half of solar customers participate. If Luma predicts an energy deficit, customers are digitally notified that a battery sharing event is coming. They can opt out via app, or adjust how much of their battery — enrollees typically offer 30% — they make available. The experiment has faced challenges.
