events.title: A dovish détente gives way to geopolitical gravity
events.summary: To be a China “hawk,” Jensen Huang declared last year, is a “badge of shame.” The former Nvidia CEO was a proud dove, one who found a dovish partner in US President Donald Trump — quite literally, in a business sense. Together, they formed an enterprise that aimed to sell high-end Nvidia chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of the profits. Their alliance represented the high-water mark of a Sino-US détente — peak dovishness, where a prime consideration in the White House was expanding Nvidia’s market share, not blocking China’s AI ambitions. Asked on CNN if it mattered who won the AI superpower race, Huang replied “I don’t think it does.” That moment has come and gone. A trade that not only sent powerful chips into China via legal channels, but also billions of dollars of hardware illicitly through Chinese-funded companies in Southeast Asia — one of the most active, Megaspeed, set up by a suspected Chinese intelligence asset with whom Huang was having an affair — has run headlong into the hard realities of US-China strategic competition. Their superpower rivalry is structural. Its main focus is technology and, whatever Huang says, AI has made the struggle existential. At times, Trump has seemed confused about the geostrategic stakes. In arguing for a let-it-rip approach to frontier AI model development, he has several times invoked the China bogeyman by insisting that “Whoever wins AI, wins.” Yet he pushed Huang and chip sales to China into the forefront of his diplomacy with Beijing. In May, Trump scrambled Huang onto Air Force One at the last minute to join his business entourage in Beijing at a Sino-US summit, reportedly despite knowing that his intelligence services were aware of the Nvidia CEO’s potential links to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Then in September, Huang was at the head table with Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a state banquet in Washington. Huang would likely be with Trump in Shenzhen this week at a meeting of Asia-Pacific leaders if he hadn’t been forced to resign. Instead, the prospect of the US Congress ratcheting up tech sanctions against China will hang over Trump’s third meeting this year with Xi, and could endanger their fragile trade truce. Beijing, at least, is clear-eyed about the nature of its competition with Washington. Although over the longer term Huang’s spectacular fall may hold back US innovation and economic dynamism — a plus for China — the short-term consequences of a tightening embargo on semiconductors and chipmaking equipment would be immensely damaging. For all its advances in critical industries, China remains heavily dependent on American IP. In retrospect, as my colleague Reed Albergotti argued, Huang’s mistake was to get mixed up in politics in Washington, where he had a target on his back. His defenders see a conspiracy involving the US intelligence services to bring down America’s foremost business supporter of engagement with China. Elon Musk posted on X that he would sign a petition reinstating Huang. Epic Games founder Tim Sweeney said his exit showed an “Apple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy.” The broader question is the appropriate role for US business leaders in forging a relationship between rival superpowers whose economies are nevertheless deeply entwined through innovation networks, finance channels, and human talent. US strategy, writes Julian Gewirtz , a scholar at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, “has come to depend, to an extraordinary degree, on powerful private-sector actors whose incentives the government cannot simply assume will align with the national interest.” In Trump’s lame-duck presidency, that issue will be taken up by an incensed Congress pushing bipartisan bills aimed at China. The doves have had their time to shape the US-China agenda. Now, geopolitical gravity takes over.

events.title: Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s report on young people not in education, employment or training?
events.summary: Former minister’s 278-page report calls for changes to employment regulations, education, healthcare and benefits Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people Five months on from a first report detailing the growing crisis of young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet), Alan Milburn has produced his recommendations on how to tackle it. Set out over 278 pages, they amount to, as he readily accepts, a major rethink of everything from employment regulations to education, healthcare and benefits. 1. The context While this was in part covered by the first report, Milburn is at pains to begin the new volume with his belief that the issue of Neets is not a failure of the younger generation but a case of them being let down by a series of structural factors. “The young people I have met over the last year are not asking for an easier life. They are asking for a fair chance to build one,” he writes. The answer must be radical, he says. “This cannot be fixed by tweaking the edges of the existing system. The response now has to be full throttle: not another initiative or another round of incremental reform, but transformational change.” At the centre of the proposed new system is a youth opportunity service (YOS), which would offer young people support in areas such as training and health – and would in return expect participation. 2. The goals Currently, about 13.5% of people aged 16-24 in the UK are classified as Neet, the highest proportion in Europe outside Romania. This is not a new problem, the report notes, pointing out that the Neet rate has stayed above 10% for most of the past 25 years. The aim over a decade-long transformational plan would be to match the records of the best-performing European nations on this metric, such as the Netherlands and Denmark. While Milburn talks playfully of aiming for “Neet zero”, he says this means an eventual consistent rate of about 5%. He says the policies in his plan would get the Neet rate to about 6.8% by 2036. 3. Employers and the labour market Noting that youth employment has declined even as overall employment rose, Milburn says opportunities are limited by issues affecting young people – for example, a lack of connections to secure work experience or first jobs – and also employers, including the costs of taking on staff and regulatory complexities. The report says this is worsened by a lack of government help. While Denmark spends about 1% of GDP on all-age hiring incentives and subsidies, in the UK it is about 0.1%. Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter | Polly Toynbee Read more The report sets out a series of recommendations, including: Doubling the salary threshold for employer national insurance for entry-level jobs for young people in retail and hospitality, possibly then expanded to other sectors. Extending the existing youth jobs grant, which gives up to £3,000 to employers who takes on a staff member on universal credit for at least six months, so it also applies to people not on benefits, with extra incentives for small employers and people facing barriers, such as those with disabilities or care leavers. Avoid minimum pay rates being a barrier – for example, any moves to put young people’s minimum wages closer the adult rate should be judged “ against the critical goal of protecting youth employment”. This should be matched with increased simplicity for companies, with a single digital gateway leading to all the schemes set up to help young workers, and more clarity on help for workers with disabilities. All this would be united in a so-called youth opportunity test, under which any future tax or regulatory policy changes would look at their effect on young workers, set out in a law. 4. Education and training The report notes that this is a long-term issue, with many of the indicators of future Neet status, such as low attainment and poor attendance, being clear during childhood. Milburn also says that while countries with low Neet rates take vocational skills seriously, in England “technical education has too often been regarded as for somebody else’s child”. Among changes the report recommends are: More investment in early years provision, such as family hubs, and individual support in school if a student is seen as being at “material risk of disengagement”. Less use of school exclusion where possible. The report notes that the Netherlands has a permanent exclusion rate 73% lower than England’s. More focus in school on preparedness for work, as well as passing exams. More investment in further education and in apprenticeships, with greater financial incentives for employers who hire apprentices. University courses “must be able to demonstrate clear value for learners, employers and the wider economy,” with funding withdrawn for poorly performing examples. 5.

events.title: Chalmers proposes rules to allow super to invest in housing, energy, startups
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Jim Chalmers announces plan to let super funds place riskier investments in housing, energy, startups Treasurer Jim Chalmers will announce long-awaited changes to super investment rules. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Super funds will be allowed to invest 5 per cent of their portfolio in longer-term assets such as housing projects and venture capital, under a new proposal. Funds would remain obligated to prioritise their members' best interests and will not be required to use the new option, or be directed towards any particular asset class. It is unclear how many funds will use the new category. Super funds will be able to take riskier, longer-term bets with their members' money, in an overhaul of fund rules which Treasurer Jim Chalmers hopes will promote investment in housing, energy and startups. Under changes to the performance test, a benchmarking exercise introduced by former treasurer Josh Frydenberg, Mr Chalmers will propose to let super funds invest 5 per cent in so-called "emerging assets" with a lower minimum return. The intention is to allow funds to choose investments which may have low or uncertain returns today but higher returns tomorrow, such as early-stage housing developments or renewable projects or venture capital funds. Funds will not be required to invest in housing, energy or any sector, or to use the new option at all, and their obligation to invest in members' best interest would not change. But the move hands a win to some industry super funds who have argued the current benchmarks, measured relative to average stock market returns year by year, have prevented them from making long-term investments with irregular return patterns. It also fulfils a longstanding ambition of Mr Chalmers to leverage the vast pool of funds tied up in super — nearly $5 trillion — to support national priorities, first articulated in a 2022 speech on whether "workers' capital" could help "to solve our biggest challenges". New class of investments would not need to be Australian The Coalition and One Nation have positioned against any such move, described by Shadow Assistant Treasurer Kevin Hogan on Tuesday in advance of this announcement as "treating your super like a piggy bank for its pet projects". But not only does the measure not direct super funds towards any particular sector, the proposal will not require the "emerging assets" to be Australian assets. That would have required a specific rule, since super funds face no general requirement to invest in Australia or any particular jurisdiction. While the move was welcomed by ASFA in a statement, and some super funds had wanted there to be no cap on their use of emerging assets, it is also unclear how many funds will use the new category. Super funds have already sought to get involved in some housing projects in Australia, such as the super-backed Assemble build-to-rent housing project in Kensington. ( Supplied: Assemble Communities ) In a submission to Treasury's consultation process, industry fund Australian Super said it did not believe the current super performance test was "constraining [its] investment in the types of assets canvassed", such as housing, energy or venture capital. One area where possible investment has been envisaged is in investor-owned housing projects (such as so-called "build-to-rent" developments), which are common in the US but less so in Australia, and which the government has tried to encourage. Venture capital funds are prime candidates because they often group together several startups, some of which will fail and others of which may have large pay-offs after a few years. Those investments would risk failing the existing benchmarks. Rather than the average returns of a benchmark portfolio, the new benchmark for emerging assets would be equal to inflation plus some additional return premium, which would be set under advice from the independent Australian Government Actuary. Treasury says performance test has improved outcomes The performance test was introduced after a Productivity Commission inquiry found some super products were failing their members, who were often too disengaged to shop around for a better fund. It compares a fund's returns over a ten-year window with a comparable portfolio, such as the S&P/ASX300 for Australian equity investments. The test also assesses whether the product fees are comparable to other similar super products. Are the super wars another Mediscare? A political war over superannuation has been inflamed in the past fortnight.

events.title: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
events.summary: The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China. In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024. It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies. Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation. Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations". In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list. Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang pictured together in Taiwan in June 2024 Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed. The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed. On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips. Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair. The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia. The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance. Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with China In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred". They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge." events.title: UK music industry hits record high of £8.4bn – but are working musicians being left behind?
events.summary: Major tours by the likes of Oasis helped make 2025 a lucrative year, with music export revenue reaching £4.8bn Major tours by Oasis, Robbie Williams and Dua Lipa, as well as hit albums by the likes of Olivia Dean, have helped to push the UK music industry to record revenues. But there are concerns over a widening gulf in income between A-listers such as these, and the less well-known artists that form the bulk of the UK’s music community. The annual report by UK Music, an umbrella organisation featuring various industry bodies, finds that music added £8.4bn to the UK economy in 2025, a record figure and an inflation-outpacing rise of 5.7% from the previous year. Export revenue rose 3.6%, to £4.8bn, encompassing money made outside the UK by British artists – including via international touring and royalties and revenues raised from sales and streaming of music abroad. There was also a slight rise in employment in the sector in the UK: 730 jobs were added, to take total recorded employment to 220,500. The success is powered in part by a live music sector in which stadium performances – once the preserve of only the very top artists – are becoming increasingly commonplace, with consumers willing to spend three-figure sums on tickets. However, the This Is Music report cautioned that “many emerging and grassroots artists experienced rising costs which reduced net incomes, and even well-known artists have found it hard to make money”. The report highlights a number of hit albums by UK artists that have helped boost recorded music revenues – including No 1s by Sleep Token, Yungblud, Sam Fender, Wet Leg, and Biffy Clyro – but also highlighted a troubling trend. In terms of album consumption figures, UK artists had historically been more popular than US ones in the domestic marketplace, but US artists overtook UK ones in 2018 and their popularity has continued to diverge, levelling out somewhat in 2025 thanks in part to blockbuster hits by Dean, Fender and others. AI also threatens to divert listeners’ attention away from human artists, with the report warning: “AI generated ‘slop’ and deepfakes are an increasing problem, which is reflected in a dramatic increase in takedown notices for AI deepfakes issued by labels,” referring to songs taken down from streaming services for imitating existing artists. There was a marked difference between two sets of data the study used to monitor the income of artists. A survey of the accounts for “top and mid-level” artists found that these musicians were flush, their earnings rising more than 14% year on year. But the Music Creators’ Survey, which asks musicians (including artists, songwriters, producers, composers and more) to self-report their income, found growth of just 0.2% in the same period. “It has never been easier to record and release music, but given the intense level of competition that has ensued, it has never been more difficult to establish a profile and build a scalable career,” reads the report. “This makes life especially tough for many music creators with average earnings. “Once artists and music creators break through beyond a certain level, more options and better terms of business can enhance their careers very significantly, but the challenge remains developing more artists and creators to that level.” UK Music is made up of industry bodies, including royalty agencies PRS for Music and PPL; the BPI, the collective body for the UK’s record labels; AIM, which represents the independent label sector; plus the Musicians’ Union and more. Tom Kiehl, UK Music’s chief executive, used the report’s launch to lobby the government on a range of issues. “The government must use the upcoming UK EU summit on 20 November to work to remove barriers to EU exports,” he said. “It must not give AI a free pass and should support a sustainably funded BBC – and deliver economic growth for music in every postcode. He added: “We are not simply asking government to act. We stand ready to be part of the solution too. The UK music industry has never lacked talent, ambition or creativity. The challenge now is ensuring the right environment exists for those strengths to flourish. If we get that right, the opportunities ahead are enormous.” Ian Murray, creative industries minister, highlighted government funding schemes such as the Music Growth Package and said: “We are investing in the grassroots infrastructure, talent pipeline and independent businesses that keep the sector competitive.” Some of the UK’s most successful acts are already eyeing a potentially lucrative 2027. Oasis will head back out on tour after the blockbuster success of their 2025 reunion, playing 11 different locations across the UK, Europe and North America; Dua Lipa has been announced as a headliner of Coachella festival and is expected to release a fourth studio album; and Sam Fender has announced the Proper Massive tour, with 12 UK and Ireland stadium dates plus major venues in North America.

events.title: Up to 99% of UK civil servants rely on Microsoft for comms, minister admits
events.summary: As many as 99 percent of Britain's civil servants rely on Microsoft to communicate, a government minister has admitted, days after Redmond demonstrated the perils of putting quite so many eggs in one basket. Ian Murray, minister for creative industries, media and online safety, laid bare the extent of Whitehall's Microsoft habit in the House of Commons on Monday, where MPs were also told that the public sector shelled out £1.9 billion on Microsoft licenses in 2024-25 alone . "We know that 98% to 99% of civil servants use Microsoft as their platform for communications, which is incredibly high," Murray told MPs . The admission followed last week's 18-hour Microsoft 365 outage , which left businesses unable to carry out transactions, public sector workers struggling to do their jobs, and even MPs unable to access their usual means of communication. Rebecca Paul, shadow technology secretary, said at least 47 NHS trusts experienced problems, with some services having to fall back on pen and paper. The Conservative MP, who cited the £1.9 billion licensing bill, pressed Murray on whether the government would seek contractual remedies from Microsoft. Murray said the government was unaware of any delays to NHS treatment or instances in which patients had been put at risk. Emergency departments remained open, and 999 services continued to operate. Only two NHS trusts activated incident response units, the minister said. The outage, which affected 74 countries, has since been blamed on a software update Microsoft rolled out in July . A surge in Teams traffic hit infrastructure already short of server capacity, exposing the months-old bug. More than 80 percent of the servers in the affected gateway stopped responding, leaving Redmond's engineers scrambling to fix their previous fix. Much of Monday's discussion centered on how the UK had allowed itself to become so dependent on a handful of American technology companies in the first place. Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of Parliament's Science and Technology Committee, pointed out that the government had been unable to tell her committee how much it spends on IT and which suppliers it uses. She also challenged ministers over their reluctance to embrace open source software, something both France and Germany have pursued to loosen Big Tech's grip on their public sectors. “Germany has 500,000 civil servants using open source products and services, but the government told my Committee that though open source could address vendor lock-in, they would not include open source targets because of a lack of what was called ‘commercial accountability’,” she said. Paul, meanwhile, reminded Murray that just last month the government had rejected the committee's recommendation to introduce supplier diversification targets. Murray conceded that the government's extensive dealings with Microsoft probably result in "vendor lock-in," but defended the arrangement, saying it gives Whitehall access to the latest technology at scale. The admission comes less than a week after research from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) revealed just how little of the British public sector's IT budget ends up in British hands . Of the £19.2 billion spent with the public sector's 150 biggest technology suppliers in 2024-25, just 15 percent went to businesses headquartered and owned in the UK, with a predominantly British workforce and which weren't reselling overseas technology. American companies took home almost twice as much as suppliers from all other foreign countries combined. Murray said the government intends to use its considerable purchasing power to give British businesses a leg up. Its national cloud infrastructure program will see departments procure cloud services collectively rather than individually, with the intention of giving more suppliers a crack at lucrative government contracts. Whitehall has also set up a technology risk group and a central IT operations function to scrutinize outages and work out what needs fixing across the public sector. Ministers intend to press Microsoft on how it plans to prevent a repeat of last week's cock-up and whether it can get services back online more quickly next time. The government, however, offered no timetable for weaning civil servants off Microsoft's software, nor did Murray commit to targets for adopting open-source alternatives. Redmond's days as Whitehall's IT supplier of choice hardly look numbered. ®

events.title: U.S. gets another D+ on premature births
events.summary: Data: National Center for Health Statistics via March of Dimes; Map: Carly Mallenbaum/Axios The U.S. earned a D+ for its preterm birth rate yet again , according to the latest March of Dimes report card . Why it matters: Babies born before 37 weeks of pregnancy face greater risks of serious health complications, hospitalization and death in their first year of life. By the numbers: The national preterm birth rate remained at 10.4% in 2025 for the fourth year in a row. It marked the fifth consecutive year at D+ (which March of Dimes considers 10.4% to 10.7%). Zoom in: Mississippi had the highest rate at 14.9%. Vermont had the lowest at 8%. Rates improved in 23 states and jurisdictions, including D.C. and Puerto Rico, per the report that relies on CDC data. But only Idaho, South Dakota and Puerto Rico recorded statistically significant declines. Between the lines: Rising rates of chronic health conditions before pregnancy are one reason the nation's preterm birth rate remains stubbornly high, Michael Warren, chief medical and health officer of March of Dimes, tells Axios. High blood pressure and diabetes became more common among women giving birth in 2025. Both conditions increase the risk of pregnancy complications and premature birth. What they're saying: "It's not just about improving care during labor and delivery," Warren says. "It's really about improving their health across the life course." That means addressing chronic conditions even before pregnancy. What we're watching: Whether strategies including expanding access to doula care and encouraging low-dose aspirin use among pregnant women at risk for preeclampsia can help bring down preterm birth rates.

events.title: Rogue Agents Hacked His Company. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?
events.summary: Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face , may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree. As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The company’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai . Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone. Despite championing the democratization of AI, however, Hugging Face was acquired by one of the industry’s biggest players, Nvidia, for $12.93 billion in September. When I caught up with Delangue recently, that was the subject of my first question. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. CLÉMENT DELANGUE: We need more resources to give open-source AI a chance. It has grown really well in the past few years and has become a really credible alternative to closed-source APIs. But the field is still dominated by closed-source. We’re gonna have the Anthropic IPO in a few weeks. They basically went from zero to a top five or top 10 most valuable company in the world in a few years. I don't think that's ever happened before. The people, inventions, and viral moments that made 2026 a little more bearable . Something we missed? Let us know in the comments. Does Anthropic's IPO suggest the closed approach is winning? It’s hard to say. I've always said that there is a very strong natural tendency for AI to concentrate capabilities and wealth. People haven't internalized how much of the future compute capacity has already been reserved by a few companies. Talent, compute, resources—these all fuel the natural tendency for AI to be dominated by a few closed-source labs. Let’s talk about the attack. When did you first realize Hugging Face was being hacked by a group of AI agents? At the beginning, it didn't go to the top of our priority list. It just wasn't bad enough to really trigger that. The goal was pretty narrow and wasn’t deemed to be very dangerous or damaging. But it was raising questions. Especially the number of actions taken compared to the narrowness of the goal. It was surprising to us, and we couldn't really fit it into a familiar pattern. That's why we started investigating. And you used the Chinese model called GLM to investigate. I actually think that 95 percent of the risks are being created by a few companies that are pushing the frontier behind closed doors. And 95 percent of the protection or defense is going to be done by the open-source ecosystem. Does the US need its own open-weight models—ones as powerful as GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen ? Yeah, I think it's very, very important for sovereignty, for understanding AI, and for academia. It’s kind of weird that most academic labs have to use Chinese models because they’re the ones that are open. If you go to Stanford or MIT, you have no choice but to use the Chinese open-weight models. There is some momentum, but I don't think it's enough. I think there's a lot more to do. A lot more investment is needed. The best open-source non-Chinese models are actually coming from outside of the US. Right from France, Mistral; Cohere from Canada; South Korea is starting to do more and more. But it’s still pretty far from what the US could do. Perhaps we don’t need to panic about AI agents, but what about the idea of AI escaping human control due to recursive self-improvement? You use a computer to write code. There's already some form of self-improvement in using the tools to build more tools. Now the question is how fast it accelerates. One thing that a lot of people realized this summer is that keeping AI behind closed doors in a few labs isn't actually safer. For recursive self-improvement, I think openness is a way to understand, follow, and regulate if we need to regulate. Can we talk about the Microduck ? I’m a bit obsessed. Oh yeah, it's so fun, no? We're probably gonna sell over 50,000 of them this year. It's probably the most popular robot of the year. We haven't talked about this much, but AI was really the unlock for the robot. We had the design for two years, but the problem was that when it fell, it couldn’t get up. And then at some point with reinforcement learning, one of our software engineers managed to get the Microduck to get itself back up. At the end of the day, how do you convince people to take an interest in open-source AI?

events.title: A Federal Women’s Prison Became a “Rape Club.” After Officials Shut It Down, Rampant Abuse Continued Elsewhere.
events.summary: Officer Felix Wilder sauntered around the women’s prison like he owned the place.  Prone to showing up to work in gold chains and stylish jeans instead of his concrete gray government uniform, the slender 35-year-old moved, one woman said, “like he had just gotten off of a horse from a long ride.” He spoke slowly and eyed the prisoners as they walked through the drab buildings and shadeless yards of the secluded federal lockup in Aliceville, Alabama. By the fall of 2024, some of the women there had begun to notice him hovering over a soft-spoken immigrant from Mexico who’d been in prison for only a few years. Ela, as she asked to be called, had dark hair, dark eyes and children to get home to back in Utah. Wilder was just a little too close, a little too familiar. Ela’s cellmate, who asked to be identified as Ana, watched it all with unease. At 40, she knew exactly what that kind of attention from an officer could mean in a women’s prison. For 15 years, Ana had served her time at Federal Correctional Institution Dublin, a low-security prison in California, where officers had preyed on the women in their care. Sexual misconduct became so rampant that staff and prisoners alike called it a “rape club.” Eventually, the FBI intervened, and prosecutors charged the warden, the chaplain and nine other officers with sexually abusing female prisoners. Hundreds of women — including Ana — came forward to tell what happened to them, not just to investigators, but also to outside lawyers who sued the system to demand change at the Bay Area prison.    Ana had hoped to leave that all behind when she was transferred out of Dublin. But tucked between the pine trees and low-slung churches of rural Alabama, the Aliceville prison had its own brand of menace. The facility had newer buildings but fewer freedoms. The roofs leaked, and sometimes the air smelled faintly of mold. The shorthanded staff often locked the women in their cells for days at a time. And then there were officers like Wilder, who seemed to be choosing their targets. Thousands of miles from families they couldn’t call during yet another lockdown, Ana and Ela became allies. They paced. They picked at the lukewarm meals delivered on Styrofoam trays. They stared out the narrow slit of a window.  And then Ela broke down, sobbing as her words tumbled out into the stale prison air.  Two years earlier, an officer had pulled her into a closet and raped her, she told Ana, her voice quavering. Now, she said, it was happening all over again — but this time it was the stylish officer in jeans: Felix Wilder. Ela said she’d reported the first assault and nothing happened. Now, she didn’t know what to do. If the prison didn’t care about one rape, why would it care about two? As she listened, Ana felt a dull rage churning in her stomach. She thought of all the things she’d seen and survived at Dublin: the rapes, the harassment, the uncertainty of a life subject to the whims of lascivious men with badges. As she tried to comfort her sobbing cellmate, she wondered whether Aliceville was any better. Maybe, she thought, no place was.  Sitting on her metal bunk, she opened the little address book she’d bought from the prison commissary and flipped to the phone numbers for the lead attorneys in the class action lawsuit against Dublin. “Here,” she told Ela, “you can talk to them.” The arrests and subsequent convictions of Dublin staff — 10 in all — marked the largest sex abuse scandal in the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ history and a rare moment of accountability in a troubled system where many women had learned to stop expecting it. Suddenly, every branch of government stepped in. A federal judge appointed an outside monitor. A slew of agencies issued reports, and the Justice Department dispatched attorneys to visit and evaluate women’s facilities. Congress passed a law to create a new, independent office to oversee the prison system. But after the judge made that unprecedented move to appoint outside oversight, in early 2024 the bureau abruptly announced it would shut down Dublin and transfer its more than 600 women — including Ana — to lockups across the country. Ana had hoped to leave the abuse behind when she was transferred out of Dublin federal prison. Then, quietly, the window of accountability shut. Little appeared to have come of the promised reforms, the site visits and the reports, and Congress never appropriated funding for the new oversight office. More than a dozen current and former federal prison employees told ProPublica and The Marshall Project they’d seen few or no meaningful improvements. One Justice Department official said the only obvious sign of progress was new sexual assault prevention posters. “Nothing has really changed,” said Alix McLearen, a top Bureau of Prisons official who retired in 2024 after serving as the agency’s first administrator overseeing the women and special populations branch. “We had a horrible crisis, and crisis leads to opportunity, and this is an opportunity that has been completely squandered.” An official with the federal prison workers union who — like nearly every current employee interviewed for this story — asked not to be named for fear of retaliation, put it even more bluntly: “Nothing has been done to effectively change sexual abuse of inmates within the BOP. Not on a large scale or small scale.” For the last five years, the culture that spawned a rape club at Dublin has persisted across the system. Reporters at ProPublica and The Marshall Project set out to determine how pervasive the problem of staff sexual abuse inside federal women’s prisons is — and what, if anything, officials have done to solve it. What we found was sexual assault, misconduct or harassment at most of the 27 facilities that currently hold women. We identified more than 185 cases in which prison employees have been accused of sexually abusing people in women’s prisons since 2021, the year the Dublin scandal broke. The cases implicate more than 96 officers at 16 prisons. Of those, just 19 officers have been arrested or convicted. In some cases, officers withheld food or medical care, or threatened to put women in solitary confinement if they refused to comply with sexual demands, court records allege. In others, officers locked them in windowless closets or bathrooms, choked them, or forced them to use sex toys or have sex with each other. In more than a dozen instances, the assaults were so brutal that the women were left bruised and bleeding. Though some abusers have been prosecuted or removed, insiders say the culture of impunity that allows officers to prey on women remains. Officials have repeatedly refused to acknowledge or failed to act on signs of sexual abuse, we found. More than 25 women said that they were abused by officers who had been reported or investigated before, according to lawsuits we reviewed. Hosted by award-winning multi-hyphenate entertainer Keke Palmer and produced by Wondery and executive produced by Palmer, the show pairs her quick wit with genuine curiosity, striking a balance between humor and thoughtful inquiry that makes even the most recognizable guests feel like close friends. Her natural ability to connect with people draws audiences into every conversation, while her candor and energy bring a refreshing and unique authenticity to the interview format. Palmer invites some of the biggest names in entertainment and culture to share the experiences that have shaped them. From exploring self-worth with Oprah Winfrey to discussing creativity, reinvention, and fatherhood with Anderson .Paak, she moves effortlessly between laugh-out-loud exchanges and thoughtful reflections on life, relationships, and success. Baby, this is Keke Palmer consistently ranks among the top video and top comedy shows on Apple Podcasts. “I’m so honored that Baby, this is Keke Palmer has been named Apple Podcasts’ Show of the Year,” said Palmer. “I love how a conversation about entertainment can open up a bigger conversation about life. There’s so much to explore in the things we watch, laugh at, and connect with, and this show gives me room to follow that curiosity. Thank you to Apple Podcasts, Wondery, our incredible guests, and everyone who listens and brings their own perspective to the conversation. This recognition means so much to me.” “Keke’s curiosity, humor, and openness make every conversation feel personal, and video brings that connection even closer,” said Oliver Schusser, Apple’s vice president of Podcasts, Music, Sports, and Beats. “Her exceptional craft and cultural impact make Baby, this is Keke Palmer Apple Podcasts’ Show of the Year. We’re proud to celebrate her talent across Apple Podcasts and Apple Music, from the conversations she creates to the music she shares.” Inside Show of the Year For Palmer, podcasting starts with connection. In an interview with Apple Podcasts for Creators, excerpted below, the host of Baby, this is Keke Palmer shares why she creates room for honest conversation, trusts her curiosity and authenticity, and celebrates being named the Apple Podcasts 2026 Show of the Year. On creating space for connection : “I’ve spent so much of my life being seen, but being seen and being known are two very different things. … I love that I get to create a space where people can just be people, myself included.” On following her curiosity : “Preparation is supposed to support the conversation, not control it. I’m always listening for that moment when somebody says something that opens up an entirely new question.” On bringing authenticity to video : “Don’t try to manufacture a personality for the camera. Develop a relationship with yourself, get comfortable expressing what is already there, and let the camera capture that.” On being named the Apple Podcasts Show of the Year : “What makes me most proud is that something rooted in genuine curiosity and connection has resonated with other people. It reminds me that being yourself isn’t just personally fulfilling; it can also create value for others. And that’s always been the goal for me.” Press Contacts Heather Norton Apple heather_norton@apple.com Rosa Oh Apple rosa_oh@apple.com Apple Media Helpline media.help@apple.com Copy text Formula 1® Las Vegas Grand Prix™ streams live on Apple TV this weekend Apple launches research study to explore the use of AI for health The latest news and updates, direct from Apple.

events.title: Nvidia forms board committee to oversee national security, export controls
events.summary: The committee is tasked with providing oversight for Nvidia’s national security and global trade compliance programmes. Nvidia formed a new board committee to oversee national security, export controls and global trade risk. Suzanne Nora Johnson will chair it, with Stephen Neal and John Dabiri. The move follows Jensen Huang’s resignation and questions over chip export oversight after revelations about his affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy. The company wants tighter control. The committee will meet at least quarterly and work with outside experts. It comes as the Trump administration plans tougher limits on China’s access to advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s. BENGALURU – Nvidia said on Nov 17 it has established a new board-level committee to oversee its national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. The move comes days after the resignation of chief executive officer Jensen Huang amid revelations of his affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy, raised questions about potential national security risks and the oversight of the artificial intelligence chip designer’s chip exports. Nvidia said that the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen Neal and John Dabiri. The committee is tasked with providing oversight for Nvidia’s national security and global trade compliance programs and will work with independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts. Nvidia’s existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report to this new committee and interim chief executive officer Colette Kress for day-to-day operations. The committee plans to meet at least quarterly, including sessions with management and in executive session. Formation of the panel also comes a day after the Trump administration said it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips from companies like ​Nvidia, tightening controls as US President Donald Trump headed to the country for talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has faced criticism for his oversight of export controls on chips to China in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, is among the officials joining Trump on his Asia trip, a White House official said. The company is due to report third-quarter earnings after the market closes on Nov 17. By some estimates, Nvidia has more than half a trillion dollars of commitments in the form of various supply and capacity backstops for chip purchases, data centre leases and equity investments, which nonetheless are a fraction of firm’s market capitalisation. events.title: AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business
events.summary: When Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the then CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion. Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology quickly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become. Steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022. He says he was regularly “heartbroken” by the outpouring of grief whenever bad news arrived about a husband, father, or son back home. “I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,” Steelberg tells WIRED. "I'm not saying this is purely altruistic,” he adds. “Of course we're going to be making money doing it." This week, their firm, Tiberius Aerospace, said it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by European technology investment firm Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, a national-security-focused investment firm licensed under the US Defense Department. Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 is also an investor. Tiberius began as Steelberg’s private research lab, incorporated in 2021, which employed people across France, the UK, and US to experiment on left-field ideas across a range of technologies, from drones and electric vertical takeoff aircraft to quantum computing. After the invasion, he pivoted the lab’s AI and aerospace engineers into writing code and building spreadsheets to objectively analyze the war’s many factors and calculate what could move the needle. The AI model they created quickly ruled out building better defensive technology because that would just harden the stalemate. With his aim narrowed to building an offensive weapon, Steelberg developed several metrics to numerically analyze the lethality of different systems, including cost-effectiveness, and used the AI engine to simulate weapons under different conditions and identify what would disrupt the market. Don’t build another drone, it suggested, build longer-range artillery munitions. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a 155-millimeter howitzer—the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine. As well as traveling farther than currently available rounds, they claim they can reach supersonic speeds and altitudes beyond jamming range. Giving Ukraine’s guns extra range is important, Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow at UK defense think tank the Royal United Services Institute, tells WIRED, because it would allow Ukrainian gunners to operate beyond the reach of Russian drone attacks. 155-mm shells “can cause massive damage to a group of vehicles or infantry,” he says. “Any technology that can help Ukraine extend the reach of its howitzers and return them to combat would be valuable.” With a prototype he’d designed with the help of AI, Steelberg also started to expand the Tiberius team, including bringing on board Baynes as chief strategy officer in 2023. Baynes had first traveled to Ukraine around a decade ago to investigate how local startup Ring , now owned by Amazon, had outdone Nest , which he’d been working on and eventually sold to Google. He fell in love with Kyiv’s ambitious software engineers and booming tech scene–responsible for globally successful tech tools like Grammarly and Snapchat’s face filters. In 2016, he bought a local life-science tech company with the aim of accelerating next-generation medicines through automating clinical trials and improving protein modeling. “What drew me into Kyiv was the hunger and ambition in the engineering community,” he tells WIRED. “It was difficult to not be enormously attracted to that and to see if it's something that could be put into really critical-mission problem sets like cancer drugs or speeding up clinical trials for life-science companies.” After the Russian invasion, Baynes set himself up in Budapest for around six months to help with the logistics of evacuating women and children and moving equipment into the country. He asked his global network for help finding medical equipment, vehicles, and accommodation for refugees—bringing him back in touch with Steelberg. Baynes believes the West’s response to the invasion has been “inadequate” and that Ukraine needs better offensive capabilities to push Russia’s army back.

events.title: Behind the Curtain: If competence were cool
events.summary: So many government problems, like last week's nationwide aviation meltdown , are foreseeable ... and foreseen. Why it matters: Again and again, we choose to do nothing until a crisis hits. A big reason: These are huge, tedious, complex, unsexy, antiquated systems that require persistence and competence to fix. A big new problem: These systems are deeply intertwined with our daily lives, and highly susceptible to malfunctions, mishaps and AI-enhanced cyberattacks. They're boring until they're vital. The big picture: We have federal agencies and congressional committees designed explicitly to monitor, protect and improve these complex systems. But they've atrophied as power has been centralized in the presidency and congressional leadership, where daily political warfare rarely includes sober discussion of competence and essential interconnected systems. Here are a few of the foreseeable (and foreseen) crises that have been staring at us, many for literally decades: The skies: We've known for years that the air-traffic system relies on copper wire and floppy disks . We've seen and known the vulnerabilities through Democratic and Republican administrations. We've known the fix is expensive: $31.5 billion, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told lawmakers last year. At Friday night's briefing at the White House, Duffy said: "I want $50 billion ." The grid: We've known for a long time that our electricity is delivered through an aging patchwork system vulnerable to accidents or attacks. The nonprofit power authority NERC (North American Electric Reliability Corp.) warned this spring that the system is so strained by rising energy needs from AI and humans that it could jam up or break. The water: Drinking and wastewater systems are old and in dangerous disrepair — a huge risk to hospitals, in particular. In July , cyberattacks hit over 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, with Iran as a likely culprit . The government's computers: Washington spends over $100 billion a year on information technology. Roughly 80% goes to keeping old systems alive. Eight of the 11 systems most in need of replacement run on dying languages like COBOL . The people who can read, write and fix them are retiring. The debt: We paid $1.052 trillion in interest last fiscal year. That's more than we spent on defense. The Congressional Budget Office sees the interest doubling to $2.1 trillion in 2036 . Every dollar of interest is a dollar that can't fix another crisis on this list. The retirement cliff: Social Security's retirement fund runs dry in 2032. Current law then cuts benefits by 22%, automatically. Medicare's hospital fund follows in 2033 . We have known those dates for decades, and they've been creeping up. Now they're just a few years away. The shriveled arsenal: Rebuilding the advanced weapons we've burned through in the Iran war will take years . Back in May, a paper from the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that replacing some interceptors used heavily in the war, including Patriot and THAAD anti-missile systems, would take three years. The minerals: China controls 91% of the world's rare-earth refining capacity, giving the other superpower a chokehold on vital ingredients of AI. We're one trade war away from slowing AI and the entire economy. The bottom line: When choosing and rating leaders in harrowing times, put a premium on competence. We'll need it. Go deeper : The chain-reaction era.

events.title: CapitaLand, Far East, Sing Holdings team up in $1.8 billion bid for Jurong Lake District site
events.summary: The top bid of $1.82 billion was from a consortium comprising CapitaLand Development, Far East Organization and Sing Holdings. CapitaLand Development, Far East Organization and Sing Holdings led a $1.82 billion bid for the Jurong Lake District Town Hall Link site, the first plot split from a larger master plan. The site can hold offices, up to 1,200 homes and other uses. Analysts said homes and retail are attractive, helped by strong MRT links and nearby schools. A key risk is office demand. Experts warned suburban office space may struggle in a hybrid work market, and the high land cost could strain financing. SINGAPORE – A mixed-use site in Jurong Lake District (JLD), where a massive business district is being planned, drew two bids at a state tender on Nov 17. The top bid of $1.82 billion, which works out to about $910 per square foot per plot ratio (psf ppr), was from a consortium comprising CapitaLand Development, Far East Organization and Sing Holdings. The second highest bid, of $1.31 billion or about $655 ppr, came from Sim Lian Land and Sim Lian Development. The 3.72ha site, zoned “white”, can be developed into a maximum gross floor area (GFA) of slightly more than 2 million square feet (sq ft). This will comprise a minimum of 430,556 sq ft of offices, up to 1,200 private housing units and about 473,612 sq ft for complementary uses (such as retail, serviced apartments, hotel, sports, recreational and community spaces, medical clinics and attractions). Analysts polled by The Business Times had predicted up to four bids for the site, with the top bid forecast to be anywhere from S$900 psf ppr to S$1,400 psf ppr. The site in Town Hall Link is the first plot carved out of an earlier tendered 6.5ha master developer site, which was to be progressively developed over 10 to 15 years to a maximum GFA of 3.93 million sq ft. This was to comprise at least 1.57 million sq ft of offices, up to 1,700 private homes and close to 800,000 sq ft of space for other uses such as retail, and food and beverage. The master developer site was intended to be a catalyst for the next phase of development in JLD as Singapore’s largest mixed-use business district outside the city centre. The tender was launched in June 2023 and closed in March 2024, with only one bidder – a five-member consortium comprising CapitaLand Development, City Developments, Frasers Property, Mitsubishi Estate and Mitsui Fudosan (Asia). In September 2024, the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) announced it would not award the tender as the shortlisted concept, at the tendered price of around $640 psf ppr, was assessed to be “too low”. The master developer site was put on the reserve list, where sites are triggered for sale only when there is an indication of interest at a minimum acceptable bid price, before the Government decided to sell the massive white site in three smaller parcels, starting with the Town Hall Link site. Initially, it was put on the first-half 2026 reserve list, before being moved to the H2 2026 confirmed list. When the tender for the carved-out plot was launched in July 2026, URA emphasised that JLD is a key pillar of Singapore’s decentralisation strategy. The Town Hall Link is intended to kickstart the next phase of JLD’s development, which will focus on the 120-hectare new Jurong Lake Central precinct, as well as support medium-term growth in demand for housing and offices. The Government has invested significantly in key infrastructure to drive the transformation of JLD, including the revitalised Jurong Lake Gardens and the addition of two new MRT lines: Jurong Region Line (JRL) and Cross Island Line (CRL). The JE5 station on the JRL will be located at the Jurong East MRT station, which is currently the interchange station for the East-West and North-South MRT lines. The JE6 station, also on the JRL, will serve the International Business Park. Both stations are scheduled to open in 2028. The Town Hall Link plot will also be a stone’s throw from the CR19 MRT station, on the CRL; the station is planned to open in 2032. To reduce development complexity and make the Town Hall Link site more attractive to developers, the Government is undertaking a greater share of the surrounding infrastructure and land preparation works, including pedestrian links to MRT stations. Property veteran Desmond Sim said: “Confidence, if not a sense of assurance, in JLD has been established. The master planning and infrastructural investments will be a testament to that.” Wong Xian Yang, head of research for Singapore and South-east Asia at Cushman & Wakefield (C&W), said the Town Hall Link site’s residential component is a key draw for developers, given the strong sales achieved by close-to-MRT station launches such as J’den and Lucerne Grand. In November 2023, CapitaLand Development’s J’den sold 88 per cent of its 368 units on launch day at an average price of $2,451 psf.

events.title: Former WH Smith chain TG Jones put up for sale after closing 130 stores
events.summary: Modella Capital plans auction of high street retailer, which employs about 3,500 people, next year The owner of TG Jones is exploring a potential sale less than 18 months after completing a deal to buy the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith. Modella Capital, which also owns businesses including Hobbycraft, completed a deal to buy the 233-year-old business for £42m in June last year. The company, which pushed through a swingeing restructure to close more than 100 stores after receiving high court approval in July, has moved to appoint advisers after receiving unsolicited expressions of interest for the business. Modella, which has closed about 150 of the 480 WH Smith stores since taking control, has appointed the corporate finance arm of Teneo, according to Sky News which first reported the news. “High-street retailer TG Jones has received unsolicited offers for the business,” said Modella and TG Jones in a joint statement. “Management and owner Modella Capital have jointly agreed to instruct Teneo Corporate Finance to review these offers and undertake a market-testing exercise.” An auction of the business, which employs about 3,500 staff, is planned for next year to avoid disruption through the key Christmas trading period. “As ever, our focus is on providing a great experience for customers, especially with the critical Christmas period coming up,” said the TG Jones chief executive, Alex Wilson. “We continue to execute our turnaround plan, which is improving our performance month by month.” WH Smith retained its almost 1,300 stores in railway stations and airports, as well as its website and the right to its name, prompting the rebrand of the high street stores to TG Jones . The potential sale comes as the future of Poundland, which employs approximately 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, remains uncertain. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Last week the chain’s owner, Gordon Brothers, won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors as it assesses three potential bids . Last month its US owners filed a notice of intention to call in administrators, but has come under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers.

events.title: Push to reinstate Jensen Huang tests superstar tech CEO accountability
events.summary: The push to reinstate Jensen Huang is set to test whether America's most powerful CEOs can still be held accountable — or if extraordinary success and political alliances have made them untouchable. Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power. Their immense wealth and growing political clout raise a fundamental question: Can corporate boards, regulators, Congress or the courts actually rein in a superstar CEO anymore? Huang's potential return — or the Nvidia board's refusal to entertain it — could signal whether that balance of power is changing. "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible," Anne Wojcicki, the founder of 23andMe and ex-wife of Google co-founder Sergei Brin, told Bloomberg . "We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Driving the news: A growing campaign to reinstate Huang has attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, following his departure after revelations of intimate relationships involving subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. President Trump said Monday he wouldn't mind seeing Huang return. Elon Musk has also backed the effort. Other supporters include Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan , Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney , Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke. Prominent investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have separately urged the board not to rule out Huang's return. Some pushing for a reexamination of the issue have focused on what they see as a lack of proof that Alice Huang, the executive with whom he had an affair, was a Chinese intelligence asset. That claim has been attributed in media reports to U.S. intelligence officials, although other stories have called it into question. Yes, but: Others have pointed to the fact that Alice Huang worked on behalf of Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer that took steps to help Chinese AI companies access cutting-edge chips. The company has been linked to more than $4 billion in Nvidia chip purchases also arranged nearly $12 billion in orders of top-end Nvidia chips destined for Chinese companies, according to The Wall Street Journal. In addition to the relationships, Huang also faces questions about whether he misled Nvidia executives . Nvidia's board isn't currently considering reinstating Huang, CNBC and Reuters reported Monday. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look outside the company for new leadership, while tech analyst Dan Ives has dismissed the idea of a comeback as unrealistic. Zoom out: Musk has become perhaps the most prominent embodiment of the superstar CEO, repeatedly defying corporate conventions and weathering controversies that might have ended other executives' careers. In 2018, Musk settled SEC fraud charges over tweets about taking Tesla private, stepping down as chairman but remaining CEO. After a Delaware judge invalidated his enormous Tesla compensation package , shareholders voted to ratify it, and the state's Supreme Court eventually restored the award. Last year, Tesla shareholders approved another potentially massive compensation package, underscoring their willingness to grant extraordinary rewards to a leader they consider indispensable. The Trump factor: Trump's return to the White House added another layer to the power of tech executives, many of whom cultivated close ties to a president whose decisions can affect their businesses through government contracts, regulation and trade policy. But this month's midterm elections demonstrated limits to Trump's political power, raising questions about whether his backing will carry the same weight going forward. Huang's fate will offer an early test, though any decision to reinstate him might reflect investor pressure as much as political influence. The intrigue: The campaign to restore Huang has echoes of Sam Altman's dramatic 2023 ouster and reinstatement at OpenAI, when employees, investors and powerful tech figures rallied to force a reversal. OpenAI's board cited vague concerns about Altman's candor and its ability to trust him. A subsequent review found that his conduct did not mandate removal. Charles Elson, corporate governance expert and founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, said Altman's departure was fundamentally a dispute with his board, whereas Huang's case involves specific allegations of misconduct. "What if they were to do nothing? Then you have no code of conduct," Elson said. Altman himself acknowledged the parallels Monday, telling a Semafor conference he has "personal strong empathy to a situation like this," but declined to endorse Huang's return. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine; heroes have flaws," he said, per Bloomberg. The bottom line: Huang's fate could help establish whether the era of the seemingly untouchable CEO is continuing — or beginning to encounter meaningful limits.

events.title: Democrats' squishy definition of Medicare expansion
events.summary: Democrats marching into a debate over expanding Medicare are about to confront difficult questions about how far to go — including for seniors who are already in the program. Why it matters: Holes in traditional Medicare leave seniors exposed to out-of-pocket costs and affordability struggles, but making the program's benefits more generous may be prohibitively expensive. The big picture: Democrats scored overwhelming gains in the midterms after making health care affordability a major priority for the next Congress. Though the election results reinvigorated progressives' push for Medicare for All, there are also less sweeping options for what expanded coverage should look like. How far to go — and what to call the plan — will become critical heading into the 2028 presidential cycle and likely determine whether Democrats can attract any Republican support. Driving the news: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is emerging as an early front-runner for what Democrats may try to pass and defy President Trump to veto. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called on Democrats to lower the eligibility age to 55 soon after the election, framing it as an "immediate first step" toward his long-sought goal of Medicare for All. Sanders also wants to add vision, dental and hearing benefits and strengthen children's coverage. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York on Friday threw his support behind that kind of package, as well as strengthening children's coverage, Stat reported . And groups of Democrats in both chambers have recently introduced legislation lowering the Medicare eligibility age to 50. What they're saying: " Medicare for All is unlikely to be enacted in the near future, but the political push for it could prompt a debate about the services Medicare itself does not cover and the high costs current Medicare beneficiaries can incur," KFF executive vice president Larry Levitt wrote last month in JAMA Forum . State of play: Some Democrats are looking at other changes beyond changing the eligibility age. More than a dozen Senate Democrats have introduced legislation capping Medicare out-of-pocket spending at $5,000 a year. House Democrats' health care working group called for both a $5,000 out-of-pocket cap and adding dental, vision and hearing benefits within the first 100 hours of taking the House majority. Between the lines: More sweeping proposals for a single-payer system would result in a Medicare program without premiums or patient cost-sharing. It would instead fund care with taxpayer dollars. Traditional Medicare now requires seniors to pay premiums, copays and other out-of-pocket costs. It doesn't include dental, vision or hearing coverage, and there are no caps on how much seniors pay out of pocket. This lack of an out-of-pocket limit leaves Medicare enrollees more exposed to high costs than they would be in an employer-sponsored plan, on an Affordable Care Act marketplace or in a Medicare Advantage plan. That's why nearly half of seniors in traditional Medicare — around 13 million — buy Medigap policies to fill the holes. What we're watching: Combining expanded Medicare access with more generous benefits only drives up the price tag, creating even more pressure to find ways to pay for it all. Democrats who ran campaigns promising to crack down on corporate bad behavior will undoubtedly look to the health care industry to ultimately pay for the changes. They'd still face GOP criticism for adding financial pressure to Medicare's trust funds and speeding up the date of the program's projected insolvency. Incoming Senate health committee Ranking Member Rand Paul (R-Ky.) "is likely to play spoiler" to Sanders' Medicare for All ambitions, Capital Alpha analyst Kim Monk said in a note on Monday.

events.title: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands
events.summary: Demonstrators take part in a protest in May at the Utah Capitol to oppose the construction of a data center in Box Elder County. Natalie Behring/Getty Images A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies. “Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them. Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth. ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules. Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers. Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land. “These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act , which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service. Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act , which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives. “I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement. Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan is one of a dozen Democratic members of Congress who have called for limiting data center construction on public lands following recent reporting by ProPublica. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress. Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority. “These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.” Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities. Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes. The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants , which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued. Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate. Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.” The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land. The post Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands appeared first on ProPublica .
