events.title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
events.summary: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models. Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International , which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia. “The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately. The rule came on the same day President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia , where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade. Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says. In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun accused Washington of arbitrarily interfering with China's trade and technological cooperation with other countries and suppressing the development of China's high-tech industries. “This is a typical example of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, runs counter to the common understanding between the two sides,” he told reporter, adding that it infringes upon the rights of Chinese companies and disrupts the stability of global supply chains. He said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests. The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology. Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House. In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed. On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship. “We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said. In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said.

events.title: Hyundai Motor takes full ownership of Boston Dynamics
events.summary: According to a third-quarter regulatory filing by Hyundai Glovis on Nov 17, all put and call options tied to Boston Dynamics’ common shares were exercised and expired during the period. Hyundai Motor Group now owns 100% of Boston Dynamics after buying SoftBank’s last 9.65% stake, giving it full control of the US robotics unit. Hyundai plans to commercialise the Atlas humanoid robot, aiming for 30,000 units a year by 2028 and first using them at its Georgia plant for simple factory tasks. Boston Dynamics’ revenue rose 29% to 136 billion won in the first nine months of 2026, but losses widened to 626.6 billion won; an IPO could come around 2029 or 2030. SEOUL – Hyundai Motor Group has acquired full ownership of its US robotics subsidiary Boston Dynamics, accelerating its push to commercialise the Atlas humanoid robot. According to a third-quarter regulatory filing by Hyundai Glovis on Nov 17 , all put and call options tied to Boston Dynamics’ common shares were exercised and expired during the period. The transaction concludes the buyout of SoftBank’s remaining 9.65% stake after the Japanese tech conglomerate triggered its put option in July under an earlier shareholder pact. Existing stake holders – including Hyundai Motor group executive chair Chung Euisun, HMG Global and Hyundai Glovis – acquired the remaining shares, giving Chung and group affiliates 100% ownership of Boston Dynamics. As part of the transaction, Hyundai Glovis injected 46.5 billion won (S$44.8 million) to raise its stake by 1.08 percentage points to 12.47% at the end of the third quarter, following a 63.1 billion won investment in the first half of 2026. Industry insiders say the ownership consolidation marks a pivotal turning point for Hyundai’s robotics push. With little need to balance external shareholder demands, the group can execute capital expenditures, R&D and cross-affiliate collaborations with greater speed and autonomy. Central to this strategy is commercialising the humanoid robot Atlas. Hyundai aims to build an annual production capacity of 30,000 Atlas units by 2028 and deploy them directly into industrial operations. The initial roll-out will take place at Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America in Georgia. The robots will first handle relatively low-intensity tasks such as sorting and transporting auto parts before expanding into complex assembly work once the technology is validated. By integrating Boston Dynamics’ AI-powered robotics with its automotive manufacturing and logistics systems, Hyundai seeks to boost factory efficiency while building a new growth engine. After securing full ownership, one key hurdle for Hyundai is to achieve profitability in its robotics unit. While Boston Dynamics’ revenue for the first nine months of 2026 rose 29% year-on-year to 136 billion won, its net loss widened to 626.6 billion won due to heavy R&D and production costs. With governance restructuring now complete, Boston Dynamics is gearing up for a potential initial public offering, which sources suggest could occur around 2029 or 2030 once production ramps up. No official timeline has been set. THE KOREA HERALD/ASIA NEWS NETWORK

events.title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
events.summary: Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests O n Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought . Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come. Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider , which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable. The trials aim to identify robust apple varieties that are resistant to diseases and pests, crop reliably and can withstand the most extreme weather that might affect Somerset . Two apples ripe for harvest, which this year ran from the middle of August to November at Myrtle Farm “Somerset is the best county in the world for making cider. But the climate is changing. It has been changing for a long time. We need to be in a position where we’ve got the experience, the knowledge and the trees in place to deal with those changes,” says Martin Thatcher, the company’s managing director. One of the biggest challenges he faces is the length of time it takes to introduce a new apple variety and change growing methods in orchards. “It doesn’t happen overnight. Each apple tree takes seven years to get to a fruit crop and could last 40 years. So it takes a very long time [for experiments] to come to fruition,” he says. The trials came about because, nearly 30 years ago, his father, John Thatcher, rescued 458 varieties of cider apples grown at the Long Ashton research station, a government-funded horticultural and agricultural research centre founded in 1903. “My father took cuttings of every single variety before the centre was closed down, so we have an orchard with 458 varieties in it.” Nestled by the Mendips, the Shiplate orchard, near Bleadon, has more than 65,000 trees across 57 hectares (140 acres) The collection includes traditional cider apples and newer varieties that cater for modern tastes. “We’re looking at that orchard now and first of all seeing which apples make fabulous cider. And then we’re looking at how the trees are doing under modern orchard conditions – and if they’re good healthy trees and they’re cropping, we will plant them out in rows of 100-tree trials, to future-proof our orchard growing.” He is trying to use fewer pesticides, so is keen to find varieties that are naturally resistant to disease and pests, and will blossom at exactly the moment when spring conditions suit apple tree pollinators such as bumblebees and honeybees. Another priority is to find varieties that need less winter chill in a warming climate: apple trees, he explains, need a sustained cold period in winter to complete their dormancy, which enables their fruit buds to develop properly in spring. “That winter chill is really important – and last year, we probably didn’t have quite enough, and some varieties are more susceptible to a lack of winter chill than others.” An apple shaker grasps the tree to shake off ripe fruit, which is then collected by the harvester and pressed within hours at the Myrtle Farm mill. The orchard is home to older cultivars such as Somerset redstreak and dabinett, as well as newer ones including three counties and red falstaff Thatchers’ orchard manager, Chris Muntz Torres, says jonagold, a cross between golden delicious and a jonathan apple, performed particularly well in trials this year. “They’ve got this vigour, this willingness to grow, whatever the weather.” He thinks this is because the tree’s vigorous growth above ground is matched by a strong root system. “That’s what we want – a variety that, irrespective of the weather, is robust enough to grow.” Myrtle Farm has also begun planting wildflower strips in its orchards, to attract insects that prey on pests such as the rosy apple aphid – a strategy that research has shown could save apple growers up to £3,000 a hectare every year and support native pollinators. Nigel Jenner, head of agronomy for tree fruit at the global fruit producer AM Fresh UK, works with independent apple farmers, who represent about 30% of Britain’s apple-growing industry. He says roughly 70% of these growers – about 220 – have planted wildflower strips in the past five years, and that number is increasing. The exhibition orchard has 458 varieties of apples, many of them rare ones such as these leathercoat russets, which date back to the 16th century “We know this is the way forward,” Jenner says. “It works and it has a meaningful effect on your chemical input and your spray bill.

events.title: HSBC offloads US$300m in troubled data centre loan at steep discount
events.summary: HSBC has sold the slice of an US$18 billion (S$23 billion) financing package for a data centre in New Mexico tied to Oracle. HSBC sold about US$300 million (S$386 million) of a troubled New Mexico data centre loan at a steep discount, showing growing fear over AI-linked debt. The loan was for the Oracle-linked Project Jupiter, an US$18 billion data centre in New Mexico. The sale came after Oracle sent a force majeure notice. The project has faced delays, permit problems and regulatory pushback, raising doubts over the Stargate AI build-out and its future pace. HONG KONG – HSBC Holdings offloaded a roughly US$300 million (S$386 million) piece of a loan to build a troubled New Mexico data centre project at a steep discount, underscoring deepening anxiety surrounding the AI boom. The bank sold the slice of an US$18 billion financing package, which funds construction of the campus in Dona Ana County tied to Oracle, at prices in the mid-80s, according to people familiar with the matter. The sale took place several weeks ago, shortly after Oracle sent a notice to the project’s developer citing force majeure, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. HSBC’s move comes as lenders weigh their exposure to AI debt alongside renewed regulatory pushback following a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections . Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure from Nvidia , a linchpin of AI’s rapid expansion, has also triggered concerns about the pace of AI growth. The massive venture in southern New Mexico, known as Project Jupiter, has been beset by regulatory hurdles and opposition. Oracle sent the force majeure notice to the developer, a unit of Blue Owl Capital, in an attempt to put off payments should the venture get derailed, Bloomberg reported in late September. A group of about 20 banks provided the US$18 billion loan to help fund the data centre’s construction, Bloomberg reported in late 2025. The construction financing is referred to as Project Miner. The loan comprises different tranches tied to various buildings at the site. While lenders in the syndicated loan market are generally free to sell their stakes in the secondary market, banks holding construction project financing loans typically keep them on their balance sheets. In some circumstances, they have to wait for a so-called pooled sell-down agreement to expire before they can sell. Banks looking to exit before the completion of a project’s construction will often have to sell their debt at a discount greater than the upfront fees received. Project Jupiter is a major part of the Stargate AI infrastructure build-out that US President Donald Trump unveiled in early 2025 alongside leaders of Oracle, OpenAI and SoftBank Group. But the campus, designed to handle 2.45 gigawatts, has hit serious setbacks, including delays in acquiring air and pipeline permits key to its plans. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Africa’s coasts are the next frontier for UAE climate finance
events.summary: As Cop31 nears its end in Antalya, Turkey, the race for Africa’s resources is accelerating. Washington has raised the investment ceiling of its International Development Finance Corporation to $205 billion and is aiming much of it at Africa's critical minerals , including a planned stake of about 20 per cent in Balama graphite mine in Mozambique. The UAE is already ahead of that curve. It has committed more than $110 billion to projects throughout Africa in recent years, making it one of the continent’s largest investors. Much of that capital sits in ports, logistics, energy and agriculture. Yet many of these assets share a vulnerability that rarely appears in investment memos: an exposed coastline . For instance, more than 60 per cent of Mozambicans live in low-lying coastal areas. In 2023, Cyclone Freddy displaced more than 184,000 people there. Parts of the country’s central coast lost three quarters of their healthy mangrove forests between 1990 and 2024, stripping away the natural buffer that once absorbed storm surges before they reached towns, roads and ports. That creates a business case for UAE investors. Coastal ecosystems are infrastructure. Researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz found mangroves prevented $1.5 billion in direct flood damage in Florida during Hurricane Irma in 2017. Mangroves also store three to five times more carbon per hectare than mature tropical forests, which allows restoration to earn revenue from carbon credits. The UAE understands this at home. It has planted about 51 million mangroves towards its target of 100 million by 2030, and it cofounded the Mangrove Alliance for Climate with Indonesia. Through Alterra, the $30 billion climate vehicle launched at Cop28, held in Dubai, it aims to mobilise $250 billion of climate investment by 2030. The question is whether that expertise and capital can be used in Africa in a way that lasts. Experience suggests one factor matters more than any other: the people who live beside the forest. Large carbon concessions negotiated with governments but not with communities have struggled. A high-profile carbon credit deal in Liberia has stalled. Restoration that pays local people, by contrast, tends to hold. A carbon credit is a promise that trees will stand for decades and that promise is only as strong as the incentives of the families who could cut them down. On Idugo Island, on Mozambique’s Zambezia coast, more than 700 families make sea salt. Most used to sell at harvest, when a 50kg bag fetched about 300 meticais ($4.70). With a community warehouse and working capital, financed partly by the UK government’s Coast Facility, they can now hold stock until the lean season, when the same bag can sell for up to 1,800 meticais. Young men who once cut mangroves for income now work in that business. The forest is worth more to them standing than cut. Development agencies are already absorbing much of the early risk. The US Millennium Challenge Corporation’s $500 million Mozambique compact includes $100 million for coastal livelihoods and climate resilience in Zambezia, led by two national institutions, ProAzul and Biofund. That grant-funded groundwork in community consent, land rights and local enterprise is exactly what makes a region investable for the private capital that follows. For UAE businesses, three opportunities stand out. First, infrastructure investors can protect their own assets. A port operator or logistics group that funds the restoration of the coast around its operations is buying insurance against storm damage and disruption, at a fraction of the cost of engineered defences. Second, UAE climate funds can co-invest alongside development finance. Blended structures, in which grants and guarantees absorb the first losses, are the most efficient way to channel Alterra-scale capital into nature-based projects that would otherwise be too small or too risky. Third, UAE companies buying carbon credits to meet their net-zero targets can insist on contracts that share revenue with communities. Credits backed by legally binding benefit-sharing carry lower reversal risk, and therefore deserve a premium. Next year, Addis Ababa hosts Cop32, putting Africa at the centre of the world’s climate talks. The UAE, a bridge between Gulf capital and African growth, is in a strong position to lead a new kind of investment there: one that treats healthy coasts not as a cost of doing business, but as an asset that protects every other investment on the shore. Vahid Fotuhi is founder and chief executive of Blue Forest, a UAE-based developer of mangrove restoration projects in Africa and Asia

events.title: Soros joins family offices selling Nvidia last quarter
events.summary: George Soros, 96, has a net worth of US$9.7 billion (S$12.4 billion), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Soros Fund Management cut its Nvidia stake by almost a fifth in the quarter to 30 Sept, selling about 206,000 shares worth up to US$47.4 million. Several family offices and firms also trimmed Nvidia, while others bought more. They still held more than US$1 billion in Nvidia shares at quarter end. Nvidia remains a key AI stock, but Jensen Huang’s sudden exit as CEO has hit sentiment. The company is searching for a successor and reports earnings on 17 Nov. LONDON – George Soros’ family office joined investment firms for the world’s ultra-rich in trimming Nvidia bets last quarter, locking in gains ahead of Jensen Huang’s dramatic exit from the vaunted chip designer. The billionaire’s namesake money manager cut its stake in Nvidia by almost a fifth in the period ended Sept 30, the biggest disclosed reduction for its Nvidia holding in 2026 after it had previously added to its position, according to data compiled by Bloomberg from quarterly regulatory filings. Michael Platt’s BlueCrest Capital Management, as well as an investment firm for Abu Dhabi ruler Sheikh Mohamed Bin Zayed Al Nahyan, also cut their Nvidia stakes during the same period. The Santa Clara, California-based company’s shares were up 22% in 2026 through the end of September, roughly double the gain of the US benchmark S&P 500 Index for the same period. The selling family offices – totalling at least a dozen – all kept at least some shares of Nvidia, with their combined holdings totalling more than US$1 billion (S$1.29 billion) at the end of the quarter. For many of those firms, Nvidia remained one of their top US stock positions. Nvidia has ranked among the world’s hottest stocks in recent years as it rapidly became a poster child of the artificial intelligence boom, but Huang’s abrupt departure last week from the company that he has overseen for more than three decades has led to a reckoning. Huang, 63, was ousted as CEO on Nov 12 after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including with Nvidia employees and a woman suspected by the US Justice Department of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia’s shares have fallen more than 25% since the New York Times first reported in late October that Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spy plot. Nvidia, which reports third-quarter earnings on Nov 17 , has begun its search for a successor, even as some of Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley – and President Donald Trump – are campaigning for his return to the top job. Nvidia’s dominance in the tech boom has made it an important part of many family offices’ investment portfolios, and some of those firms increased their positions in the stock in the third quarter. Among those buying Nvidia were firms managing fortunes on behalf of duty-free shopping tycoon Alan Parker, Brazil’s Moreira Salles finance dynasty and Missouri’s Van Tuyl family. Soros Fund Management, led by former UBS Group AG executive Dawn Fitzpatrick, sold about 206,000 shares in Nvidia last quarter worth as much as US$47.4 million, filings show. Its remaining Nvidia stake was worth nearly US$200 million as of Sept 30. Soros, 96, has a net worth of US$9.7 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Money managers overseeing more than US$100 million in US equities have to file a 13F form within 45 days of the end of each quarter to list their holdings in stocks that trade on US exchanges. It offers one of the few glimpses into how hedge funds and some large family offices invest. Other highlights from the latest 13F filings include: Jeffrey Skoll’s Capricorn Investment Group slashed its biggest holding, selling 9.8 million shares of SpaceX worth almost US$1.5 billion as of Sept 30. Alta Advisers, an investment firm for a branch of Sweden’s Rausing dynasty, increased its number of equity holdings by more than a third last quarter, with 114 new positions including stakes in ExxonMobil, Blue Owl Capital and AMC Entertainment. WIT LLC, which manages a portion of the Walton family fortune, is comprised solely of stakes in exchange-traded funds. It sold 2 million shares of the iShares ESG Aware MSCI EM ETF and bought 2.75 million shares of the Vanguard FTSE Developed Markets ETF. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Simply telling the AA about my minor no-fault, no-claim prang doubled my insurance quote
events.summary: A recent £364 renewal quote suddenly increased to an extortionate £796 My car was involved in a minor no-fault accident. The other driver admitted responsibility and said they would pay for repairs without involving insurers. I informed my insurer, the AA, without making a claim. It had recently sent a renewal quote for £364, but after reporting the accident I was sent a revised figure of £796.86. I was told by a call handler that any insurance company would do the same. However, they eventually lowered the quote to £452.31. This seems extortionate for a no-fault, no-claim prang. You’re damned if you do and damned if you don’t. Failure to report an accident, even if it’s minor, not your fault and you don’t plan to claim, could invalidate your policy. The algorithms that insurers use to assess risk tend to assume that one prang makes you statistically more likely to have another, regardless of blame. Plus, you, or the at-fault driver, might later decide to claim for said incident. However, when I asked the AA how it justified doubling your premium, it discovered that its system and the call handler had boobed. It didn’t say what you should have been quoted, but has decided to honour the original £364 to make up for its failings. We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. events.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
events.summary: New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores S porting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients. But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market . Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each. Anthropic’s millionaire factory promises to expand the group of tech buyers, who range from senior staff at major AI labs to founders who have sold their startups, with budgets that range from £2m to £40m, Eccles says. Tech’s wave of wealth has already reshaped Silicon Valley – notably in San Francisco – driving up demand for already scarce housing as young entrepreneurs and engineers became millionaires overnight. Now, that money is washing up on British shores too. Anthropic, which employs about 5,000 people worldwide, has more than 200 employees in the UK. The company, founded in San Francisco in 2021, has announced plans to expand its presence in London, with a new office that is capable of accommodating up to 800 people. The company’s UK filings show that it spent £24.1m employing an average of 43 staff in 2024 alone – a mean average of £560,000 per person. Job listings this year have advertised base salaries of up to £630,000 before stock options for research engineers. Salaries across Britain’s AI sector are flying: OpenAI’s staff in London each received £2.3m on average last year – about 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings. That puts them on par with partners at top law firms such as Linklaters and Clifford Chance, and ahead of some bankers in the City. UK-based investors in these companies are also watching the value of their stakes grow at breakneck speed. Alex Gerko, the billionaire founder of the trading firm XTX and an early investor in Anthropic via the venture arms of the business, is expected to make hundreds of millions of pounds in paper gains when the company joins the stock market this week. The flush of technology cash is already evident in London’s commercial property market. First, a wave of startups led to Shoreditch being nicknamed Silicon Roundabout , before tech firms began expanding across the capital. Now, US AI firms are expanding at pace in the UK, clustering tightly inside the King’s Cross “knowledge quarter” where Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta all work a stone’s throw from each other. They have followed in the footsteps of Demis Hassabis , a totemic figure in AI’s breakthrough era who co-founded DeepMind in 2010 and sold it to Google for £400m four years later. He was one of the first to set up in the north London enclave. Isomorphic Labs, his AI drug discovery startup that is also now owned by the Google parent Alphabet, is in the area. The AI gold rush is already being felt at the highest end of London’s housing market. Although tech bosses may be younger than the sector’s traditional client base, agents report that interest – while spread across London – includes plenty of familiar wealthy haunts. In February, the Times reported that Igor Babuschkin, the billionaire co-founder of Elon Musk’s AI venture xAI, had bought a £57m penthouse overlooking Hyde Park, in one of the biggest deals in the city this year. Meanwhile, Providence House, the Reform UK treasurer Nick Candy’s former mansion on the grounds of the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London, was reportedly sold for £270m to the founder of the quantitative investment firm Quadrature Capital, Suneil Setiya. Aidan Devane, the chief executive of the firm, attributed its success partly to its proximity to AI labs in the city, telling the Financial Times: “We are probably in the golden age of London quant.” Tech wealth, increasingly generated by gains in the AI sector, “has become a force at the very top of the prime central London market”, according to the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates, which has a portfolio including a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park. Jeremy Gee, a managing director at Beauchamp, says inquiries from tech and AI buyers have risen noticeably over the past year. “Some are international buyers, principally from the US, but a growing number are based here in London,” he says, adding that many have amassed their fortunes with remarkable speed.

events.title: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
events.summary: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger. Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign , export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing. Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms. “For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University. Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan. One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity. “This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan. The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion. The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t. “I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.” Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense. Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said. Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales. Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low. “I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said. Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.

events.title: Aboriginal protester guilty of trespass despite 'cultural responsibility' to forests
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Aboriginal woman Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna found guilty of trespass despite 'cultural responsibility' Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna has been found guilty of one count of trespass. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Tasmanian-born Yorta Yorta/Dja Dja Wurrung woman Ruth Langford, also known as Tipruthanna, had pleaded not guilty in the Hobart Magistrates' Court to one count of trespass. While the court agreed she had a cultural obligation to protect forests, it found she did not have a legal excuse to remain on a logging coupe after being asked to leave. The matter has been adjourned until December 18 for sentencing submissions. An Aboriginal woman has been found guilty of trespass after a magistrate rejected her claim that she was innocent because she had a "cultural obligation" to protect forests from logging. Tasmanian-born Yorta Yorta/Dja Dja Wurrung woman Ruth Langford, also known as Tipruthanna, pleaded not guilty in the Hobart Magistrates' Court to one count of trespass. It related to an incident in January 2025, when she and other activists protested at a logging coupe at Snow Hill in state's northern midlands. Ms Langford was accused of refusing police orders to leave the site, which was managed by the state-owned forestry company, Sustainable Timbers Tasmania (STT). During hearings earlier this year, Ms Langford argued that STT had failed to comply with their legal obligations to identify and protect Aboriginal cultural heritage. She told the court that she held cultural responsibilities within the Palawa Aboriginal community that required her to "protect lands that are being slaughtered". US tech billionaire flags interest in Hurricanes, Hobart stadium MP declares shares in data centre developer before calling for moratorium Man charged with murder of two-week-old Hobart baby Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna spoke to the media and her supporters outside court. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Ms Langford said she had permission to be on the site from Palawa/Pakana elder Uncle Jim Everett, whom she described as the rightful owner of the cultural landscape. In a written decision handed down on Tuesday, Chief Magistrate Catherine Geason agreed that Ms Langford had cultural obligations. "Ms Langford was entitled to engage in cultural practices and prevent the logging contractors from commencing their work," Ms Geason stated. However, she said that once Ms Langford was asked to leave, that entitlement ended. Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna was charged with trespassing at an anti-logging protest at Snow Hill. ( ABC News: Paul Yeomans ) Ms Geason said that while it was accepted Uncle Jim was a senior elder, he did not hold the authority to grant lawful permission for Ms Langford to remain at the coupe. "I also acknowledge the evidence of Ms Langford and her witnesses regarding the profound grief and responsibility experienced by Aboriginal people when old-growth forests are cleared. "However, the court is bound to apply the law as enacted by parliament." Ms Geason said, on the balance of probabilities, Ms Langford had not established that her cultural obligations amounted to a "reasonable or lawful excuse" to remain on the land. "As such, the charge of trespass is proved." Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna at the anti-logging protest in January last year. ( Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation ) Ms Langford told the court she was "exceptionally disappointed". Outside court, Ms Langford addressed the media and her supporters. "And regardless of what the colonial court may determine, we know that our law, our obligation, is in country and country has spoken. Ruth Langford/Tipruthanna says she is pleased with some parts of the chief magistrate's decision. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Despite the verdict, she said she was pleased with some parts of the written decision. "In my hands is the written reasons why this court denied my internationally recognised rights as an Aboriginal person," she said. "I am delighted to see that she has clearly recognised that as an Aboriginal woman, I have an obligation to protect country. "That those old trees hold our law, that that law exists, and that in the finding, the magistrate has recognised that that is true." Ms Langford said she would continue to practice her cultural obligations. "We will assert that our law is in country and we are the law holders," she said. In Tasmania, trespassing on land can incur a maximum penalty of six months jail, or a $5,325 fine.

events.title: Singapore must stand firm under pressure, cannot be a ‘laundromat for contraband’: George Yeo
events.summary: The Republic must defend its reputation as a trusted international financial centre, even if doing so comes at a cost, says former foreign minister George Yeo. SINGAPORE – Singapore must be prepared to withstand pressure from bigger powers and defend its reputation as a trusted international financial centre, even if doing so comes at a cost, former foreign minister George Yeo said. The Republic cannot become a “laundromat for contraband”, he added, stressing that while Singapore must remain flexible in navigating an increasingly fragmented world, there must be limits to how far it is willing to accommodate the demands of other countries. “Being small, we can come under pressure. But beyond a point, we say no. We have to be ourselves,” he said. He was speaking at a panel discussion titled Fault lines: Investing In A Fragmented World, at the inaugural HSBC Singapore Wealth Investment Summit 2026, where he joined fellow panellist Justin Muzinich, chief executive of Muzinich & Co, in looking at the implications of geopolitical tensions, shifting trade relationships and changing investment patterns. Yeo’s remarks come amid growing scrutiny of Singapore’s role as an international financial and wealth management hub , where its reputation for strong institutions, regulatory credibility and the rule of law is central to attracting global capital. He cited the controversy involving Singapore and Alice Huang – a Chinese former executive at Singapore-based firm Megaspeed and alleged spy who former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair with – saying the Government had responded firmly after The Wall Street Journal allegedly distorted the country’s role in the matter. Singapore cannot act on allegations without evidence, Yeo said. “If you tell us it’s contraband, we’ll investigate it, and please give us information. But if it’s just an allegation without proof, then we cannot continue withholding or impounding or detaining someone at your behest,” he added. For a small country deeply connected to the global economy, such situations can put Singapore in a difficult position, particularly when demands come from larger, more powerful nations. But Yeo said the Republic’s credibility depends on its willingness to stand by its principles rather than buckle under pressure. He recalled the 1994 Michael Fay case in which the American teenager was sentenced to caning for vandalism in Singapore. Then US President Bill Clinton appealed for clemency, and Singapore reduced the sentence from six strokes to four. The episode strained bilateral relations, with then Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong unable to visit the White House for three years, Yeo said. Singapore paid a price for its position, but the country’s standing among other nations, including China and India, rose because it demonstrated it would not compromise its principles under external pressure. “So we are flexible, but beyond a point, no. And if there’s a price to be paid, so be it,” he said. Yeo said this firmness was not a departure from Singapore’s approach, but a longstanding reason other countries trust the Republic as a jurisdiction. His comments come as the global order becomes increasingly fragmented, with the rivalry between the United States and China reshaping trade, investment flows and the movement of technology and capital. Yeo described the world as undergoing a major transition, with geopolitical fault lines shifting and a new equilibrium gradually emerging. “We are entering an earthquake,” he said, adding that countries would have to remain watchful and careful as the transition unfolds. For Singapore, preserving its ability to manoeuvre will require a combination of flexibility and firmness, particularly as economic relationships become increasingly entangled with national security and political considerations. Yeo also cautioned investors against assuming that existing trends would continue uninterrupted. History, he said, has often been punctuated by sudden disruptions that could produce winners and losers. Investors should therefore consider potential failure scenarios, including a sharp disruption to the US dollar, an artificial intelligence bubble or geopolitical escalation in the Middle East. Yeo urged them to think beyond conventional market projections and consider what could bring entire economic or financial structures down. In an uncertain world, Singapore’s greatest asset may ultimately be the trust it commands. For Yeo, protecting that trust means knowing when to accommodate international pressures – and when to draw the line. Angela Tan is senior correspondent at The Straits Times’ business desk.

events.title: 'Bragyu' beef a milestone for famous outback station
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Remote Bullo River Station producing branded Wagyu Brahman beef Bullo River beef for sale in Kununurra. ( ABC Rural: Jess Baker ) Bullo River Station in the NT has started producing branded beef, using its herd of Wagyu-Brahman cross cattle. The first animals have been processed and are now for sale at some local butcher shops in the north. A butcher from Kununurra says it is the first time he has been able to sell locally produced beef. One of the most remote cattle stations in northern Australia has started producing its own branded beef, which is now being sold in local butcher shops either side of the WA/NT border. Bullo River Station in the Northern Territory is located about 800 kilometres south-west of Darwin and becomes impossible to access via road during the wet season months. Managers Joe and Catherine Atkins run a herd of Wagyu-Brahman cross cattle and said it had been a dream come true to supply local beef to communities in the region. "About six years ago the owners of this station, the Burt family, put this idea together and we started breeding what we've branded the Bragyu," Mr Atkins said. "So this is a long time coming, but it's now on the shelves for local people and it's very exciting." Wagyu Brahman cross cattle at Bullo River Station, NT. ( Supplied: Bullo River ) Mr Atkins said the station sent a trial consignment of animals to the Rum Jungle abattoir near Batchelor for a service kill and would look to ramp up next year if all went to plan. "We want to initially support butchers in Katherine and Kununurra and also give visitors here at Bullo River the paddock to plate experience," he said. "It's a very different game to what I'm used to; I've long done live export, that was my world, but this is exciting. Butcher Murray Salter cutting beef from Bullo River Station. ( ABC Rural: Jess Baker ) Murray Salter took over the butcher shop in Kununurra 10 years ago and said being able to sell locally produced beef was a milestone for his business. "I've been waiting 10 years for a moment like this to source local beef for our customers," he said. "The local Brahman stock all get sent to the live export trade, but by crossing them with the Wagyu it's brought a quality meat to the Kimberley. "Our beef supply normally travels 3,000 to 4,000 kilometres to get here, but this is from just down the road, which is nice." Beef from Bullo River Station packaged up, ready for sale. ( Supplied: Tenderspot Kununurra ) Mr Salter said the beef was tender, juicy, could be cut "with a butter knife", and local customers had been excited to support it. The Bullo River beef is the latest in a growing trend of northern cattle stations selling products locally, including KAPCO beef in the Kimberley, Eva Valley Meats in the NT, and the Niceforo family processing its cattle near Katherine for a new Darwin steakhouse. Joe Atkins said in terms of dollars, selling branded beef was not too different to selling direct to the live export trade, but there were other benefits. Bullo River Station is located 800km south-west of Darwin and 200km east of Kununurra. ( ABC Rural: Matt Brann ) "There's satisfaction for us is supporting local people and not doing live export," he said. "I've lived up here 40 years and have never been able to buy local beef from our local butcher store, so yeah, I think this is the future. "Actually 45 years ago there was a small abattoir here on Bullo River Station, so it's funny how the wheels have turned around and that is definitely our grand plan to have a micro-abattoir on the property.

events.title: Hundreds of tonnes of rubbish illegally dumped on WA roadsides each year
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Large amounts of fencing has been dumped by the roadside in Noranda. ( ABC News: Nadia Mitsopoulos ) Main Roads says it removed more than 600 tonnes of litter and dumped material from Perth's road network over the past two financial years. Perth resident Robert Parker says he reported what appeared to be asbestos and fencing dumped on Reid Highway, and blames costly, restrictive tip rules. Main Roads says the dumped material on Reid Highway will be cleared by a maintenance crew within the coming week. Tonnes of rubbish and potentially toxic old building material are being dumped on Perth roadsides and nature strips by what is believed to be contractors and others avoiding council tip fees. WA's Main Roads department says it has removed more than 600 tonnes of litter and dumped material from the Perth metropolitan road network over the past two years. Dianella resident Robert Parker told 102.5 ABC Perth he recently saw what appeared to be 10 tonnes of material by the side of Reid Highway when he was out walking. "There's what appeared to be a bit of asbestos or fencing being dumped in the scrub down there," he said. "Later on, I was driving and [it appeared] a commercial contractor has chosen to use the verge on Reid Highway as his yard and dumped asbestos material and other products that should go to landfill or the appropriate recycling facility." Mr Parker said he reported the dumping to Main Roads, but also believed councils were making it too expensive for people to legally dispose of their hard rubbish. "You go to the tips, and they say, 'Oh no, we don't accept super six fencing here anymore, we don't take hardy fence', or it's only so many sheets per time. Construction waste dumped on the southern side of Reid Highway. ( ABC News: Nadia Mitsopoulos ) Listeners to 102.5 ABC Radio Perth said there were significant barriers to disposing of rubbish legally. Matt : 'It's very expensive to take waste to the recycling centre. Last week they would not accept some bathroom tiles. They said it was construction waste, and won't be accepted. No wonder people do illegal dumping.' Anon : "It's a no-brainer: getting rid of waste in the community is far too expensive. It should be free and funded by the state government through our taxes, a clean city with proper disposal is good for everyone and everyone should pay through the taxes. Illegal dumping goes away then, and we return to a beautiful litter-free city." Anon : "I took a broken office chair to the local tip. The guy on the gate said it would cost me $45 to dump it. I guess that's why people dump stuff illegally.' Sivwarr : 'I drive up to Gidgegannup quite regularly on Toodyay road the illegal dumping starts at the bottom of the hills and just doesn't stop." Rick : "The reason for illegal dumping is laziness, selfishness and a sense of self-entitlement." Rubbish dumped on the southern side of Reid Highway between Camboon Road and Alexander Drive. ( ABC News: Nadia Mitsopoulos ) In a statement, a Main Roads spokesperson said the department was aware of the fencing material on the southern side of Reid Highway. "The material has been programmed for removal and will be cleared by a maintenance crew within the coming week," the spokesperson said. "Across the 2024/25 and 2025/26 financial years, Main Roads removed more than 600 tonnes of litter and dumped material from the metropolitan road network alone." They said the department continued to monitor known dumping hotspots and used "targeted measures" to deter offending.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Attackers try logging in to Earth’s ninth most powerful machine after status page hack exposed credentials America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states 31 minutes ago REIT move? Blackstone joint venture buys AWS campuses to lease back to the cloud giant 6 hours ago China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion 1 day ago Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric 1 day ago Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed 1 day ago The RIKEN Center for Computational Science, the home of the Fugaku supercomputer, has revealed unauthorized attempts to access the machine after a data leak. According to a statement issued by RIKEN yesterday, between November 10 and 13 an unknown entity attacked a web dashboard that displays operational status data for Fugaku. It sounds like whatever the attackers did to that dashboard allowed them to move across the RIKEN network, because they were able to reach several servers that store data belonging to authorized users, and install malware. The servers stored users’ names and email addresses, plus credentials used to access supercomputers and services not operated by RIKEN. The attacker has tried to use those credentials. RIKEN is working with the organizations that host those other supercomputers to investigate whether the attackers succeeded. The research outfit doesn’t know how the attack happened and can’t say with certainty what information attackers were able to access and/or steal, beyond saying that 4,222 registered users of Fugaku are at risk, along with 375 registered users of its smaller Rikyu supercomputer. RIKEN does know that on November 13, someone attempted to log onto Fugaku. RIKEN quickly took the machine offline. Fugaku comprises 158,976 nodes, each packing a 48-core processor and 32GiB of available RAM, for a total of 7,630,848 cores and over five petabytes of memory. Those specs saw Fugaku lead the Top 500 lists of Earth’s mightiest supercomputers for two years between 2020 and 2022. It ranks ninth on the update of the list released on Tuesday. RIKEN’s other super, Rikyu, operates 288,000 cores. If attackers managed to run a workload on either machine, they could do a lot of damage. The intrusion has already had serious consequences because Fugaku is currently offline. As the machine is used for scientific research, and RIKEN schedules use of the machine, the outage will disrupt researchers who were waiting for their turn to use the supercomputer. At the time of writing, RIKEN has found no evidence that users’ research data has leaked but isn’t yet sure what info did make it out of the building and whether it contains any data describing third parties. The research org has promised to conduct a detailed investigation into the incident, which is the latest in a long string of significant cyberattacks that have struck Japanese clouds , telcos , retailers and government agencies, leading Tokyo to release emergency funds in the hope that extra money can quickly shore up the nation’s cyber-defenses. ® Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’ If you design a test to find misalignment, you will find misalignment America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states Harvard study claims emissions attributable to datacenters are two to three times higher than in 2018 The future of datacenters depends on behind-the-meter energy generation PARTNER CONTENT: PARTNER CONTENT: Hyperscalers and colos have distinct power strategies, but for both, securing flexible, fast power relies on self-generated solutions Inspiring FOSS project Crosspoint Reader has lessons about tech, communities, and LLMs Cheap tiny e-readers and the perils of LLM-generated drive-by pull requests – plus much more We don't need no education platform evolution.

events.title: ‘Due for a reset’: Mubadala CEO says global AI economy faces compute shortage
events.summary: The global AI buildout and broader economy is due for “a reset of sorts,” Mubadala CEO Khaldoon Al Mubarak said Monday. Asked whether “winter is coming” — a nod to fears that the AI boom could face a correction — Al Mubarak said it was, but that “winter doesn’t mean minus 30 degrees. It could be a nice pleasant winter,” he said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The AI buildout is part of “a cycle,” Al Mubarak said, adding that the global economy has had “a very good run.” The Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund is a major investor in AI infrastructure and software, with big bets on data center developers and both OpenAI and Anthropic, through MGX, a separate funding vehicle it co-founded. Mubadala has become one of the most aggressive Gulf sovereign wealth funds, embarking on a dealmaking spree , tying up with some of the biggest names in global finance, and taking a more active role leading on investments rather than being a passive capital provider. About 44% of Mubadala’s assets are in North America, and it has aligned itself with the US’ efforts to dominate the AI race with China. “There’s no navigating” between the US and China, Al Mubarak said Monday. “You either go US or China, and we’re betting on the US technology stack.” Al Mubarak said he’s “hoping that any US government, Republican or Democrat, is going to be partnership-oriented.” He said he isn’t worried about energy, and that access to capital is “OK,” but that getting enough compute is the biggest challenge. — J.D. events.title: Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang comeback despite backing from big names
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang comeback despite big names backing his return Jensen Huang stepped down from the Nvidia board last week. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) Nvidia is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang, despite Elon Musk and Donald Trump supporting his return. Mr Huang was forced to step down amid revelations about affairs, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Ms Huang's relationship with China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating the scandal-hit Jensen Huang as chief executive, three people have told Reuters. Mr Huang was forced to step down last week amid revelations about affairs involving employees and a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The former chief executive's departure plunged the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sent shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll. More than 180,200 people, including thousands identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, have signed a petition demanding Mr Huang's return. Elon Musk has also thrown his support behind the effort, and US President Donald Trump, who reportedly held millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares, said he would not mind seeing Mr Huang reinstated as CEO . Mr Trump's reported trades this year suggest he held between $US13 million ($19m) and $US62m in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, The Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures. Taiwan's tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Monday with messages including "Taiwan Loves Jensen". The message "Taiwan heart Jensen" was projected on the Taipei 101 building in Taipei in support of Jensen Huang. ( Reuters: Ann Wang ) It came as the Stand With Jensen campaign gained traction online. "We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts," an open letter published on the campaign's website said. The campaign listed SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its signatories. Prominent shareholders such as Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace Mr Huang before all the facts are known. However, a person familiar with the matter said: "The Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen back." The uncertainty over Mr Huang's future has divided investors and complicated the board's search for a successor. Nvidia has lost $US800 billion in market value since Mr Huang stepped down. After news broke of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset Nvidia's value plummeted. Why? The company's shares closed down more than 4 per cent on Monday, a day before the chipmaker was due to report third-quarter earnings. Independent technology researcher Richard Windsor said he expected "very risk-averse" large institutional Nvidia investors to oppose Mr Huang's return while investigations remained unresolved, because of the legal exposure and uncertainty it could create. At the centre of the scandal is Chinese businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang (no relation), who Mr Huang admitted to having an affair with. US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine the extent of Ms Huang's relationship with China's Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Evidence gathered so far indicates she was likely an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, sources said. Mr Huang's reach is especially visible in Taiwan, where he was born, and where he enjoys celebrity-like status dubbed "Jensanity". Nvidia relies on a local manufacturer to make its most advanced chips, and a sprawling network of suppliers to manufacture other chips and systems underpinning the AI boom. For many Taiwanese, Mr Huang's exit marks the loss of a charismatic champion who helped put the island at the heart of the global AI boom. Jimmy Yang, a 42-year-old marketing worker, said Mr Huang's departure was a loss for Taiwan. He expressed hope that Mr Huang could eventually return to Nvidia. "His private life is his own choice," Mr Yang said. "But whether it's the night market economy he's driven or his help for the tech industry, it has been massive," he said.

events.title: Anthropic's IPO: How do you price the future of AI?
events.summary: Like most AI companies, Anthropic is burning through cash and has not found a path to profitability, which makes its future cash flows hard to forecast. Anthropic wants a market value of up to US$1.4 trillion in its IPO, as investors try to price the future of AI and its uncertain profits. Valuing Anthropic is hard because it is still losing money and has few listed rivals, so bankers and investors are negotiating the price. CEO Dario Amodei said the firm is going public for funding to build advanced AI, but experts warn there is “no guarantee” it will keep growing. WASHINGTON – Speculation over Anthropic’s stock market valuation has highlighted one of the riskiest bets in finance: trying to put a price on the future of artificial intelligence. A few days before its initial public offering, the maker of the AI agent Claude said it was aiming for a market capitalisation of up to US$1.4 trillion (S$1.81 trillion). That figure would put the young company among the largest stock market debuts on record, though it falls short of the US$2 trillion some estimates had floated until a few weeks ago. Since then, concern about AI development and profits has swept the market. OpenAI, a rival which plans to go public in 2027, is valued at US$1.025 trillion on the private market, according to US media reports. There are two main ways to value a company, said Michelle Lowry, a finance professor at Drexel University. The first is to estimate how much cash the company will bring in over the coming years. Money expected far in the future counts for less than money today, especially when it is uncertain, so those future amounts are reduced to work out what the company is worth now. The second compares the company with similar listed firms. If those firms are valued at, say, five times their annual revenue, the same ratio is applied to the company being valued. Both methods are well established, but “in the case of Anthropic, both of these approaches are quite difficult”, Lowry told AFP. It also has few listed peers. The closest is SpaceX, which made a record debut on Wall Street in June with a valuation of US$1.77 trillion. But that comparison is imperfect, since the Elon Musk-led company combines a social network, space operations and an AI lab. SpaceX also rides on Musk’s star power among retail investors. So, how was the US$1.4 trillion figure set? “There’s some back and forth” between companies seeking to go public and institutional investors, said Minmo Gahng, an assistant professor of finance at Cornell University. Investment banks act as intermediaries between the two sides, he said, in a process that can be time-consuming. A company’s valuation is its share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding. A company going public wants that price as high as possible, since it determines how much money it raises. But it also has to leave enough room to attract buyers, since weak demand would drag down the stock. Investors, for their part, want to be sure they can later sell their stakes at a profit – and are hoping for a “pop”, or sharp rise in the share price, on the first day of trading. Speaking on Nov 13 with JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon, Anthropic co-founder and chief executive officer Dario Amodei cited a company motto when discussing the IPO: “Under-promise and over-deliver.” He also said the company was going public mainly because it needs funding. Anthropic is set to raise a total of US$90 billion through the offering, money it plans to use to develop cutting-edge AI. Jay Ritter, an IPO specialist at the University of Florida, said investors accept such valuations because a handful of companies, such as Amazon, Alphabet and Nvidia, have shown “you can earn profits of US$100 billion a year or more without competition eroding those profits”. But there is no guarantee that Anthropic will do the same, he warned. “It could be the case that 10 years from now, Anthropic will have been left in the dust where nobody is using frontier large language models because open-source models are good enough and cheap.” Anthropic’s growth has already shown signs of slowing and 90 pages of its IPO prospectus are devoted to risks facing the future of the company – and even of humanity – depending on the direction AI takes. events.title: S’pore has $7 trillion in assets under management as AI reshapes wealth management: Alvin Tan
events.summary: Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development Alvin Tan (right) and CEO of HSBC Singapore Kee Joo Wong at the HSBC Singapore Wealth Investment Summit. Singapore will use AI to grow wealth and protect its role as a global financial centre, while keeping strong safeguards for financial integrity. Alvin Tan said wealth management has reached "$7 trillion" in assets under management, with about 2,000 single-family offices and a financial sector that makes up about 14% of GDP. Singapore will deepen capital markets, support philanthropy, and use AI safely in finance, while planning long term for jobs, innovation and future generations. SINGAPORE – Singapore must harness artificial intelligence to generate new wealth and strengthen its position as a global financial centre, even as it maintains strong safeguards to protect the integrity of its financial system, said Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development Alvin Tan. Speaking at the inaugural HSBC Singapore Wealth Investment Summit 2026 on Nov 17, he said the Republic is not seeking to compete with global technology giants in developing cutting-edge AI models, but positioning itself as a centre for the research, development and application of AI across industries, including financial services. He added that the country’s wealth management industry had grown on the back of trust, with assets under management reaching $7 trillion, and private banking client assets have increased by about 50% over the past five years. Singapore now has about 2,000 single-family offices, reflecting the continued flow of wealth into the Republic. The financial sector contributes about 14 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product and employs about 200,000 people, said Tan, who is a Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) board member. He outlined three priorities for Singapore’s development as a wealth centre: growing wealth through trust, generating wealth through innovation, and giving wealth through philanthropy and legacy planning. He said trust and innovation go hand in hand, stressing that Singapore must remain a trusted regulatory hub while ensuring its financial sector remains competitive and responsive to global investors’ needs. AI is expected to play an increasingly important role in this ambition. Tan highlighted five areas where Singapore can apply AI to create economic opportunities: connectivity, advanced manufacturing, healthcare, national development housing projects and financial services. In financial services, AI could significantly improve the way banks serve wealthy clients by reducing the time needed to gather information and prepare investment recommendations. He cited the example of wealth managers preparing annual portfolio reviews for clients. Previously, bankers had to obtain information from different divisions , including investment banking, trading and wealth management, before consolidating the data into a client portfolio presentation – a process that could take several hours . With AI, information from different sources can be pulled together and a presentation prepared in minutes, allowing bankers to spend more time engaging clients. Tan said about 30 financial institutions, including HSBC, had established centres of excellence in Singapore to develop AI capabilities and financial applications. These include tokenised money market funds, agentic commerce and AI-powered advisory services. He also cited Google’s DeepMind AI research lab and OpenAI’s recently announced US$200 million (S$258 million) investment in AI research in Singapore as examples of the growing ecosystem. But the expanding use of AI in finance must be accompanied by appropriate safeguards, particularly as agentic AI takes on more responsibilities in financial transactions and advisory services. Tan said HSBC had been working with MAS on safeguards for agentic finance, including measures to ensure AI systems operate safely at runtime. Beyond AI, Singapore is also seeking to deepen its capital markets and broaden opportunities for wealth creation. Tan pointed to initiatives to strengthen the equities market, establish Singapore as a gold trading hub and develop a growth capital market group to help start-ups raise funds and find exit opportunities in both public and private markets. On the regulatory front, he said Singapore must strike a balance between maintaining rigorous anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing safeguards, and ensuring that legitimate wealth can enter the financial system efficiently. Following past money laundering concerns, the authorities have adopted a risk-proportionate approach to managing fund flows and account openings. Tan said the Government has been working with the private banking industry and MAS to improve account-opening processes while maintaining the necessary checks on source of wealth and source of funds.

events.title: Greens offer government a path to pass trusts and capital gains tax changes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Greens narrow demand on trusts and capital gains tax changes David Shoebridge has raised concerns about an exemption to Labor's trust tax for private schools and other tax-exempt entities. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The Greens want the government to commit to reforming charity rules in exchange for passage of its tax bills. A "name and shame" proposal for trusts and beneficiaries is not a red line and the Greens have no major issues with the government's CGT carve-out. The government is trying to pass two tax bills through the Senate by the end of next week. The Greens could pass Labor's two major tax bills by the end of next week if the minor party can extract a promise to reform the charities sector. Treasurer Jim Chalmers wants parliament's support for legislation to impose a minimum tax on some trusts and to carve out start-ups from the new capital gains tax (CGT) regime. The Coalition is opposed, making the Greens the only viable pathway in the Senate. The minor party is comfortable with the principle of both measures and would support them subject to a small number of changes, several Greens sources told the ABC. The party's red line is an exemption for private schools and other non-tax-paying recipients, which they want repealed along with a commitment to consider broader charitable sector reform, including the tax treatment of religious institutions. But the Greens have no apparent red lines on the CGT start-up carve-out and appear unlikely to support independent MP Allegra Spender's proposed alternative, despite expressing openness to it yesterday. Mr Chalmers revealed this morning that he had written to Ms Spender outlining Treasury's concerns with her proposal. That letter, seen by the ABC, said her idea would be "neither simple nor straightforward" and would be inequitable. Spender proposal not 'fairer', Chalmers says The CGT issue relates to a workaround the government devised in response to a complaint from start-ups that the new inflation-based discount would unfairly penalise them, because they start from scratch and so had no cost base to be "inflated". The government's proposed concession would apply to businesses less than 15 years old, subject to a test to establish whether they were developing or commercialising "genuinely innovative products, processes, services or methods". Government won't promise net savings Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update. Ms Spender said the exemption was too narrow and subjective and that any "active" business assets should instead get a 40 per cent discount, which she said would raise a similar amount of money but be simpler. In his letter to Ms Spender, Mr Chalmers said Treasury had "identified a number of issues and concerns". "Their analysis suggests that your proposal is unlikely to be simpler, fairer or enhance productivity, as you suggest," he wrote. "Your proposal would introduce a second set of tax arrangements for capital gains and replaces one arbitrary distortion in the tax system with another, for the majority of assets. [It] risks introducing more complexity, not less." In the letter, Mr Chalmers said early-stage start-ups, which were most likely to be innovative, would likely stand to pay higher taxes under the 40 per cent idea and that identifying which assets were "active" would be complex. "This would need to occur regularly and across all businesses to ensure shareholders understand an entity's status, as opposed to the current definition that only applies to small businesses in years where CGT events arise," he wrote. He added that the proposal could "introduce pervasive incentives to restructure for tax reasons", such as by putting properties and other assets into an "active" business vehicle to pay less tax. In a statement, Ms Spender told the ABC her proposal was "gathering wide support in the business community" and reiterated her call to the government to "listen seriously to what business is saying and carefully analyse and evaluate the advantages" of her model. "I would welcome a thorough and serious parliamentary inquiry," she said. Ms Spender added that she "appreciated" the letter but that it had "failed to recognise the concerns of the business community" with the existing approach "and its real-world impacts on risk-taking and investment... "The business community wasn't consulted on the government's original CGT direction but is willing to compromise. The government should be willing to listen now.
