AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Bunnings Warehouse needs a technology model its current employees somehow can’t deliver Australia may make knowingly selling unsafe AI a crime 6 days ago Royal London plans IT outsourcing shake-up as staff brace for redundancies 12 days ago After threatening AI export bans, China allows DeepSeek to keep selling 22 days ago South Korean president calls for creation of tools that stop all cyber-attacks October 7, 2026 Atos lands £350M beat keeping Met Police applications running October 6, 2026 Indian tech giant Tata Consultancy Services has a new client, iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse which has made a third of its IT department redundant. Bunnings is Australia’s equivalent of big box hardware retailers Home Depot and B&Q and earlier today advised its IT teams to attend a town hall meeting. The Register understands the invitation to that meeting was sent twice, after the first effort contained an error. We hear from staff that the botched invitation was taken as a clue of what was to happen next, namely the announcement of 230 redundancies plus an end to 120 contracted roles. The town hall meeting was not interactive, with a Bunnings rep speaking from a script and not taking questions. Staff whose roles will end then received an email inviting them to a meeting. Bunnings, whose logo is a hammer, has tried to explain the decision in a statement that says, “We need a technology model and partner that keeps pace with our customers so that we can continue to deliver the service, value and helpful advice people expect from us.” “These changes reflect the way customers are choosing to shop and the increasingly competitive retail environment,” the statement adds, before pointing out “Bunnings is already investing in technology and digital experiences to respond to these changes, earlier this year becoming the first Australian retailer to launch an AI-powered shopping agent using Google's Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience platform through Buddy.” Some of the TCS workers Bunnings is hiring will work in Australia. Others will work from India and the Philippines. While Bunnings follows the template of a big box retailer, each of its stores allows charities and community groups to run fundraising barbeques in its forecourt every weekend. Those barbeques are a significant source of income for many non-profits and have earned the chain a broad social license. The hardware barn is so well-known that children’s TV show Bluey – the most viewed program of 2024 and 2025 in the US – gently parodied it as "Hammerbarn" it in an episode. The Register mentions this because we understand the reference to TCS staff helping to deliver the Bunnings experience has gone down badly, as the chain’s employees wonder how offshore workers who have not experienced its stores and atmosphere can deliver a service that preserves its culture. Bunnings says its new IT operating model will commence in July 2027 and that “Impacted team members will be supported in their roles through Christmas, with any changes taking effect in the new year.” The company’s IT team will still employ around 500 people. These job losses add to a rotten year for Australia’s tech scene, which this year saw local heroes Canva and Atlassian farewell hundreds of staff. Iconic Australian airline Qantas last week outsourced hundreds of jobs to India through Accenture.

events.title: Dubai airport on target for 70 million passengers this year amid recovery from war
events.summary: Dubai International Airport handled 50.4 million passengers in the first nine months of 2026, even as the Iran war disrupted travel. The airport sustained vital connections for tourism, trade and business during the period, with continued investment in artificial intelligence, connected systems and smarter processes aimed at boosting future growth, state-owned operator Dubai Airports said on Tuesday. Passenger traffic in the nine months to the end of September fell 28.1 per cent year on year, while third-quarter volumes declined 22.1 per cent to 18.8 million passengers, Dubai Airports said. August was the busiest month of the quarter, with 6.6 million passengers. The airport expects to welcome more than 70 million passengers this year, as airlines resume services and its global network strengthens, Dubai Airports’ chief executive Paul Griffiths said. That is down from 95.2 million passengers last year , the highest annual international passenger traffic recorded by any airport. DXB has also delayed its target of 100 million passengers to 2027. “We are focused on continuing to accommodate future growth … innovation is central to that approach,” he said. Return of global airlines The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted air travel this year, driving up fuel prices and causing flight delays, cancellations and diversions across the Middle East and beyond. International airlines have been forced to adjust schedules for Middle East flights in the aftermath of the war, which broke out on February 28, as airspace restrictions persist. Airlines have gradually begun to restart flights to the region. This month, British Airways resumed flights between London Heathrow and Dubai after an eight-month suspension caused by the conflict. Lufthansa Group also said last week that it would resume Dubai services on November 25, joining Royal Air Maroc, SunExpress and Cebu Pacific. Other airlines are scheduled to resume operations in the coming weeks, Dubai Airports said. DXB, the world’s busiest international hub for passengers in 2025, is served by 57 airlines connecting Dubai to 235 destinations across 101 countries. Mr Griffiths said in September that DXB was determined to hold on to the top spot despite war-related disruption. India was DXB’s largest country market in the third quarter of this year, accounting for 2.6 million passengers, followed by Saudi Arabia with 1.4 million and the UK with 1.3 million, Dubai Airports aid on Tuesday. London was the leading city destination, with 784,000 passengers, followed by Mumbai with 528,000 and New Delhi with 525,000. No spillover impact from war Mr Griffiths said he is not expecting a spillover impact from the ongoing attacks in the neighbouring countries of Saudi Arabia and Bahrain. “People tend to lump the [Middle East] region as one big trouble spot,” he said. “Yeah, but it's not. You can't say that the whole of the Middle Eastern area is one homogenous area because it isn't. And obviously, the issues between the Saudis and the Yemenis are one thing. The issues between Iran and the rest of the region is another thing.” He said there is a “sense of optimism” now. “I think the collective view now is that hopefully a diplomatic solution to the position we find ourselves in here is perhaps more likely than a military solution. I think that is the optimism,” he said. Mr Griffiths also said he is not seeing any deterrence in the number of international travellers that want to come back to Dubai. “In fact, the appetite is incredibly healthy and I think we feel quite positive about the prospects,” he said. “We may even see close to our magic 100 million by the end of next year.” In terms of capacity, the airport chief said it is about “83 per cent” back. “There's absolutely no barriers for us to get back to 100 per cent capacity and I think if you look at the recovery rates of the airlines, particularly Emirates, they are in the 90s [per cent], so they're very, very close to where they were last year,” he said. Technology leads the way Dubai Airports is investing in AI, predictive analytics and biometric technology to improve passenger flows and increase capacity within existing facilities, it said. The initiatives bring together data and visual feeds from airport systems to give operations teams a real-time view of passenger movements, aircraft activity and airport facilities. AI tools help identify potential bottlenecks and allow staff to address pressure points before they affect operations. “Every process we simplify and every bottleneck we remove helps us use our existing facilities more efficiently,” Mr Griffiths said. “By combining technology with better ways of working, we can unlock additional capacity without expanding the airport’s footprint, while improving the experience for our guests.” Operational performance Aircraft movements fell 27.6 per cent to 243,000 in the first nine months, while cargo volumes declined 23.2 per cent to 1.215 million tonnes. The average passenger load factor stood at 74 per cent, three percentage points lower than a year earlier, Dubai Airports said. The airport processed 48 million bags during the nine-month period, with 91 per cent delivered within 45 minutes of arrival. In the third quarter, 99.9 per cent of passengers waited less than 10 minutes at departure passport control, while the same proportion cleared arrival passport control within 15 minutes, Dubai Airports said.

events.title: Bunnings cuts 230 jobs in partial offshoring of tech services
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bunnings to make 230 jobs redundant amid partial offshoring of tech services Bunnings is planning to cut more than 200 permanent jobs. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) Bunnings has announced plans to cut 230 tech jobs and end 120 contractor agreements. The retail giant has signed an agreement with an Indian-based tech firm to offshore some of its tech services. The company says job cuts will begin in the new year. Hardware retailer Bunnings will cut roughly 230 jobs and end 120 contractor agreements as it shifts part of its technology department offshore. The Australian retail giant announced today it had penned a new agreement with Indian-based tech firm Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) as part of a restructure of its technology services. Roughly 230 permanent roles will be made redundant and an additional 120 contractor roles will end as a result. Australia cashes in on India's IT jobs machine India has positioned itself as a global hub of skilled, cheap labour, and Australian companies are moving more jobs to its shores. In a statement, Bunnings managing director Mike Schneider said the changes aimed to respond to evolving consumer needs. "This is a necessary but important change. We need a technology model and partner that keeps pace with our customers so that we can continue to deliver the service, value and helpful advice people expect from us," Mr Schneider said. The transition is due to begin in December and continue through to June next year, the company said. Affected staff will be supported in their roles over Christmas, with job losses to begin in the new year, while the retailer will retain a core in-house technology team of approximately 500 people based in Australia. Remaining services will be delivered by TCS teams based in Australia, India and the Philippines. Mike Schneider says impacted staff are being offered support. ( Supplied: Bunnings ) Mr Schneider said Bunnings would support impacted team members through various means, including redundancy packages. "We know that this is difficult for our Technology team members, particularly those impacted by the change," he said. "We're managing these changes with care and respect, including through redundancy packages, career transition, redeployment wherever possible and wellbeing support." Bunnings is the latest in a growing list of Australian companies , including Qantas, NAB, Officeworks, Woolworths and Coles, to announce plans to outsource jobs overseas. 'Difficult news to share', executive says Staff were given the news earlier today by Bunnings chief information officer Genevie Elliott, who said it was "difficult news to share". In a virtual meeting with employees, Ms Elliott said many of those impacted by today's announcement had helped build up the company's technology services, which remained in use across its network of stores. Bunnings is the latest major Australian company to offshore part of its operation. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) "I want you to know these changes we're announcing are not a reflection of anyone's performance or their contribution or value," she told staff. "So I think it's really important you all understand why we've made this decision. Over the last two years, we've deliberately strengthened our tech function. "We've evolved our structure, our ways of working, how we prioritise and deliver work, and that structure has served us well. "I don't want anyone thinking those changes didn't work. They did. But this decision that I'm sharing today builds on that work." Ms Elliott said bringing TCS on board would allow the company to drive down business costs and tap into "specialist expertise and global retail experience". "We need a model that allows us to remain competitive without continually increasing our costs. This partnership will help us do that," she said. She said the company had to evolve alongside a rapidly transforming online retail environment impacting how consumers shop. "And we all know that tech is rapidly evolving, and the pace of change is only going to increase. That means we need to respond to keep up.

events.title: Robert Pattinson as James Bond throws out the 007 playbook
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts As James Bond, Robert Pattinson prepares to lead his biggest franchise yet Robert Pattinson has capped off a blockbuster year by snagging the coveted role of 007. ( AP: Scott A Garfitt/Invision ) Who knew Twilight would have predicted the next 007? Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next James Bond , succeeding fellow Englishman Daniel Craig in one of Hollywood's most recognisable roles . But it's a scene from Pattinson's breakout film that has resurfaced for its eerily prophetic nature. In the 2008 vampire hit, the prom theme is Monte Carlo, with the students of Forks High School told to think "gambling, tuxedos and Bond … James Bond". The camera than cuts to Pattinson's Edward Cullen, who steps out of a sleek silver Volvo sporting Ray-Bans and a smirk. Fast forward nearly 20 years and that parallel is now a reality. Pattinson brings maximum star power to the James Bond role, reportedly beating out fellow Brits Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O'Connor. "I think Robert Pattinson is one of the most dynamic and most interesting actors working in Hollywood," film critic Luke Goodsell says, noting his roles in this year's Primetime , The Drama and The Odyssey . Several of Robert Pattinson's projects have hit theatres this year, including Primetime. ( Supplied: A24 ) Pattinson's appointment also marks the first time James Bond has been cast since Amazon reportedly paid more than $1 billion for the 007 intellectual property in February last year. The announcement of a new actor to play James Bond gives the franchise an opportunity to reinvent itself for a new audience. "It's been remarked on that it's the first time the Bond franchise has cast a big A-Lister," Goodsell says. "Obviously, Roger Moore was famous for The Saint and Pierce Brosnan was famous to some degree for Remington Steele, but this is the first time they've really gone for an A-list actor. Which is unusual, Goodsell says, because "the former producer Barbara Broccoli was always adamant that the actor should not be bigger than 007". "But I think repeating the same old playbook where they cast a relative unknown would be the least interesting choice at this point in the franchise," Goodsell says. "For them to dive straight in, headlong into a major movie star, and a really interesting and slippery actor who is also a movie star, is a really fascinating choice." Pattinson is no stranger to franchises. One of his first major roles was in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in 2005, where he played the dashing but doomed Cedric Diggory, his death marking the moment the series goes from whimsical to something much darker. But Pattinson was launched to stratospheric levels of fame in 2008 when he landed the role of Edward Cullen in Twilight, the film's success cementing his heart-throb status in Hollywood and making him a household name, in the homes of teenage girls, at least. Robert Pattinson shot to fame as Edward Cullen in Twilight. ( Reuters: Mario Anzuoni ) Despite his fame, Pattinson rallied against his handsome, alluring on-screen persona, instead using his countless interviews on the Twilight press junket to begin a years-long affinity for creating bizarre, fabricated stories. In a 2024 interview with The New York Times , the actor revisited a 2011 interview in which he spoke extensively about watching a clown die in a little-car explosion as a kid. "There was absolutely no hesitation at all [in my voice]," Pattinson said with a combination of "pride and alarm". His reason? Boredom, explaining "the only thing people would ever ask me about was being famous" and "you go into, like, a fugue state". Goodsell says Pattinson's career has been "compelling to watch". Post Twilight, Goodsell says Pattinson and his co-star Kristen Stewart were "assumed, I think, to be doomed after that, and both of them went out and said, 'OK, we're going to revive our careers in different ways'". With five Twilight movies complete, Pattinson had the freedom to get weird. Robert Pattinson (right) starred alongside Willem Dafoe (left) in The Lighthouse. ( Supplied: Universal ) He dived into independent films, teaming up with David Cronenberg for Cosmopolis, starring in the Safdie brothers' Good Time, and Robert Eggers' psychological horror The Lighthouse. In 2020, he would star in one his most Bond-esque roles to date: Christopher Nolan's Tenet. He even explored voice acting for the English dub of Hayao Miyazaki's The Boy and the Heron. "He really kind of, let's just say it, lets his freak flag fly. He loves a weird voice," Goodsell says.

events.title: Top Trump aides to meet with Europeans, Ukrainians on peace plan
events.summary: President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are planning to meet with Ukrainian and European officials this week to work on security guarantees and a postwar economic recovery plan for Ukraine, a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The Thursday meeting in Berlin comes a week after Witkoff and Kushner urged Russia to propose a postwar security framework for Europe — a parallel effort they hope will help bring the war to a close. On the same day, Trump will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. Trump said on Monday that he expects to talk about the war in Ukraine. Zoom in: The aim of the Berlin meeting is to develop security guarantees to deter future Russian attacks on Ukraine as well as plans to rebuild its economy, the official said. The Trump aides have been in regular contact with Ukrainian and European officials as they engage Russia simultaneously, the person said. The U.S. official described the Berlin meeting and Trump's visit to China as a coordinated diplomatic effort. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — who are joining Trump in China — have been briefed on the Ukraine negotiations, the person said. Zoom out: Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin in Moscow last Thursday. They also spoke Monday with his foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the war talks. Axios reported last week that the U.S. asked Russia for a European security proposal that includes steps by Moscow to ease tensions. Many European governments, however, are highly skeptical that Russia would honor any agreement. Earlier this month, Axios reported that the U.S. hoped easing Russian diesel sanctions would win concessions, but Putin still rejected a ceasefire. The big picture: One overarching question is whether Europe will participate directly with Russia in negotiations to resolve the war. Witkoff and Kushner said Russia agreed that Europe would have a seat at the table, but Ushakov said Monday that no such agreement had been reached.

( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Tasmania's parliament is set to debate a bill for a moratorium on new data centre developments until binding rules are put in place. The MP who put forward the moratorium bill — Franklin independent Peter George — has disclosed shares in an Australian property company which has almost 80 per cent of its development pipeline in data centres. Mr George says his interest in Goodman Group centres on its commercial buildings, which have "a wide range of uses". A Tasmanian independent MP who has tabled a bill for a moratorium on new data centres has declared shares in a property giant whose global development pipeline is almost 80 per cent data centres. Franklin MP Peter George listed Sydney-headquartered Goodman Group among the interests in his "retirement plan", previously described as his self-managed super fund. The company was not included in his disclosure 12 months earlier, when the Climate 200-backed MP listed shares in Origin Energy and poker machine venue operator Endeavour Group , both of which he divested as being "inappropriate" to his values. In its full-year results, released in August, Goodman Group outlined that data centre development accounted for more than $15 billion out of its total $19.7 billion global work in progress. The proportion has increased substantially in the past 18 months for the industrial and logistics property group, rising from 57 per cent to 68 per cent by September last year, and now at 78 per cent, building large facilities aimed at cloud and AI customers. US tech billionaire flags interest in Hurricanes, Hobart stadium Aboriginal protester guilty of trespass despite 'cultural responsibility' to forests Man charged with murder of two-week-old Hobart baby Peter George with supporters during his election campaign. ( ABC News: Maren Preuss ) Mr George has been critical of the Tasmanian government's lack of specific planning controls and broader framework for data centre development in Tasmania, describing "deep uncertainty" about their costs and benefits, with "growing resistance from communities globally". He tabled a bill for a moratorium on data centres on Tuesday until issues around location, energy and water use had been addressed, saying there is concern in Tasmania "about the impact of giant data centres on communities and natural resources". His bill would ensure data centres could only be built in specially designated zones, and that public consultation and appeal rights are retained. Mr George confirmed he bought the shares in the past 12 months and said his interest in Goodman Group was due to its commercial holdings. He said he would review his shares as Goodman "changes its portfolio listings" to ensure he is comfortable with the company's direction. "It just shows that I am technologically neutral," he said. "I am quite happy to engage with a company which, in part, develops data centres but also other commercial undertakings, other commercial buildings at the same time. Goodman Group recently withdrew plans for its proposed $1.2 billion Project Mars facility in Sydney's north shore after community opposition and regulatory changes . It does not have any publicly announced proposals for Tasmania. Mr George said data centres needed to be placed "in the right places and under the right conditions". Approach is 'one of caution', MP says The Tasmanian government last week released an "expectations" document for data centre developments. It included partnering with new renewable energy projects, but not be expected to procure or construct new firming capacity if this was already available from Hydro Tasmania. They would need to "use water efficiently" and minimise water demand through the design phase. Progressive politician has shares in mining, pokies An independent MP who received more than $72,000 in donations from Climate 200 says he will divest his shares in a fossil fuel company, miner and pokies venue operator, as they conflict with his "approach to life". A community benefit fund would also be established, a common method for any new development type involving large companies. The expectations were criticised by Labor and the Greens, who both called for binding rules prior to developments proceeding. They both supported a pause on new data centres until these are in place. Mr George has also supported a moratorium for some months, questioning the government about this in August.

events.title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex boss
events.summary: Donald Trump greeting Jensen Huang in September this year Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort. Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign. But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs , including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy. The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia. The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance. Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted. Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return. The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 5 days ago The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive. They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process". Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back. Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , external , though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report. The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House. Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy". Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company. The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy. It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models. The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping , whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development. The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China. The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said. Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US. He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company". In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington. How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? Published 4 days ago How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House Published 4 days ago The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad . The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore. Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.

events.title: S’pore to lead ASEAN association on social security as region tackles ageing population
events.summary: Acting Minister for Manpower and Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information Jasmin Lau speaking at the ASEAN Social Security Association conference on Nov 17. Singapore has taken over the ASEAN Social Security Association for 2026/2027. Leaders will share ways to handle ageing, changing work, and digitalisation. At the 43rd ASSA Conference in Singapore, about 90 delegates from 21 groups are discussing stronger safety nets. Lau said ASEAN is at “different stages of demographic transition” and by 2050 all members are expected to be ageing, aged or super-aged, with about one in six people aged 65 or older.. Lau warned that “Digital-first must never mean digital-only” and said members must improve digital safety without excluding seniors. SINGAPORE – Singapore takes the helm of the ASEAN Social Security Association (ASSA) for 2026/2027 from Brunei, at a time when the region is dealing with an ageing population, the changing nature of work and digitalisation. The handover took place at the 43rd ASSA Conference and Meeting, which is being held at Orchard Hotel Singapore from Nov 17 to 19. About 90 delegates from 21 social security organisations across ASEAN, as well as regional and international experts, are attending the three-day conference. They will exchange experiences and explore practical ways to strengthen social safety nets for their populations. Acting Minister for Manpower and Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information Jasmin Lau noted in her opening speech that the ASEAN countries are at “different stages of demographic transition”. Some still have young populations while others – such as Singapore, with 21.4% of its citizens aged 65 or older – have already crossed the United Nations’ 21% threshold for a super-aged society. She added that by 2050, all ASEAN countries are projected to be ageing, aged or super-aged societies, with around one in six people in the region aged 65 or older. “Longer lives are something for us all to celebrate. But because none of us knows whether we will live to 75 or 95, or whether we will need years of care at the end – that uncertainty is the part that is too much for us to bear, and that is why we pool risk,” she said. CPF LIFE, Singapore’s national longevity insurance annuity scheme, shares the risks across members, so everyone receives a steady monthly payout for life. To ensure these payouts keep pace with inflation, rising living standards and longer lifespans, the Government has been increasing retirement sums by about 3.5% annually from 2023 to 2027. The full retirement sum (FRS) will rise from $220,400 for those turning 55 in 2026 to $228,200 in 2027. The FRS for 2028 and beyond is not yet available as the Government is currently reviewing the figures, Lau said. The nature of work is also evolving as the rise of platform jobs and other non-traditional work arrangements creates new opportunities, while making it more challenging for workers to build up retirement savings. Before January 2025, platform workers contributed only to MediSave for healthcare needs, and lacked mandatory work injury compensation and collective representation. The Government introduced the Platform Workers Act in January 2025 to close these gaps. Under the Act, those born on or after January 1995, or older workers who opt in, make CPF contributions in increments, with their employers having to do so as well. Their contribution rates will reach standard employee-employer rates of 20% and 17% by 2029. This Platform Workers project has been nominated for the Insurance Coverage Recognition Award. During the conference, Singapore will share its learnings in strengthening retirement and housing adequacy for platform workers. Lastly, Lau touched on the digitalisation trend. She said that while technology can speed up transactions – for example, eligible CPF members can now withdraw their CPF savings online almost instantaneously – greater digital convenience also brings more risks. Member organisations will discuss how they strengthen digital safeguards without making the services too difficult for people to use. “Digital-first must never mean digital-only. Not everyone is equally comfortable with technology, particularly our seniors,” Lau added. As ASEAN countries navigate these triple challenges, she sees value in learning from one another. There are hardly perfect solutions to complex problems and Singapore does not claim to have all the answers, she said, adding that the Republic can learn from some of the solutions that ASEAN peers are trying out. Ultimately, it is through mutual learning and sharing that ASEAN can build a resilient social security system that is here to stay. “The real test of a social security system is not whether it works today. It is whether a 25-year-old starting work today can trust that it will work for him when he turns 85,” Lau said. “That is what all of us are building together.

events.title: Jensen Huang’s daughter, a close ally, remains in senior role at Nvidia
events.summary: The continued presence of Madison Huang has raised concerns among senior executives that she has conflicted loyalties between the company and her father. Madison Huang has become a powerful figure at Nvidia, acting like Jensen Huang’s chief of staff and shaping marketing, communications and key decisions. Her temper and direct access to her father have upset staff and helped drive departures, while some executives worry about her loyalties after Jensen Huang’s resignation. Nvidia must now decide Madison Huang’s role, along with other family members, as interim CEO Colette Kress takes control and faces pressure over the company’s future. SAN FRANCISCO – Madison Huang was yelling. Her father, Nvidia’s chief executive officer Jensen Huang , had been scheduled to headline a conference in New Delhi in February. Shortly before the event, he had pulled out and tapped a long-time lieutenant, Jay Puri, to attend in his place. But Nvidia had not buttoned up its plans for the conference, infuriating Madison Huang. On a call before the event, she berated other employees – including Puri – for being unprepared, said three people familiar with the meeting. Eventually, Puri interrupted and told her he could answer her questions if she stopped yelling at him. Less than six months later, Puri left his role at Nvidia. The tense meeting highlighted the powerful and sometimes disruptive role Huang, 35, played at the company her father co-founded, according to more than a dozen current and former employees who spoke on condition of anonymity about the family’s leadership of Nvidia. Before Jensen Huang resigned last week , Madison had become his de facto chief of staff, with considerable authority over more seasoned executives. That influence creates an immediate challenge for Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim CEO, who replaced Jensen Huang after his resignation last week. Kress must quickly determine how much power Madison Huang will have in the company after her father’s exit. She must also decide what to do about Jensen Huang’s other family members employed at the company: his son, Spencer Huang, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez. Huang resigned after revelations that he had had extramarital relationships with an Nvidia executive and a customer that US intelligence concluded was working for Chinese intelligence. Those concerns were heightened over the last few days as Jensen Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street started a campaign to reinstate him, and US President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” if Huang returned to his job. The Huang family – including Jensen, Madison and Spencer, as well as Puri – did not respond to requests for comment. Jensen Huang, who employees say also has a hot temper, was aware of his daughter’s behaviour. He occasionally threatened to sic an angry Madison Huang on other employees and told them to be afraid of her, said two people familiar with the comments. And even senior executives thought they could not disagree with her because of her direct line to the boss. “Nepotism is almost always a bad idea,” said David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who has served on more than dozen corporate boards. “There are few examples of it even working modestly well.” Jensen Huang has said he was not around much as a father. On a podcast recorded in April, he said he “missed a lot” of Madison’s and Spencer’s childhoods, including “all of their karate tournaments”. Jensen Huang’s wife, Lori , an accomplished electrical engineer, left her job to raise their children shortly before he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. His children learnt from an early age to care about Nvidia. “Both kids have read every shareholder letter, gone to every shareholder meeting, been to every single conference that I’ve ever done,” Jensen Huang said on the podcast. “Despite the fact that I was gone a lot, they found a way to always love the company.” Huang’s children took winding paths to Nvidia. Madison Huang received her bachelor’s degree from the Culinary Institute of America in 2012 and studied baking and wine at Le Cordon Bleu in Paris and London from 2013 to 2015, according to her profile on LinkedIn. She then managed luxury hotels and an Italian pastry shop owned by Louis Vuitton Moet Hennessey for four years. In 2019, she started at London Business School and then joined the family business in 2020. Spencer, 36, received his bachelor’s degree from Columbia College Chicago, an arts school, in 2013, according to his profile on LinkedIn. He then owned a bar in Taipei, Taiwan, called R&D Cocktail Lab for eight years. In 2022, he joined Nvidia, where he is now a director of product management for its robotics efforts. He is considered to be quiet and focused on his responsibilities, said seven people familiar with his work. Caprez, who met Madison Huang at London Business School, joined Nvidia in 2024 and became heavily involved in dealmaking.

events.title: Singapore discussing effect of new chip rules with US, minister says
events.summary: Singapore is pressing Trump administration officials for details on new rules designed to crack down on China’s access to advanced US-made chips, and which pose a potential threat to the country’s booming AI sector. Josephine Teo, Singapore’s minister for digital development and information, said Monday her government is “engaging with our US counterparts as to the scope of implementation.” “I think more importantly, how we can facilitate trusted access to this very important AI infrastructure,” Teo said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, noting she has spoken with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau. The new US Commerce Department rules include closing a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to access advanced US semiconductors via third-country data centers, which the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, at the center of the Nvidia scandal that took down CEO Jensen Huang, is accused of exploiting. Singapore has also been added to a list of countries that faces export restrictions on advanced chips, a move US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had postponed repeatedly until his agency came under scrutiny in recent days. “Singapore takes very seriously the upholding of the rule of law,” Teo said, noting that there are about 6,000 US companies in Singapore: “We safeguard our integrity in the business environment and we do not condone anyone… violating the laws of other countries.” “If they also violate our laws, they can be very certain that we will actively investigate and also hold them to account,” Teo said. Teo declined to comment on her government’s claim that the US had been unhelpful in the city state’s investigation of Megaspeed — whose former executive, Alice Huang, is accused of acting as a Chinese intelligence asset — but noted that Singapore’s own investigation into the company predated its knowledge of an investigation by the US Bureau of Industry and Security. “Suffice to say, investigations into Megaspeed are still continuing,” Teo said. Teo said the environment in Singapore for AI companies would continue to remain favorable, and pointed out that firms including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind had deepened their presence in Singapore in recent months. “There is positive momentum. We’d like to keep it going.” “I think we will try our best to understand the impact and help ensure that we continue to have trusted access to the critical infrastructure needed for legitimate businesses,” Teo said. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Government backflips on backpacker policy
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government backflips on backpacker regional work policy Tony Burke has backed down on proposed changes to backpacker visas. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) The government has backed down on planned changes to working holiday visas. The cap on third-year visas will rise from 5,000 to 25,000, while second-year applicants will have tougher regional work requirements. British backpackers remain exempt from regional work rules. The government has backed down on its planned overhaul of the working holiday-maker program, agreeing to increase the number of backpackers eligible for a third-year visa and tightening regional work requirements. Under changes announced by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, working holiday-makers would need to complete 120 days of regional work, up from 88 days, to qualify for a second-year visa. In a major speech in September, Mr Burke had announced third-year visas would be capped at 5,000 places, a reduction on the current level of about 31,000. That cap will now be set at 25,000 places, while the introduction of a ballot system called the Next Year Regional Work Guarantee has also been delayed to next year after it was originally scheduled to start in November. The shift follows months of pressure from the agriculture, tourism and hospitality sectors over the government's original proposal, with businesses warning it would significantly reduce the supply of seasonal workers and leave them struggling to fill jobs over summer. The new arrangements will apply from March 1, while backpackers who complete their regional work requirements before that date will remain eligible under the existing rules, creating a transition period for those already in the country. A visa is the reason backpackers take on the tough jobs in regional Australia. The cap on second-year places would be set at 45,000. Mr Burke rejected suggestions the government was abandoning its original reforms, arguing the final package had been shaped by consultations with industry and would ultimately deliver more workers to regional Australia. "From the day after the speech … we started consultation with industry to work through what is the best landing place to deliver the total numbers that we're talking about, but to do it in a way that works best for industry," he said. "This creates a very significant shift, but also means for the people who are wanting to qualify for their second year, we're getting more regional days out of them." He said the government had been able to refine its approach because of a go-slow in visa processing which had created "head room" to adjust the broader working holiday-maker reforms while still pursuing an overall lower migration number. The number of backpackers getting visas to Australia has fallen dramatically since July, when the go-slow was introduced as a temporary fix designed to put the brakes on international arrivals. Since then, 44,469 visas have been approved, which means a total of 177,876 backpackers would be granted entry to Australia this financial year, if the government maintains its current rate of processing. Last financial year, a record 323,077 backpacker visas were granted in Australia. Mr Burke said Australia would continue to welcome working holiday-makers. "These reforms make the program fairer, more targeted and sustainable for the long term," he said. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the changes were 'complete nonsense'. ( ABC News: Andrew O'Connor ) Opposition rubbishes changes as 'complete nonsense' Opposition Leader Angus Taylor described the proposal as "complete nonsense" and vowed to repeal the changes if the Coalition was elected. "They've created a complete mess with this raffle, this ballot. They've said they're going to delay it … they should just axe it," he said. The sentiment was echoed by Nationals leader Matt Canavan, who said the backdown was "inevitable" but warned the government had already damaged confidence in the sector. The National Farmers' Federation welcomed the changes but said key questions remained unanswered. "We need more details on the logistical realities of this reform before we can fully throw our support behind it," president Hamish McIntyre said. In WA, Premier Roger Cook acknowledged the federal government's need to bring down net overseas migration, but said he would make sure it "doesn't impact on Western Australia's economy". He said he hoped further adjustment to the system would improve the number of working holiday-makers heading west. "What I want to see is less people going to the east coast and more people coming to the west coast," Mr Cook said.

events.title: The tech industry has a public image problem, Arianna Huffington says
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has joined a group of “brilliantly intelligent” corporate leaders who “just lack wisdom,” Arianna Huffington said Monday. Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Huffington called the Nvidia scandal a teachable moment. “We see incredibly intelligent people all around who are incredibly deluded, incredibly destructive, and self-destructive,” said Huffington, the founder and CEO of Thrive Global, a behavioral change tech company. “We need to invest in making humans better.” Speaking alongside Huffington on the panel, Willett Advisors CEO Steven Rattner said the idea of bringing Huang back as CEO is “ridiculous.” Some in the tech industry are calling for Huang to come back, though the Nvidia board reportedly isn’t considering it . Rattner said the comparison between Huang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who returned to his post after an ouster in 2023, “doesn’t even come close to computing. You can’t bring Jensen back.” Both Huffington and Rattner agreed the tech industry needs to do a better job making a case for itself to a skeptical and anxious public. “The crisis that the tech industry faces is the fact that people hate the tech industry and they hate AI,” Rattner said, referencing the recent US midterm elections that were widely seen as a rebuke of tech. He said tech leaders face the same responsibility as politicians or public officials “to communicate and explain to people. And the tech industry just blew it.” Huffington said that people’s anxieties and fears stem from how life — not just the economy — is changing. “There was no effort to really tell a story that would touch people’s hearts and minds, that would explain how AI would benefit their lives.” Rattner, who led the Obama administration’s 2009 rescue of the auto industry, said the US government shouldn’t take stakes in AI companies. “We did not to have stakes in the auto companies. We had to have stakes in the auto companies because they needed our money and there was no other way to do it except putting equity in,” he said. “I think it’s a slippery slope and a murky bit of business when you start doing that.” — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Medical students should ‘learn the hard way,’ AI startup CEO says
events.summary: The CEO of a major medical AI startup said on Monday that medical students should do paper exams and master the material, even if they also use AI. “The risk of cognitive offloading is really, really acute,” OpenEvidence CEO Daniel Nadler said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. He would advise students to “train classically, learn classically, learn the hard way, do paper exams, do paper tests, make sure you actually know it,” he told Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie. Nadler’s company aims to cover a niche within the medical business, synthesizing complex medical information with AI trained on millions of medical papers. The startup has hit a $15 billion valuation on the promise that AI can condense the complexities of the medical field into information palatable to physicians. The threat of cognitive offloading, or deskilling, is real. Early studies have found that deferring work to AI can weaken neural networks, leading to lower cognitive performance. Nadler says the concern is especially pressing for younger generations, those who have grown up in academic environments with access to AI. He noted that all of his company’s engineers use “dozens and dozens of AI buddies.” Benjamine Liu, the CEO of Formation Bio, which uses AI to accelerate drug development, also noted onstage on Monday that in the pharmaceutical industry “AI systems can begin to now do the work of entire teams.” Noting that the GLP-1 drugmakers “did more revenue than OpenAI and Anthropic combined last year,” he told Sergie that “some people underestimate how big pharma is.” “We’re early innings in these things that help you live longer and healthier — and in an area that our industry sometimes misses,” Liu said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: OpenAI CFO says latest funding round was unplanned, prompted by news report
events.summary: Anthropic’s IPO is “good for the ecosystem” and “good for us,” Sarah Friar, CFO of OpenAI said Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, adding that the company was unconcerned with being second. Retail investors are ready for access to frontier models, not just hyperscalers which come with “pros and cons,” she said. After OpenAI closed a $122 billion fundraise in March this year, Friar said that the company was closing out a smaller fundraise at a $1.25 trillion valuation. But she suggested that the latest round was unplanned and “opportunistic,” and was prompted after a “very well-respected, well-known publication… announced we were fundraising, which we weren’t.” “That caused a whole bunch of inbounds from investors, and so we said, okay, if we can be super fast and in kind of a six-week period, go in and out of the market, be done by the midterms, let’s do it because why not?” Friar said. Friar also said that OpenAI’s advertising model has been very successful, garnering more than $1 billion in revenue in under 200 days — a record for the company. Addressing the public resentment in the US over data centers, Friar said that for companies to regain trust, “you have to show up in those communities” and “be accountable.” She noted that in Georgia, where the company is hoping to build a 3.2 gigawatt data center, OpenAI has sponsored school lunches, a local park, and an AI summit for small businesses. But she acknowledged that OpenAI is still seeing the backlash to the AI buildout that was evident in the US midterm elections. “People are getting way too bombarded by kind of the rage element to not feel that there’s something they should be reacting to,” Friar said. “But when you go talk to people in real life, and show up for them, you have a very different conversation, and I believe a very different outcome.” — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Trump cyber director: FAA, other outages not a cyberattack
events.summary: White House cyber director Sean Cairncross said Monday that a cyberattack was not behind the Trump administration’s nationwide ground stop of air traffic or other outages reported on Monday, attributing the problems to upgrades of old technology. “No, this is not any sort of coordinated, nefarious cyberattack from a malicious actor,” Cairncross told Semafor. “What we are seeing, and frankly I’d expect to see more of it, are service disruptions coming from updating and modernizing legacy systems.” He said the US government is tracking all recent software outages in the last few days. Cairncross told Semafor in an earlier interview that the Trump administration has no plans to release, or require compliance with, its voluntary framework for review of new advanced AI models — adding that frontier labs have cooperated. “The labs have been extremely good about being in communication with us and giving their new models for evaluation to be assessed,” Cairncross said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Putting a strict regulatory regime in place “isn’t going to work at the speed that we need,” he added. Cairncross said that the administration did not release the full text of the framework, which was set in motion by a June executive order, to enable a “frank conversation” with AI companies. He did say he believed the White House will soon make “it much more clear how this is working in practice.” The White House has taken a lighter-touch regulatory approach to the AI industry compared with Europe or the Biden administration; it has also taken steps to block states from stepping in. On the question of cybersecurity, Cairncross was bullish on AI’s defense capabilities, which were “unimaginable even a short time ago,” he said. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, appearing on stage with Cairncross, pointed out that Russia’s hacking capabilities have improved along with AI in the last year. Michal said the country’s ultra-wired government has been increasingly under attack, blaming private actors, as well as Russia, North Korea and Iran. When asked whether cyber attacks could be considered acts of war, Michal said he believes some could rise to the NATO definition of “attack” covered by the alliance’s Article 5. “It’s mainly a question about the consequences,” he said. — Laura McGann

events.title: Bloom Energy sees 'nothing but a huge opportunity' amid AI headwinds
events.summary: The CEO of fuel cell maker Bloom Energy said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that he’s not worried about rising natural gas prices or political pushback to data centers, as the economy-wide scramble for electrons marks an “architectural shift” for the grid that will favor onsite power production. Bloom, whose gas-fueled mini power plants are used by data centers, hospitals, retailers, and other big power consumers, has faced some headwinds recently: Its share price is down 20% in the past month thanks in part to economy-wide jitters about the pace of the AI buildout, and its flagship data center project in New Mexico has been held up by permitting issues . Still, CEO KR Sridhar said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday, “I see nothing but a huge opportunity.” Power use continues to surge across the economy, and if the price of natural gas — Bloom’s crucial input — rises because of increased demand or trade disruptions like the war in Iran, “our value proposition gets even better,” Sridhar told Semafor’s Liz Rappaport, as the technology can operate more efficiently than conventional gas turbines. Bloom is on a steep growth trajectory: Its net profit hit $250 million in the third quarter, up from a $23 million loss in the same period last year. The company is expanding its manufacturing base, and targeting projects in the Middle East and elsewhere, Sridhar said. Though he is eyeing projects abroad, the company will continue to invest in the US. “We should not cede this opportunity to any other country, but from our perspective, we will be happy to sell our power to neighboring countries,” he said. “Nothing is NIMBY-proof,” he said, of backlash to data centers in the US. Still, “AI happens to be a catalyst pushing everything to the right very steeply.” — Tim McDonnell

events.title: US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China
events.summary: The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has decided to ban remote access to certain GPUs and servers running in datacenters located in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. The agency has also introduced a requirement to secure a license before selling what it describes as “advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers” that are sufficiently powerful to “be used for training or running of advanced SI models” into the five nations. The interim final rule [PDF] containing the new regulations says they’re needed “to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.” Similar language can be found in previous US bans on sales of GPUs and other advanced tech to China, which Washington fears will use advanced tech to improve its military capabilities. US authorities understood that export bans wouldn’t prevent Chinese entities from renting GPUs housed elsewhere. So from 2021 to 2024, Washington introduced a series of regulations that required US-based clouds to make sure they didn’t serve Chinese customers. No such obligation existed for cloud operators elsewhere, which created a market for resources that Chinese customers could access from afar. It is widely felt that datacenter building booms in Malaysia and Thailand, both of which are generally on good terms with China, aimed to cater to Middle Kingdom customers who wanted to rent GPUs they could not import. Megapseed – whose former employee Alice Huang had an intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and may have been a Chinese intelligence asset – built datacenters in Malaysia and was suspected of catering largely to offshore customers. Neil Shah, vice president of research at analyst firm Counterpoint, said the new rules shift the regulatory burden of complying with export controls from hardware manufacturers to cloud operators. “Data center operators in hubs such as Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia will now face massive ‘Know Your Customer's Workload’ requirements,” he told The Register by email, likening it to the KYC restrictions imposed on financial services firms. “They must prove to US regulators that their compute is not being funneled back to embargoed nations, or risk losing their own access to US silicon.” He feels the new rules represent “a severe short-term compute bottleneck for Chinese tech giants” and “a massive long-term catalyst for decoupling.” “Washington is forcing domestic capital and engineering talent to double down on full-stack sovereign alternatives, accelerating ecosystems like Huawei's Ascend.” Shah’s observation came days after Alibaba decided to spin out its T-Head chip design unit, which it described as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China.” That description suggests Alibaba doesn’t think T-Head has strong prospects of selling its wares outside China. It remains to be seen if the new BIS rules will slow datacenter development across Asia and Brazil. All five nations the US has regulated are all enjoying the economic impact of the AI boom. They’re also trying to manage its impact. Singapore limits datacenter construction, as befits a tiny and resource-constrained island nation. Malaysia is very much open for business but has introduced increasingly strict building codes and requirements to minimize energy and water consumption. Thailand recently introduced new regulations that new builds of large datacenters must take place in designated industrial zones. Indonesia also has strong regulations but is not currently a major datacenter hub. Brazil requires datacenter operators to reserve at least 10 percent of capacity for local users, suggesting some operators are more interested in offshore customers. Interestingly, the new BIS rules don’t impact infrastructure used for “commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat.” Chinese e-tailers operate at vast scale and have already attracted regulatory attention in Europe and the USA. Asian and Brazilian datacenter operators therefore probably do not see the likes of Temu and Alibaba as a lifeline, but might see a role as regional hosts for outfits like Amazon or Meta. ® UDPATED AT 05:45 UTC, November 17 to add news that late on Monday the US Departments of Commerce and Justice confirmed an ongoing criminal investigation into Megaspeed. In the announcement, the two departments detail investigative activities they conducted across 2024 and 2025, including a June meeting with Alice Huang in Singapore, and state those details "address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting." Singaporean authorities have also said that meeting took place, but say they asked asked US counterparts for help with their own investigations and received frustratingly little support. Singapore also investigated Supermicro's possible role at Megapseed, and complained that the server-maker didn't co-operate either. Supermicro today told The Register it " does not conduct business with these entities" and operates a "robust compliance program." "We are committed to complying with all applicable U.S. export and re-export control laws and regulations, and we require our distributors and resellers to do the same," according to a Supermicro statement sent to The Register .

events.title: Democrats dig in for grueling leadership fight
events.summary: The News Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., mimed a coin flip on Monday night when asked if he’ll support Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer over his insurgent opponent, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. It was a joke — but one that also showed how Democrats are wrestling with the decision. “Leave it to the Democrats. We flip nine seats and the person who actually helps put it together and do all that, all of a sudden there’s a revolt,” Hickenlooper said. He quickly made clear he didn’t mean that as a Schumer endorsement: “I haven’t picked a position. I do think it’s useful to go and look at: How could the caucus be better?” If the first few days of the leadership race are any indication, it’s going to be a very long two weeks for Senate Democrats. Several declined to comment on Monday night after days of celebrating their big election wins, with one senator saying Schumer’s challenge is all reporters have been asking about. But that’s because it’s such an unusual moment for the party: The vast majority of sitting Senate Democrats have never experienced a contested leadership race for the top job. And Van Hollen’s rebel campaign isn’t following crushing losses, but instead a historic victory. “No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer. Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anyone else in the caucus and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge,” said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. “The voters are also demanding change.” Kaine, who will chair the Budget Committee next year, also declined to publicly come out for or against Schumer. Van Hollen’s pitch for change Van Hollen is not exactly an obvious change agent: He previously chaired the party’s campaign arms in both the House and Senate and has been in elected office since 1991. But he is seeking to draw bright contrasts with Schumer, pushing for a prohibition in the next spending bill on offensive weapons for the Iran war and highlighting Schumer’s opposition to the Obama-era Iran nuclear deal. And while Schumer has several times the public support of Van Hollen, most of the incoming 56 Democratic Caucus members next year have declined to publicly endorse either one. Van Hollen said he knows “for a fact” some public reporting about senators’ support for Schumer is not true: “Some are voting for me and others are undecided on that list.” “People are still listening. They’re very interested in having a debate,” Van Hollen said on Monday evening. One of his supporters, Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., said he thinks the Maryland Democrat has a real chance to defeat Schumer. Most Democrats still see Schumer as the heavy favorite given the election results, however. Still, a number of other longtime Democratic senators who know Schumer well are keeping their powder dry. Asked about the race, Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said only that he’s “laser-focused” on his agenda next year leading the Finance Committee and pushing Medicare for All, a billionaire’s income tax, and repealing tariffs. “Everybody deserves to be heard and then our caucus will make a decision,” said Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., who will chair the Appropriations Committee. “I have not declared anything,” The next leader will decide when Murray or Wyden’s legislation will come to the Senate floor over the next two years — giving them incentive to stay neutral. And many Democrats are still digesting how to handle a secret ballot election that comes after the party’s most commanding win since Barack Obama became president. “Every candidate should make their pitch. And I’ll hear out any candidate for leader,” said Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who obliterated his opponent in his reelection bid. “I’m grateful to everyone for their efforts, including Leader Schumer.” Schumer has served as Democratic leader for a decade, during which time the party’s activist base has soured on him; he’s also the architect of multiple Democratic majorities and made the most of a 50-seat Democratic majority during the first two years of Joe Biden’s presidency. But no leader hangs on forever: both former Democratic Leader Harry Reid and former Republican Leader Mitch McConnell lost a handful of votes in their last leadership races, before stepping down from the job. Schumer’s given no indication he would do that, but he’s up for reelection in 2028 and has a big decision ahead of him. And Van Hollen knows it. “That’s a decision for him,” he said of Schumer’s 2028 plans. Room for Disagreement Some Democrats said it’s healthy to have this debate after more than three decades without a real contested battle for the leadership race. “We’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats,” Kaine said. “We like democracy.” “It just comes with the territory,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. Burgess’s view Van Hollen’s leadership challenge to Schumer has made things very awkward for Senate Democrats. The contest will supercharge the debate about the party’s agenda in 2027 as well as how they handle the lame duck. And regardless of the outcome, it’ll have long term consequences for the usually tight-knit caucus. Notable Democratic voters prefer Van Hollen over Schumer but not by an overwhelming margin , according to polling from Data for Progress.

events.title: 'Unfair and unjust': Anger from David Jones suppliers as debt revealed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts David Jones creditors owed at least $459 million, administrators confirm David Jones creditors have been updated. ( ABC News: Fletch Yeung ) The first David Jones creditors meeting has revealed the company has almost half a billion dollars in debt. Suppliers left unsure if they would ever have their debts paid. The second creditors meeting is expected to be held in March 2027. David Jones is deeply in debt, with its liabilities revealed so far reaching almost half a billion dollars. The retailer owes at least $180 million to suppliers, more than $200 million to lenders and more than $10 million to its own staff. 6,242 employees: Estimated claims of $11 million including annual leave, long service leave and potential redundancy payments Secured creditors Hilco: Estimated claim of $155 million and ACP estimated claims of $80 million 940 unsecured creditors: Estimated claims of $180 million 802,319 gift cards: Estimated claims of $33 million The debts were revealed at the almost two-hour first creditors meeting for the embattled department store, which was placed into voluntary administration earlier this month. It has already been announced that the receiver will close 19 of the retailer's 38 stores by the end of 2027 . Administrators are now trying to find a buyer for David Jones to keep the legacy brand alive. McGrathNicol's role as voluntary administrator is to tally the company's debts and possibly find a buyer to recoup cash for entities owed money, such as suppliers and landlords. The retailer's key secured lender, Hilco, will be first in line to claw back money. It has appointed a receiver, FTI Consulting, to David Jones and now controls its day-to-day operations. The 188-year-old department store's collapse came after negotiations broke down with Scentre Group, the owner of key shopping centre chain Westfield, which confirmed David Jones was behind on its rent since September. David Jones has more than 1,000 suppliers. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) A long list of woes is blamed for David Jones's collapse, including difficult trading as the cost of living bites, competition from online retail, and an "unsustainable" business model, McGrathNicol said. The meeting, attended by just under 500 people, heard from suppliers of everything from clothing to truffles, with anxious brand owners asking questions about when, if ever, they would see debts paid. "It has become pretty apparent to others in the market that some suppliers, specifically the larger ones, were given preferential treatment," one supplier told the meeting. Store suppliers have told ABC News they have been struggling to get invoices paid for months. Some are owed more than $100,000. David Jones has more than 1,000 suppliers, 6,000 employees and a similar number of concession staff, all impacted by the collapse. The main retail union, the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employee's Association (SDA) confirmed after the meeting that 1,689 direct jobs were on the line and only 170 positions have been offered redeployment. NSW branch secretary Bernie Smith said the union expected further job losses from staff employed by concessions, but did not have exact numbers. Unsecured creditors, which include suppliers, are lower on the list to be repaid, behind employees and secured creditors Hilco, Anchorage Capital Partners (ACP) and Commonwealth Bank. David Jones is due to close half of its stores. ( ABC News ) One supplier asked if for a possible range of how much they might receive to the dollar, which McGrathNicol administrator Matthew Hutton said it was too soon to know the value or an exact timeline. He said there were "too many variables", including not having engaged with enough bidders to know the value, pre-Christmas trade and the upcoming store closures, adding they might not know the potential return to creditors until mid to late January. Brands that have been selling stock in David Jones stores within their own sub-leases under concession arrangements, also asked about whether they would see sales revenue repaid. "If David Jones was to go into liquidation can partners take their stock back prior to the company being liquidated?" asked one brand owner, with McGrathNicol confirming this was the case. Administrators also confirmed some brands had pulled out of David Jones since the administration, but this was "limited" and the receivers now controlling the stores were experiencing record sales. Several suppliers expressed frustration with a lack of correspondence from FTI regarding stock levels and sales since November 5. Julie Mathers left the meeting frustrated.

events.title: AI leaders helping drive ‘unnaturally negative’ narrative, Palo Alto Networks CEO says
events.summary: The leaders of the world’s most advanced AI companies are helping drive an “unnaturally negative” narrative around the technology, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. In an interview with MIT Technology Review’s Mat Honan, Arora argued that the focus on AI’s risks is overshadowing its potential benefits of the fast-moving technology. “I find it strange that sometimes the leaders of frontier [large language models] want to come up here and talk about the dark side of AI. Every technology has a dark side,” Arora said at the event, adding that the negative narrative has “been driven by some of the people who should be espousing the benefits.” Arora described AI as a “transformational technology” with “the potential of uplifting a huge amount of humanity” and “democratiz[ing] intelligence.” “A villager sitting in India or anywhere in the world will have the ability to not just read 10 websites, but have them summarized and have the best intelligence available to them,” he said. Arora also challenged concerns that growing domestic resistance to data center construction could slow innovation, arguing that constraints on computing capacity would instead accelerate efforts to make the technology more efficient. “Scarcity breeds innovation,” Arora said. “If you say there’s only so many data centers that can be built, think about the amount of companies that are going to come back and say, wait, I’ve got this compression technology which makes tokens more efficient.” But Arora also acknowledged that AI’s growing capabilities are inevitably intensifying cybersecurity risks by making it easier to uncover vulnerabilities in software. “All the bad software we’ve written for the last 50 years as humans, is now going to be found out,” he said, warning that as more vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited, the higher the risk of systems being forced offline as companies scramble to patch longstanding weaknesses. “I don’t think there’s a panacea. I don’t think there’s a quick solve. I just think we’re gonna power through all of these and grind ourselves through them,” he said. — Lauren Morganbesser
